primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Avoid for a quick single answer when Copilot Chat or a specialized agent is sufficient.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot and select Cowork beside Chat. Describe the outcome you want rather than a single question, then review the work at each checkpoint it presents.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

resources.title: Sales Home (SME&C Hub)
resources.description: The SME&C seller surface inside Sales Agent. Covers My View, Prospecting and Pipeline today, with Campaign, Planning, Renewal and Realization & Usage on the roadmap. Sales Home is part of Sales Agent rather than a separate product, and works alongside chat rather than replacing it. In preview for SME&C individual contributors since late July 2026; it does not replace MSX.

resources.title: Role Hub
resources.description: Always-available hub for role guidance and enablement.

secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Sales Home is in preview for SME&C sellers who use MSX, and is enabled for individual contributors only - managers will not see it. Renewal, Campaign, Planning, Realization and Deal Agent integration are roadmap, not available today, so do not build an activity that depends on them.
stepsToGetStarted: Opens Sales Agent. Sales Home is the seller surface inside it - My View for alerts and quota attainment, Prospecting for signals, account research, contacts and outreach, and Pipeline for opportunities, forecast comments, close plans and deal risks. It is not a separate product and has no separate link.

secondaryAgents.name: Researcher
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: Deep research agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot that produces structured, source-cited reports.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Combines work content and web research across multiple steps.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Customer, market, competitor, industry, and strategic research requiring citations. Researcher is also reachable inside Sales Agent, which uses it to answer research questions; call Researcher directly when you want the full sourced report rather than an answer inside a sales conversation.
keyBenefits: Produces source-cited research reports rather than unattributed summaries, combining work content and web research across multiple steps so claims can be traced.

resources.title: Frontier Accelerator Content and Learning Model
resources.description: Working model for huddle content, practice cards, experiments, validation, and app rendering.

secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Avoid for quick summaries or lightweight drafting.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot and select the Researcher agent, then state the research question and sources.

secondaryAgents.name: Agent J.ai
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: Text-based coaching experience grounded in Microsoft 365 context and curated content.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Helps users sharpen messages, rehearse conversations, anticipate objections, and plan next steps.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Customer conversation preparation and role-play.
keyBenefits: Rehearsal before the real conversation. Sharpens messages, surfaces objections you had not anticipated, and coaches on clarity and next step, grounded in Microsoft 365 context and curated content.

resources.description: MCAPS agent reference for coaching and conversation rehearsal.

secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use as the authoritative source for CRM or commercial data.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

stepsToGetStarted: Opens Sales Agent. Sales Home is the seller surface inside it - My View for alerts and quota attainment, Prospecting for signals, account research, contacts and outreach, and Pipeline for opportunities, forecast comments, close plans and deal risks. It is not a separate product and has no separate link.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Account planning fails when it becomes an inventory. Today is about a short operating plan that helps you decide where attention goes this week.
keyTalkingPoints: Prioritization requires saying no. AI can assemble customer, pipeline, renewal, whitespace, partner, and investment signals. The AE decides which account deserves action and why.
discussionQuestions: Which accounts get your attention by habit rather than evidence? Where is the account plan missing a decision? What signal would change your priority list?
suggestedTransitions: Move from account list discussion to one AE selecting a top account and naming the next action.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the top accounts you will act on and the evidence behind the priority.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one territory or account list and one account where the next action is unclear.
facilitatorQuestions: Which account deserves attention that it is not getting? Which account gets attention mostly by habit? What evidence would change your top three?
listenFor: Listen for planning as annual documentation, prioritization by revenue alone, unclear next actions, missing role coverage, and customer priorities not connected to pipeline.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tools are unavailable, run the prioritization manually and record the prompt or Scout/Cowork skill candidate for later.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Use AI to build or refine one account priority view, then choose one next action you will actually take.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the prioritized account list, source signals, the action chosen, and any assumptions you rejected.

activities.name: Keep pipeline hygiene current between reviews
activities.description: Stand up a recurring sweep of your owned pipeline so hygiene problems surface on a schedule instead of the night before a review.
activities.prompt: Check my owned pipeline on a recurring basis and report only what has changed since the last run. Flag opportunities with a close date in the past, no activity in the last 30 days, a missing or generic next step, or a stage that has not moved while the close date has. For each one, draft the specific update or question I would need to resolve it. Rank by revenue at risk within the current period. Do not change any record - produce a review list for me to action.
activities.expectedOutput: A recurring change-only hygiene list ranked by revenue at risk, with a drafted resolution for each flagged opportunity.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE confirms each flagged item is genuinely stale before updating, and makes every record change themselves rather than delegating the write.
activities.requiredContext: Access to your owned pipeline; your current period close dates; your team's definition of a healthy next step.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm your team's definition of a healthy next step so the check flags the right things.
2. Run the prompt against your owned pipeline.
3. Review the first list and confirm each flagged opportunity is genuinely stale rather than deliberately paused.
4. Set the cadence to land before your pipeline review, not after it.
5. Make every record change yourself; do not let the check write to MSX.
activities.whyThisMatters: Pipeline hygiene fails because it is a periodic scramble rather than a standing habit. A recurring check that reports only what changed turns a two-hour clean-up into a five-minute review.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about restoring trust in the pipeline signal before it becomes a forecast argument.
keyTalkingPoints: Bad data creates bad inspection. Stage, close date, next step, customer engagement, and partner attach should reflect reality. AI can flag issues; the AE verifies and decides the correction.
discussionQuestions: Where does your pipeline data most often mislead you? Which field do you trust least? Which opportunity would you hesitate to defend in a review?
suggestedTransitions: Move from aggregate gap to one opportunity that needs correction or verification.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one opportunity record to correct, verify, or escalate for missing evidence.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring the scope you normally inspect for pipeline reviews and one opportunity you suspect may be stale or misrepresented.
facilitatorQuestions: Which opportunity would you not want inspected right now? What field, date, or next step might be telling the wrong story? What correction would change the forecast conversation?
listenFor: Listen for manual reconciliation, stale dates, close-date optimism, missing customer engagement, and records corrected only right before reviews.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If certified reports are unavailable, map the inspection routine and identify where evidence should come from.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Run one pipeline signal-quality check and correct or flag one material issue.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the before/after record state or issue list, the source signal, and the decision you made as the owner.

activities.name: Draft the first contact for the top-priority lead
activities.description: Turn the top-ranked lead into a specific, short first message that connects the signal to a reason for the customer to respond.
activities.prompt: Here is the top lead from my follow-up plan: [paste source signal, account, role, likely interest, and any prior interaction]. Draft a first contact message under 100 words that references the specific signal, states one reason this is relevant to their business now, and asks for one small next step. Give me two versions: one for a business decision maker and one for a technical decision maker. Do not claim knowledge of their environment we do not have, and do not assert a product feature I have not given you.
activities.expectedOutput: Two short first-contact drafts, one business and one technical, tied to the originating signal.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP confirms consent and outreach appropriateness, verifies every factual statement about the customer, and owns the wording before sending.
activities.requiredContext: The prioritized lead plan; the source signal; the contact's role; prior interaction history; consent and outreach appropriateness.
activitySteps: 1. Take the top lead from the prioritized plan.
2. Confirm consent and context are appropriate for outreach.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Edit into your own voice.
5. Send one, and note the date.
activities.whyThisMatters: A prioritized list that never becomes a message is just a better-sorted backlog.

activities.name: Close the loop on what the follow-up produced

activitySteps: 1. List the leads worked and the outcome of each.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Record the outcome in the opportunity or lead record.
4. Name the one signal source you will deprioritize.
activities.whyThisMatters: Lead follow-up improves only if you find out which signals were worth following.

activities.name: Close the loop on outreach that never got an answer
activities.description: Track the outreach you have sent so the follow-ups that matter are surfaced and drafted rather than remembered.
activities.prompt: Review the outreach I have sent over the last 30 days and identify every message where I asked for something - a meeting, an introduction, a decision, or information - and did not receive a substantive reply. For each one, tell me how long it has been waiting, how important it looks based on the opportunity involved, and draft a short follow-up in my own voice that adds a new reason to respond rather than simply repeating the ask. Do not send anything.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of unanswered asks with elapsed time and a drafted follow-up for each that adds new value rather than repeating.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP reviews and edits every draft before sending, and removes any follow-up where the silence is itself the answer.
activities.requiredContext: Access to your sent messages; your current lead and opportunity list; your team's follow-up cadence norms.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm the check can see your sent messages for the last 30 days.
2. Run the prompt.
3. Review the ranked list and remove any thread where the silence is itself the answer.
4. Edit every drafted follow-up so it adds a new reason to reply rather than repeating the ask.
5. Send them yourself; do not let the check send on your behalf.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most lost specialist opportunities are not rejected - they are dropped. The follow-up that would have converted was never sent because it was never surfaced.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Lead and account signals are noisy. Today is about turning them into a focused follow-up plan.
keyTalkingPoints: Qualification is evidence work. Solution relevance, owner, message, consent, and next action must be explicit.
discussionQuestions: Which lead or signal deserves attention first? What evidence makes it real? Who owns the next action?
suggestedTransitions: Move from noisy signals to one prioritized follow-up plan.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to ranking one lead or prospect list and owning the top next action.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live solution pursuit, solution play, lead list, opportunity, or investment case relevant to this huddle; confirm tool access; review last commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: Which lead or account signal deserves follow-up first? What evidence supports solution relevance?
listenFor: Listen for undifferentiated lead lists, vague ownership, weak message fit, and missing consent/context.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If systems are unavailable, manually rank one lead list and draft the prompt for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Turn your top-priority lead into an actual first contact this week.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the message you sent and whether the signal was worth following.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.description: Practice putting the real decision, its options and its tradeoffs to an executive.
activities.prompt: Use Agent J.ai to role-play the executive who has to make this decision. I will present the options and their tradeoffs rather than a recommendation. Push back where an option sounds like a pitch, where a tradeoff has been softened, or where what this executive is personally backing has not been named. Pause for my response before coaching me on whether the decision was put clearly and the tradeoffs stated honestly. Do not invent customer facts or commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A rehearsed decision conversation, the objections raised, and coaching on where an option was pitched rather than offered.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS decides which tradeoffs are material enough to put in front of this executive. Review the downsides the rehearsal raises and add the material ones it missed, since not everything it raises bears on the decision being made.
activities.requiredContext: The approved narrative; the decision being asked for; the options and their tradeoffs; who the executive is and what they are accountable for.
activities.whyThisMatters: An executive decision put badly sounds like a pitch. Rehearsing it is how you hear the difference before they do.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about assemble an executive technical customer narrative without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is An executive-ready technical narrative with sourced claims, proof points, decision questions, and a technical ask. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: When did an executive last stop you to ask what something meant?
Which part of your technical story do you find hardest to say without jargon?
What decision do you actually need from the executive, and have you ever asked for it directly?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the technical story to the one decision you want the executive to make, and the proof they need to make it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the executive audience, the single decision you will ask for, and the proof point they still need. If there is no ask, the narrative is not ready.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: Read your opening line aloud. Would a CFO know what you meant?
Which claim in your narrative rests on a proof point you do not have?
What are you asking the executive to decide, stated in one sentence?
listenFor: Listen for architecture described rather than translated, value asserted without evidence, narratives that end without an ask, and jargon that survived because nobody in the room questioned it. Also listen for a narrative aimed at the technical stakeholder while claiming to target the executive.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Rewrite one technical narrative for an executive audience, and state the single decision you are asking for.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the narrative, the ask, and the proof point you still need.

secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the next step is to build something rather than to plan or describe it. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Architecture validation works best when options, criteria, assumptions, and risks are visible before the technical debate starts.
keyTalkingPoints: Compare options against the agreed decision criteria.
Name the assumptions and validation steps, not just the recommended design.
Use AI to assemble evidence and decision records while keeping architecture judgment human.
discussionQuestions: Which architecture assumption would hurt most if wrong?
What criteria will decide between options?
What validation step should happen before the customer sees the recommendation?
suggestedTransitions: Move from option comparison to creating the architecture decision record.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to one architecture assumption or option you will validate against agreed criteria.
preparationChecklist: Bring one architecture decision, relevant customer criteria, approved technical sources, and known constraints.
facilitatorQuestions: Which option should be compared, and against what criteria?
Which assumption needs validation first?
What would make the architecture recommendation unsafe to share?
listenFor: Listen for unchallenged assumptions, uncited guidance, missing security or operations review, and options that are not tied to criteria.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If authoritative sources are unavailable, identify required sources and reviewers before drafting.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Design one solution and name the constraint that most limits it.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the design and the constraint you validated.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Discovery should end with decision criteria, not a second discovery meeting. Today focuses on making the customer decision explicit early.
keyTalkingPoints: Start from the customer decision and work backward to criteria and evidence.
Separate sourced facts from hypotheses and open questions.
Capture what must be validated before architecture, demo, or PoC work begins.
discussionQuestions: Which decision is the customer actually trying to make?
What evidence gap would make the next technical step unsafe?
What criteria need to be agreed rather than inferred?
suggestedTransitions: Move from discovery discussion to building the actual decision-criteria brief.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to one discovery brief that includes decision criteria and evidence gaps.
preparationChecklist: Bring one upcoming or recent technical discovery conversation, approved context, known constraints, and any open technical questions.
facilitatorQuestions: Which discovery question would most change the technical decision?
What evidence is missing or only assumed?
Which criteria must be agreed with the customer?
listenFor: Listen for vague decisions, inferred criteria, missing evidence, and questions that sound impressive but do not advance the decision.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, draft the criteria and evidence-gap structure manually.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Run one discovery conversation with the decision criteria written down before you go in.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the criteria you took in and the one that turned out to be wrong.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Risk you find this week is a conversation. The same risk found by the customer is an escalation. Today is about finding it earlier.
keyTalkingPoints: A health score can tell you something is wrong. It rarely tells you what to do.
Every risk needs an owner and a date or it is an observation.
AI is good at surfacing signal. Prioritizing it is judgment.
discussionQuestions: Which account is at risk in a way the reporting does not show?
What stops a known risk from getting an owner?
Which part of this carries policy or precedent risk?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how risk surfaces to one account that is actually at risk now.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one risk, one intervention and one owner.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm tool access for this huddle, bring one real commercial structure and policy example you are working on now, and review the commitment you made last week.
facilitatorQuestions: Which activity here is closest to what you are working on this week?
What would you need to see before you trusted the output?
Where would this break in your real commercial structure and policy work?
listenFor: Through the lens of commercial structure and policy, listen for: risk described without an owner or a date; health reported by score rather than cause; and interventions discussed but never started.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If status data is unavailable, work from what people know and note where the evidence should have come from.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Rank your commercial risks, then take the top one to its owner with a proposed intervention.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the risk, the intervention, and the authoritative source behind it.

activities.whyThisMatters: Comparing viable commercial structures surfaces the difference that actually changes the decision.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Commercial structure decides whether a deal can move. Today is about comparing options before the structure hardens.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is not to create an offer. The goal is to compare viable structures, surface trade-offs, and name the approval path while options still exist.
discussionQuestions: What option is the deal implicitly assuming? Which approval or exception would surprise the team later? What trade-off should be explicit before negotiation?
suggestedTransitions: Move from possible structures to the smallest options matrix that makes the decision clearer.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Create one commercial options matrix and names the approval path or missing evidence.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live opportunity, approved commercial context, known constraints, and the current approval or exception question.
facilitatorQuestions: Which commercial option is most plausible? What trade-off would change the decision? Where would this break if an approval requirement appears late?
listenFor: Listen for: one default structure being treated as the only option; approval path ambiguity; pricing, term, or concession trade-offs not stated; and assumptions that need CE or Deal Desk review.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, build the options matrix manually and name the missing source evidence.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Build a commercial options matrix for one live deal and identify which option needs approval you do not hold.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the options, the trade-offs, and the approval requirement you found.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. activities.name: Stress-test the assumptions the value claims depend on
activities.description: Expose what each outcome number quietly assumes, and record which assumptions the customer would have to accept.
activities.prompt: Here is our value narrative and the evidence brief behind it: [paste both]. For every outcome claim, produce a row containing: the claim, the assumption it depends on, who has to accept that assumption for the claim to hold, the evidence we currently have, and what happens to the claim if adoption is half as fast as projected. Rank the rows by how much the claim collapses when its assumption fails. Do not add claims that are not in my narrative, and do not supply evidence I have not given you.
activities.expectedOutput: An assumption and risk table ranked by how much each claim depends on an unproven assumption.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP decides which assumptions are defensible with this customer, and owns every outcome figure before it reaches them.
activities.requiredContext: The value narrative; the evidence brief; the customer's financial context; adoption expectations already discussed with them.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the value narrative and evidence brief.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Find the claim that collapses hardest.
4. Either find proof for its assumption or remove the claim.
5. Bring the assumption table to the huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: The value claim you cannot defend is the one the customer will ask about.

For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Renewal readiness starts before the renewal motion. Today is about seeing risk and growth conditions early.
keyTalkingPoints: Consumption, MACC or usage trajectory, adoption gaps, value evidence, support health and stakeholder signals all shape renewal confidence.
discussionQuestions: Which renewal are you least confident about, and what specifically drives that?
What consumption signal would you want to see six months before a renewal conversation?
Where is growth genuinely available versus where are you hoping?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the forecast to the one early signal you will start tracking, and who you will align it with.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the renewal you are least confident about, the early signal you will start tracking, and who you will align the forecast with.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account with renewal, consumption, usage or expansion relevance in the near planning horizon.
facilitatorQuestions: What is your forecast based on, and how far ahead does the signal reach?
Which growth opportunity is supported by consumption evidence?
What would you need to know now to avoid a surprise at renewal?
listenFor: Listen for forecasts driven by relationship confidence rather than consumption evidence, growth assumed from headroom rather than intent, renewal risk surfacing late because nobody looked early, and commercial ownership blurring between CSAM and CE. Also listen for consumption trends read without seasonality.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Start tracking one early consumption signal and hand it to the account owner.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the signal, why it matters, and who you handed it to.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: CSAM orchestration is making the customer-success system observable enough to run.
keyTalkingPoints: Handoffs need an input, owner and date. Escalation is not a failure when it is used to unblock the system and protect customer outcomes.
discussionQuestions: Where does work currently stop between Microsoft, the partner, and the customer?
Who believes they own something that someone else also believes they own?
Which handoff have you personally been compensating for?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the coordination map to the one handoff you will make explicit, with both sides named.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the handoff you will make explicit, both parties by name, and the date it will be agreed rather than assumed.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one workstream involving Microsoft, customer, partner, support or delivery handoffs.
facilitatorQuestions: Where exactly does work stop between the three parties?
Who thinks they own that step, and have you asked them?
What are you personally absorbing because the handoff does not work?
listenFor: Listen for the CSAM compensating for a broken handoff rather than fixing it, ownership assumed across company boundaries, partner commitments with no date, and coordination meetings that report rather than decide. Also listen for the customer's own team being left out of the orchestration picture.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Make one handoff explicit this week by agreeing it with both sides rather than assuming it.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the handoff, both owners, and the date it was agreed.

activities.name: Track commercial policy and licensing changes that affect your accounts
activities.description: Set up a monitored, source-locked watch on the commercial policy and licensing guidance you rely on, so changes reach you before a customer raises them.
activities.prompt: Set up a recurring check against a fixed list of authoritative Microsoft commercial policy and licensing sources that I will confirm with you first. Each time, report only what has changed, quote the change, cite the source, and state plainly which of my accounts it plausibly affects and why. Do not interpret the change into commercial advice and do not draw on any source outside the confirmed list. Where the implication is unclear, say so and name the owner who can rule on it.
activities.expectedOutput: A recurring change-only digest quoting and citing each change, with plausible account impact and the named owner for anything requiring a ruling.
activities.humanCheckpoint: CE confirms the source list before the watch is enabled, and routes every interpretation to the accountable policy owner rather than acting on the summary.
activities.requiredContext: The authoritative policy and licensing sources your team treats as canonical; your account list; your escalation owners.
activitySteps: 1. Agree the fixed list of authoritative policy and licensing sources with your team before you enable anything.
2. Run the prompt with that confirmed list.
3. Check the first digest quotes and cites each change rather than paraphrasing it.
4. Set the cadence and confirm the watch is not drawing on sources outside the agreed list.
5. Route every interpretation to the accountable policy owner rather than acting on the summary.
activities.whyThisMatters: Commercial policy changes are only a problem when the customer knows before you do. A locked source list is what separates a reliable watch from confident invention.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Policy questions found at approval cost weeks. Today is about finding the question early and routing it to the authoritative owner.
keyTalkingPoints: AI can assemble the context and possible questions. It cannot interpret policy, approve exceptions, or invent authority. The useful output is a routed question with evidence, not a guessed answer.
discussionQuestions: Which policy or licensing question most often causes rework? Where did an approval path surprise you? Which interpretation must come from an authoritative source?
suggestedTransitions: Move from policy categories to one live deal question and the owner who can answer it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Route one policy, licensing, or approval question to an authoritative owner with the evidence needed.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one real commercial structure or policy example, the approved source you would check, and the decision or approval path currently unclear.
facilitatorQuestions: Which Practice helps you route the policy or licensing question fastest? What would you need to see before trusting the output? Where must the answer come from an authoritative owner instead of AI?
listenFor: Through the lens of commercial structure and policy, listen for: policy interpreted from memory; uncertainty left unflagged; approval paths discovered late; and questions that need an authoritative owner rather than a generated answer.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If guidance is unavailable, list the questions, required evidence, and routing owner. Do not guess the answer.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Take one open policy or licensing question to its authoritative owner rather than answering it yourself.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the question, the owner, and the answer you received.

secondaryAgents.name: GitHub Copilot
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: AI pair programmer available in VS Code, the CLI and the GitHub Copilot app. It works against a repository or a working folder rather than against your mail and meetings.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Write, explain, refactor and test code; scaffold infrastructure-as-code and deployment artifacts; build the smallest spike that proves or disproves an architecture assumption; generate sample data and validation scripts; and reproduce a reported failure so you can see it rather than describe it.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the next step is to build something rather than to plan or describe it. Validating an architecture assumption with a spike, standing up a demo or workshop environment, iterating a proof of concept, reproducing a deployment or integration failure, or packaging a reusable asset with tests and setup steps.
keyBenefits: Turns a technical opinion into evidence. A spike that takes twenty minutes settles an argument that would otherwise run for a week, and a reproduced failure is a fact the account team can act on rather than a claim the customer has to accept.
secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for customer, market or account research; that is Researcher. Do not use it to assemble a customer-facing document or deck; that is Cowork. Do not point it at production without the review your team already requires, and do not paste customer data into it. It works on code and configuration, not on the CRM record.
stepsToGetStarted: Use it where the code already is: the Copilot extension in VS Code, the gh copilot CLI, or the GitHub Copilot app in the browser for work not tied to a local checkout. Open the repository or folder first so it has the context. Start with: Explain what this deployment does, then write the smallest test that would prove the assumption I am least sure about.

activitySteps: 1. Choose the asset worth reusing.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Reuse only works when an asset has enough context for someone else to trust and adapt it.
keyTalkingPoints: Package purpose, prerequisites, steps, parameters, validation checks, limitations, owner, and example use.
Remove sensitive content before reuse.
Use Skill Blueprints for repeatable workflows that are not validated assets yet.
discussionQuestions: What did you build recently that another SE will rebuild?
What context would make someone trust and adapt it?
What should not be reused without review?
suggestedTransitions: Move from asset selection to packaging or Skill Blueprint creation.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Package one reusable technical asset or drafts one Skill Blueprint.
preparationChecklist: Bring one demo, script, architecture, checklist, response, or pattern that could become reusable.
facilitatorQuestions: Which asset is worth reusing?
What context would make it usable by another SE?
What must be removed, validated, or tested before sharing?
listenFor: Listen for assets without owner, missing prerequisites, sensitive content, unclear limitations, and reuse patterns that should become blueprints.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the repository location is unclear, package the asset and record the placement decision as a blocker.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Turn one piece of work you already did into something another SE could reuse.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the asset and who you gave it to.

primaryAgents.shortDescription: AI-powered experience layer, available through Sales Agent and Microsoft 365, that connects the systems used across the end-to-end ECIF journey.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Understand eligible investment offers; create compliant ECIF workscopes with guided, auto-populated inputs; identify suitable suppliers; submit requests; and track status, milestones, overdue actions, and delivery progress.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Preparing or refining an ECIF funding request; selecting an eligible offer or supplier for an Opportunity and location; submitting a request; or tracking milestones and delivery across internal or partner-led projects.
keyBenefits: Reduces seller toil by bringing ECIF guidance and actions into one conversational flow; improves workscope completeness and first-pass quality; speeds the path from scope creation to IO/PO; and provides a connected view of requests, milestones, alerts, and delivery progress.

resources.description: The investment path across systems. Sales Agent and the ECIF Agent for guidance, ECIF Central for the workscope, MSX Deal Assistance for submission and tracking, MCAPS Help when blocked. For Azure offers, start at Azure Offer Navigator.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat the agent as the final authority for policy, eligibility, compliance, funding approval, or supplier selection. Review generated content and required evidence before submission, and use governed ECIF channels for exceptions or approvals.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Investment should be connected to a real customer barrier, not added as a side process. Today is about the AE’s role in naming the investment hypothesis and routing the next decision.
keyTalkingPoints: Eligibility, funding, and approval are governed human decisions. AI may help assemble context, status, and evidence, but the AE should not overstate approval or commitment.
discussionQuestions: Where could investment remove a barrier? Which part is yours to advance? Who owns the next governed decision?
suggestedTransitions: Move from investment concept to the AE’s next governed action on one live case.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the investment hypothesis, evidence gap, and next governed owner.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live opportunity or account barrier where investment may be relevant, plus any approved context you can safely use.
facilitatorQuestions: Where might investment remove a real barrier? What evidence supports that barrier? Who owns eligibility, funding, approval, delivery, or value proof?
listenFor: Listen for funding implied as approved, hidden open questions, unowned handoffs, and investment ideas not tied to an account priority or decision.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized scenario if live data is not appropriate. Do not infer eligibility, approval, or funding status.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Test whether investment could remove one real barrier, then route the next decision without implying approval.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the investment hypothesis, source evidence, open questions, owner, and the next governed action.

WF-ORIENT-01.todayObjective: Understand how the AE huddle path runs and where the human checkpoints protect account, deal, and forecast judgment.
WF-ORIENT-01.whyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
WF-ORIENT-01.desiredOutcome: AEs know how the huddle motion works, which tools may show up, what to review, and what AI experiences to bring back before next week.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This session sets the operating model for the AE path. The point is not tool fluency for its own sake; it is better account, pipeline, deal, and customer-conversation execution with human judgment visible.
keyTalkingPoints: The huddle is workflow-first. Every session uses real AE work, a practical AI-supported practice, and a human checkpoint. AI can assemble evidence, summarize, draft, and monitor; the AE owns judgment, customer trust, commitments, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted account, pipeline, or customer-facing output?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the workflow-discovery prompt below. Week 1 is for finding the recurring work worth automating.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the tools named for this path, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
facilitatorQuestions: Which account, pipeline, or customer-facing work do you repeat every week without thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where must the AE judgment stay human no matter how good the output gets?
listenFor: Listen for unvoiced scepticism, access blockers stated as disinterest, the assumption that this is a tool rollout, and people who describe only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat. The recurring, unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the discovery conversation and record access blockers separately from interest. The discovery prompt can be run in whichever tool the person already has.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

"I am an Account Executive at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with."
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation, or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

WF-ORIENT-01.keyTakeaway: The point of the motion is better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake.

activities.name: Map the workflow the team chose and find where it leaks
activities.description: Make the chosen workflow visible end to end, then locate the specific steps where time, confidence, or quality is lost.
activities.prompt: I run this recurring workflow: [describe the workflow, what triggers it, how often, and who depends on the output]. Here is a recent example of it going badly: [describe what happened]. Break the workflow into its actual steps. For each step, identify what input it needs, what decision it requires, and who owns it. Then tell me which two or three steps most likely cost time or quality, and why you think so. Ask me for anything you need rather than assuming it. Do not propose tools yet.
activities.expectedOutput: A step-by-step map of the chosen workflow with the two or three highest-friction steps named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The person who owns the workflow confirms the step map matches how the work is really done, not how it is supposed to be done.
activities.requiredContext: A recurring workflow you personally run; a recent concrete example; who owns each step; what inputs the workflow depends on.
activitySteps: 1. Describe the workflow and one recent example.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Correct the step map where the model got your work wrong; that correction is where the learning is.
5. Agree as a group which step leaks the most.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most workflow friction is invisible to the person living with it, because they have already adapted to it.

activities.name: Design one bounded experiment you can finish this week
activities.description: Turn the highest-friction step into a test small enough to run before the next huddle and specific enough to judge.
activities.prompt: Here is the workflow step I want to test: [paste the step and why it costs time or quality]. Design a one-week experiment. Specify: the exact input I will supply, the action I will take, the output I expect, who reviews it before it is used, what evidence I will bring back, and the stop condition that tells me to abandon it. Keep it small enough to run in under an hour total. If the step as described is too large to test in a week, tell me how to narrow it rather than proposing a bigger plan.
activities.expectedOutput: A bounded experiment card with input, action, output, reviewer, evidence, and stop condition.
activities.humanCheckpoint: You decide whether the experiment is genuinely small enough to finish, and you own the judgment about what output is safe to use in real work.
activities.requiredContext: The friction step from the previous activity; what data or systems you can actually access this week; who could review the output.
activitySteps: 1. Take the step your group identified.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Cut the experiment down until it fits in an hour.
4. Name your reviewer and your stop condition out loud.
5. Put it in your calendar before you leave the huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: An experiment that does not fit in a week does not get run, and an experiment without a stop condition never ends.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This huddle has no pre-written workflow. The team chooses one, which means the value depends entirely on picking a workflow people actually run. Anchor the session in real work and trusted context before anyone opens a tool.
keyTalkingPoints: The workflow must be recurring, not a one-off.
Someone in the room must actually own it.
A specific recent example beats a general description.
If the team cannot name a real example, the workflow is too abstract to work on.
discussionQuestions: What workflow are we improving today?
What triggers it, and how often does it run?
What inputs, constraints, and approvals shape it?
Whose work is it, and who else depends on the output?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the friction people named to one specific assistable step, then from that step to a single bounded experiment with an owner.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the workflow you chose, the one step you will test, the human checkpoint you will keep, and the evidence you will bring back. If you cannot name an owner or a date, the experiment is not real yet; shrink it until it is.
preparationChecklist: Bring one recurring workflow you personally run and one recent example of it, including what made that run harder than it needed to be.
facilitatorQuestions: Where in this workflow is effort or quality lost today?
What is the smallest step AI could assist, rather than the whole workflow?
What must a person verify before the output is used?
What would a one-week version of this experiment look like?
listenFor: Listen for scope that is too broad to test in a week, inputs the person cannot actually access, an output nobody would notice if it were wrong, and enthusiasm for a tool without a workflow behind it. Also listen for the opposite problem: a step so small that automating it changes nothing.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If a tool or data source is unavailable, map the workflow on paper and design the experiment for later execution. Use a hypothetical process shape if needed, but do not invent business facts, customer detail, or system behavior.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: What will you test this week? State the input, the action, the output, who reviews it, and what would tell you to stop.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the actual output from your experiment, whether it worked or not. A failed experiment with evidence is more useful to the group than a success without it.

WF-X-TRANSITION-01.todayObjective: Take one account you are inheriting or handing over and get it to the point where the customer conversation can happen with confidence.
WF-X-TRANSITION-01.whyItMatters: More than two thousand account transitions happen every year, and a poor one measurably depresses customer experience scores. The incoming seller inherits whatever the outgoing seller failed to write down, and the customer pays for the gap in repeated conversations they have already had.
WF-X-TRANSITION-01.desiredOutcome: One transition moved forward with the inherited context understood, the gaps named, the customer conversation prepared, and the follow-up owned.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.
