primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

activities.name: Find out what you actually inherited
activities.description: Assemble the history, relationships, open work and unresolved risk on an account you are taking on, before you speak to anyone.
activities.prompt: I am taking over [Account name or TPID]. Build me a picture of what I am inheriting: the customer's stated priorities, the open opportunities and their current stage, active commitments and milestones, recent support or delivery escalations, who the known stakeholders are and who owns each relationship, and anything that looks unresolved or overdue. Tell me plainly where the record is thin or stale, because that is what I most need to know before I meet this customer.
activities.expectedOutput: An inherited-context brief covering priorities, open opportunities, commitments, escalations and stakeholders, with the thin or stale parts of the record explicitly named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what the silence means. An account with no recorded risk is not a healthy account, it is an unwritten one, and the incoming seller must treat an empty field as unknown rather than as good news.
activities.requiredContext: The account you are inheriting or handing over, with its TPID; access to MSX for that account; the name of the outgoing or incoming seller.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one account you are inheriting, or one you are handing over.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate what the record says from what it does not say. The gaps matter more than the summary.
5. Write down the three questions only the outgoing seller can answer.
6. Do not contact the customer yet. The internal handoff comes first.
activities.whyThisMatters: You inherit whatever the last person wrote down, and most of what mattered was never written down. Finding that out before the customer meeting is the difference between a handover and a restart.

activities.name: Run the internal handoff conversation properly
activities.description: Turn the gaps you found into the specific questions for the outgoing seller, and capture the answers where the next person will find them.
activities.prompt: Here is what I found on [Account name or TPID] and here is what is missing: [paste your gaps]. Help me prepare the internal handoff conversation with the outgoing seller. Draft the specific questions I should ask about relationships, unwritten history, sensitivities, commitments made verbally, and anything that would embarrass me in front of this customer. Prioritise the questions whose answers exist only in that person's head.
activities.expectedOutput: A prioritised question list for the outgoing seller, the answers captured in MSX rather than in private notes, and an agreed plan for who notifies the customer.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what is safe to record. Some relationship context is candid and belongs in a conversation rather than a permanent field, and the seller owns that line rather than transcribing everything.
activities.requiredContext: Your inherited-context brief and its gaps; time with the outgoing seller; access to update the account record in MSX.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the gaps you named in the previous practice.
2. Paste those gaps into the prompt where it asks for them, then run it.
3. Separate what the customer actually said from your interpretation of it, and label both.
4. Put the notes in the record, not in a chat message. Chat is not where the next person will look.
5. Hold the handoff conversation as well. The notes make the conversation shorter, not unnecessary.
activities.whyThisMatters: The handoff conversation is the only chance to collect what was never written down. Held badly, the next transition starts from the same empty record.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Find out what you actually inherited

activities.name: Prepare the customer conversation that earns the relationship
activities.description: Plan the introduction so the customer hears continuity and a reason to invest in a new relationship, not an administrative notification.
activities.prompt: I am being introduced to [Account name or TPID] as their new [role]. Help me prepare the first conversation. I want to show I already understand their priorities and open commitments, ask what the record cannot tell me, and give them a reason to invest in this relationship. Draft the opening, the three questions worth their time, and how I acknowledge anything that has gone wrong recently without over-promising. Do not invent history I have not confirmed.
activities.expectedOutput: A first-conversation plan with an opening that demonstrates continuity, three questions the record could not answer, and a considered position on any recent problem.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what to acknowledge. Raising a known problem you cannot yet fix builds credibility only if you also say what happens next, and the seller judges whether that is ready.
activities.requiredContext: Your inherited-context brief and the handoff answers; the outgoing seller's introduction plan; the customer stakeholders you will meet.
activitySteps: 1. Use the context and the answers from the internal handoff.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Cut anything you cannot personally stand behind. Confidence about details you have not verified is what damages a first meeting.
5. Agree with the outgoing seller how the introduction is made.
6. Hold the meeting. The transition record stays open until you have.
activities.whyThisMatters: The customer did not choose this change and is measuring whether it costs them. The first conversation is where they decide whether to invest in you or wait you out.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Run the internal handoff conversation properly

activities.name: Pressure-test what you are handing over
activities.description: Look at an account you are handing on and find what only exists in your own head, before it is lost.
activities.prompt: I am handing over [Account name or TPID]. First, based on what is recorded in MSX, tell me what an incoming seller would and would not understand about this account. Then interview me: ask me up to six questions, one at a time, designed to surface what I know that is not written anywhere, covering informal relationships, the history behind a decision, sensitivities, verbal commitments and who actually influences outcomes. Do not guess my answers. After I have answered, organise what I told you into what belongs in the record and what is better said in conversation.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on what the record fails to convey, plus your own tacit knowledge drawn out through questioning and sorted into what to record and what to say in person.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The outgoing seller decides which commitments must be written down. A verbal commitment that dies with the handover becomes the incoming seller's credibility problem and the customer's evidence that Microsoft does not remember.
activities.requiredContext: An account you are handing over; your own knowledge of its unwritten history; access to update the record.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an account you are handing over, or one you know well.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt. It will read the record first, then ask you questions; answer them as you go.
4. Be specific in your answers. The value of this is entirely in what you say, not what the tool retrieves.
5. Record the parts it identifies as belonging in the system, and plan to say the rest in conversation.
6. Check whether any verbal commitment you mentioned is captured anywhere.
activities.whyThisMatters: Every seller who inherited a thin account was handed it by someone who knew more than they recorded. This is where that stops being someone else's problem.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Find out what you actually inherited

activities.name: Own the ninety days after the introduction
activities.description: Convert what the customer said in the first meeting into commitments with dates, so the transition is judged on follow-through rather than on the meeting.
activities.prompt: Here is what came out of my first conversation with [Account name or TPID]: [paste your notes]. Turn this into a follow-through plan: what I committed to, what the customer asked for, what needs someone else at Microsoft, and what I should have demonstrably delivered before the ninety-day mark. Flag anything I appear to have committed to that I have not confirmed I can deliver.
activities.expectedOutput: A ninety-day follow-through plan with commitments, owners, dates, and any unconfirmed promise flagged for resolution.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms every commitment is one they can actually keep. A transition is judged on whether the first promise was kept, and an unkept one costs more than the original change did.
activities.requiredContext: Your notes from the first customer conversation; the commitments you made; the Microsoft roles who would own anything outside your control.
activitySteps: 1. Open your notes from the first customer conversation.
2. Paste those notes into the prompt where it asks for them, then run it.
3. Check every commitment it identifies. Deal with anything you promised without meaning to.
4. Put dates against each item and name owners for anything that is not yours.
5. Diarise the ninety-day point now, while it still feels urgent.
activities.whyThisMatters: Transitions are not judged by the introduction meeting. They are judged ninety days later, on whether the thing you said you would do happened.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Prepare the customer conversation that earns the relationship

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Every seller in this room has inherited an account with nothing useful written down, and every seller has handed one over. This session is about the transition you are in the middle of right now, on either side of it.
keyTalkingPoints: Enterprise transitions are expected to complete within 30 days of the record being created, and 60 days for SME&C, CASA and Elevate. The transition record is closed only after the customer meeting has happened, not when the fields are populated. There is no mandatory transition document; the requirement is current contacts, a current plan, and a documented customer conversation.
discussionQuestions: What is the worst account you have ever inherited, and what specifically was missing?
What do you know about your accounts that exists nowhere in MSX?
When a customer is handed a new seller, what does it actually cost them?
suggestedTransitions: Move from what the record is missing to the one conversation each person needs to have this week, internal or customer-facing.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the account and the specific next conversation, internal or customer. A transition moves when someone talks, not when a field is updated.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account you are currently inheriting or handing over. If you have neither, bring the account you would find hardest to hand to someone else.
facilitatorQuestions: What did the record fail to tell you that you needed?
What do you know that would be lost if you handed this account over tomorrow?
What would this customer say if you asked them how the last transition went?
listenFor: Listen for transitions treated as administration rather than as a customer experience, for records closed before the customer meeting happened, for verbal commitments nobody has captured, and for sellers assuming an empty risk field means there is no risk.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live transition, run it on the account each person would find hardest to hand over. The exercise of naming what is unwritten works either way.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you find missing from an account record that you assumed would be there, and what will you write down differently because of it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, record one thing about an account you own that currently exists only in your own head.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the account, what you found missing, the conversation you had, and what you recorded so the next person does not have to ask.

activities.name: Test whether the qualification would survive the receiving role
activities.description: Check that an opportunity being handed on has the qualification evidence the receiving role needs, before you transfer it rather than after they reject it.
activities.prompt: I am handing over [opportunity name or ID] to the specialist team. Review what is documented and tell me whether a specialist receiving this could act on it immediately. Specifically: is the customer outcome clear, are the business and technical decision makers identified, is the budget and timing evidenced, are the blockers named with a mitigation, and does the milestone carry a real estimated value and date rather than a placeholder. Tell me what is missing rather than summarising what is there.
activities.expectedOutput: A gap list against the qualification the receiving role needs, covering outcome, decision makers, budget, timing, blockers and milestone completeness.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The sending role decides what is genuinely known versus assumed. Handing over an assumption dressed as a qualified fact is worse than handing over an acknowledged gap, because the receiving role will act on it.
activities.requiredContext: One opportunity being transferred, with its ID; the milestone attached to it; the qualification criteria your team applies.
activitySteps: 1. Choose one opportunity you are about to hand over, or one you recently received.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Treat every gap as work to do before the transfer, not after.
5. Check the milestone has an estimated date and a value that is not zero.
6. If you received this handoff, send the gap list back rather than rebuilding it silently.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most handoffs are rejected or quietly rebuilt because the receiving role cannot act on what arrived. The gap was always visible before the transfer; nobody looked.

activities.name: Write the handoff so the next role does not have to ask
activities.description: Capture the qualification, the customer context and the unwritten detail in the record itself, so the transfer survives without a meeting.
activities.prompt: Help me write the handoff notes for [opportunity name or ID] moving to [receiving role]. Cover what the customer is trying to achieve and in their own words where I have them, what has been agreed and what has not, who influences the decision and how, what I have already tried, and what I would warn the receiving person about. Write it so someone who has never spoken to this customer could pick it up. Flag anything I have written that is my opinion rather than something the customer said.
activities.expectedOutput: Handoff notes covering customer outcome, agreed and unagreed items, decision influence, what has been tried, and warnings, with opinion separated from evidence.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The sending role decides what belongs in a permanent record. Candid relationship context may be better said than written, and the sender owns that judgement rather than transcribing everything.
activities.requiredContext: Your gap list; what the customer has said in their own words; the receiving role and who specifically will take it.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the gap list you produced in the previous practice.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate what the customer actually said from your interpretation of it, and label both.
5. Put the notes in the record, not in a chat message. Chat is not where the next person will look.
6. Hold the handoff conversation as well. The notes make the conversation shorter, not unnecessary.
activities.whyThisMatters: The handoff conversation happens once and is forgotten. The record is what the receiving role actually works from, and what the person after them inherits.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Test whether the qualification would survive the receiving role

activities.name: Find the handoffs that stalled in the gap between roles
activities.description: Look across your opportunities and milestones for transfers that were started and never completed, where ownership is ambiguous and nothing is moving.
activities.prompt: Across my opportunities and milestones, find where a transfer between roles looks incomplete or stalled: ownership that changed but where nothing has happened since, milestones sitting at the same stage well past their estimated date, opportunities where the specialist or customer success team was engaged but no activity followed, and anything where I cannot tell from the record who currently owns the next action. Rank by how long each has been static.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of stalled or incomplete transfers with time static, and the ownership ambiguity named for each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms actual ownership with the other role directly. A record showing a transfer completed is not evidence that anyone picked it up.
activities.requiredContext: Your opportunities and milestones; the expected transfer windows your team works to; the roles you routinely hand off to.
activitySteps: 1. Run the prompt across your own opportunities and milestones.
2. For each result, establish who actually believes they own it. It is often nobody, and sometimes two people.
3. Pick the one that has been static longest and resolve ownership today.
4. Check whether the customer is waiting on any of these. That changes the priority.
5. Record the owner in the system rather than agreeing it verbally.
activities.whyThisMatters: Work does not usually stall inside a role. It stalls in the space between two, where both parties believe the other has it.

activities.name: Rehearse receiving a handoff you were given badly
activities.description: Practise the conversation that recovers a thin handoff without damaging the relationship with the role that sent it.
activities.prompt: I have received a handoff for [opportunity name or ID] and it is thin. Play the role of the person who sent it. I will ask for what I need. Push back the way a busy colleague would, including being defensive if I imply they did it badly. Afterwards, tell me which of my questions got the most useful information, where I put them on the defensive unnecessarily, and how to ask for the missing context without making it a complaint.
activities.expectedOutput: A rehearsed recovery conversation with coaching on which questions produced information and where the approach created defensiveness.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The receiving role decides how hard to push. The relationship with that colleague outlasts this opportunity, and a handoff recovered at the cost of a working relationship is a poor trade.
activities.requiredContext: A handoff you received that was insufficient; what specifically you still need; your relationship with the sending role.
activitySteps: 1. Use a real handoff you received that was not enough.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the role-play.
4. Notice where you made it about the process rather than the customer.
5. Rewrite your opening so it leads with what the customer needs.
6. Have the real conversation.
activities.whyThisMatters: Nobody sends a bad handoff deliberately. Getting what you need without making it an accusation is the skill that keeps the next one better.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Work rarely stalls inside a role. It stalls in the gap between two, where the sending role believes it is done and the receiving role cannot act. This session is about closing that gap on one live handoff.
keyTalkingPoints: Ownership transfers between the account, specialist and customer success teams are expected to complete within seven business days. A handoff is not complete when ownership changes; it is complete when the receiving role can act. The record is what the next person works from, not the conversation.
discussionQuestions: What is the least useful handoff you have ever received, and what was missing?
When you hand something over, what do you assume the other person already knows?
How would you know today if a handoff you sent had gone nowhere?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the gap analysis to the one handoff each person will prepare, repair or chase this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the handoff each person will complete or repair, and who they need to speak to.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one opportunity or milestone you are currently handing over or have recently received. If you have neither, bring the one that went worst.
facilitatorQuestions: Could the receiving role act on what you sent, without asking you anything?
Where in your own list has a transfer stalled with nobody owning it?
What do you know about this opportunity that is written nowhere?
listenFor: Listen for handoffs described as notifications, for ownership that changed without anyone accepting it, for milestones carrying placeholder values or dates, and for sellers rebuilding a thin handoff silently rather than sending it back.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live handoff, use one that has already completed and ask whether the receiving role could have acted on it. The gaps are just as visible in hindsight.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you assume the receiving role already knew, and what will you write down next time instead of assuming?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one handoff you have sent or received and make it complete enough that the other role could act without contacting you.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the handoff, what was missing, what you added, and whether the receiving role could then act.

WF-X-HANDOFF-01.keyTakeaway: A handoff is a gated transfer with exit criteria, not a notification. If the receiving role cannot act on what they were given, the handoff has not happened.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Most of us have at some point defended a number we were not fully sure about. Today is about fixing the signal, not the spreadsheet.
keyTalkingPoints: A gap is usually three problems wearing one label: not enough, not moving, or dated wrong.
Certified data settles arguments opinion cannot.
Correction is judgment work. The agent proposes, you decide.
discussionQuestions: Where do consumption or usage signals become technical work for you?
Which shortfall signal is most likely to hide a technical cause?
What evidence would you need before owning an intervention?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the report signal to one technical cause or blocker that can be validated this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one consumption signal you will validate and one technical question you will answer.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the relevant certified report, bring one consumption or usage signal you are reviewing, and note what technical context the report does not show.
facilitatorQuestions: Which consumption or shortfall activity is closest to what you inspect today?
What would you need to verify before trusting the signal?
Where would this break if the report lacks architecture context?
listenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: report signals separated from technical cause; assumptions about customer intent; missing owners; and interventions that require architecture or workload context.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the data source is unavailable, map the current inspection routine and draft the prompt and human checkpoint for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Name the technical cause behind one consumption gap, and start the intervention with an owner.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the cause you identified and who owns the intervention.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

activities.name: Find out which recorded sponsors are still actually engaged
activities.description: Check the senior relationships your account depends on against real engagement, and find the ones that have gone quiet without anyone noticing.
activities.prompt: For [Account name or TPID], focus only on the senior stakeholders recorded as sponsors, executive contacts or decision makers, not the full contact list. For each, show me when they were last genuinely engaged, whether that engagement was with me or with someone else at Microsoft, and whether it has become less frequent over time. Separately, identify any senior person now appearing regularly in meetings or correspondence who is not recorded as a sponsor at all. I am testing whether the sponsorship this account depends on still exists, not building a contact list.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on each recorded sponsor covering last genuine engagement, who at Microsoft holds it, and whether it is declining, plus any unrecorded senior contact now engaging.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what absence means. A sponsor who has not been in a meeting may still be engaged through a colleague, and the seller judges that rather than the activity data.
activities.requiredContext: One account and its TPID; the senior stakeholders currently recorded as sponsors or decision makers; the outcomes the account depends on them for.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one account, ideally one you feel confident about.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Look first at recorded sponsors with no recent engagement. That is the dangerous category.
5. Note whether the engagement that does exist is yours or a colleague's, because a relationship held by someone else is not yours to rely on.
6. Look last at unrecorded senior contacts. You may be misreading who holds influence.
activities.whyThisMatters: Sponsorship decays quietly. The person your account depends on may have changed role or priority months ago, and the account plan will keep listing them as your sponsor until someone checks.

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

activities.name: Separate real sponsorship from polite interest
activities.description: Apply an honest test to each senior relationship, distinguishing executives who would act on your behalf from those who merely take the meeting.
activities.prompt: Here are the senior stakeholders on [Account name or TPID] and what I know about each: [paste your list with what each has actually done]. Help me test each one honestly. For each, tell me what evidence exists that they would spend their own political capital for this, what evidence suggests they are merely being courteous, and what I would need to see to be confident either way. Be direct where the evidence is thin. Do not soften a weak relationship into a strong one.
activities.expectedOutput: An honest assessment of each senior relationship separating evidenced sponsorship from courtesy, with the evidence gap named for each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller owns the honesty of the input. An overstated relationship produces a confident assessment of something that does not exist, which is worse than no assessment.
activities.requiredContext: The senior stakeholders on the account; what each has actually done rather than said; the outcomes the account depends on them for.
activitySteps: 1. List each senior stakeholder and what they have actually done, not what they have said.
2. Paste that into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Be honest in what you supply. This exercise is worthless if you overstate the relationship.
4. Identify the single relationship the account most depends on.
5. If no relationship passes the test, that is the finding, and it is worth knowing now.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most accounts believe they have executive sponsorship. Far fewer have someone who would spend their own credibility to unblock something. The difference only becomes visible under pressure.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Find out which recorded sponsors are still actually engaged

activities.name: Design the investment that earns sponsorship
activities.description: Plan what you will give an executive relationship over the coming quarter, so sponsorship is earned before it is needed rather than requested when it is.
activities.prompt: I want to deepen the relationship with [executive name and role] at [Account name or TPID] over the next quarter. Here is what I know about their priorities and here is what I am genuinely able to offer them, whether that is access, insight, introductions or influence: [paste their priorities and your realistic offer list]. Using only what I have supplied, help me sequence the investment across the quarter: what to lead with, what earns the right to the next conversation, and what would signal the relationship is strengthening. Do not suggest anything I have not told you I can actually provide, and do not give me generic executive engagement advice.
activities.expectedOutput: A sequenced quarter of relationship investment built only on what you can genuinely provide, with what to lead with, what earns the next conversation, and the signals that sponsorship is strengthening.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what can actually be offered and delivered. Sponsorship built on something you cannot provide costs more than the relationship you were trying to build.
activities.requiredContext: The executive and their role; what the record and your own knowledge show about their priorities; what you can genuinely offer, meaning access, insight, introductions or influence you actually control.
activitySteps: 1. Write down what this executive appears to care about, and separately what you can genuinely offer them.
2. Paste both into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Discard anything that would be true of any executive at any company. That is the test of whether it is useful.
4. Sequence it across the quarter rather than planning a single meeting; sponsorship is built over time.
5. Diarise the first step. An intention to deepen a relationship is not a plan.
activities.whyThisMatters: Executive relationships deepen through usefulness delivered over time, not through contact frequency or a single well-prepared meeting. The investment has to start from what they need and what you can actually give.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Separate real sponsorship from polite interest

activities.name: Work out what happens when your sponsor leaves
activities.description: Establish how much of an account rests on one person, and what would survive if that person moved on.
activities.prompt: For [Account name or TPID], I want to understand my exposure if a key relationship ended. Here is who I rely on and what each of them does for us: [paste the senior relationships and what each one enables]. For each person, tell me what would stop working if they left tomorrow, whether anyone else at the customer could carry that, and how much of our position depends on that single individual. Then tell me which relationship I should be building now as insurance. Be blunt about concentration.
activities.expectedOutput: An exposure read per key relationship covering what would stop working, who could carry it, the degree of single-person dependency, and the relationship to build as insurance.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller judges how much concentration is tolerable. Some accounts genuinely run through one executive, and the decision is whether to accept that risk or invest in reducing it.
activities.requiredContext: One account and its TPID; the senior people you rely on and what each one enables; who else at the customer operates at that level.
activitySteps: 1. List the senior people you rely on and what each one actually enables, from renewals to unblocking decisions.
2. Paste that into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Be honest about how much depends on one person. Most accounts depend on more than the seller admits.
4. Identify the second relationship you would need if the first one ended.
5. Start building that relationship now, while it is insurance rather than emergency.
activities.whyThisMatters: Sponsors leave, get promoted and change priorities, and the account discovers its dependency at the worst moment. The insurance relationship has to be built before it is needed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Every account plan claims executive sponsorship. Far fewer accounts have someone senior who would actually spend their own credibility to unblock something. This session is about finding out which kind you have.
keyTalkingPoints: Stakeholder maps age quietly; the person you are counting on may have changed role or priority. Sponsorship is built over quarters and cannot be assembled in the week you need it. An executive relationship you only use when you need something is not sponsorship.
discussionQuestions: Who on your biggest account would take your call today, and when did you last test that?
Which senior relationship are you assuming is stronger than it is?
When did a sponsor last change without you noticing?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the tested map to the one relationship each person will act on, and what they will offer.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the executive each person will engage and what they will offer, not what they will ask for.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account you feel confident about, and its current stakeholder map. Confidence is what makes this exercise useful.
facilitatorQuestions: Which recorded sponsor has not actually engaged recently?
Which relationship would hold under pressure, and what is your evidence?
What could you offer that this executive cannot easily get elsewhere?
listenFor: Listen for sponsorship asserted without evidence, for relationships described by meeting frequency rather than by what the person has done, for engagement plans that would suit any executive at any company, and for sellers softening a weak relationship rather than naming it.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If engagement data is unavailable, run it from memory: name each senior stakeholder and what they have actually done for the account. The honesty of the input matters more than the data source.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which relationship turned out to be thinner than you assumed, and what will you do about it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, test one assumed executive relationship by offering something useful and seeing what comes back.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the relationship, what you offered, what the response told you, and whether the sponsorship is real.

WF-X-SPONSOR-01.keyTakeaway: An executive relationship you only use when you need something is not sponsorship. Sponsorship is the relationship that already exists when you need it.

WF-X-FYPLAN-01.roleTopicName: Pressure-Test the Territory Plan Before Someone Else Does
WF-X-FYPLAN-01.roleTopicDescription: Work the arithmetic behind your territory and coverage plan, find where it does not add up, and prepare the support request that closes the gap.
WF-X-FYPLAN-01.wiifm: You will be asked to defend this plan. Better to find its weakest assumption yourself, while there is still time to do something about it.

activities.name: Work out whether your territory actually covers your number
activities.description: Do the arithmetic between what your territory can realistically produce and what you have been asked to deliver, and quantify the gap.
activities.prompt: Help me test whether my territory covers my number. Here is what I have: [paste your quota, your pipeline by stage with values, your renewal base, and the conversion rate your team actually achieves at each stage]. Using the conversion rates I supplied rather than any assumed benchmark, work out what the existing pipeline could realistically produce, and show the arithmetic so I can check it. Keep the renewal base separate from new business in your working rather than netting them together, because how renewals count toward quota depends on how my plan is structured. Then tell me how much new pipeline would be needed to close the remaining gap, and by when it would have to exist in order to close within the year.
activities.expectedOutput: A coverage calculation with the arithmetic shown, new business and renewal base kept separate, the remaining gap quantified, and the date by which new pipeline must exist.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller owns both the conversion rates and the treatment of renewals. Optimistic conversion produces a plan that looks covered and fails in the second half, and how renewals count toward attainment varies by plan rather than being a universal rule.
activities.requiredContext: Your quota for the year; current pipeline by stage with values; your renewal base; the conversion rates your team actually achieves at each stage; how renewals are treated in your own compensation plan.
activitySteps: 1. Gather your quota, your pipeline by stage with values, your renewal base, and the conversion rates your team actually achieves.
2. Paste all four into the prompt where it asks for them, then run it. Without your own conversion rates it will have nothing to calculate from.
3. Check the arithmetic yourself. This is the number you will be held to.
4. Check how renewals count toward your own quota before treating the renewal base as coverage; that varies by plan and the calculation deliberately keeps them separate.
5. Note the date by which new pipeline must exist, not the date it must close.
activities.whyThisMatters: A territory plan is a claim about where the number comes from. Most are never tested against arithmetic until a review tests them, which is the worst moment to find out.

activities.name: Find where the growth is most likely to come from
activities.description: Identify which accounts in your territory have the strongest evidence for growth, so coverage planning is based on signal rather than familiarity.
activities.prompt: Across my assigned accounts, help me find where new pipeline is most likely to come from. Consider consumption trending against commitment, workloads the customer owns but has not deployed, renewal timing, recent engagement levels, and any account where activity has increased without a corresponding opportunity. Rank by strength of evidence rather than account size, and tell me what the evidence actually is in each case. Flag accounts where I have no basis for a judgement either way.
activities.expectedOutput: Accounts ranked by evidenced growth potential with the evidence named, accounts lacking any basis flagged, and the top three matched to a specific play.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides which evidenced opportunity is realistic given their capacity. A ranked list that exceeds the hours in the year is not a plan, and the seller owns that trade-off.
activities.requiredContext: Your assigned account list; consumption and renewal data; your coverage gap from the previous practice.
activitySteps: 1. Run the prompt across your assigned accounts.
2. Compare the ranking against your own instinct, and take seriously anywhere they disagree.
3. Note the accounts flagged as having no basis for judgement. Those need research, not a forecast.
4. Pick the top three and name the specific play for each.
5. Check the total against the coverage gap you calculated. If it does not close, say so now.
activities.whyThisMatters: Territory planning defaults to the accounts you already know. The growth is often in the ones you have not looked at, and the evidence for that is usually already sitting in the data.

activities.name: Build the support ask you can actually defend
activities.description: Turn the coverage gap into a specific, evidenced request for the help you need, rather than a general statement that the number is hard.
activities.prompt: I have a coverage gap and I need to ask for support. Here is what I have: [paste your gap calculation, your ranked opportunities, what support you have already tried to get and what came back, and the specific resource or investment you think you need]. Using only what I have supplied, help me turn this into a request a manager could act on: state the ask precisely, tie it to the specific accounts and evidence, show what has already been attempted, and set out what changes if it is not provided. Flag any part of the ask my evidence does not support, and do not invent a consequence I have not described.
activities.expectedOutput: A support request naming the specific ask, the accounts and evidence behind it, what has already been attempted, and the consequence of not getting it, with unevidenced elements flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what consequence to state. Overstating what happens without support costs credibility in the next review, and the seller is the one who will be there for it.
activities.requiredContext: Your coverage gap; your ranked growth opportunities; what support you have already tried to secure and the response; the specific resource, specialist or investment you need.
activitySteps: 1. Gather your gap calculation, your ranked opportunities, what you have already tried, and the specific support you need.
2. Paste all four into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Cut anything you cannot evidence. An unevidenced ask weakens the parts that are real.
4. Check the consequence it states is one you would defend in a review.
5. Take it to your territory review or your manager rather than waiting to be asked.
activities.whyThisMatters: Support goes to the people who ask for something specific and evidenced. A general statement that the territory is difficult competes with everyone else saying the same thing.

activities.name: Stress-test the plan against the thing most likely to go wrong
activities.description: Find the single assumption your territory plan most depends on, and work out what happens if it does not hold.
activities.prompt: Here is my territory plan and coverage calculation: [paste your plan]. Identify the single assumption it most depends on, whether that is a renewal landing, one large opportunity closing, a conversion rate holding, or a consumption ramp continuing. Then tell me what happens to my coverage if that assumption fails, how early I would know, and what I could do now to reduce the dependency. Be direct about how concentrated the risk is.
activities.expectedOutput: The plan's most load-bearing assumption named, the coverage impact if it fails, the earliest warning signal, and a contingency to reduce the dependency.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides how much concentration is acceptable. Some territories are genuinely dependent on one renewal, and the judgement is whether that is a risk to manage or a plan to change.
activities.requiredContext: Your territory plan and coverage calculation; the largest single opportunities and renewals within it; the conversion assumptions you used.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your plan and coverage calculation.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Be honest about how much rests on one deal or one renewal.
4. Work out the earliest signal that the assumption is failing, and diarise a check.
5. Decide now what the contingency is, while there is still time to build one.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most territory plans fail on one assumption, not many. Knowing which one, and how early it would show, is the difference between adjusting in month three and explaining in month nine.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Your territory plan is a claim about where the number comes from. This session tests that claim against arithmetic, while there is still time to do something about the answer.
keyTalkingPoints: Fiscal year planning, quota acknowledgement and territory review are annual obligations, and territory reviews recur later in the year. The plan is what you will be held to, so it is worth being the person who finds its weakest assumption first.
discussionQuestions: Do you know, arithmetically, whether your pipeline covers your number?
What single deal or renewal is your year most dependent on?
What support would actually change your position, and have you asked for it specifically?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the coverage gap to the specific, evidenced support request each person will make.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the coverage gap and the specific support ask each person will make, to a named person, by a date.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your quota, your current pipeline by stage, and your renewal base. Bring real numbers; the exercise does not work on estimates.
facilitatorQuestions: What is your uncovered gap, and by when would new pipeline have to exist to close it?
Where is the growth evidence strongest, and does it match where you spend your time?
What is the one assumption your plan cannot survive without?
listenFor: Listen for optimistic conversion rates used to make a plan look covered, for growth ranked by familiarity rather than evidence, for concentration risk nobody has named, and for support asks phrased as a general complaint about difficulty.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If pipeline data is incomplete, run the arithmetic on what is known and treat the missing part as the first finding. An incomplete pipeline view is itself a planning problem.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did the arithmetic tell you that your instinct had not, and what changes because of it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take your coverage gap to your manager or territory review with a specific evidenced ask rather than a general concern.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the gap, the ask you made, who you made it to, and what came back.

WF-X-FYPLAN-01.keyTakeaway: Your territory plan is a claim about where the number will come from. It is worth the hour it takes to find out whether that claim survives contact with the arithmetic.

WF-X-CLOSE-01.roleTopicName: Land the Fiscal Year Without Damaging Next Year
WF-X-CLOSE-01.roleTopicDescription: Separate what is genuinely pinned to the fiscal calendar from what only feels urgent, and act on the part that is real while there is still time.
WF-X-CLOSE-01.wiifm: The costly year-end mistakes are a record nobody fixed in time and a deal that was forced early and discounted for no reason. Both are avoidable and both are decided now.
WF-X-CLOSE-01.name: Land the Fiscal Year and Protect What Books
WF-X-CLOSE-01.description: Work out what can still book before the fiscal year closes, get the records right before the systems stop accepting changes, and tell the difference between a real deadline and a self-imposed one.

WF-X-CLOSE-01.todayObjective: Establish what can still book this fiscal year, what has to be corrected before the systems close, and what should be left on its own clock.
WF-X-CLOSE-01.whyItMatters: Year end is where a deal that was always going to close in July gets pushed into June and damaged, while a record that could have been corrected in a day quietly misses the cutoff. Knowing which is which is most of the skill.
WF-X-CLOSE-01.desiredOutcome: A list of what can still book with the runway it needs, the records to correct before cutoff, and the deals you have deliberately left in the new year.

activities.name: Work out what can still realistically book this fiscal year
activities.description: Separate the deals that can still be fully executed and processed before the period ends from the ones that are already next year's.
activities.prompt: For [my patch, or a named account or TPID], list the opportunities with a close date in the current fiscal period. For each, tell me what the record shows about its approval state, what is still outstanding, whether it has been signed, and whether anything indicates it will arrive for processing after the guaranteed cutoff. Tell me first which of these you can actually see. Do not tell me whether it will book, because the rule that decides that is set by my own segment's bookings policy and you do not have it. Tell me what still has to happen for each deal to be capable of booking in the period.
activities.expectedOutput: Each in-period opportunity with its approval state, what is still outstanding, its signature position, any indication it will miss the processing cutoff, and what still has to happen for it to be capable of booking.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms the bookings rule locally and decides what is genuinely closeable. An approval state in the record is a snapshot, and only the person in the deal knows whether the customer will actually sign in time or is simply being polite about the date.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one account and its TPID; the opportunities you expect to close in the period; their current approval state; what each is waiting on; your Deal Desk or operations contact for the bookings rule that applies to your segment.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your own patch or one account, and the deals you believe are landing this period.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details, then run it.
3. Confirm the bookings rule that applies to your own segment with Deal Desk or operations rather than assuming it. What has to be true for a deal to book in a period, and by when, is set locally.
4. Separate deals waiting on Microsoft approvals from deals waiting on the customer. Only one of those is inside your control, and check the processing runway rather than only the signature date.
5. Decide which deals you are deliberately leaving in the new year, and say so out loud rather than carrying them as hope.
activities.whyThisMatters: Every year some deals get forced into June that were always going to close in July, and are discounted for the privilege. The deals worth pushing are the ones that only need a signature, not the ones that still need a decision.

activities.name: Find the renewals whose expiration timing will cost you the booking
activities.description: Identify renewals whose expiration date sits at the period boundary, where how they are handled decides whether they land in this year or the next.
activities.prompt: For [my patch, or a named account or TPID], list the renewals with expiration dates at or near the end of the current fiscal period. For each, tell me the actual expiration date, whether it has been committed as on-time, what is still outstanding to complete it, and what the record shows about customer engagement on it. Flag any renewal where the expiration falls on the final day of the period, since the booking and billing calendars treat that date differently and it needs handling deliberately rather than by default. Tell me what you cannot see rather than assuming it is fine.
activities.expectedOutput: Renewals at the period boundary with their actual expiration dates, commitment status, outstanding work and customer engagement, with last-day expirations flagged for deliberate handling.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms the processing runway with the person who owns it. Renewal processing has a real lead time and the deadline that matters is when the work has to arrive, not when the agreement expires.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one account and its TPID; renewals with expiration dates near the period end; their commitment status; your renewals or operations contact.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your patch or one account with renewals near the period boundary.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details, then run it.
3. Pay particular attention to anything expiring on the last day of the period. That is the case that behaves differently and gets missed.
4. Confirm the processing runway with your renewals or operations contact rather than assuming it.
5. Commit the ones that are genuinely on-time and stop describing the others as on-time.
activities.whyThisMatters: A renewal at the period boundary is the easiest booking to lose and the hardest to explain, because nothing about it looked at risk until it was.

activities.name: Correct the records that stop being correctable at close
activities.description: Find the records whose correction window closes with the fiscal year, and separate them from the hygiene items that are worth fixing but can be fixed at any time.
activities.prompt: For [my patch, or a named account or TPID], help me find records on my accounts that look wrong, and separate them into two groups. The first is detail that stops being correctable once the fiscal year closes: agreement, licensing and enrollment detail and the amounts tied to them. The second is pipeline hygiene, such as close dates already in the past, mis-categorised forecast or stale commitments, which is worth fixing but is not tied to the fiscal calendar. For each item, tell me what looks wrong, what the correct position appears to be, and what evidence you are basing that on. Tell me which of these you can actually see and which I would have to check somewhere else.
activities.expectedOutput: Records that appear incorrect, split into detail that stops being correctable at close and year-round hygiene, each with the apparent correct position and the evidence for it, and a separation of what you can correct yourself from what must be raised with another team.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller verifies the correct position against the agreement before changing anything. A confidently inferred correction is still a guess, and a wrong correction made in the last week of the year is materially harder to undo than a wrong original.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one account and its TPID; the agreements and amounts as actually agreed; your operations or Deal Desk contact for anything you cannot correct yourself.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your patch or one account.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details, then run it.
3. Do the first group first. The hygiene backlog will still be fixable in July; the agreement and licensing detail will not.
4. Confirm the correct position from the agreement or the customer, not from the model's inference.
5. Raise anything you cannot correct yourself with the owning team now rather than at the cutoff, when their queue is longest.
activities.whyThisMatters: Once the year closes, the agreement and licensing detail stops being editable and only limited fields remain open. The hygiene backlog will still be there in July. This group will not.

activities.name: Separate the real deadlines from the ones you have invented
activities.description: Sort your year-end pressure into work genuinely pinned to the fiscal calendar and work that belongs on the customer's own timeline.
activities.prompt: Here is everything I am treating as urgent because of year end: [paste the list, and for each say what I believe the deadline is and where that deadline comes from]. Sort it into two groups. The first is work genuinely pinned to the fiscal calendar, meaning it must happen before the period closes because a system, an approval chain or a booking rule requires it. The second is work I am pulling forward into this month even though the real driver is the customer's own decision, contract or delivery timeline. For anything in the second group, tell me what it would cost to force it early. Where I have not said where a deadline comes from, ask me rather than assuming there is one.
activities.expectedOutput: Your year-end work sorted into genuinely fiscal-dated and customer-dated, the cost of forcing each item that is being pulled forward, and an owner and date for the items that are genuinely fixed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what to force. Some work is worth pulling forward even at a cost, and that is a judgement about the customer relationship and the number, not one a model can make.
activities.requiredContext: Your own list of what you are treating as year-end urgent; where you believe each deadline comes from; the customer decision or contract timing behind each item.
activitySteps: 1. Write down everything you are treating as urgent because of year end, and where you think each deadline comes from.
2. Paste the list into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Be honest about the ones where the only deadline is that it is June.
4. For anything you are pulling forward, decide whether the cost of forcing it is worth it. Often it is; the point is to decide rather than to drift.
5. Take the genuinely fiscal-dated items and make sure each one has an owner and a date that is earlier than the cutoff.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most of what feels like a June deadline is a deal on its own clock being pulled forward. Doing that deliberately is fine. Doing it because the month feels urgent is how good deals get discounted and customers get pushed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Year end generates a lot of urgency and only some of it is real. This session separates the part that is genuinely fixed by the calendar from the part that only feels that way, and acts on the first while there is still room.
keyTalkingPoints: There is no single worldwide month-by-month year-end calendar for Enterprise sellers, and looking for one is why people end up inventing deadlines. What is genuinely fixed is the systems close: for the FY26 close, licensing and agreement detail had to be submitted by 26 June, all revenue had to reach MS Sales by close of business on 30 June, and the close publish landed on 2 July, after which only limited fields remain editable. Confirm this year's exact dates locally, because they shift by a few days. For a deal to book in a period it must be fully approved, final and fully executed before the end of the last day of that period, and it needs processing runway on top of that. Renewals expiring on the final day of a period are treated differently by the booking and billing calendars and need deliberate handling. Facilitator note: ECIF publishes its own detailed year-end milestone calendar, but the milestone quarter-end validation warning is documented for the Americas only, so do not present it as a worldwide rule.
discussionQuestions: Which of the things you are rushing right now would still be urgent if it were March?
What did you find out too late at the last year end?
Which deal did you pull forward last year, and what did it cost to do it?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the closeable list to the single record each person will correct and the single deal each person will deliberately release into the new year.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming, for each person, one record they will correct before cutoff and one thing they are deliberately not forcing into this period.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your own patch or one account, the deals and renewals you expect to land in this period, and a written list of everything you are currently treating as year-end urgent.
facilitatorQuestions: Which of your in-period deals is waiting on Microsoft, and which is waiting on the customer?
What could you correct today that stops being correctable after close?
Which of your urgent items has a deadline you could actually point to?
listenFor: Listen for signature dates being treated as booking dates with no processing runway, for renewals at the period boundary assumed to be fine, for corrections being deferred to the week when every queue is longest, and for deadlines whose only source is that it is June.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If someone carries no quota and no renewals, run the third practice only. The record-correction window applies to anyone who owns milestones or agreement detail, and it is the part most often left to somebody else.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which of your year-end deadlines turned out to have no source other than the month it is?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, correct one record that stops being correctable at close, and tell one customer or one internal owner that a deal you had been pushing is landing in the new year instead.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the record you corrected, the deal you released, and what happened when you said so.

WF-X-CLOSE-01.keyTakeaway: Almost nothing about June is a seller deadline. What is genuinely fixed is when the systems stop accepting changes, and that is the part most often discovered too late.

WF-X-SIGNAL-01.roleTopicName: Judge Which Engagement Signals Are Real
WF-X-SIGNAL-01.roleTopicDescription: Work the Highly Engaged and program signals in your solution area, separate genuine buying intent from activity, and route each one before the window closes.
WF-X-SIGNAL-01.wiifm: Engagement data tells you someone clicked, not that someone is buying. Being able to tell the difference quickly is most of the job.
WF-X-SIGNAL-01.name: Work the Signal Queue Before It Expires
WF-X-SIGNAL-01.description: Take an inbound queue of marketing signals and plan priorities, decide fast which ones are real, and act on them inside the window rather than after it.
WF-X-SIGNAL-01.todayObjective: Take the engagement signals in your solution area and decide, with evidence, which represent real intent and which do not.
WF-X-SIGNAL-01.whyItMatters: Signals arrive faster than anyone can work them, and the ones that expire do so silently. Whoever is deliberate about which signals they drop ends up ahead of whoever tries to work them all.

activities.name: Separate real buying intent from engagement activity
activities.description: Look at the engagement behind a signal and judge whether it indicates someone is buying or merely reading.
activities.prompt: Here is an engagement signal in my solution area: [paste the account, the signal type, and what engagement the record shows]. Help me judge whether this is buying intent or activity. Tell me what the engagement pattern actually supports, what would distinguish genuine evaluation from general interest, and what I would need to see to be confident either way. Be explicit about what you cannot tell from this data. Do not assume that more engagement means more intent.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on what the engagement pattern supports, what would distinguish evaluation from interest, and what evidence is still missing.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what the engagement means. Marketing engagement is a weak proxy for intent, and the specialist who knows the solution area is the only person who can judge whether this particular pattern is meaningful.
activities.requiredContext: One engagement signal in your solution area; the account and what it already owns; the engagement detail the record shows.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one engagement signal in your solution area, ideally one you are unsure about.
2. Paste the account, signal type and engagement into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Look for whether several people at the account engaged or only one. One person reading is not an evaluation.
4. Check whether the engagement matches something they already own or something new. Those mean different things.
5. Decide what you would need to see to be confident, and whether it is worth the time to find out.
activities.whyThisMatters: Engagement data tells you someone clicked. Treating it as intent is how specialists spend a week on an account that was never evaluating anything.

activities.name: Decide the route before the window closes
activities.description: Choose deliberately whether a signal is yours to pursue, belongs with a partner, or should be declined.
activities.prompt: I have to decide what to do with this signal before its window closes: [paste the signal, the account, what I have established about intent, and what capacity I have this week]. Help me choose between pursuing it myself, routing it to a partner, or declining it. For each route, tell me what makes it the right choice and what it costs. Take seriously that declining is a legitimate answer. Where the decision depends on something I have not told you, ask rather than assuming.
activities.expectedOutput: A recommendation across pursue, route to partner and decline, with what makes each right and what it costs, and the decision you have taken with its reason.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS owns the routing decision. Whether a partner is the right home depends on that partner's current capacity and relationship with the account, which is not in any system the agent can read.
activities.requiredContext: The signal and its account; what you have established about intent; your genuine capacity this week; which partners cover this solution area.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the signal you assessed in the previous practice.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, including your honest capacity this week, then run it.
3. Answer its questions rather than letting it guess at your capacity or partner coverage.
4. If routing to a partner, make the decision now rather than after you have half-worked it. A partner picking up a warm signal is very different from a partner inheriting a stalled one.
5. Record the decision and the reason, including for the ones you decline.
activities.whyThisMatters: The worst outcome for a signal is not being declined. It is being half-worked by someone who never decided whether they were working it.

activities.name: Open the conversation without revealing how you found them
activities.description: Prepare a first approach informed by the customer's likely situation, without referencing the internal engagement data that surfaced them.
activities.prompt: I am making first contact with a customer who surfaced through an internal engagement signal. Here is what I know: [paste the account, the solution area, and what I have established about their situation]. Prepare an opening built on their likely business situation and what companies like them are typically working through. Do NOT reference or allude to anything they viewed, clicked, downloaded or attended, and do not imply I know what they have been looking at - that information is internal and referencing it damages trust. Give me the question I should lead with, what I should not assume, and what would tell me quickly that this is not an evaluation after all. Keep it usable in a short call or message, and do not write me a pitch.
activities.expectedOutput: An opening grounded in the customer's likely business situation with no reference to internal engagement data, the assumptions to avoid, and what would show this is not a real evaluation.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS is accountable for what the customer hears. Internal engagement data is exactly that - internal - and an opening that reveals how closely someone has been tracked costs the relationship far more than the signal was ever worth.
activities.requiredContext: The account and its solution area; what you have established about their situation; a contact that exists in MSX if you intend to draft outreach.
activitySteps: 1. Take a signal you have decided to pursue.
2. Paste the account, solution area and situation into the prompt where it asks. Do not paste the engagement detail itself; you are not trying to reference it.
3. Read the opening back and check it does not hint at how you found them. If it would sound like surveillance to the customer, it is wrong regardless of how it was generated.
4. Check the opening question is genuinely open. If it can be answered yes or no, it will be.
5. Confirm the contact exists in MSX before relying on any drafting help, and note that outreach drafting in Sales Home is English only during preview.
activities.whyThisMatters: The signal tells you who to call. It does not give you anything you can say. Openings that leak how the seller found the customer are the fastest way to make a first conversation the last one.

activities.name: Read what the signals are telling you about your solution area
activities.description: Look back at recent signals in your solution area for what customers consistently react to, and what that says about where demand is forming.
activities.prompt: Here are the engagement signals in my solution area recently: [paste the list, with the topic or offer, the account profile, and whether each went anywhere]. Tell me what customers are consistently engaging with, which topics or offers generate engagement that goes nowhere, and whether the pattern differs by customer size or industry. Separate what this genuinely supports from what would be over-reading a small sample. I want to know where demand is actually forming, so be direct if the honest answer is that there is not enough here to say anything.
activities.expectedOutput: What customers consistently engage with, what generates engagement that does not convert, whether patterns hold across customer profiles, and an honest statement where the sample is too small.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS tests the pattern against real conversations. A pattern in engagement data can be an artefact of what marketing happened to send, and the specialist is the only one positioned to know the difference.
activities.requiredContext: Recent engagement signals in your solution area with topic, account profile and outcome; your own recollection of recent customer conversations to test findings against.
activitySteps: 1. Pull the recent signals in your solution area from Sales Accelerator or your own records.
2. Mark each as converted, still open, or went nowhere. The last group is the useful half.

activities.whyThisMatters: You see more signals in your solution area than anyone else does. What consistently fails to convert is intelligence nobody else in the territory can give.

activities.name: Watch for the engagement that turns into real intent
activities.description: Set a standing watch across your solution area so repeat engagement surfaces as it builds rather than after the window has closed.
activities.prompt: Watch engagement across the accounts in my solution area and tell me, on a schedule I set, where activity is repeating or building rather than one-off, where a signal has gone quiet after I responded, and where the same pattern is showing up across more than one account. Carry forward what you reported last time so I can see what built and what faded.
activities.expectedOutput: A standing watch across the solution area showing where engagement is building, where it went quiet after a response, and the patterns appearing across more than one account.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what repeat engagement means. Activity that repeats can be a buying signal or one person doing their research, and the difference is not in the count.
activities.requiredContext: The accounts in your solution area, access to the engagement signals for them, and the cadence you want to be told on.
activitySteps: 1. Set the cadence and the accounts in scope.
2. Say what repeat engagement looks like in your solution area.
3. Ask for what changed since the last check, not the full picture.
4. Review the first run before relying on it.
5. Use the cross-account patterns to decide where your solution area is actually landing.
activities.whyThisMatters: A pattern across several touches says something a single event does not, and watching for it by hand is the part that does not get done.
