facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Engagement data tells you someone clicked. This session is about telling the difference between that and someone buying, quickly enough to matter.
keyTalkingPoints: Highly Engaged and program signals carry a 5-day SLA and are yours to action, while Contact Me signals sit with the account executive. Engagement is a weak proxy for intent: several people engaging is a different thing from one person reading. Declining a signal is a legitimate outcome and is far better than half-working it. Facilitator note: Sales Home is in preview and enabled for individual contributors only, with English-only outreach drafting, so some of the room may be working in Sales Accelerator.
discussionQuestions: When did engagement data last mislead you into pursuing something that was never real?
What does genuine evaluation look like in your solution area, as opposed to interest?
How often do you decline a signal outright, and how does that feel?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the intent judgement to the routing decision each person will make and record before the window closes.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the routing decision each person has taken and the reason, including for anything they are declining.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one Highly Engaged or program signal in your solution area that you are genuinely unsure about.
facilitatorQuestions: What in this engagement pattern would you actually bet on?
Is this one person reading or several people evaluating?
If you route this to a partner, what are you handing them?
listenFor: Listen for volume of engagement being read as strength of intent, for signals being carried rather than routed or declined, for partner routing decided after the signal has gone cold, and for openings built on how closely the customer has been tracked.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live signal, use one that was pursued and went nowhere, and work backwards to what in the engagement should have been the warning.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you believe the engagement meant before you looked at it properly?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one engagement signal, decide whether it is real, route or decline it, and record why.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the signal, what you judged, what you decided, and whether the outcome supported your read.

WF-X-SIGNAL-01.keyTakeaway: A signal is an unqualified lead with a clock on it. The skill is deciding quickly which ones deserve your time, not working all of them equally.

WF-X-PARTNER-01.roleTopicName: Keep Pinned-Partner Deals Moving Between Stages
WF-X-PARTNER-01.roleTopicDescription: Track where your pinned-partner deals actually sit across the co-sell stages, find the ones that have stopped moving, and use the partner rhythm to unblock them.
WF-X-PARTNER-01.wiifm: Partner deals stall between stages rather than failing outright, and nobody raises it because it is nobody's obvious job. It is yours.
WF-X-PARTNER-01.name: Hand Work to a Partner and Keep It Moving
WF-X-PARTNER-01.description: Decide what genuinely belongs with a partner, hand it over with enough for them to act, and stay on it through the acceptance and conversion windows rather than assuming it landed.
WF-X-PARTNER-01.todayObjective: Establish where your pinned-partner deals are stuck and take one of them into the next partner conversation with a specific ask.
WF-X-PARTNER-01.whyItMatters: Partner-led is structural in this segment rather than optional help, which means referrals that quietly expire are lost coverage you chose to give away. The difference between a partner motion that works and one that does not is almost entirely about what happens after the handoff.
WF-X-PARTNER-01.desiredOutcome: A stage-by-stage read on your pinned-partner deals, the stalled ones identified with a likely cause, and one specific ask prepared for the partner.

activities.name: See where your pinned-partner deals actually sit
activities.description: Build a stage-by-stage picture of the partner deals you track, and find where the picture and the evidence disagree.
activities.prompt: Here are the pinned-partner deals I track: [paste the list from Partner Center, with the co-sell stage of each, when it last moved, and what the partner last reported]. The co-sell stages run Created and Accepted at 10 percent, Qualified at 20, Developed at 40, Proposed at 60, Negotiated at 80 and Won at 100. For each deal, tell me what the stage claims is true and what would need to be true for that stage to be genuine. Identify deals whose stage has not moved for a long time relative to the others, and deals where the reported stage looks ahead of what the partner has actually described. Do not assume a stage is accurate because it is recorded.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on each deal covering what its stage claims, what would make that stage genuine, which have not moved, and which look stage-inflated.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS judges whether a stage is real. Partners set their own stages and have every reason to be optimistic, and the specialist who knows the deal is the only one who can tell an advancing deal from an advancing number.
activities.requiredContext: Your pinned-partner deals and their current co-sell stage from Partner Center; when each last moved; what the partner last reported; your partner meeting cadence.
activitySteps: 1. Open Partner Center and pull the current stage of each pinned-partner deal you track. The agent cannot see Partner Center, so this list has to come from you.
2. Paste it into the prompt where it asks, with when each last moved, then run it.
3. Look for stages that are ahead of what the partner has actually described. Optimistic stage-setting is the most common distortion.
4. Pick the deal with the longest gap since it last moved.
5. Take that one into your next partner meeting rather than raising all of them at once.
activities.whyThisMatters: Partner deals rarely fail loudly. They sit at a stage that looks respectable while nothing underneath it moves, and nobody asks because the number is not obviously wrong.

activities.name: Work out what is actually blocking the stalled one
activities.description: Establish why a partner deal has stopped between stages and who is genuinely able to move it.
activities.prompt: A pinned-partner deal has stopped moving between stages. Here is what I know: [paste the deal, its current stage, how long it has been there, what the partner has told me, and anything I know from the customer side]. Help me work out what is most likely blocking it: partner capacity or skills, a customer-side decision, a technical dependency, a commercial or licensing issue, or the partner deprioritising it. For each possibility, tell me what evidence would confirm or rule it out, and which role would own it - partner seller, partner development manager, the account executive, or me. Name the role rather than a person, since you cannot know the individuals. Do not guess at a cause the evidence does not support.
activities.expectedOutput: Ranked likely causes with the evidence that would confirm each, the owning role for each, and the cause you have chosen to act on.

activitySteps: 1. Take the deal with the longest gap from the previous practice.

activities.name: Prepare the partner conversation with one specific ask
activities.description: Turn a stalled deal into a partner conversation that produces a commitment rather than an update.
activities.prompt: I am taking a stalled deal into a conversation with the partner. Here is the situation: [paste the deal, its stage, what I believe is blocking it, and what I am able to offer to help]. Help me prepare the conversation: how to raise it as a shared problem rather than an inspection, the one specific thing I am asking them to commit to, what I will do in return, and how we will both know within a short period whether it moved. Do not invent support or resources I have not told you I can offer. Keep it to a single ask; a conversation with four asks produces none.
activities.expectedOutput: A conversation plan framing the stall as a shared problem, with one specific ask, what you will do in return, and how both sides will know shortly whether it moved.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides how hard to push. Partners choose where to put their capacity, and a conversation that feels like an audit moves this deal at the cost of the next five.
activities.requiredContext: The stalled deal and its stage; what you believe is blocking it; what you are genuinely able to offer; your partner meeting or deal clinic cadence.
activitySteps: 1. Take the stalled deal and its likely cause.
2. Decide what you can genuinely offer before you run anything, and include it. If you do not, it will invent something you cannot deliver.
3. Paste the situation into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Cut it down to one ask. This is the step people skip and it is the one that decides whether anything happens.
5. Raise it in the deal clinic or partner rhythm rather than as a separate escalation, so it lands as working the deal rather than checking up on them.
activities.whyThisMatters: Partner conversations default to status updates, which change nothing. A single specific ask with something offered in return is what turns a rhythm into progress.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Work out what is actually blocking the stalled one

activities.name: Look at where your recent deals stopped
activities.description: Take a small number of recent partner deals and check whether they stopped at the same stage.
activities.prompt: Here are a few partner deals I have tracked recently and what happened to each: [paste up to five, with the partner, the stage each reached, and whether it progressed or stalled]. Looking only at these, tell me whether they stopped at a similar stage and what is different about any that got through. Be explicit that this is too small a set to establish a pattern, and tell me what I would need to see to know whether it is real. Give me one thing worth watching for rather than a conclusion.
activities.expectedOutput: Whether the small set stopped at a similar stage, what differs about any that progressed, an explicit caveat about sample size, and one thing worth watching for.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides whether a repeated stage is a real bottleneck. It may equally be the stage where optimistic early staging finally meets reality, and telling those apart needs someone who saw the deals.
activities.requiredContext: Up to five recent partner deals with the partner, the stage reached and the outcome; your partner rhythm or deal clinic.
activitySteps: 1. Bring up to five recent partner deals from Partner Center. The agent cannot see Partner Center, so this comes from you.
2. Note the partner, the stage reached and the outcome for each.
3. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Treat any apparent stage boundary as something to watch for, not as a finding. Five deals cannot tell you where your portfolio stalls.
5. If it does keep recurring, raise it in your partner rhythm as something to look at earlier, not as a scorecard.
activities.whyThisMatters: Chasing individual stalled deals is endless. Noticing that several stopped at the same point is what turns it into something you can change upstream.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Partner deals rarely fail loudly. They sit at a respectable stage while nothing underneath them moves, and nobody asks because the number does not look wrong.
keyTalkingPoints: The co-sell stages run Created and Accepted at 10 percent, Qualified at 20, Developed at 40, Proposed at 60, Negotiated at 80 and Won at 100. Partners set their own stages and have every reason to be optimistic, so a stage is a claim rather than evidence. Your accountability is visibility and Stage 2 to 3 acceleration rather than execution ownership; the partner owns delivery in the later stages and partner performance issues belong with the partner development manager. Facilitator note: Partner Center is a separate system from MSX, so the agent cannot read it - sellers must bring their own stage data into the session.
discussionQuestions: Which of your partner deals would you actually bet on at the stage it claims?
Where do your deals most often stop moving?
When did you last ask a partner for a specific commitment rather than an update?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the stage review to the one stalled deal each person will take into their next partner conversation with a specific ask.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the deal each person will raise, the single ask they will make, and what they are offering in return.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: pull the current co-sell stage of your pinned-partner deals from Partner Center, with when each last moved.
facilitatorQuestions: Which stage is ahead of what the partner has actually described?
What is genuinely blocking the one that stopped?
What is the single thing you would ask this partner to commit to?
listenFor: Listen for recorded stages treated as evidence, for causes assumed rather than confirmed, for partner performance problems being worked one deal at a time instead of raised with the PDM, and for conversations planned with several asks and therefore no ask.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If Partner Center data is not to hand, work from what each partner last told you and treat the missing data as the first thing to fix.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which deal turned out to be stalled for a different reason than the one you had been assuming?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one stalled partner deal into a partner conversation with a single specific ask and something offered in return.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the deal, the ask you made, what the partner committed to, and whether the stage moved.

WF-X-PARTNER-01.keyTakeaway: Handing something to a partner is not the end of your involvement. The windows run whether or not anyone is watching them, and the system closes the lead for you if nobody acts.

WF-X-TERRITORY-01.roleTopicName: Decide Who Is Actually Covering Each Account
WF-X-TERRITORY-01.roleTopicDescription: Segment a territory you cannot work account by account into what you cover, what a partner covers and what nobody covers, then take the uncovered part into the joint plan instead of leaving it to chance.
WF-X-TERRITORY-01.wiifm: The accounts that lapse are almost never the ones you decided to drop. They are the ones that were never on anybody's list, and you find out at renewal.
WF-X-TERRITORY-01.name: Plan the Territory With the Partners Who Cover It
WF-X-TERRITORY-01.description: Decide who is genuinely covering which accounts across a territory far larger than one person can work, and build that decision into a joint plan with the partners who cover the rest.
WF-X-TERRITORY-01.todayObjective: Produce an honest coverage read on your territory and name the accounts currently covered by nobody.
WF-X-TERRITORY-01.whyItMatters: A territory of roughly fifty accounts cannot be covered account by account, so most of it is covered by partners or not at all. The plan is where that becomes deliberate. Left implicit, the accounts that get worked are the ones that shout, and the ones that quietly lapse were never assigned to anybody.
WF-X-TERRITORY-01.desiredOutcome: A territory segmented by actual coverage, the uncovered accounts named, and one of them either taken on or deliberately routed to a partner.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Home
primaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Split the territory into covered, partner-covered and neither
activities.description: Produce an honest three-way coverage read across the whole territory rather than a list of the accounts already front of mind.
activities.prompt: List every account in my territory and group them three ways: accounts where I have had direct activity recorded this quarter, accounts with an open partner referral or co-sell opportunity of any status, and accounts with neither. For the second group, show the referral or co-sell record and whatever status field it currently carries, without interpreting what that status means. For the third group, show the account name, its segment, any open opportunity, and the date of the most recent recorded activity of any kind.
activities.expectedOutput: A three-way coverage read across the full territory with the uncovered accounts named and counted, not estimated.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DAE decides what counts as coverage, and confirms partner acceptance in the Partner Timeline before counting an account as covered. The agent can see that a referral exists but not whether a partner picked it up, and an unaccepted referral is an account you have told yourself is handled.
activities.requiredContext: Your assigned territory in MSX. Your open partner referrals and their acceptance status from the Partner Timeline view.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Replace nothing - it runs against the territory already assigned to you in MSX.
3. Read the third group first and count it.
4. For every account in the second group, open the Partner Timeline view on the plan priority and confirm whether the referral was actually accepted. A sent referral is not coverage.
5. Move anything not accepted into your uncovered count.
6. Note the accounts where the most recent activity date surprises you.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most territory reads start from the accounts already in mind, which is exactly the set that is already covered. Starting from the whole list is what surfaces the accounts nobody has touched.

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

agents.name: Sales Home
agents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
agents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Test the plan priorities that were assigned to you
activities.description: Work the preloaded plan priorities against their window and decide which ones genuinely fit the territory rather than working them in the order they arrived.
activities.prompt: Show my open plan priorities with the date each was created, the account it sits against, and any recorded activity on that account since. For each, state what the priority is asking me to do and whether anything in the account record suggests it is already underway, already lost, or still untouched. Flag any where the account has had no activity at all.
activities.expectedOutput: Plan priorities sorted by remaining window with an explicit worked-or-declined decision recorded against each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DAE decides which priorities are worth the window. A priority that was generated for you is not evidence that the account is ready, and declining one deliberately is a legitimate answer that a priority left to expire silently is not.
activities.requiredContext: Your open plan priorities in MSX Plans, with their creation dates.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Check each priority against the fourteen-day window from its creation date.
3. Separate the ones that fit your territory strategy from the ones that arrived because a model scored them.
4. Decide explicitly which ones you are not going to work, and record the reason.
5. Take the one closest to expiring into an action today.
activities.whyThisMatters: Preloaded priorities carry a fourteen-day SLA and expire whether or not anyone looked. A declined priority and an ignored one are identical in the data and completely different in practice.

activities.name: Prepare the uncovered accounts for a partner conversation
activities.description: Turn the uncovered part of the territory into something a partner can act on, inside the rules that govern what may be shared.
activities.prompt: For these accounts [paste the uncovered accounts from your coverage read], summarize what would help a partner decide whether to take them on: industry, size band, the workloads already in place, any open opportunity and its stage, and the reason the account is uncovered. Write it as a briefing for someone outside Microsoft. Do not include contact names, contact details, seat counts, spend figures or anything that reads as an export from our systems.
activities.expectedOutput: A partner-ready briefing on the uncovered accounts with the data-sharing boundary respected before anything leaves Microsoft.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DAE owns what crosses the boundary to a partner and checks the output against the CELA rules before the conversation, not after. A model asked for a helpful summary will include contact and commercial detail because it is helpful, and the sender is the only control on that.
activities.requiredContext: Your uncovered accounts from the coverage read. The CELA rules on what may be exchanged with a partner.
activitySteps: 1. Take the uncovered accounts from your coverage read._x000D_
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [paste the uncovered accounts from your coverage read] with your actual list._x000D_
3. Read the output specifically for anything CELA rules exclude: personal data, seat-level or financial detail, or anything that looks like a screenshot or export._x000D_
4. Remove anything that crosses that line before the partner conversation._x000D_
5. Decide which accounts you are genuinely offering rather than offering everything at once.
activities.whyThisMatters: Partner-led coverage is structural in this segment, so the uncovered part of the territory is usually a partner conversation rather than a personal to-do list. The constraint is that partner exchange is governed.

activities.name: Build the coverage position you will defend at Territory Health
activities.description: Prepare the coverage argument for the bi-weekly review, including the part that does not look good.
activities.prompt: Using my coverage read, draft the position I will take into a territory health review: how many accounts I am working directly, how many sit with a partner and are confirmed accepted, how many are covered by neither, and what I am doing about the third group. State plainly where the coverage is thin. Identify the two questions a manager is most likely to ask about this position and what evidence would answer them.
activities.expectedOutput: A defensible coverage position with the thin areas surfaced deliberately and a specific support ask attached.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DAE decides which gap to raise first. Bringing your own worst number to a review is a judgement about credibility that pays off over quarters, and no analysis can make that call for you.
activities.requiredContext: Your completed coverage read. The territory health review cadence for your pod.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Check the numbers against your own coverage read rather than accepting them.
3. Decide which gap you are going to raise yourself rather than waiting to be asked.
4. Prepare the specific support ask that follows from it.
activities.whyThisMatters: The bi-weekly territory health review runs with the full v-team present. The coverage position is going to be discussed whether or not you prepared it.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A territory of roughly fifty accounts cannot be worked account by account, which means most of it is covered by a partner or by nobody. This session is about finding out which.
keyTalkingPoints: The territory plan is the primary planning construct in this segment, and individual account plans still sit underneath it for Unified and MACC customers. Territory Planning in MSX Plans is shipped and operational, and Partner Center is the partner-facing surface alongside it. Preloaded plan priorities carry a fourteen-day SLA, with an FY27 target of at least eighty-five percent of TPP and Sales Accelerator signals actioned. Facilitator note: coverage model is a property of the account rather than of the seller, so a single territory will usually span Unified, non-Unified and partner-led accounts at the same time.
discussionQuestions: How many accounts are in your territory, and how many did you touch last quarter?
Of the ones you did not touch, how many is a partner genuinely working?
Who would notice if one of your accounts stopped being covered by anyone?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the coverage read to the specific uncovered accounts, then to what each person will do about one of them.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person name the number of accounts they believe are covered by nobody, and one they are going to act on.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: open your territory in MSX Plans and bring your account list, including the accounts you have not touched this quarter.
facilitatorQuestions: Which accounts in your territory are you genuinely working, and which are you assuming somebody else has?
What evidence do you have that the partner is actually working the ones you handed over?
Which account would you be most embarrassed to discover nobody has contacted?
listenFor: Listen for coverage assumed from a referral being sent rather than accepted, for partner coverage claimed without evidence from the Partner Timeline, for territory reads built from memory rather than from the plan, and for the uncovered set being described as small without anyone having counted it.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If someone cannot reach MSX Plans, have them work from their account list and reconstruct the coverage read from what they know, which usually exposes the gap faster anyway.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which account did you assume was covered until you looked?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, produce a coverage read on your full territory and take one uncovered account either onto your own list or into a partner conversation.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the count of uncovered accounts you found and what you did with one of them.

WF-X-TERRITORY-01.keyTakeaway: Coverage is a decision whether or not you make it. An account nobody named is an account nobody is working.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Satisfaction is decided during the delivery, not at the survey. Today is about reading it early enough to act.
keyTalkingPoints: The customer already knows how they feel. The survey only tells us.
Responsiveness, clarity and expectation-setting move scores as much as technical outcomes do.
A satisfaction risk you cannot evidence is a feeling. Name what you saw.
discussionQuestions: Where in a current delivery would the customer say we are harder to work with than we need to be?
Which satisfaction signal have you noticed and not acted on?
What would this customer say if they were asked today rather than at the end?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the general idea of satisfaction to one live delivery and the specific moment that would show up in the score.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one satisfaction risk, the evidence behind it, and the action you will take before the delivery closes.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live delivery, any customer feedback or escalation on it, and the moment you would least like the customer to remember.
facilitatorQuestions: Which delivery are you least confident about, and what is the evidence rather than the feeling?
What would the customer say we did slowly or explained badly?
Which satisfaction risk is yours to fix and which belongs to another role?
listenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: satisfaction inferred from the absence of complaints; technical success treated as the whole of the customer experience; risks named without a specific moment behind them; and anything the CSA plans to absorb that belongs to the CSAM or to delivery.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized delivery. Do not speculate about individual customer contacts or attribute dissatisfaction to named people.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Take one live delivery, name the satisfaction risk you would least like to see in the survey, and act on it this week.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the risk you named and what changed after you acted.

WF-X-VSAT-01.keyTakeaway: Satisfaction is decided long before the survey. The signals are there during delivery if you go looking for them.

facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the technical gap you are closing, why this customer makes it urgent, and the first step.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one customer, what you know of their technical direction, and one question you were recently unable to answer.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the next technical decision this customer faces, and could you hold that conversation today?
Which gap is real and which is imagined?
What is the smallest step that would make you credible on it?

facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized customer. Keep the focus on technical direction rather than commercial detail.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.

activities.name: Look for the proof before you build one
activities.description: Check whether you or a colleague have already proven this, at a customer with a comparable estate.
activities.prompt: I need to prove [describe what the customer doubts] for a customer running [describe their estate]. Across the opportunities in my patch, show me any where a similar workload or configuration was involved, what stage they reached, and any recorded notes, objections or outcomes. activities.expectedOutput: Comparable prior work identified with an honest read on whether it transfers, or a clear statement that this proof is genuinely new.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE judges whether a prior proof actually transfers. Two customers on the same product can differ in the one respect the proof depended on, and a borrowed proof that quietly does not apply is worse than building a new one, because nobody re-examines it.
activities.requiredContext: The technical doubt to be settled, and the customer's environment as you understand it.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Look for the closest environment rather than the closest product name.
3. If something transfers, find out who ran it before rebuilding it.
4. If nothing transfers, you now know why this one is genuinely new.
activities.whyThisMatters: A bespoke proof for every customer does not survive the customer count in this segment. Reuse is the constraint that makes the job possible, and it only works if somebody looks first.

activities.name: Cut your proof down before you build it
activities.description: State the proof you are considering, then test it against what comparable customers actually needed.
activities.prompt: A customer at [account name] is unsure about [describe the doubt]. I am considering this proof: [describe the proof you have in mind]. Across the opportunities in my patch, show me any where a similar doubt or objection was recorded, what was proposed, what stage the opportunity reached, and any note about what convinced the customer. Do not design a proof or judge whether mine is the right size.
activities.expectedOutput: Your proposed proof tested against what comparable customers actually needed, cut to the smallest sufficient version with exclusions stated.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what the customer is really doubting, which is frequently not what they asked to see. A request for a pilot is often a request for reassurance about operational effort, and building the pilot answers a question nobody had while leaving the real one open.
activities.requiredContext: The customer, what they are unsure about, and the proof you are considering including its exclusions.
activitySteps: 1. Write down the proof you have in mind first, including what it will not cover. That scoping is yours.
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace all three bracketed sections.
3. Look at what actually convinced comparable customers. It is frequently smaller than what was offered.
4. Cut yours to the smallest version that still settles the doubt, and write down explicitly what it excludes.
5. Get the customer to agree that this settles it, before you build anything.
activities.whyThisMatters: Proof work expands to fill whatever time it is given, and at this customer count that time comes straight out of another customer. What convinced somebody comparable is the cheapest available check on your own scoping.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Look for the proof before you build one

activities.name: Leave it in a state the next engineer can use
activities.description: Spend the extra hour that makes this proof reusable, rather than rebuilding it from memory next quarter.
activities.prompt: I have built a proof demonstrating [describe what it shows] for a customer running [describe the environment]. Help me write it up so another engineer could reuse it: what it demonstrates, what environment it assumes, what it deliberately does not cover, what would have to change for a different customer, and what someone should check before reusing it. Write it for an engineer who was not involved. Do not include the customer name, contact details, or anything identifying them.
activities.expectedOutput: A reuse note covering what the proof shows, what it assumes, what it excludes, and what to check before reusing it, with the customer anonymized.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE states what the proof deliberately does not cover. A reuse note that lists only capabilities gets applied to a situation it was never valid for, and the engineer who inherits the failure will not know which assumption broke.
activities.requiredContext: The proof you built, what it demonstrates, and the environment it assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the assumptions section as somebody who was not there. Anything implicit will be missed.
3. Remove anything identifying the customer.
4. Put it where your colleagues will actually find it, and tell the ones covering similar estates.
activities.whyThisMatters: Reuse only works if somebody wrote down the limits. The capabilities are obvious from the artifact; the boundaries exist only in the head of whoever built it.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Building a bespoke proof for every customer does not survive contact with this many customers. This session is about proving the point with less.
keyTalkingPoints: Enterprise engineers can afford a tailored proof per pursuit; at this customer count that arithmetic does not work, so reuse is the constraint rather than a nice-to-have. A partner may be able to run the proof instead, which is covered separately in the design session. What matters here is deciding the smallest thing that would actually settle the customer's doubt. Facilitator note: the most common failure is building a technically impressive proof of something the customer was never doubting.
discussionQuestions: How long does a proof take you, and how many can you run at once?
When did you last build something that already existed?
What was the customer actually unsure about?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the decision in doubt to what each person will reuse or scope.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming what each person is reusing rather than building.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one customer asking for a demo, pilot or proof.
facilitatorQuestions: What decision is this proof supposed to settle?
Does something already exist that would settle it?
What is the smallest version that would still be convincing?
listenFor: Listen for proofs scoped to what is interesting to build rather than to what is in doubt, for reuse dismissed without looking, for success criteria that were never agreed with the customer, and for effort that exceeds the value of the deal.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live request, use the last proof that was built and work out what the smallest sufficient version would have been.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you build that you could have borrowed?

bringBackEvidence: Bring what you found already existing, and what you still had to build.

AE-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand how the AE huddle path runs and where the human checkpoints protect account, deal, and forecast judgment.
AE-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
AE-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: AEs know how the huddle motion works, which tools may show up, what to review, and what AI experiences to bring back before next week.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This session sets the operating model for the AE path. The point is not tool fluency for its own sake; it is better account, pipeline, deal, and customer-conversation execution with human judgment visible.
keyTalkingPoints: The huddle is workflow-first. Every session uses real AE work, a practical AI-supported practice, and a human checkpoint. AI can assemble evidence, summarize, draft, and monitor; the AE owns judgment, customer trust, commitments, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted account, pipeline, or customer-facing output?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the workflow-discovery prompt below. Week 1 is for finding the recurring work worth automating.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the tools named for this path, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
facilitatorQuestions: Which account, pipeline, or customer-facing work do you repeat every week without thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where must the AE judgment stay human no matter how good the output gets?
listenFor: Listen for unvoiced scepticism, access blockers stated as disinterest, the assumption that this is a tool rollout, and people who describe only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat. The recurring, unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the discovery conversation and record access blockers separately from interest. The discovery prompt can be run in whichever tool the person already has.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

"I am an Account Executive at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with."
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation, or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

AE-ORIENT.keyTakeaway: The point of the motion is better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

activities.name: Build or assess the account plan with approval gates
activities.description: Use a reusable planning skill to propose account-plan updates while keeping every write or commitment AE-approved.
activities.prompt: For [Account] and [TPID], assess the current account plan, research evidence gaps, propose additive updates to priorities, stakeholders, opportunities, and next actions, and require approval before any MSX write.
activities.expectedOutput: Account-plan assessment with proposed updates, evidence gaps, and explicit approval/rejection decisions.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE approves or rejects each proposed change and confirms nothing is written or committed without review.
activities.requiredContext: The account and its TPID; the current account plan; your authority to approve or reject an MSX write.
activitySteps: 1. Open Scout and start the account plan skill.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Supply the account and TPID.
4. Review the proposed additions against your own knowledge.
5. Approve or reject each proposed MSX write.
6. Confirm nothing was written without your approval.
activities.whyThisMatters: Account planning becomes usable when it creates next actions, not just more content.

activities.name: Pressure-test the account priority list
activities.description: Challenge whether your account priorities are driven by evidence or by habit and familiarity.
activities.prompt: Review my account priority list. For each of the top accounts, state the evidence behind the priority and whether it reflects a current signal or a standing assumption. Identify the account most likely to be wrongly prioritized, the account most likely to be wrongly ignored, and what would confirm either.
activities.expectedOutput: A priority challenge showing evidence per account, plus the most likely over-prioritized and under-prioritized account.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides which account is genuinely mis-prioritized. A model sees only the signals that were recorded, and the account most often wrongly ignored is the one whose activity happens off-system.
activities.requiredContext: The prioritized account list; the source signal behind each priority; the accounts you have not touched recently.
activities.whyThisMatters: If the decision path for Prioritize Accounts and Build an Actionable Account Plan is going to fail, it should fail here rather than in front of the customer.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Account planning fails when it becomes an inventory. Today is about a short operating plan that helps you decide where attention goes this week.
keyTalkingPoints: Prioritization requires saying no. AI can assemble customer, pipeline, renewal, whitespace, partner, and investment signals. The AE decides which account deserves action and why.
discussionQuestions: Which accounts get your attention by habit rather than evidence? Where is the account plan missing a decision? What signal would change your priority list?
suggestedTransitions: Move from account list discussion to one AE selecting a top account and naming the next action.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the top accounts you will act on and the evidence behind the priority.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one territory or account list and one account where the next action is unclear.
facilitatorQuestions: Which account deserves attention that it is not getting? Which account gets attention mostly by habit? What evidence would change your top three?
listenFor: Listen for planning as annual documentation, prioritization by revenue alone, unclear next actions, missing role coverage, and customer priorities not connected to pipeline.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tools are unavailable, run the prioritization manually and record the prompt or Scout/Cowork skill candidate for later.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Use AI to build or refine one account priority view, then choose one next action you will actually take.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the prioritized account list, source signals, the action chosen, and any assumptions you rejected.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Keep pipeline hygiene current between reviews
activities.description: Stand up a recurring sweep of your owned pipeline so hygiene problems surface on a schedule instead of the night before a review.
activities.prompt: Check my owned pipeline on a recurring basis and report only what has changed since the last run. Flag opportunities with a close date in the past, no activity in the last 30 days, a missing or generic next step, or a stage that has not moved while the close date has. For each one, draft the specific update or question I would need to resolve it. Rank by revenue at risk within the current period. Do not change any record - produce a review list for me to action.
activities.expectedOutput: A recurring change-only hygiene list ranked by revenue at risk, with a drafted resolution for each flagged opportunity.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE confirms each flagged item is genuinely stale before updating, and makes every record change themselves rather than delegating the write.
activities.requiredContext: Access to your owned pipeline; your current period close dates; your team's definition of a healthy next step.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm your team's definition of a healthy next step so the check flags the right things.
2. Run the prompt against your owned pipeline.
3. Review the first list and confirm each flagged opportunity is genuinely stale rather than deliberately paused.
4. Set the cadence to land before your pipeline review, not after it.
5. Make every record change yourself; do not let the check write to MSX.
activities.whyThisMatters: Pipeline hygiene fails because it is a periodic scramble rather than a standing habit. A recurring check that reports only what changed turns a two-hour clean-up into a five-minute review.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about restoring trust in the pipeline signal before it becomes a forecast argument.
keyTalkingPoints: Bad data creates bad inspection. Stage, close date, next step, customer engagement, and partner attach should reflect reality. AI can flag issues; the AE verifies and decides the correction.
discussionQuestions: Where does your pipeline data most often mislead you? Which field do you trust least? Which opportunity would you hesitate to defend in a review?
suggestedTransitions: Move from aggregate gap to one opportunity that needs correction or verification.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one opportunity record to correct, verify, or escalate for missing evidence.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring the scope you normally inspect for pipeline reviews and one opportunity you suspect may be stale or misrepresented.
facilitatorQuestions: Which opportunity would you not want inspected right now? What field, date, or next step might be telling the wrong story? What correction would change the forecast conversation?
listenFor: Listen for manual reconciliation, stale dates, close-date optimism, missing customer engagement, and records corrected only right before reviews.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If certified reports are unavailable, map the inspection routine and identify where evidence should come from.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Run one pipeline signal-quality check and correct or flag one material issue.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the before/after record state or issue list, the source signal, and the decision you made as the owner.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A forecast narrative explains what changed, what is at risk, and what decision is needed. Today is about building that story from evidence.
keyTalkingPoints: The number alone does not create confidence. Movement, risk, timing, and inspection questions need to be visible. AI can draft the story, but the AE owns the commitment and caveats.
discussionQuestions: What changed since the last review? Which commit has the weakest evidence? What question from your manager would be hardest to answer?
suggestedTransitions: Move from report output to the narrative the AE would actually use in a forecast review.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one forecast risk and the inspection question that will resolve it.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring the current forecast scope and the report or meeting notes you use for weekly inspection.
facilitatorQuestions: What changed since last week? Which commit carries the most risk? What would your manager ask that the current narrative cannot answer?
listenFor: Listen for forecast narrative built from memory, risk without evidence, unclear inspection questions, and confusion between confidence and wishful thinking.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If data access is unavailable, build the narrative structure and mark which claims need certified data.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Draft one forecast narrative for your scope and use it in your next inspection or manager discussion.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the narrative, supporting metrics, unresolved questions, and what you changed after human review.

activities.name: Pressure-test the opportunity hypotheses
activities.description: Separate the opportunity signals that are genuinely evidenced from the ones that reflect optimism.
activities.prompt: Review my opportunity hypotheses. For each, state the trigger event, the evidence it rests on, and whether a customer has actually indicated intent or the intent is inferred. Identify which would create duplicate or unsupported pipeline, and what one piece of evidence would qualify or kill each.
activities.expectedOutput: A qualification challenge per hypothesis, with evidence status, duplication risk, and the single test that would qualify or kill it.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides whether the customer has actually indicated intent or the intent is inferred. Building pipeline from an inferred signal is how forecast credibility is lost, and the distinction is usually visible only to whoever had the conversation.
activities.requiredContext: The opportunity hypotheses; the trigger and evidence behind each; your existing pipeline so you can spot duplication.
activities.whyThisMatters: If the decision path for Create and Qualify New Opportunities is going to fail, it should fail here rather than in front of the customer.

activities.name: Watch your accounts for buying signals worth acting on
activities.description: Set up a standing watch across your account list so external and internal signals reach you while they are still actionable.
activities.prompt: Set up a recurring watch across my named accounts. Each week, surface publicly reported changes - leadership moves, earnings commentary, announced initiatives, regulatory or funding events - alongside internal signals such as new support volume, usage shifts, or newly opened engagements. For each signal, state what it plausibly implies for a Microsoft opportunity and what would have to be true for that to hold. Separate what is evidenced from what is inference, and cite the source for every external claim.
activities.expectedOutput: A recurring signal digest per account with sourced external events, internal activity changes, and an explicit evidence-versus-inference split.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE validates each signal against what they know about the account before acting, and never repeats an unsourced claim to a customer.
activities.requiredContext: Your named account list; access to internal account activity; the priority solution areas for your territory.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your named account list and confirm which of those accounts you can see internal activity for.
2. Run the prompt.
3. Check the first digest against one account you know well, and confirm every external claim carries a source.
4. Set the cadence you will actually read; weekly is usually enough.
5. Discard any signal you cannot trace to a source before acting on it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Opportunity creation is mostly a timing problem. The trigger events that make an account ready are public or visible internally - the constraint is noticing them while there is still time to act.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: The next opportunity is often already visible in customer signals. Today is about finding and testing those signals without creating pipeline noise.
keyTalkingPoints: Whitespace is not just a product gap. A qualified opportunity has a trigger, stakeholder, business problem, next action, and evidence. AI can surface signals; the AE tests whether they are real.
discussionQuestions: Where did your last real opportunity come from? What makes a signal qualified rather than hopeful? Where might you be missing a signal because it sits outside MSX?
suggestedTransitions: Move from signal discovery to one opportunity hypothesis and the first outreach or discovery action.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to testing one opportunity signal with a real customer or account-team action.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account with recent meetings, engagement, or whitespace that might become an opportunity.
facilitatorQuestions: Which signal looks promising but not yet qualified? What evidence would make it real? What customer action would test the hypothesis?
listenFor: Listen for opportunities created to fill coverage, whitespace treated as product absence, duplicate opportunities, and signals without a named stakeholder or trigger.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, work from one account’s known context and draft the prompt to run later.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Qualify one opportunity hypothesis and document the trigger, evidence, next action, and uncertainty.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the opportunity hypothesis, evidence, outreach or discovery step, and whether it became qualified or was rejected.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Decide whether the satisfaction signal changes your ask
activities.description: Test the ask you were planning to make against the customer's current satisfaction and support experience, and change it if the evidence says you should.
activities.prompt: I am going into a conversation with [Customer name - TPID] and the ask I intend to make is [state your ask]. Based on this customer's current satisfaction and support experience, tell me whether that ask is well timed. Name anything in the recent evidence that a customer could reasonably raise in this meeting that I would struggle to answer, and suggest what I should resolve or acknowledge first. If the evidence does not justify changing the ask, say so plainly rather than inventing a concern.
activities.expectedOutput: A judgement on whether the intended ask is well timed, the issues a customer could raise that you are not ready for, and what to resolve or acknowledge before making the ask.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides whether to proceed with the ask. The tool can flag a poorly timed ask, but only the AE knows what the relationship can carry and what has already been discussed offline.
activities.requiredContext: The account and its TPID; the specific ask you intend to make; the meeting date.
activitySteps: 1. Write down the ask you intend to make before you run anything. The point is to test it, not to discover it.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt with that ask included.
4. Decide whether to proceed with the ask, soften it, or resolve something first.
5. Prepare an answer for anything the customer could reasonably raise.
6. Never quote the internal satisfaction data in the meeting. It shapes your preparation and stays out of the room.
activities.whyThisMatters: Preparation usually fails at the ask, not the agenda. Walking a growth ask into a customer whose support experience is deteriorating is how a relationship gets set back a quarter.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Customer conversations are where decisions move. Today is about preparing the position, evidence, objections, and ask before the meeting starts.
keyTalkingPoints: A brief is not a recap. It should state the intended outcome, customer context, evidence, open questions, likely objections, and the ask. The AE validates tone and relationship nuance.
discussionQuestions: What do you often walk into a meeting still not knowing? What would change if the ask were explicit before the meeting? Which claim would need validation before customer use?
suggestedTransitions: Move from preparation concept to one live meeting brief and the ask the AE will use.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Pick one customer meeting and names the primary ask and fallback ask.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one upcoming customer meeting, the desired decision, and any approved source materials you want to use.
facilitatorQuestions: What decision should the meeting move? What claim must be validated? What objection is likely but uncomfortable to prepare for?
listenFor: Listen for recaps instead of positions, meetings with no intended outcome, generic value language, unsupported claims, and missing fallback asks.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tools are unavailable, build the brief skeleton manually and identify source gaps.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Prepare one customer conversation brief and validate the claims before use.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the brief, source signals, validated or removed claims, primary ask, fallback ask, and meeting outcome if available.

secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Your AI desktop assistant for seller work. Prepare for customer meetings, summarize communications, organize actions, monitor priorities, and automate repetitive work across Microsoft 365 and sales systems.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Continuous or proactive work that should persist beyond one chat.
keyBenefits: Keeps work moving between sessions rather than inside one chat. Monitors signals, coordinates follow-through, and prepares materials within organizational controls.

secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for a quick single answer that Copilot Chat would handle, and do not use it to bypass a human checkpoint just because it can run unattended. Anything it produces while running on its own still needs the same review as anything else.

activities.name: Inspect deal context before customer action
activities.description: Use the deal making features in Sales Agent to assemble agreement, enrollment, renewal, discount, and consumption context, then shape the deal from real data rather than recollection.
activities.prompt: Show me the list of enrollments for [Account name or TPID], then list all agreements with type and status. For the agreement I name, provide license estate details grouped by SKU, list the SKUs whose discount is between 40 and 60 percent, and show the upcoming renewals with expiry dates. Lead with the identifier I give you. Tell me which figures you could not retrieve rather than estimating them, and flag anything that needs licensing or entitlement validation before I use it with the customer.
activities.expectedOutput: A deal context brief covering enrollments, agreements, license estate by SKU, discount posture, and upcoming renewals, with retrieval gaps named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE verifies the figures came from the source systems rather than inference, and routes pricing approval, policy exceptions, and final commercial authority to the accountable owner.
activities.requiredContext: Approved account, TPID, enrollment, or agreement identifier and current deal context.
activities.whyThisMatters: Deal making answers depend on the identifier. A named enrollment or agreement returns real deal data; a vague account reference returns a generic summary.

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.
