activities.name: Generate the Deal Book for a renewal and choose your scenario
activities.description: Compile the renewal summary for one agreement, then decide which pricing scenario to lead with and why.
activities.prompt: Create Deal Book for agreement number [agreement number]. If the agreement number does not resolve, try the enrollment number instead. When it returns, summarize the pricing scenarios it produced, what each assumes about the customer, and what evidence in the purchase history and current licensing footprint supports each one. Tell me which scenario you would lead with for [customer context] and what would have to be true for that to be wrong. Flag any upsell or cross-sell recommendation that is not supported by the consumption data. Do not present a scenario as approved or as a commitment.
activities.expectedOutput: A Deal Book with purchase history, current licensing footprint, pricing scenarios, and upsell or cross-sell recommendations, plus your reasoned choice of which scenario to lead with.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE validates the deal facts against the source data, decides which scenario fits this customer, and routes pricing approval, exceptions, and material amendments to the accountable owner and approval chain rather than acting on the recommendation alone.
activities.requiredContext: An agreement number or enrollment number for a real renewal. Customer context that would make one scenario more appropriate than another. Sales Agent access with your CRM scope connected.
activitySteps: 1. Have the agreement number ready; the enrollment number also works.
2. Run the prompt.
3. Review the Agreement Details sheet, including year-over-year revenue, before the scenario tabs.
4. Check the Reason to Believe tooltips on the List Price column for SKUs marked discontinued, new, or replaced.
5. Treat the first output as a draft; re-run if the data looks stale.
6. Decide which scenario to lead with and why.
activities.whyThisMatters: The Deal Book assembles in minutes what used to take weeks across seven or eight portals. The judgment that matters is which scenario fits this customer.

activities.name: Turn the chosen scenario into a quote and start the approval
activities.description: Create the EA quote from the scenario you selected, check the pricing fields, and request the approval you know it will need, rather than discovering the approval requirement later.
activities.prompt: Create an EA Quote for [enrollment number] based on the scenario I selected from the Deal Book. Then show me the price settings so I can check them, and tell me which fields you populated from the Deal Book versus which need my input. Identify any discount level in this quote that will require approval, and what the approval path would be. Do not submit anything or represent any discount as approved. If a guardrail or validation issue applies to this deal, including anything multi-year or multi-tenant, surface it now rather than at submission.
activities.expectedOutput: A draft EA quote with price settings visible, a clear split between populated and required fields, and the approval requirement and path named before submission.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE verifies every pricing field before submission, treats the draft as a draft rather than a final quote, and routes discount approval, exceptions, and any material amendment through the accountable owner and the legal approval chain rather than around it.
activities.requiredContext: The enrollment number and the Deal Book scenario you selected. Knowledge of your own empowerment level and who owns approval beyond it. Sales Agent access with your CRM scope connected.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the enrollment number and the scenario you chose from the Deal Book.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Review the price settings and correct anything that came across wrong.
5. Note the approval that will be needed and who owns it.
6. If a discount needs approval, request it: Request approval for a [X percent] discount on this renewal.
7. Keep this in the same chat thread as the rest of this deal.
activities.whyThisMatters: Deals stall between a good scenario and a submitted quote. Knowing the approval requirement before you build the quote is what keeps that gap short.

activities.name: Test whether customer investment would unblock this deal
activities.description: Check the deal for a barrier that customer investment could remove.
activities.prompt: Using the approved opportunity, account priorities and current blockers, identify whether a customer investment could remove a decision, deployment or adoption barrier on this deal. Separate evidence from assumption. Do not determine eligibility, funding or approval.
activities.expectedOutput: Deal-linked investment hypothesis with barrier, evidence, assumptions, owner, and next human decision.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE confirms the barrier is real, investment is appropriate, and funding or eligibility remains a governed decision.
activities.requiredContext: Approved opportunity context, current blockers, account priorities
activities.bestFitJob: Check the deal for a barrier that customer investment could remove.
activities.whyThisMatters: Investment belongs in the deal conversation only when it changes a real blocker.

activities.name: Pressure-test the deal inspection
activities.description: Find the blocker, approval or stakeholder gap that the deal plan assumes is handled but nobody owns.
activities.prompt: Review this deal inspection. Identify the next decision the customer must make, whether the evidence to support it exists, and which blocker has no named owner. Name the assumption that, if wrong, would move the close date most, and what would confirm it.
activities.expectedOutput: A deal challenge naming the next customer decision, unowned blockers, and the assumption with the largest close-date impact.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE names the assumption that would most move the close date. A model can list unowned blockers, but which one actually threatens the date depends on customer dynamics that were never written down.
activities.requiredContext: The deal inspection brief; the exit criteria for the current stage; the account-team roles involved.
activities.whyThisMatters: If the decision path for Accelerate a Strategic Deal is going to fail, it should fail here rather than in front of the customer.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Inspect deal context before customer action

activities.name: Create the deal follow-through plan
activities.description: Convert the deal inspection into owned actions and checkpoints that move the next customer decision.
activities.prompt: Turn the deal inspection into a follow-through plan. For each blocker and open decision, define the action, the owner, the date, the customer-facing step if there is one, and the checkpoint where you will verify movement. Separate what you own from what the account team owns.
activities.expectedOutput: A deal follow-through plan separating seller-owned from team-owned actions, with dates and verification checkpoints.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE separates what they own from what the account team owns, and confirms the account team agrees before the plan is used. A plan that silently assigns work to another role produces neither the work nor the escalation.
activities.requiredContext: The reviewed deal inspection; the account-team owners; the customer decision date you are working toward.
activities.whyThisMatters: You spend your time editing the follow-through plan for Accelerate a Strategic Deal rather than staring at a blank version of it.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Inspect deal context before customer action

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Strategic deals stall when the next decision, blocker, or owner is unnamed. Today is about making the deal inspectable.
keyTalkingPoints: A close date is not a plan. Exit criteria, approvals, commercial dependencies, stakeholder coverage, and customer actions determine whether the deal can move. AI can organize the deal picture; the AE routes decisions to the right owners.
discussionQuestions: What is your deal really waiting on? Which approval, customer action, or role gap is not yet explicit? What should not be decided by AI?
suggestedTransitions: Move from deal summary to the next decision and owner map.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the next decision on one live deal and the owner for every blocker.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live opportunity, the current stage, and the next decision you believe is needed.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the next decision, not the next task? Which blocker has no owner? Which commercial, technical, or partner decision needs another role?
listenFor: Listen for close date as proxy for plan, approval paths discovered late, role gaps, unsupported deal assumptions, and AI outputs that overstep CE or SME authority.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If systems are unavailable, whiteboard the decision path, blockers, and accountable owners.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Inspect one strategic deal and route at least one blocker or decision to the right owner.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the deal inspection, blocker-owner map, routed ask, and what changed in the deal plan.

AE-DEAL.keyTakeaway: Deals stall on structure more often than on merit. Getting the shape right early is the cheapest work available.

AE-RENEW.roleTopicName: Manage Renewal Risk and Expansion Readiness
AE-RENEW.roleTopicDescription: Read renewal timing, consumption and usage gaps, value evidence, recent engagement, and commercial review needs early enough to change the outcome.
AE-RENEW.wiifm: A renewal is decided long before the renewal date. Seeing risk and value evidence early gives you time to change the result.

activities.name: Assemble the renewal and expansion package
activities.description: Pull the renewal position, consumption evidence, value story and expansion options into one package the customer and the account team can both work from.
activities.prompt: Build a renewal and expansion package for [Customer]. Work across the agreement and renewal position, consumption and usage evidence, the value delivered so far, open risks, and the expansion options we believe are supported. Produce a short customer-facing summary, an internal account-team view with the risks stated plainly, and a one-page value story. Show me the plan before you build it, and check in before each document so I can redirect you.
activities.expectedOutput: Renewal package with a customer-facing summary, an internal risk view, and a one-page value story.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE validates every claim in the customer-facing material, confirms commercial statements with the Commercial Executive, and decides what is shared externally.
activities.requiredContext: Approved renewal, consumption, usage and value evidence for the account; the expansion hypotheses already tested.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the customer, the renewal date, and the value evidence you can actually support.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Separate what the package claims as delivered value from what is projected.
5. Flag every pricing or commercial statement for CE review before the package goes near the customer.
6. Confirm the expansion options are grounded in usage evidence rather than aspiration.
activities.whyThisMatters: The renewal conversation needs a package, not a chat answer. This is multistep work across several sources, with checkpoints, which is what Cowork is for.

activities.name: Test renewal risk against how the customer actually feels
activities.description: Put the customer's satisfaction signal next to your own renewal risk read, and investigate every account where the two disagree.
activities.prompt: For these accounts renewing in the next six months, show me the satisfaction picture for each: current OSAT and its trend, DSAT drivers, the most negative recent verbatims, and the support experience measured by ATQ. Here are the accounts and how I have currently rated their renewal risk: [paste your renewal list with your own risk rating for each]. Tell me which accounts show a deteriorating satisfaction signal, and present it next to the rating I gave so I can see where the two disagree.
activities.expectedOutput: A renewal list showing satisfaction evidence alongside your own risk rating, with the accounts where a declining signal contradicts a favourable rating explicitly identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE owns the renewal risk call. Satisfaction is one input, not a verdict, and a satisfied customer can still leave for commercial reasons no CX metric will show.
activities.requiredContext: Your renewal portfolio for the next six months with TPIDs; your own current risk rating for each of those accounts, since the tool does not hold your risk read.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your renewal view for the next six months, with your own current risk rating for each account.
2. Paste that list into the prompt. The satisfaction data and your risk ratings live in different places, so you supply the ratings.
3. Run it in Sales Agent and look only at the disagreements.
4. For each disagreement, decide which signal you trust and write down why.
5. Raise any renewal you downgrade with the account team before it appears in a review.
activities.whyThisMatters: Renewal risk assessed on pipeline signals alone misses the customer who is quietly unhappy and has not told you yet.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Renewal risk is usually visible before the renewal conversation. Today is about finding it while there is still time to act.
keyTalkingPoints: Renewal health depends on value evidence, usage or consumption signals, relationship recency, commercial readiness, and expansion logic. AI can surface patterns; the AE validates intent and next action.
discussionQuestions: Which upcoming renewal has the weakest value evidence? What expansion hypothesis is already visible? Where do you need CSAM, CSA, CE, or SSP input?
suggestedTransitions: Move from renewal principles to one account and the action that changes risk this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one renewal risk, one value evidence gap, and one expansion hypothesis.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account renewing in the next planning window and the evidence you currently use to judge risk.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the largest renewal risk? What value evidence would the customer recognize? Which expansion signal is supported by usage, consumption, or customer priority?
listenFor: Listen for renewals treated as admin, value evidence built too late, expansion detached from customer outcomes, and unclear CSAM/CSA/CE ownership.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If data is unavailable, work from known context and list evidence gaps to close.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Assess one upcoming renewal and take one action that reduces risk or strengthens value evidence.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the renewal assessment, risk, evidence gap, expansion hypothesis, and the owner for the next action.

ATS-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand how the ATS huddle path runs and where AI fits technical strategy and account planning.
ATS-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
ATS-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: ATSs know how the huddle motion works, which tools may show up, what to review, and what AI experiences to bring back before next week.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This session explains how the huddle motion works and how ATS team members should test AI on real technical strategy work.
keyTalkingPoints: Huddles are workflow-led, not tool demos. Every session ends with one experiment. Human judgment stays explicit.
discussionQuestions: Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted technical strategy output?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the workflow-discovery prompt below. Week 1 is for finding the recurring work worth automating.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the tools named for this path, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
facilitatorQuestions: Which technical strategy work do you repeat every week without thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where must the ATS judgment stay human no matter how good the output gets?
listenFor: Listen for unvoiced scepticism, access blockers stated as disinterest, the assumption that this is a tool rollout, and people who describe only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat. The recurring, unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the discovery conversation and record access blockers separately from interest. The discovery prompt can be run in whichever tool the person already has.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

"I am an Account Technology Strategist at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with."
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation, or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

ATS-ORIENT.keyTakeaway: The point of the motion is better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake.

activities.name: Build a standing account intelligence hub the v-team can use
activities.description: Consolidate the scattered sources behind account planning into one maintained hub that refreshes rather than being rebuilt each planning cycle.
activities.prompt: Build me a standing account intelligence hub for this account. Pull together the business context, current opportunities, stakeholder map, installed estate and licensing position, recent engagement history, and open risks into one structured place. Then keep it current on a recurring basis and tell me specifically what changed since the last refresh. Where a source is unavailable to you, list it as a gap rather than filling it with inference.
activities.expectedOutput: A maintained account intelligence hub with a change summary each refresh and an explicit list of unavailable sources.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS reviews the hub for accuracy before sharing with the v-team, and confirms that no customer-confidential material has been placed where it should not sit.
activities.requiredContext: The account name; access to your account planning sources; the v-team members who need visibility.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm which account planning sources you can reach, and name the ones you cannot.
2. Run the prompt.
3. Review the first hub build against what you already know about the account.
4. Check that nothing customer-confidential has been placed where the wider v-team should not see it.
5. Set the refresh cadence and agree with the v-team who reads the change summary.
activities.whyThisMatters: Account planning quality is usually limited by assembly time, not thinking time. When the assembly is standing and self-refreshing, the v-team spends its hour on the judgement instead of the gathering.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about build an account intelligence and meeting prep brief without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is An account intelligence brief with technical risks, workload signals, stakeholder context, and next actions. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: Which account are you least confident you could brief someone on right now?
Where does your current account picture come from, and how old is it?
What technical signal would change your priorities this week if you knew it today?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the assembled account picture to the single signal that should change this week's priorities.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the account you will brief, the signal you will chase down, and the source you will use to close it. If the brief will not change a decision, pick a different account.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: What is in your account brief that you could not source if challenged?
Which signal in the brief actually changes what you do next week?
What is missing that you only notice once it is written down?
listenFor: Listen for briefs assembled from memory rather than systems, KPI figures quoted without their definition or date, technical risks with no named owner, and stakeholder context that is a year old. Also listen for the brief becoming an end in itself rather than driving a decision.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Build an account intelligence brief for one account, and chase down the one signal you could not source.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the brief and the signal you had to verify manually.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

Sales Home is part of Sales Agent rather than a separate product, and works alongside chat rather than replacing it. In preview for SME&C individual contributors since late July 2026; it does not replace MSX.

Renewal, Campaign, Planning, Realization and Deal Agent integration are roadmap, not available today, so do not build an activity that depends on them.
stepsToGetStarted: Opens Sales Agent. Sales Home is the seller surface inside it - My View for alerts and quota attainment, Prospecting for signals, account research, contacts and outreach, and Pipeline for opportunities, forecast comments, close plans and deal risks. It is not a separate product and has no separate link.

activities.name: Pressure-test the options and tradeoffs with an executive
activities.description: Practice putting the real decision, its options and its tradeoffs to an executive.
activities.prompt: Use Agent J.ai to role-play the executive who has to make this decision. I will present the options and their tradeoffs rather than a recommendation. Push back where an option sounds like a pitch, where a tradeoff has been softened, or where what this executive is personally backing has not been named. Pause for my response before coaching me on whether the decision was put clearly and the tradeoffs stated honestly. Do not invent customer facts or commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: A rehearsed decision conversation, the objections raised, and coaching on where an option was pitched rather than offered.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS decides which tradeoffs are material enough to put in front of this executive. Review the downsides the rehearsal raises and add the material ones it missed, since not everything it raises bears on the decision being made.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about assemble an executive technical customer narrative without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is An executive-ready technical narrative with sourced claims, proof points, decision questions, and a technical ask. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: When did an executive last stop you to ask what something meant?
Which part of your technical story do you find hardest to say without jargon?
What decision do you actually need from the executive, and have you ever asked for it directly?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the technical story to the one decision you want the executive to make, and the proof they need to make it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the executive audience, the single decision you will ask for, and the proof point they still need. If there is no ask, the narrative is not ready.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: Read your opening line aloud. Would a CFO know what you meant?
Which claim in your narrative rests on a proof point you do not have?
What are you asking the executive to decide, stated in one sentence?
listenFor: Listen for architecture described rather than translated, value asserted without evidence, narratives that end without an ask, and jargon that survived because nobody in the room questioned it. Also listen for a narrative aimed at the technical stakeholder while claiming to target the executive.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Rewrite one technical narrative for an executive audience, and state the single decision you are asking for.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the narrative, the ask, and the proof point you still need.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

secondaryAgents.name: GitHub Copilot
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: AI pair programmer available in VS Code, the CLI and the GitHub Copilot app. It works against a repository or a working folder rather than against your mail and meetings.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Write, explain, refactor and test code; scaffold infrastructure-as-code and deployment artifacts; build the smallest spike that proves or disproves an architecture assumption; generate sample data and validation scripts; and reproduce a reported failure so you can see it rather than describe it.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the next step is to build something rather than to plan or describe it. Validating an architecture assumption with a spike, standing up a demo or workshop environment, iterating a proof of concept, reproducing a deployment or integration failure, or packaging a reusable asset with tests and setup steps.
keyBenefits: Turns a technical opinion into evidence. A spike that takes twenty minutes settles an argument that would otherwise run for a week, and a reproduced failure is a fact the account team can act on rather than a claim the customer has to accept.
secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for customer, market or account research; that is Researcher. Do not use it to assemble a customer-facing document or deck; that is Cowork. Do not point it at production without the review your team already requires, and do not paste customer data into it. It works on code and configuration, not on the CRM record.
stepsToGetStarted: Use it where the code already is: the Copilot extension in VS Code, the gh copilot CLI, or the GitHub Copilot app in the browser for work not tied to a local checkout. Open the repository or folder first so it has the context. Start with: Explain what this deployment does, then write the smallest test that would prove the assumption I am least sure about.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about develop a technical strategy and decision trajectory without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is A technical trajectory with priority bets, proof needs, owners, risks, milestones, and open decisions. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: What is the next technical decision this customer has to make, and when?
Which of your technical bets is least supported by evidence?
What would have to be true for the customer to commit to the direction you are recommending?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the technical direction to the next decision it requires, with an owner and the evidence that unblocks it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the next technical decision, its owner, the date it must happen by, and the proof the customer needs to make it.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the next decision in the trajectory, and who makes it?
Which bet would you abandon first if evidence went against it?
What proof does the customer need before they will commit, and do you have a path to producing it?
listenFor: Listen for a strategy that is a destination without a sequence, bets with no falsification condition, proof needs identified after the customer already asked, and milestones with no owner. Also listen for technical direction set without the customer's own objectives in the room.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Name the next technical decision on one account, its owner, and the date it must happen by.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the decision, the owner who agreed to it, and the proof the customer needs.

secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about design an executive briefing experience without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is An EBC plan with desired decisions, participants, evidence, preparation milestones, and follow-through ownership. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: What is the one thing the customer should leave the briefing believing?
Who in the room can actually approve the next step?
What would make this briefing worth their time rather than ours?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the briefing design to the single decision it is meant to produce and who must be present for that.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the briefing, the decision it should produce, and the one person who must be in the room for that decision to be possible.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: What will the customer do differently after this briefing?
Who in the room can approve that, and are they invited?
Which part of the agenda serves us rather than them?
listenFor: Listen for agendas built around what we want to present, attendee lists without a decision maker, briefings with no ask, and content density that leaves no room for the customer to talk. Also listen for an experience designed for the meeting rather than for what happens after it.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Design one executive briefing around a single decision, and confirm the person who can make it will be there.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the decision the briefing targets and confirmation the approver is invited.

secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about adjust the technical talk track from customer signals without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is A signal-adjusted talk track with opening language, questions, objections, responses, and human review flags. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: What did the customer say recently that should change how you talk about this?
Where is your current talk track still answering last quarter's objection?
What signal are you choosing to ignore because it is inconvenient?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the customer signal to the specific line in your talk track that has to change because of it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the customer signal you are acting on and the specific line in your talk track that changes because of it.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: What specifically did the customer say, and what did you infer from it?
Which part of your talk track is now answering a question they stopped asking?
What would you change if you took their last objection at face value?
listenFor: Listen for signals interpreted to confirm what we already planned, talk tracks updated in wording but not in substance, and customer silence read as agreement. Also listen for adjustments based on one conversation with one person treated as the account's position.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Change one line in your talk track based on something a customer actually said this month.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the customer signal and the line that changed because of it.

Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Keep the v-team commitments moving between huddles
activities.description: Set up a recurring check that watches the technical v-team commitments and tells you what has slipped, without you having to go looking.
activities.prompt: Set up a recurring check on the technical v-team commitments for [Account or opportunity]. Each week, look across our meetings, mail and the account record for the commitments made, and tell me which ones have no activity since they were made, which have passed their date, and which have gone quiet on the customer side. Give me the specific chase for each one and who should make it. Keep a memory of what you already flagged so you are not repeating the same item back to me every week.
activities.expectedOutput: A recurring commitment check that reports slipped, stalled and quiet items with a named chase for each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS decides whether silence actually means a stall, and owns the judgment about which chases are appropriate given the relationships involved.
activities.requiredContext: The v-team commitments and owners from the alignment brief; approved access to your own mail, meetings and account record.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the current v-team commitments with owners and dates.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Confirm each flagged commitment is genuinely stalled rather than progressing somewhere you cannot see.
5. Set the cadence to run before your v-team call.
6. Raise slipped items with the owner directly rather than in the group thread.
activities.whyThisMatters: Technical commitments do not fail loudly. They go quiet, and by the time anyone notices the customer has moved on. This is exactly the persistent, between-sessions work that Scout is built for.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about mobilize the technical v-team around priorities and risks without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is A technical v-team alignment brief with owners, dependencies, investment signals, checkpoints, and next actions. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: Who on your technical v-team could not state the current priority if asked today?
Which dependency has gone quiet in the last two weeks?
What are you carrying yourself that should belong to someone else?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the coordination picture to one specific ask, to one named person, with a date.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one v-team ask you will send this week, to one named person, with a date and what you will supply to make it easy.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: If I asked each v-team member the current priority, would I get the same answer?
Which dependency is at risk, and does its owner know?
What are you doing yourself that is really someone else's accountability?
listenFor: Listen for priorities that live only in the ATS's head, owners assigned in a document but never agreed in a conversation, dependencies tracked without dates, and the ATS absorbing work because delegating it feels slower. Also listen for v-team meetings that report status without deciding anything.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Send one specific v-team ask to one named person with a date and what you will supply.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ask you sent and whether it was accepted.

SSP-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand how the SSP huddle path runs and where AI fits solution pursuit, with human judgment explicit.
SSP-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
SSP-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: SSPs know how the huddle motion works, which tools may show up, what to review, and what AI experiences to bring back before next week.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This session explains the motion and sets expectations for using AI in solution pursuit work.
keyTalkingPoints: Huddles are workflow-led, not tool demos. Every session ends with one thing to try. Human judgment stays explicit.
discussionQuestions: Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted solution or pursuit output?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the workflow-discovery prompt below. Week 1 is for finding the recurring work worth automating.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the tools named for this path, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
facilitatorQuestions: Which solution or pursuit work do you repeat every week without thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where must the SSP judgment stay human no matter how good the output gets?
listenFor: Listen for unvoiced scepticism, access blockers stated as disinterest, the assumption that this is a tool rollout, and people who describe only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat. The recurring, unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the discovery conversation and record access blockers separately from interest. The discovery prompt can be run in whichever tool the person already has.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

"I am a Solution Sales Professional at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with."
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation, or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

SSP-ORIENT.keyTakeaway: The point of the motion is better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake.

activities.name: Draft the first contact for the top-priority lead
activities.description: Turn the top-ranked lead into a specific, short first message that connects the signal to a reason for the customer to respond.
activities.prompt: Here is the top lead from my follow-up plan: [paste source signal, account, role, likely interest, and any prior interaction]. Draft a first contact message under 100 words that references the specific signal, states one reason this is relevant to their business now, and asks for one small next step. Give me two versions: one for a business decision maker and one for a technical decision maker. Do not claim knowledge of their environment we do not have, and do not assert a product feature I have not given you.
activities.expectedOutput: Two short first-contact drafts, one business and one technical, tied to the originating signal.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP confirms consent and outreach appropriateness, verifies every factual statement about the customer, and owns the wording before sending.
activities.requiredContext: The prioritized lead plan; the source signal; the contact's role; prior interaction history; consent and outreach appropriateness.
activitySteps: 1. Take the top lead from the prioritized plan.
2. Confirm consent and context are appropriate for outreach.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Edit into your own voice.
5. Send one, and note the date.
activities.whyThisMatters: A prioritized list that never becomes a message is just a better-sorted backlog.

activities.name: Close the loop on outreach that never got an answer
activities.description: Track the outreach you have sent so the follow-ups that matter are surfaced and drafted rather than remembered.
activities.prompt: Review the outreach I have sent over the last 30 days and identify every message where I asked for something - a meeting, an introduction, a decision, or information - and did not receive a substantive reply. For each one, tell me how long it has been waiting, how important it looks based on the opportunity involved, and draft a short follow-up in my own voice that adds a new reason to respond rather than simply repeating the ask. Do not send anything.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of unanswered asks with elapsed time and a drafted follow-up for each that adds new value rather than repeating.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP reviews and edits every draft before sending, and removes any follow-up where the silence is itself the answer.
activities.requiredContext: Access to your sent messages; your current lead and opportunity list; your team's follow-up cadence norms.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm the check can see your sent messages for the last 30 days.
2. Run the prompt.
3. Review the ranked list and remove any thread where the silence is itself the answer.
4. Edit every drafted follow-up so it adds a new reason to reply rather than repeating the ask.
5. Send them yourself; do not let the check send on your behalf.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most lost specialist opportunities are not rejected - they are dropped. The follow-up that would have converted was never sent because it was never surfaced.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Lead and account signals are noisy. Today is about turning them into a focused follow-up plan.
keyTalkingPoints: Qualification is evidence work. Solution relevance, owner, message, consent, and next action must be explicit.
discussionQuestions: Which lead or signal deserves attention first? What evidence makes it real? Who owns the next action?
suggestedTransitions: Move from noisy signals to one prioritized follow-up plan.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to ranking one lead or prospect list and owning the top next action.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live solution pursuit, solution play, lead list, opportunity, or investment case relevant to this huddle; confirm tool access; review last commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: Which lead or account signal deserves follow-up first? What evidence supports solution relevance?
listenFor: Listen for undifferentiated lead lists, vague ownership, weak message fit, and missing consent/context.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If systems are unavailable, manually rank one lead list and draft the prompt for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Turn your top-priority lead into an actual first contact this week.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the message you sent and whether the signal was worth following.

agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.

For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. activities.name: Map who actually decides and who is missing
activities.description: Build the real decision map for this solution play, including the people who can stop it, not only the people who like it.
activities.prompt: Here is my solution-selling plan and the stakeholders I have engaged: [paste plan and stakeholder list with roles and engagement level]. The solution play is [paste], the decision type is [paste, for example new workload, renewal, or migration], the customer's organizational model is [paste, for example centralized IT, business-unit autonomy, or shared services], and their known procurement and technical governance constraints are [paste]. Build a decision map showing who decides, who influences, who implements, and who can block. For each person, state what they need to believe for this to move forward and what evidence would convince them. Then identify missing roles ONLY where the solution play, decision type, organizational model, or governance constraints I gave you imply that role is required. Do not list generic enterprise buying-committee roles. Do not invent names; describe missing roles by function. If my context is too thin to identify missing roles, say so rather than guessing.
activities.expectedOutput: A decision map with what each stakeholder needs to believe, plus a named list of missing roles and the risk each creates.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP validates the stakeholder reality against what the account team actually knows, and owns the plan to reach anyone missing.
activities.requiredContext: Solution-selling plan; stakeholders engaged with roles; the solution play and decision type; the customer's organizational model; known procurement and technical governance constraints; who owns the customer relationship.
activitySteps: 1. List stakeholders engaged so far with role and engagement level.
2. Gather the solution play, decision type, customer organizational model, and governance constraints.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Identify the highest-risk absence.
5. Decide who introduces you to that person and by when.
activities.whyThisMatters: Solution plans usually fail on a person nobody engaged, not on a fact nobody knew.

activities.name: Convert the plan into dated commitments
activities.description: Reduce the plan to the few actions that will actually happen in the next 30 days, each with a named owner and a date.
activities.prompt: From this solution-selling plan [paste], extract only the actions that must happen in the next 30 days to clear the next customer decision. For each: what it is, who owns it by role, the date it must be done by, and what it unblocks. Limit to five actions. If the plan implies more than five critical actions in 30 days, tell me which ones are not realistic and what to cut. Do not assign an action to a person or team I have not named.
activities.expectedOutput: Five or fewer dated actions with named owners and what each unblocks.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP confirms each owner has actually agreed to the action and the date, rather than being assigned it in a document.
activities.requiredContext: The pressure-tested solution-selling plan; the account team and their availability; the next customer decision and its timing.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the pressure-tested plan.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Cut to five or fewer.
4. Confirm each owner has agreed.
5. Record the dates where the account team will see them.
activities.whyThisMatters: A plan without dates and owners is a description of intentions.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A solution-selling plan is useful only if it changes pursuit execution. Today is about building a plan that can be worked.
keyTalkingPoints: Plan around customer outcome, solution play, stakeholders, proof needs, demo or workshop sequence, and next decision.
discussionQuestions: Which solution pursuit needs a clearer plan? What proof or stakeholder coverage is missing?
suggestedTransitions: Move from plan structure to one active pursuit.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to building or improving one solution-selling plan for a live pursuit.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live solution pursuit, solution play, lead list, opportunity, or investment case relevant to this huddle; confirm tool access; review last commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: What makes this solution pursuit worth SSP time? What next decision is the plan built to advance?
listenFor: Listen for generic solution plans, missing stakeholder coverage, unclear proof path, and no 30-day plan.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, sketch the plan on paper and capture evidence gaps.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Map who really decides on one pursuit, then reach the person missing from your list.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the decision map and the absence that carried the most risk.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Stress-test the assumptions the value claims depend on
activities.description: Expose what each outcome number quietly assumes, and record which assumptions the customer would have to accept.
activities.prompt: Here is our value narrative and the evidence brief behind it: [paste both]. For every outcome claim, produce a row containing: the claim, the assumption it depends on, who has to accept that assumption for the claim to hold, the evidence we currently have, and what happens to the claim if adoption is half as fast as projected. Rank the rows by how much the claim collapses when its assumption fails. Do not add claims that are not in my narrative, and do not supply evidence I have not given you.
activities.expectedOutput: An assumption and risk table ranked by how much each claim depends on an unproven assumption.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP decides which assumptions are defensible with this customer, and owns every outcome figure before it reaches them.
activities.requiredContext: The value narrative; the evidence brief; the customer's financial context; adoption expectations already discussed with them.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the value narrative and evidence brief.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Find the claim that collapses hardest.
4. Either find proof for its assumption or remove the claim.
5. Bring the assumption table to the huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: The value claim you cannot defend is the one the customer will ask about.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Tailor the solution value narrative

Remove anything that only makes sense if a seller is explaining it. Remove any claim that is not supported by the evidence brief I gave you. Keep it under 350 words.
activities.expectedOutput: A one-page, forwardable value summary with a specific next ask.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP verifies every claim survives without a seller present, and approves the wording before the champion receives it.
activities.requiredContext: The rehearsed value narrative; the evidence brief; who the champion is and who they would forward it to; the next ask.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the rehearsed narrative with weak claims removed.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.

activities.whyThisMatters: Most internal customer decisions happen in rooms the seller is not in.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Value needs to be created before the conversation, not after the objection. Today is about the customer-specific story.
keyTalkingPoints: The customer defines value. Use sourced evidence, caveats, use cases, and a clear next ask.
discussionQuestions: What customer priority does this solution map to? Which claim is supported, assumed, or missing evidence?
suggestedTransitions: Move from value logic to the conversation or proof it supports.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to one customer-specific value narrative with sourced evidence and caveats.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live solution pursuit, solution play, lead list, opportunity, or investment case relevant to this huddle; confirm tool access; review last commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: Which customer priority does the value narrative serve? Which claims are sourced?
listenFor: Listen for generic value claims, unsupported ROI, customer priorities inferred rather than sourced, and missing caveats.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If evidence sources are unavailable, build the narrative skeleton and list missing proof.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Test the assumptions behind one value claim, and remove any claim you cannot defend.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the assumption table and the claim you dropped.

secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Rehearse solution discovery and objection handling
activities.description: Rehearse the solution conversation and receive coaching before customer use.
activities.prompt: Use Agent J.ai to role-play the upcoming [meeting type] with [customer or stakeholder]. Use the approved conversation plan and focus on solution discovery, differentiation, proof points, likely objections, next solution decision, and primary ask. Pause for the team member response, then coach clarity, evidence, listening, and next step. Do not invent customer facts or commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Interactive role-play, targeted coaching, objections, and improvement list.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP validates facts, claims, commitments, guidance, and decides what to change before customer use.
activities.requiredContext: Approved conversation plan; meeting type; customer context; desired outcome.
activities.whyThisMatters: Ten minutes rehearsing is cheaper than improvising in the room.

agents.name: Agent J.ai
agents.shortDescription: Text-based coaching experience grounded in Microsoft 365 context and curated content.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Helps users sharpen messages, rehearse conversations, anticipate objections, and plan next steps.
agents.whenToUseIt: Customer conversation preparation and role-play.
keyBenefits: Rehearsal before the real conversation. Sharpens messages, surfaces objections you had not anticipated, and coaches on clarity and next step, grounded in Microsoft 365 context and curated content.

resources.title: Agent J.ai Reference
resources.description: MCAPS agent reference for coaching and conversation rehearsal.

agents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use as the authoritative source for CRM or commercial data.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Agent J.ai in Microsoft 365 Copilot, then describe the conversation you want to rehearse and who you will be speaking to.

activities.name: Find the discovery gap before the meeting, not after
activities.description: Check what you still do not know that would change your recommendation, and build the question that closes it.
activities.prompt: Here is what we currently know about [account] for [solution play]: [paste priorities, environment, stakeholders, constraints, prior conversations]. Identify what we do not know that would materially change our recommendation, ranked by how much it would change it. For the top three unknowns, write one open question each that could be asked naturally in the upcoming conversation without sounding like a survey. Distinguish what we actually know from what we have assumed.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of decision-changing unknowns and three natural questions to close the top ones.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP verifies which items are genuinely known versus assumed by the account team, and chooses which question is worth the meeting time.
activities.requiredContext: Everything currently known about the account and solution context; prior conversation notes; the recommendation you intend to make.
activitySteps: 1. Assemble what is known about the account.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Separate known from assumed.
4. Choose one question to definitely ask.
5. Add it to the conversation plan.
activities.whyThisMatters: The most expensive assumptions are the ones nobody noticed they were making.
