activities.name: Turn the conversation into decisions and commitments
activities.description: Convert meeting notes into what changed, what was agreed, and what the customer actually committed to.
activities.prompt: Here are my notes from the customer conversation: [paste notes or transcript summary]. Produce three separate lists: what we learned that changes our understanding, what was explicitly agreed and by whom, and what remains open. Then draft a short follow-up note to the customer confirming only what was actually agreed. Do not record something as agreed if the notes only show it was discussed. Flag anything ambiguous rather than resolving it.
activities.expectedOutput: Separated lists of learnings, agreements, and open items, plus a short confirming follow-up note.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP confirms that anything recorded as agreed was actually agreed, and owns the follow-up wording before sending. When Sales Agent offers a confirmation card before writing to the opportunity, that card is the last point at which a misheard agreement is still only a note rather than the record everyone downstream works from.
activities.requiredContext: Meeting notes or transcript summary; who attended; what was asked for; the conversation plan you went in with.
activitySteps: 1. Capture notes immediately after the meeting._x000D_
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it._x000D_
3. Check the agreed list against your memory._x000D_
4. Send the follow-up note._x000D_

5. Update the opportunity with what changed. Sales Agent can do this without you leaving the chat - ask it to add a forecast comment or change the close date. It will show a confirmation card setting out exactly what it is about to write._x000D_
6. Read the card against your notes before you confirm. Nothing is committed until you do.
activities.whyThisMatters: Deals slip on the gap between what was discussed and what was agreed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Preparation is the difference between explaining a solution and advancing a decision.
keyTalkingPoints: Prepare discovery questions, proof points, likely objections, role contributions, and a primary/fallback ask. Rehearse where useful.
discussionQuestions: What decision should this conversation advance? What objection is most likely? What proof will you use?
suggestedTransitions: Move from preparation to rehearsal or next customer ask.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Pick one upcoming solution conversation and prepares the brief or rehearsal.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live solution pursuit, solution play, lead list, opportunity, or investment case relevant to this huddle; confirm tool access; review last commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the intended decision from this meeting? What objection is most likely?
listenFor: Listen for meetings framed around content rather than customer decision, objections first discovered live, and unclear ask.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If Agent J.ai is unavailable, role-play manually with one person acting as the customer.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Find the unknown that would change your recommendation, and ask about it in your next conversation.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the question you asked and what the answer changed.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

Sales Home is part of Sales Agent rather than a separate product, and works alongside chat rather than replacing it. In preview for SME&C individual contributors since late July 2026; it does not replace MSX.

secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Sales Home is in preview for SME&C sellers who use MSX, and is enabled for individual contributors only - managers will not see it. Renewal, Campaign, Planning, Realization and Deal Agent integration are roadmap, not available today, so do not build an activity that depends on them.

activities.name: Make each ask specific enough to be accepted
activities.description: Turn a role requirement into an ask a busy colleague can say yes to without a meeting to clarify it.
activities.prompt: From this pursuit orchestration plan [paste], write the individual ask for each role involved. Each ask must state: what specifically is needed, why this pursuit needs that role rather than someone else, what the person receives from me to make it easy, the date it is needed by, and how long it should take. Keep each ask under 80 words. Do not represent funding, approvals, or customer commitments as secured if the plan does not show them as secured.
activities.expectedOutput: One short, specific, dated ask per role, ready to send.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP verifies that no ask overstates funding, approval, or customer commitment status, and owns what is promised in return.
activities.requiredContext: The pursuit orchestration plan; the roles required; what you can supply to each; the customer timeline.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the orchestration plan.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Check each ask states a realistic time commitment.
4. Send the asks.
5. Record who accepted.
activities.whyThisMatters: A vague ask gets a polite yes and no calendar time.

activities.name: Catch the checkpoint that quietly slipped
activities.description: Compare the plan against what has actually happened and surface the dependency nobody has mentioned in two weeks.
activities.prompt: Here is the pursuit orchestration plan with its checkpoints and owners [paste], and here is what has actually happened since [paste updates, meeting notes, or status]. Identify every checkpoint that has passed without evidence of completion, every dependency that has gone quiet, and every owner who has not confirmed. Rank by impact on the customer timeline. For the top item, draft the one message that would restart it. Do not assume something is complete because it was not mentioned.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked list of stalled checkpoints and quiet dependencies, plus one message to restart the highest-impact item.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP confirms an item is genuinely stalled rather than simply undocumented before escalating to an owner.
activities.requiredContext: The orchestration plan with checkpoints and owners, written down even if only informally; recent updates, notes, or status; the customer timeline. If checkpoints and owners do not exist yet, create them before running this activity.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the plan and recent activity. If the plan has no dated checkpoints or owners recorded, write them down first; the activity does not work without them.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Confirm which items are genuinely stalled.
4. Send the restart message for the top one.
5. Reset the checkpoint date.
activities.whyThisMatters: Pursuits rarely stop. They go quiet, and quiet looks like progress until the date arrives.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Pursuits stall at handoffs. Today is about making every role, partner, funding dependency, and checkpoint explicit.
keyTalkingPoints: Name the objective, contributors, asks, owners, dates, dependencies, and escalation points.
discussionQuestions: Which handoff is currently assumed rather than owned? Where could partner or funding support change the path?
suggestedTransitions: Move from orchestration principles to one stalled handoff.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Make one stalled contributor, partner, or funding handoff explicit.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live solution pursuit, solution play, lead list, opportunity, or investment case relevant to this huddle; confirm tool access; review last commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: Which role, partner, or funding dependency is assumed but not owned?
listenFor: Listen for unnamed owners, handoffs without dates, partner input treated as optional, and funding status overstated.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If systems are unavailable, map the contributor chain and identify the break point.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Send one specific, dated ask to each role you need on a live pursuit.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the asks you sent and which were accepted.

activities.name: Test the differentiator against the customer's real decision criteria
activities.description: Pressure-test each claimed differentiator against what this customer actually said they will decide on, and drop the ones that do not connect.
activities.prompt: You are helping a specialist seller sharpen a competitive position. Here is the customer's stated decision criteria and evaluation process: [paste criteria, evaluation team, timeline]. Here are the differentiators we plan to lead with: [paste differentiators and proof]. For each differentiator, state which specific decision criterion it addresses, how directly it addresses it, and what proof the customer would need to accept it. Identify any differentiator that does not map to a stated criterion and recommend dropping or reframing it. Flag any criterion we currently have no answer for. Do not add differentiators that are not in my list.
activities.expectedOutput: A shortened differentiator list mapped to decision criteria, plus a named list of criteria with no current answer.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP confirms the decision criteria are what the customer actually said rather than what the team assumes, and owns the decision to drop a differentiator.
activities.requiredContext: Customer decision criteria and evaluation process; current differentiators and supporting proof; who is on the evaluation team.
activitySteps: 1. Gather the customer's stated decision criteria from meeting notes or MSX.
2. List current differentiators and their proof.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Cut differentiators that do not map to a criterion.
5. Name the gaps you cannot yet answer.
activities.whyThisMatters: A differentiator the customer is not deciding on is noise, however true it is.

activities.name: Rehearse the competitive conversation and build the objection handler
activities.description: Practice the response out loud, then convert what broke into a written objection handler tied to approved proof.
activities.prompt: Play the role of a technical evaluator at [customer] who currently favors [competitor]. I will present our competitive position. Challenge me the way that evaluator would, including on price, migration effort, and lock-in. After three exchanges, stop the role-play and produce an objection handler table: each objection you raised, my response, the approved proof that supports it, and a note where no approved proof exists. Do not soften the objections and do not supply proof I have not given you.
activities.expectedOutput: An objection handler table mapping each objection to a response and the approved proof behind it, with proof gaps named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP judges whether the rehearsed language is accurate, appropriate for this customer, and consistent with approved competitive guidance before using it externally.
activities.requiredContext: Competitive position and differentiators; the competitor in play; approved competitive proof sources; known evaluator concerns; customer role you will be speaking to.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the differentiator list from the previous activity and the approved competitive proof.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run a short rehearsal with the agent as the skeptical evaluator.
4. Have it produce the objection handler table.
5. Fill or remove any row where proof is missing.
6. Bring the table to the huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: Competitive conversations are lost in the moment, not in the brief.

activities.name: Convert the competitive position into the next customer step
activities.description: Turn the position into a concrete next action in the opportunity rather than a document that stops at the brief.
activities.prompt: Using this competitive position and the customer's decision criteria [paste], propose the single next step that would most reduce competitive risk in this opportunity. Then draft the short note I would send to the customer to set it up. Keep the note under 120 words and do not overstate what we have proven.

activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP owns the choice of next step and the customer-facing wording, and confirms it fits the account team's plan before sending.
activities.requiredContext: Tested differentiators and open gaps; opportunity stage and close plan; who owns the customer relationship.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the tested differentiator list and the open gaps.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Pick one next step.
4. Adjust the draft note in your own voice.
5. Record the next step in the opportunity.
activities.whyThisMatters: A competitive brief that does not change the next customer interaction has not changed the deal.

activities.name: Build a reusable objection and language library from real calls
activities.description: Mine your own customer conversations for the objections and language that keep recurring, and turn them into something the team can reuse.
activities.prompt: Work across my customer meeting transcripts and mail from the last quarter for [solution area]. Identify the objections that keep recurring, the language customers actually use to describe the problem we solve, the competitor claims that come up, and the points where conversations stall. Group them by how often they appear. For each recurring objection, show me the customer's own words rather than a paraphrase, and note which conversations it came from so I can go back to the source.
activities.expectedOutput: An objection and customer-language library grouped by frequency, quoted in the customer's own words, traceable back to source conversations.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SSP verifies the quotes against the source conversation, removes anything customer-identifying before sharing, and decides what is safe to circulate beyond the account team.
activities.requiredContext: Approved access to your own meeting transcripts and mail; the solution area in scope; a quarter or more of conversations.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm you can reach your own meeting transcripts and mail for this solution area.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Check the recurring objections against your own memory of those calls before treating them as a pattern.
5. Keep the customer language the customer actually used rather than rewriting it into product language.
6. Share the library with your solution area only after removing customer-identifying detail.
activities.whyThisMatters: The most useful competitive content is already sitting in conversations you have had. Reading a quarter of transcripts by hand is not realistic, which is why this pattern only became available recently.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Competitive response should be built on customer context and proof, not generic battlecards.
keyTalkingPoints: Use current approved competitive evidence, win/loss context, differentiators, objections, risks, and review flags.
discussionQuestions: Which competitor or alternative is shaping the decision? What proof is strongest and where is it weak?
suggestedTransitions: Move from competitor context to one proof-backed response plan.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Build one proof-backed competitive response for a live pursuit.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live solution pursuit, solution play, lead list, opportunity, or investment case relevant to this huddle; confirm tool access; review last commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: Which competitive claim matters to the customer decision? What proof supports it?
listenFor: Listen for stale battlecard claims, unsupported competitor statements, and differentiators not tied to customer priorities.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If current sources are unavailable, separate what is known, assumed, and requiring Researcher/SME validation.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Build one objection handler tied to approved proof, and use it in a live conversation.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the handler, the objection it met, and whether the proof held.

activities.description: Rewrite the close plan as the customer's path to their outcome, so it can be shared with them rather than kept internal.

SE-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand how the SE huddle path runs and which human checkpoints protect technical accuracy.
SE-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
SE-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: SEs know how the huddle motion works, which tools may show up, what to review, and what AI experiences to bring back before next week.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This huddle sets the working contract for SE use of AI: faster assembly, stronger evidence checks, and explicit human accountability.
keyTalkingPoints: The huddle motion is workflow-led, not a tool demo.
AI can assemble briefs, options, responses, and reusable packages, but SEs keep technical judgment and customer commitments.
Each huddle ends with one small test on live or sanitized work.
discussionQuestions: Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted technical output?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the workflow-discovery prompt below. Week 1 is for finding the recurring work worth automating.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the tools named for this path, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
facilitatorQuestions: Which technical work do you repeat every week without thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where must the SE judgment stay human no matter how good the output gets?
listenFor: Listen for unvoiced scepticism, access blockers stated as disinterest, the assumption that this is a tool rollout, and people who describe only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat. The recurring, unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the discovery conversation and record access blockers separately from interest. The discovery prompt can be run in whichever tool the person already has.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

"I am a Solution Engineer at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with."
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation, or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

SE-ORIENT.keyTakeaway: The point of the motion is better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Technical responses move faster when supported answers, assumptions, confidence, exceptions, and required reviewers are visible.
keyTalkingPoints: Answer with sources and confidence, not just fluency.
Preserve unsupported areas instead of smoothing them over.
Use the response package to route review, not to bypass it.
discussionQuestions: Which technical answer needs evidence before it can be used?
Where do we usually hide uncertainty?
Who must review the response before it goes to the customer?
suggestedTransitions: Move from answer drafting to response governance and exception routing.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to one technical answer matrix or exception list with reviewer flags.
preparationChecklist: Bring one RFP question, security or architecture questionnaire item, technical ask, or objection that requires a governed response.
facilitatorQuestions: Which answer is most consequential?
What source supports it?
Where should the response show confidence, caveat, exception, or SME-needed flag?
listenFor: Listen for confident but unsourced answers, hidden uncertainty, overbroad commitments, and missing reviewers.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If sources are not approved, create the exception list and reviewer path instead of drafting final language.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Prepare one technical conversation by finding the unknown that would change your recommendation.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the unknown you found and the question you used to close it.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Write, explain, refactor and test code; scaffold infrastructure-as-code and deployment artifacts; build the smallest spike that proves or disproves an architecture assumption; generate sample data and validation scripts; and reproduce a reported failure so you can see it rather than describe it.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the next step is to build something rather than to plan or describe it. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Architecture validation works best when options, criteria, assumptions, and risks are visible before the technical debate starts.
keyTalkingPoints: Compare options against the agreed decision criteria.
Name the assumptions and validation steps, not just the recommended design.
Use AI to assemble evidence and decision records while keeping architecture judgment human.
discussionQuestions: Which architecture assumption would hurt most if wrong?
What criteria will decide between options?
What validation step should happen before the customer sees the recommendation?
suggestedTransitions: Move from option comparison to creating the architecture decision record.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to one architecture assumption or option you will validate against agreed criteria.
preparationChecklist: Bring one architecture decision, relevant customer criteria, approved technical sources, and known constraints.
facilitatorQuestions: Which option should be compared, and against what criteria?
Which assumption needs validation first?
What would make the architecture recommendation unsafe to share?
listenFor: Listen for unchallenged assumptions, uncited guidance, missing security or operations review, and options that are not tied to criteria.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If authoritative sources are unavailable, identify required sources and reviewers before drafting.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Design one solution and name the constraint that most limits it.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the design and the constraint you validated.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A demo or workshop should advance a customer decision, not tour a product. Today narrows the experience to proof that matters.
keyTalkingPoints: Anchor the experience in the customer scenario and decision.
Prepare evidence, objections, roles, environment needs, and fallback plan.
Do not rely on demo energy to cover unclear criteria.
discussionQuestions: What decision should the demo or workshop make easier?
Which scenario proves the most important customer concern?
Where could environment, permission, or data issues derail the experience?
suggestedTransitions: Move from scenario selection to the demo or workshop plan.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to one demo or workshop plan tied to a specific customer decision.
preparationChecklist: Bring one demo, workshop, or technical customer session and the decision it needs to advance.
facilitatorQuestions: What decision should the demo or workshop advance?
Which scenario proves that decision?
What could fail because of data, tenant, permission, or environment constraints?
listenFor: Listen for feature tours, unclear audience, unsupported claims, missing fallback plans, and proof not tied to criteria.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the environment is unavailable, build the plan and mark environment validation as the human checkpoint.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Build one demo or workshop around the customer's decision rather than the product's features.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what you cut and what the customer actually asked about.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

Sales Home is part of Sales Agent rather than a separate product, and works alongside chat rather than replacing it. In preview for SME&C individual contributors since late July 2026; it does not replace MSX.

secondaryAgents.name: GitHub Copilot
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: AI pair programmer available in VS Code, the CLI and the GitHub Copilot app. It works against a repository or a working folder rather than against your mail and meetings.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Write, explain, refactor and test code; scaffold infrastructure-as-code and deployment artifacts; build the smallest spike that proves or disproves an architecture assumption; generate sample data and validation scripts; and reproduce a reported failure so you can see it rather than describe it.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the next step is to build something rather than to plan or describe it. Validating an architecture assumption with a spike, standing up a demo or workshop environment, iterating a proof of concept, reproducing a deployment or integration failure, or packaging a reusable asset with tests and setup steps.
keyBenefits: Turns a technical opinion into evidence. A spike that takes twenty minutes settles an argument that would otherwise run for a week, and a reproduced failure is a fact the account team can act on rather than a claim the customer has to accept.
secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for customer, market or account research; that is Researcher. Do not use it to assemble a customer-facing document or deck; that is Cowork. Do not point it at production without the review your team already requires, and do not paste customer data into it. It works on code and configuration, not on the CRM record.
stepsToGetStarted: Use it where the code already is: the Copilot extension in VS Code, the gh copilot CLI, or the GitHub Copilot app in the browser for work not tied to a local checkout. Open the repository or folder first so it has the context. Start with: Explain what this deployment does, then write the smallest test that would prove the assumption I am least sure about.

activities.prompt: Create a PoC plan for [technical decision]. Define hypothesis, in-scope scenario, success and exit criteria, milestones, data and environment needs, roles, risks, dependencies, review gates, final decision and handoff if successful.

activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides whether the proof is necessary at all. A proof absorbs weeks of engineering time, and the ones that were never going to change a decision are the most expensive thing on the calendar.
activities.requiredContext: Technical decision; constraints; resources.
activities.whyThisMatters: A small, criteria-led PoC reduces waste and makes the exit decision clear before work starts.

activities.name: Pressure-test PoC readiness
activities.description: Review a proposed PoC plan for gaps and ambiguity.
activities.prompt: Review this PoC plan. Identify vague success criteria, unowned dependencies, unrealistic milestones, missing security or data assumptions, weak linkage to the customer decision and unclear exit paths. Return five review questions and the smallest revisions needed.
activities.expectedOutput: Readiness review and revision list.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE owns the go or no-go call and confirms the required reviewers have seen the plan before it is called ready. A readiness checklist can be entirely green while the one thing that will actually break the proof was never on it, and that thing is usually known to the engineer rather than to the checklist.
activities.requiredContext: Proposed PoC plan.
activities.whyThisMatters: Readiness issues should be found in planning, not after the customer expects a proof.

activities.name: Validate PoC success and exit criteria
activities.description: Test whether the PoC has measurable success criteria and a real exit condition, or whether it will quietly become a project.
activities.prompt: Review the PoC plan for measurable success criteria, exit conditions, dependencies, security or data assumptions, milestones, and owner clarity.
activities.expectedOutput: PoC criteria and readiness review.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE owns the exit criteria and sets them before the PoC starts. A proof without a defined exit runs until someone loses patience, and then it proves nothing either way.
activities.requiredContext: The PoC plan with its stated criteria; the data and environment assumptions; the owner of the exit decision.
activities.whyThisMatters: Measurable success and exit criteria prevent the PoC from becoming open-ended work.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A PoC is valuable only if it has a bounded hypothesis, success criteria, and an exit decision before work starts.
keyTalkingPoints: Define the smallest useful proof.
Make success, exit, milestones, owners, dependencies, and review gates observable.
Pressure-test readiness before the customer or delivery team absorbs ambiguity.
discussionQuestions: What is the smallest proof that would answer the technical decision?
Which success criterion is too vague?
What should trigger exit, handoff, or no-go?
suggestedTransitions: Move from proof idea to readiness pressure test.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to one PoC scope revision that improves success criteria, dependencies, or exit path.
preparationChecklist: Bring one proposed PoC or proof motion, constraints, resources, dependencies, and desired technical decision.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the smallest useful proof?
Which success criterion is measurable?
Which dependency or owner is missing?
listenFor: Listen for vague success criteria, PoCs that duplicate demo work, unowned dependencies, and no exit path.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If customer data or resources are unavailable, use the missing dependency as the main readiness finding.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Scope one proof with success criteria and a stop condition agreed before it starts.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the criteria, the stop condition, and who agreed to them.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Discovery should end with decision criteria, not a second discovery meeting. Today focuses on making the customer decision explicit early.
keyTalkingPoints: Start from the customer decision and work backward to criteria and evidence.
Separate sourced facts from hypotheses and open questions.
Capture what must be validated before architecture, demo, or PoC work begins.
discussionQuestions: Which decision is the customer actually trying to make?
What evidence gap would make the next technical step unsafe?
What criteria need to be agreed rather than inferred?
suggestedTransitions: Move from discovery discussion to building the actual decision-criteria brief.

facilitatorQuestions: Which discovery question would most change the technical decision?

facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, draft the criteria and evidence-gap structure manually.

facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Run one discovery conversation with the decision criteria written down before you go in.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Monitor technical blockers across your accounts between reviews
activities.description: Set up a standing watch on the technical signals that predict a stalled deployment, so intervention happens before the review rather than at it.
activities.prompt: Set up a recurring check across the accounts I support. Surface where deployment or consumption has flattened or declined, where a technical blocker has been open longer than expected, where a support pattern suggests an unresolved architectural issue, and where a planned milestone has slipped without a new date. For each, state the technical hypothesis and the evidence behind it, and name what you would need to confirm it. Do not diagnose root cause with confidence you do not have.
activities.expectedOutput: A recurring technical risk list with a stated hypothesis, supporting evidence, and the confirmation step for each item.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SE validates each hypothesis technically before raising it with the customer or the account team, and corrects any signal that reflects a known planned change.
activities.requiredContext: The accounts you support; access to deployment, consumption and support signals; the committed technical milestones.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm which deployment, consumption and support signals you can reach for the accounts you support.
2. Run the prompt.
3. Review each technical hypothesis and check the evidence actually supports it.
4. Set the cadence to land before your account or delivery review.
5. Confirm any blocker technically yourself before raising it with the customer.
activities.whyThisMatters: Technical blockers are cheapest to fix early and most expensive to fix at a review. The signal is usually present weeks before anyone names the problem.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Technical risk should be named while it is still a decision, not after it becomes a customer escalation.
keyTalkingPoints: Inspect exit criteria, blockers, proof gaps, objections, dependencies, and handoffs.
Every risk needs evidence, owner, mitigation, checkpoint, and next decision.
Use AI to surface signals, but use SE judgment to prioritize them.
discussionQuestions: What technical risk is blocking progression right now?
Which proof gap is being treated as if it were already closed?
Who owns the next technical action?
suggestedTransitions: Move from risk naming to action plan and handoff.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one technical risk, the evidence needed, the owner, and the next checkpoint.
preparationChecklist: Bring one opportunity or technical workstream with a blocker, proof gap, objection, or dependency.
facilitatorQuestions: Which technical risk is blocking progression?
What evidence would clear or confirm it?
Who owns the mitigation and next checkpoint?
listenFor: Listen for risks without owners, proof gaps treated as closed, delivery handoffs without requirements, and blockers framed too broadly.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If opportunity context is unavailable, build the risk register from known facts and flag missing source context.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Identify one technical risk early enough to be a conversation rather than an escalation.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the risk, when you found it, and what you did about it.

secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the next step is to build something rather than to plan or describe it. keyBenefits: Turns a technical opinion into evidence. A spike that takes twenty minutes settles an argument that would otherwise run for a week, and a reproduced failure is a fact the account team can act on rather than a claim the customer has to accept.
secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for customer, market or account research; that is Researcher. Do not use it to assemble a customer-facing document or deck; that is Cowork. stepsToGetStarted: Use it where the code already is: the Copilot extension in VS Code, the gh copilot CLI, or the GitHub Copilot app in the browser for work not tied to a local checkout. Open the repository or folder first so it has the context. Start with: Explain what this deployment does, then write the smallest test that would prove the assumption I am least sure about.

agents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for customer, market or account research; that is Researcher. Do not use it to assemble a customer-facing document or deck; that is Cowork. CE-ORIENT.roleTopicDescription: Introduce the eight-session huddle motion, where AI supports commercial work, where its boundaries sit, which tools may appear, and what to review before next week's topic.
CE-ORIENT.wiifm: Commercial work has the least tolerance for AI error. This session sets out where the boundaries are before you rely on anything.
CE-ORIENT.name: Frontier Accelerator Orientation
CE-ORIENT.description: Introduces the motion, the huddle format, the AI tools in scope, and what team members are expected to try between sessions.

CE-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand how the CE huddle path runs and where the boundaries sit for AI in commercial work.
CE-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
CE-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: CEs know how the huddle motion works, which tools may show up, what to review, and what AI experiences to bring back before next week.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This is the session that explains the rest. Be honest about scepticism now rather than carrying it for eight weeks.
keyTalkingPoints: Huddles are 30 minutes and workflow-led, not tool demos.
Every session ends with one thing you will try.
Human judgment stays explicit at every step. That is the point, not a caveat.
discussionQuestions: Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted commercial output?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the workflow-discovery prompt below. Week 1 is for finding the recurring work worth automating.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the tools named for this path, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
facilitatorQuestions: Which commercial work do you repeat every week without thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where must the CE judgment stay human no matter how good the output gets?
listenFor: Listen for unvoiced scepticism, access blockers stated as disinterest, the assumption that this is a tool rollout, and people who describe only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat. The recurring, unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the discovery conversation and record access blockers separately from interest. The discovery prompt can be run in whichever tool the person already has.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

"I am a Commercial Executive at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with."
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation, or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

CE-ORIENT.keyTakeaway: The point of the motion is better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Risk you find this week is a conversation. The same risk found by the customer is an escalation. Today is about finding it earlier.
keyTalkingPoints: A health score can tell you something is wrong. It rarely tells you what to do.
Every risk needs an owner and a date or it is an observation.
AI is good at surfacing signal. Prioritizing it is judgment.
discussionQuestions: Which account is at risk in a way the reporting does not show?
What stops a known risk from getting an owner?
Which part of this carries policy or precedent risk?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how risk surfaces to one account that is actually at risk now.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one risk, one intervention and one owner.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm tool access for this huddle, bring one real commercial structure and policy example you are working on now, and review the commitment you made last week.
facilitatorQuestions: Which activity here is closest to what you are working on this week?
What would you need to see before you trusted the output?
Where would this break in your real commercial structure and policy work?
listenFor: Through the lens of commercial structure and policy, listen for: risk described without an owner or a date; health reported by score rather than cause; and interventions discussed but never started.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If status data is unavailable, work from what people know and note where the evidence should have come from.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Rank your commercial risks, then take the top one to its owner with a proposed intervention.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the risk, the intervention, and the authoritative source behind it.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Commercial structure decides whether a deal can move. Today is about comparing options before the structure hardens.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is not to create an offer. The goal is to compare viable structures, surface trade-offs, and name the approval path while options still exist.
discussionQuestions: What option is the deal implicitly assuming? Which approval or exception would surprise the team later? What trade-off should be explicit before negotiation?
suggestedTransitions: Move from possible structures to the smallest options matrix that makes the decision clearer.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Create one commercial options matrix and names the approval path or missing evidence.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live opportunity, approved commercial context, known constraints, and the current approval or exception question.
facilitatorQuestions: Which commercial option is most plausible? What trade-off would change the decision? Where would this break if an approval requirement appears late?
listenFor: Listen for: one default structure being treated as the only option; approval path ambiguity; pricing, term, or concession trade-offs not stated; and assumptions that need CE or Deal Desk review.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, build the options matrix manually and name the missing source evidence.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Build a commercial options matrix for one live deal and identify which option needs approval you do not hold.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the options, the trade-offs, and the approval requirement you found.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Reviewers do not need more history. They need the recommendation, options, assumptions, risks, and decision requested.
keyTalkingPoints: A commercial decision narrative should separate facts from judgment. It should show why this structure, what alternatives were considered, and who must review it.
discussionQuestions: What would a reviewer need to say yes, no, or not yet? Which assumption is unsupported? What customer impact needs to be explained plainly?
suggestedTransitions: Move from deal facts to the internal recommendation and the decision being requested.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Draft one commercial decision narrative with options, assumption flags, and required reviewers.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring a reviewed deal option, known assumptions, transition considerations, and the audience for the recommendation.
facilitatorQuestions: Which recommendation would a reviewer understand quickly? What assumption needs evidence? Which reviewer or decision owner is missing?
listenFor: Listen for: narratives that bury the ask; options without trade-offs; customer impact omitted; and transition or migration risks stated without a source.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, draft the decision narrative outline and identify the evidence gaps.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Write the commercial recommendation for one deal in a form a reviewer could act on without asking you a question.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the recommendation and the assumption a reviewer challenged.

activities.name: Build an MCA-E proposal from a validated product list you already have
activities.description: Bring your own product data into proposal creation for an MCA-E or EA to MCA-E transition, and resolve what does not map before it reaches the customer.
activities.prompt: I have product and quantity data for an MCA-E proposal in a spreadsheet. Walk me through bringing it in: what format you need, how you will validate the SKUs and products against the agreement, and what happens to anything that does not match. Then generate the draft proposal in MSX from the validated inputs. List every unmatched product separately so I can resolve it, and tell me if the upload has to be split across multiple proposals to stay within platform limits. Do not drop unmatched items silently.
activities.expectedOutput: A validated input set, a named list of unmatched products for follow-up, and a draft proposal in MSX ready for commercial review.
activities.humanCheckpoint: CE confirms the SKU mapping is commercially correct rather than merely valid, resolves unmatched products rather than accepting the gap, and owns the pricing and structure before the proposal reaches the customer.
activities.requiredContext: Product and quantity data in Excel or CSV. The MCA-E agreement or the EA being transitioned. The opportunity the proposal attaches to.
activitySteps: 1. Prepare the product and quantity data as Excel or CSV.
2. Run the prompt and follow the validation guidance.
3. Review the unmatched product list; those are the ones that will cause problems later.
4. Resolve or consciously defer each one.
5. Generate the draft proposal in MSX.
6. Check the proposal against the customer's actual commercial expectation before it goes anywhere.
activities.whyThisMatters: Unmatched products found before proposal creation are a cleanup task. Found after, they are a customer conversation.

activities.name: Rehearse the commercial negotiation
activities.description: Practice objections, value trades and decision control.
activities.prompt: Role-play the upcoming commercial negotiation using the approved plan. Simulate realistic customer objections and requests. Pause for my response, then coach clarity, value trading, concession discipline, policy boundaries and the next decision. Do not invent terms or authority.
activities.expectedOutput: Negotiation rehearsal and coaching actions.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE owns every position rehearsed. Practice makes a concession sound available whether or not it has been approved, and in a live negotiation that distinction disappears.
activities.requiredContext: Approved negotiation plan.
activities.whyThisMatters: Ten minutes rehearsing the commercial negotiation is cheaper than improvising it in the room.
