activities.name: Stress-test negotiation assumptions
activities.description: Test the concession logic and authority boundaries in a negotiation plan before customer pressure exposes them.
activities.prompt: Review the negotiation plan for unsupported commercial assumptions, customer constraints, policy dependencies, approval needs, concession risks, and unresolved authority boundaries.
activities.expectedOutput: Negotiation assumption register with authority gaps, concession risks, and required decisions.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE owns the concession authority boundary. Entering a negotiation unclear about what can be conceded without approval is how unapproved cost gets absorbed, and that boundary is set by policy rather than by the deal.
activities.requiredContext: The negotiation plan with its concession logic; your confirmed authority limits; known customer constraints and alternatives.
activities.whyThisMatters: If the negotiation position will fail, it should fail in rehearsal rather than across the table.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Negotiation is where vague structure becomes expensive. Today is about authority boundaries, give/get logic, and rehearsal before the customer asks.
keyTalkingPoints: The agent can help prepare scenarios and objections. The CE stays accountable for authority, customer commitments, concession discipline, and escalation triggers.
discussionQuestions: Where is your concession logic unclear? Which customer ask would trigger escalation? What must not be said before review?
suggestedTransitions: Move from negotiation principles to one realistic customer objection and the reviewed response.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Rehearse one negotiation scenario and identifies authority, concession, and review boundaries.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one negotiation scenario, approved position, authority boundaries, and any known customer asks.
facilitatorQuestions: Which customer ask would test your authority boundary? What give/get logic is clear enough to use? What must be reviewed before customer-facing use?
listenFor: Listen for: concession logic that is not tied to value; authority boundaries not explicit; likely objections unrehearsed; and customer commitments that require review.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If role-play tooling is unavailable, rehearse manually using the approved negotiation plan.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Prepare one negotiation with your concession boundaries and escalation triggers set before the conversation.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the plan, what you would not concede, and what actually happened.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Commercial execution stalls when owners, evidence, and approval handoffs are implied. Today is about making them explicit.
keyTalkingPoints: Execution is not just follow-up. It is approval routing, evidence readiness, exception handling, ownership, and escalation without overstating authority.
discussionQuestions: Which handoff is implicit today? What evidence is missing for the next approver? Where could ECIF, Deal Desk, finance, policy, or legal review be needed?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the full execution path to the single blocker and owner that must be handled next.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one approval or execution blocker, its owner, evidence needed, and next governed action.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one in-flight deal or investment dependency, its known approval stage, and the evidence or owner currently missing.
facilitatorQuestions: Which handoff or approval is the deal actually waiting on? What evidence is missing? Who owns the next decision, and what should not be represented as approved?
listenFor: Listen for: approval status overstated; handoffs without owners; ECIF, finance, Deal Desk, legal, or policy dependencies hidden; and blockers described without the next governed action.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized scenario. If systems are unavailable, map the route, owner, evidence, and next decision without inferring approval state.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Map the approval path for one deal and confirm the first owner knows it is coming.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the path, the owners, and the blocker you cleared.

primaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. When it offers a confirmation card before creating or changing an MSX record, read what it is about to write rather than confirming by reflex - nothing is committed until you tap, and that tap is the only check on it.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Microsoft 365 Copilot in Teams or Outlook, or install the Microsoft 365 Copilot app on your phone. Use the agent picker to find and select Sales; no separate install is required. Start a new chat with a deal prompt such as: List my upcoming renewals this quarter. Deal Agent triggers automatically. Keep one chat thread per deal so the context stays clean. On mobile, name the account or opportunity explicitly - Sales Agent is sharpest when pointed at a specific record. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

activities.name: Build the CE-led renewal strategy view
activities.description: Surface renewal economics, risk and expansion early.
activities.prompt: For [account name or TPID], show the upcoming renewals with expiry dates and current agreement details, then for the agreement I name provide the license estate grouped by SKU, the SKUs whose discount is between 40 and 60 percent, and ACR trends month over month. Build a CE-led renewal strategy view covering structure, MACC trajectory, consumption signals, current discounts and concessions, risk, expansion potential, and amendments in play. Separate what the source systems returned from what you inferred, and do not represent any concession or discount as approved.
activities.expectedOutput: Renewal strategy brief with commercial structure, risk, expansion potential, approval path, and evidence gaps.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE reads the contract itself rather than a summary of it. Renewal terms carry conditions that summaries drop, and the dropped condition is usually the one that decides the strategy.
activities.requiredContext: Account and approved renewal context.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most of the effort in the renewal strategy view is assembly. The strategy decision stays human-led.

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

activities.name: Inspect upcoming renewal portfolio for CE intervention
activities.description: Prioritize renewals requiring CE intervention.
activities.prompt: Show upcoming renewals in the selected period for my scope. Prioritize by revenue, discount exposure, consumption or MACC risk, execution complexity, expansion potential, approval requirements, and evidence quality. Explain the certified signal behind each priority.
activities.expectedOutput: Prioritized renewal radar with intervention rationale, evidence quality, and missing data.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE decides which renewals genuinely need commercial intervention. Every renewal can be made to look like it needs attention, and spreading commercial time across all of them is how the one that needed it gets missed.
activities.requiredContext: Approved renewal report and scope.
activities.whyThisMatters: Reviewing the renewal portfolio is judgment work. The agent proposes; the CE stays accountable.

activities.name: Watch the renewal portfolio for commercial trigger dates
activities.description: Set up a standing check across your renewal portfolio so commercial trigger dates surface with enough runway to act on them.
activities.prompt: Set up a recurring check across my renewal portfolio. Each week, tell me which agreements are approaching a commercial trigger date, which have consumption or usage moving in a direction that changes the commercial position, and which have an approval dependency that has not started yet. Rank by how much runway is left rather than by value. Do not interpret pricing or policy; where a question needs an authoritative answer, name the owner instead.
activities.expectedOutput: A recurring portfolio check ranked by remaining runway, with approval dependencies and the owner for each open question.
activities.humanCheckpoint: CE confirms the commercial reading of every flagged item and routes pricing, discount and policy interpretation to the accountable owner rather than acting on the output.
activities.requiredContext: Your renewal portfolio with dates; approved consumption and usage data; the current approval requirements.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your renewal portfolio with dates and the current approval requirements.
2. Run the prompt.
3. Confirm the runway ranking matches your own read on which renewals are genuinely tight.
4. Set the cadence far enough ahead of approval lead times to be useful.
5. Route pricing, discount and policy questions to the accountable owner rather than answering them yourself.
activities.whyThisMatters: Commercial leverage is a function of how early you saw it coming. A renewal found with three weeks left is a different negotiation from the same renewal found with three months.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Renewal risk is visible before the renewal date if commercial structure, value evidence, and approval needs are inspected early.
keyTalkingPoints: A renewal is not only a date. It is a commercial strategy with structure, risk, expansion potential, concessions, and approval path.
discussionQuestions: Which renewal risk is already visible? What expansion is supported by evidence? What approval or structure question should not wait?
suggestedTransitions: Move from renewal principles to one renewal actually on the horizon.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one renewal risk, one supported expansion hypothesis, and the approval or structure question to resolve.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one renewal, approved context, current structure, risk signal, and expansion or approval question.
facilitatorQuestions: Which activity here is closest to what you are working on this week?
What would you need to see before you trusted the output?
Where would this break in your real commercial structure and policy work?
listenFor: Through the lens of commercial structure and policy, listen for: renewals treated as administrative; risk noticed inside the last quarter; and expansion pursued without evidence of realized value.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If data is unavailable, work the renewal from what the team knows and note the evidence gaps.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Build a renewal strategy for one account using real agreement and discount data, not recollection.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the strategy, the data you retrieved, and the expansion you found or ruled out.

activities.name: Track commercial policy and licensing changes that affect your accounts
activities.description: Set up a monitored, source-locked watch on the commercial policy and licensing guidance you rely on, so changes reach you before a customer raises them.
activities.prompt: Set up a recurring check against a fixed list of authoritative Microsoft commercial policy and licensing sources that I will confirm with you first. Each time, report only what has changed, quote the change, cite the source, and state plainly which of my accounts it plausibly affects and why. Do not interpret the change into commercial advice and do not draw on any source outside the confirmed list. Where the implication is unclear, say so and name the owner who can rule on it.
activities.expectedOutput: A recurring change-only digest quoting and citing each change, with plausible account impact and the named owner for anything requiring a ruling.
activities.humanCheckpoint: CE confirms the source list before the watch is enabled, and routes every interpretation to the accountable policy owner rather than acting on the summary.
activities.requiredContext: The authoritative policy and licensing sources your team treats as canonical; your account list; your escalation owners.
activitySteps: 1. Agree the fixed list of authoritative policy and licensing sources with your team before you enable anything.
2. Run the prompt with that confirmed list.
3. Check the first digest quotes and cites each change rather than paraphrasing it.
4. Set the cadence and confirm the watch is not drawing on sources outside the agreed list.
5. Route every interpretation to the accountable policy owner rather than acting on the summary.
activities.whyThisMatters: Commercial policy changes are only a problem when the customer knows before you do. A locked source list is what separates a reliable watch from confident invention.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Policy questions found at approval cost weeks. Today is about finding the question early and routing it to the authoritative owner.
keyTalkingPoints: AI can assemble the context and possible questions. It cannot interpret policy, approve exceptions, or invent authority. The useful output is a routed question with evidence, not a guessed answer.
discussionQuestions: Which policy or licensing question most often causes rework? Where did an approval path surprise you? Which interpretation must come from an authoritative source?
suggestedTransitions: Move from policy categories to one live deal question and the owner who can answer it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Route one policy, licensing, or approval question to an authoritative owner with the evidence needed.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one real commercial structure or policy example, the approved source you would check, and the decision or approval path currently unclear.
facilitatorQuestions: Which Practice helps you route the policy or licensing question fastest? What would you need to see before trusting the output? Where must the answer come from an authoritative owner instead of AI?
listenFor: Through the lens of commercial structure and policy, listen for: policy interpreted from memory; uncertainty left unflagged; approval paths discovered late; and questions that need an authoritative owner rather than a generated answer.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If guidance is unavailable, list the questions, required evidence, and routing owner. Do not guess the answer.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Take one open policy or licensing question to its authoritative owner rather than answering it yourself.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the question, the owner, and the answer you received.

CSA-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand how the CSA huddle path runs and where AI fits customer architecture and delivery.
CSA-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
CSA-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: CSAs know how the huddle motion works, which tools may show up, what to review, and what AI experiences to bring back before next week.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This is the session that explains the rest. Be honest about scepticism now rather than carrying it for eight weeks.
keyTalkingPoints: Huddles are 30 minutes and workflow-led, not tool demos.
Every session ends with one thing you will try.
Human judgment stays explicit at every step. That is the point, not a caveat.
discussionQuestions: Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted architecture or delivery output?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the workflow-discovery prompt below. Week 1 is for finding the recurring work worth automating.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the tools named for this path, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
facilitatorQuestions: Which architecture or delivery work do you repeat every week without thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where must the CSA judgment stay human no matter how good the output gets?
listenFor: Listen for unvoiced scepticism, access blockers stated as disinterest, the assumption that this is a tool rollout, and people who describe only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat. The recurring, unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the discovery conversation and record access blockers separately from interest. The discovery prompt can be run in whichever tool the person already has.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

"I am a Cloud Solution Architect at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with."
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation, or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

CSA-ORIENT.keyTakeaway: The point of the motion is better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

activities.name: Analyze consumption trajectory and shortfall drivers
activities.description: Ask what certified consumption data says.
activities.prompt: For [Customer] and [period], analyze enabled consumption trajectory and compare it with the relevant plan or milestone view. Break down largest changes by available dimension, identify data-supported contributors to potential shortfall, show supporting metrics and state what the report cannot answer.
activities.expectedOutput: Consumption trajectory analysis.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms what the consumption figure actually counts. Similarly named measures include different workloads, and a shortfall diagnosed from the wrong measure sends the intervention to the wrong place.
activities.requiredContext: Enabled certified report; customer; period.
activities.whyThisMatters: Working through consumption trajectory and shortfall drivers forces a position, and a position is what the decision needs.

activities.description: Connect customer context to intervention planning.
activities.prompt: Using approved consumption analysis and available context for [Customer], identify technical blockers, workload milestones, stakeholders, commitments and dependencies relevant to the potential shortfall. Propose intervention options, owner candidates, customer touchpoints and evidence needed. Do not assume cause or make commitments.
activities.expectedOutput: Intervention options with evidence, owners and gaps.

activities.requiredContext: Approved analysis and authorized context.
activities.whyThisMatters: Settling a technical shortfall intervention before the work starts is the only version of that decision that holds.

activities.name: Validate the consumption gap analysis
activities.description: Test whether the consumption gap has been traced to a real technical cause or to a plausible-sounding assumption.
activities.prompt: Review the consumption analysis. For each shortfall, state the technical cause proposed, the signal that evidences that cause, and the alternative explanations that have not been ruled out. Identify which gaps are technically caused, which are commercial or customer-driven, and which are still unexplained.
activities.expectedOutput: A consumption gap analysis separating evidenced technical causes from unruled-out alternatives and non-technical drivers.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA separates technically caused shortfalls from commercial or customer-driven ones. A technical intervention applied to a commercial problem consumes weeks and changes nothing, and the distinction is rarely visible in telemetry alone.
activities.requiredContext: The consumption position against plan; the telemetry and deployment signals behind it; known customer events that affect usage.
activities.whyThisMatters: Confirming the technical health evidence for Forecast Consumption and Intervene on Shortfall Risk now costs a conversation. Discovering it late costs a decision.

activities.name: Design the consumption intervention plan
activities.description: Build the intervention that changes the consumption trajectory, with the owner and the checkpoint that will show whether it moved.
activities.prompt: Turn the evidenced consumption causes into an intervention plan. For each, define the technical action, who owns it on both sides, the dependency that could block it, the date you would expect to see movement, and the telemetry that would confirm it. Rank by the size of the gap each one closes.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked consumption intervention plan with owners, blocking dependencies, expected movement dates, and confirming telemetry.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA confirms the customer-side owner exists before the intervention plan is used. Consumption interventions depend on customer action, and a plan with an unconfirmed owner on the other side simply does not start.
activities.requiredContext: The validated consumption causes; the deployment and architecture levers available; the customer owners for each dependency.
activities.whyThisMatters: Settling the technical intervention plan for Forecast Consumption and Intervene on Shortfall Risk before the work starts is the only version of that decision that holds.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Most of us have at some point defended a number we were not fully sure about. Today is about fixing the signal, not the spreadsheet.
keyTalkingPoints: A gap is usually three problems wearing one label: not enough, not moving, or dated wrong.
Certified data settles arguments opinion cannot.
Correction is judgment work. The agent proposes, you decide.
discussionQuestions: Where do consumption or usage signals become technical work for you?
Which shortfall signal is most likely to hide a technical cause?
What evidence would you need before owning an intervention?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the report signal to one technical cause or blocker that can be validated this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one consumption signal you will validate and one technical question you will answer.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the relevant certified report, bring one consumption or usage signal you are reviewing, and note what technical context the report does not show.
facilitatorQuestions: Which consumption or shortfall activity is closest to what you inspect today?
What would you need to verify before trusting the signal?
Where would this break if the report lacks architecture context?
listenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: report signals separated from technical cause; assumptions about customer intent; missing owners; and interventions that require architecture or workload context.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the data source is unavailable, map the current inspection routine and draft the prompt and human checkpoint for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Name the technical cause behind one consumption gap, and start the intervention with an owner.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the cause you identified and who owns the intervention.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Preparation is rarely the thing people disagree about. The problem is finding an hour for it. Today is about making it take ten.
keyTalkingPoints: A brief is not a summary. It is a position plus the questions that would change it.
The intended outcome is the part most preparation leaves out, and it changes how the meeting runs.
Anticipated objections are cheaper than recovered ones.
discussionQuestions: Which upcoming conversation needs a recommendation, not just a summary?
What evidence would make the advisory position credible?
What customer decision should the conversation advance?
suggestedTransitions: Move from generic preparation to one upcoming conversation and its intended customer decision.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Pick one upcoming advisory conversation and names the decision it should advance.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one upcoming technical advisory conversation, the intended decision, and the approved sources you would trust for preparation.
facilitatorQuestions: Which advisory conversation is worth preparing with AI support?
What evidence would you need before using the recommendation?
Where would the conversation fail if the ask is not clear?
listenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: preparation that summarizes but does not decide; evidence gaps; customer facts needing review; and advisory recommendations without a named decision.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, build the brief structure for a real upcoming meeting and note where the evidence would come from.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Prepare one advisory conversation around the decision you need, not the content you have.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the recommendation, the evidence, and the decision you asked for.

secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Write, explain, refactor and test code; scaffold infrastructure-as-code and deployment artifacts; build the smallest spike that proves or disproves an architecture assumption; generate sample data and validation scripts; and reproduce a reported failure so you can see it rather than describe it.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the next step is to build something rather than to plan or describe it. Validating an architecture assumption with a spike, standing up a demo or workshop environment, iterating a proof of concept, reproducing a deployment or integration failure, or packaging a reusable asset with tests and setup steps.
keyBenefits: Turns a technical opinion into evidence. A spike that takes twenty minutes settles an argument that would otherwise run for a week, and a reproduced failure is a fact the account team can act on rather than a claim the customer has to accept.
secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for customer, market or account research; that is Researcher. Do not use it to assemble a customer-facing document or deck; that is Cowork. Do not point it at production without the review your team already requires, and do not paste customer data into it. It works on code and configuration, not on the CRM record.
stepsToGetStarted: Use it where the code already is: the Copilot extension in VS Code, the gh copilot CLI, or the GitHub Copilot app in the browser for work not tied to a local checkout. Open the repository or folder first so it has the context. Start with: Explain what this deployment does, then write the smallest test that would prove the assumption I am least sure about.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A design that has not been argued against has not really been validated. Today is about the proof, not the diagram.
keyTalkingPoints: Design and proof are one motion. A design the customer cannot see is a document.
Success criteria set before the work are the only ones that count.
AI accelerates the assembly. The architecture judgment stays human.
discussionQuestions: Which architecture option is still being treated as obvious?
What decision criteria would change the recommendation?
What evidence would you need before supporting this design?
suggestedTransitions: Move from architecture principles to one live architecture decision with explicit criteria.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one architecture assumption or option you will compare against explicit criteria.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one architecture decision or design assumption, the known constraints, and the evidence you would use to compare options.
facilitatorQuestions: Which architecture option comparison is worth doing now?
What decision criteria must be explicit before recommending?
Where could current guidance conflict or lack evidence?
listenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: untested assumptions; option comparisons without decision criteria; public guidance used without applicability review; and controls, governance, or resilience claims needing SME validation.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the environment is unavailable, define the validation approach and the success criteria on paper.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Draft one production-ready design and name the dependency most likely to break it.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the design and the dependency you validated.

secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A design that has not been argued against has not really been validated. Today is about the proof, not the diagram.
keyTalkingPoints: Design and proof are one motion. A design the customer cannot see is a document.
Success criteria set before the work are the only ones that count.
AI accelerates the assembly. The architecture judgment stays human.
discussionQuestions: Which dependency could make the design fail in production?
What proof is small enough to validate the decision?
Who owns the next technical decision after validation?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the design to the smallest validation path that can change the decision.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one validation or delivery-readiness dependency you will make explicit.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one validation path, proof plan, or delivery-readiness question tied to a real workload or customer scenario.
facilitatorQuestions: Which validation or proof plan would reduce delivery risk fastest?
What dependency must be owned before committing the design?
Where does ECIF or delivery-readiness change the technical plan?
listenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: validation scoped too broadly; unowned prerequisites; proof criteria written after work begins; and investment-funded scope that may not be deliverable as designed.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the environment is unavailable, define the validation approach and the success criteria on paper.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Define the validation path for one design, including what would tell you to stop.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the validation path and the stop condition you set.

secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not treat Deal Agent as a separate agent to select; it is a skill inside Sales Chat. Do not rely on it alone for complex negotiations or sensitive disclosures, and do not bypass the legal approval chain for material amendments. Do not treat a first response as final on a complex deal; re-run and verify against current data. Do not use it for work outside the CRM such as decks, emails, and documents; that is Cowork. MCAPS Help is built in, so you can also ask how to complete an MSX task.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Watch consumption and health signals between reviews
activities.description: Set up a standing check on the accounts you carry, so a health or consumption change reaches you when it happens rather than at the next review.
activities.prompt: Set up a recurring check on technical health across the accounts I carry. Each week, tell me where consumption has moved against plan, where a deployment or adoption blocker has appeared, and where a previously flagged risk has not changed. For each one, state what the data shows, what it does not tell us, and the single technical question I should ask next. Remember what you flagged before so you can tell me what is new and what is unchanged.
activities.expectedOutput: A recurring health check separating new movement from unchanged risk, with the next technical question for each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: CSA confirms the technical reading of each signal and decides which movement is significant enough to act on.
activities.requiredContext: The accounts you carry; approved consumption, usage and support data; the risks currently on your register.
activitySteps: 1. Confirm which telemetry, support and consumption sources the check can reach.
2. Run the prompt.
3. Review the first output and separate genuinely new movement from risk you already knew about.
4. Set the cadence to land before your delivery review.
5. Validate each technical hypothesis yourself before raising it with the customer or the account team.
activities.whyThisMatters: Risk found early is a conversation and the same risk found late is an escalation. Between reviews is exactly where that gap opens, and it is where an always-on agent earns its place.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Risk you find this week is a conversation. The same risk found by the customer is an escalation. Today is about finding it earlier.
keyTalkingPoints: A health score can tell you something is wrong. It rarely tells you what to do.
Every risk needs an owner and a date or it is an observation.
AI is good at surfacing signal. Prioritizing it is judgment.
discussionQuestions: Which technical risk is visible now but not yet owned?
What is evidence, and what is interpretation?
What intervention could prevent this from becoming customer-visible?
suggestedTransitions: Move from health signal to one risk, its evidence, owner, and next intervention.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one technical risk, its evidence, its owner, and the next intervention.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one technical health signal, risk, or dependency you are tracking, plus the source you would use to validate it.
facilitatorQuestions: Which technical health activity is closest to a real account risk?
What evidence separates the risk from a hunch?
Who owns the intervention if the risk is real?
listenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: health scores treated as causes; risks without owners or dates; technical blockers becoming customer-visible; and actions that require CSAM, support, delivery, or commercial alignment.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If status data is unavailable, work from what people know and note where the evidence should have come from.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Find one technical health risk that is not visible in the data, and take it to its owner.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the risk, where the signal came from, and who now owns it.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Value without evidence tends to read as opinion. Today is about the evidence, and who needs to hear it.
keyTalkingPoints: The customer defines value. Our job is to evidence it in their terms.
Causality is easy to claim and hard to support. Say what the data supports.
A value story nobody hears is not value realized.
discussionQuestions: Which technical progress has not yet been translated into customer value?
Which cost, consumption, or optimization signal is credible enough to use?
What claim would you refuse to make without stronger evidence?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the signal to one bounded recommendation or technical value narrative.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to one evidence-backed optimization or technical value recommendation.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one optimization, consumption, or delivery-progress signal and the outcome it might support.
facilitatorQuestions: Which optimization or progress signal could become a value story?
What financial or technical claim requires review?
What evidence is missing before recommending action?
listenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: invented savings; correlation presented as causality; optimization divorced from architecture tradeoffs; and value claims not tied to supported outcomes.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If evidence sources are unavailable, build the value structure and identify what evidence you would need.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Evidence one technical outcome in terms the customer would use themselves.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the outcome, the evidence, and how you phrased it.

CSA-VALUE-1.keyTakeaway: Value that is not evidenced is an opinion. Value that is not communicated is invisible.

CSA-VALUE-2.roleTopicName: Translate Technical Progress into a Customer Value Narrative (2 of 2)
CSA-VALUE-2.roleTopicDescription: Turn technical progress into a value story the customer recognizes, with the evidence behind every claim checked before it is shown.
CSA-VALUE-2.wiifm: Technical work is only credited when someone connects it to what the customer wanted. Unverified claims lose that credit instantly.
CSA-VALUE-2.name: Prove and Communicate Value
CSA-VALUE-2.description: Turn what has actually happened into a value story the customer recognizes and will act on.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Track delivered value against what was promised
activities.description: Keep a running comparison between the outcomes committed in the business case and what consumption and usage data actually show.
activities.prompt: Set up a recurring comparison between the outcomes we committed to in this account's business case and what the consumption and usage data now shows. Report the direction of travel for each committed outcome, flag any where the trend will not reach the commitment on the current trajectory, and state what evidence would be needed to make the value claim defensible to the customer's finance function. activities.expectedOutput: A recurring value tracker per committed outcome, showing measured versus projected, trajectory against commitment, and the evidence gap.
activities.humanCheckpoint: CSA verifies the measurement basis has not changed and confirms every figure before it is shown to the customer as a delivered result.
activities.requiredContext: The agreed business case and its committed outcomes; current consumption and usage data; the baseline used at commitment.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the agreed business case, its committed outcomes, and the baseline used at commitment.
2. Run the prompt.
3. Confirm the tracker distinguishes measured results from projected ones on every outcome.
4. Check that the measurement basis has not changed since the commitment was made.
5. Verify any figure yourself before it is shown to the customer as delivered value.
activities.whyThisMatters: Value claims lose credibility the moment a customer's finance function finds the number is projected rather than measured. Tracking continuously is what makes the claim survive scrutiny.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Value without evidence tends to read as opinion. Today is about the evidence, and who needs to hear it.
keyTalkingPoints: The customer defines value. Our job is to evidence it in their terms.
Causality is easy to claim and hard to support. Say what the data supports.
A value story nobody hears is not value realized.
discussionQuestions: What value story would the customer actually recognize?
Which evidence supports the story, and which part is still only expected?
What next technical action would make the value more real?
suggestedTransitions: Move from value language to the evidence package and next technical action.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to one technical value story and the evidence that will travel with it.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one technical review, business review, or value-realization example and the evidence behind it.
facilitatorQuestions: Which customer review package would benefit from AI assembly?
What evidence must travel with the value story?
Which next technical action makes the value more credible?
listenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: progress not connected to agreed outcomes; unsupported realization claims; missing source links; and follow-through that lacks owners.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If evidence sources are unavailable, build the value structure and identify what evidence you would need.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Produce one costed optimization recommendation the customer could act on this quarter.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the recommendation, the cost basis, and the customer response.

CSA-VALUE-2.keyTakeaway: Value that is not evidenced is an opinion. Value that is not communicated is invisible.

CSAM-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand how the CSAM huddle path runs and where AI fits the customer-success work you already do.
CSAM-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
CSAM-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: CSAMs know how the huddle motion works, which tools may show up, what to review, and what AI experiences to bring back before next week.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This is the session that explains the motion through the CSAM lens: less status assembly, more customer outcome leadership.
keyTalkingPoints: Huddles are 30 minutes and workflow-led. CSAM work stays human-led: AI helps gather, synthesize, draft and monitor; the CSAM validates context, trust, commitments and customer-facing messages.
discussionQuestions: Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted customer success output?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the workflow-discovery prompt below. Week 1 is for finding the recurring work worth automating.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the tools named for this path, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
facilitatorQuestions: Which customer success work do you repeat every week without thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where must the CSAM judgment stay human no matter how good the output gets?
listenFor: Listen for unvoiced scepticism, access blockers stated as disinterest, the assumption that this is a tool rollout, and people who describe only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat. The recurring, unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the discovery conversation and record access blockers separately from interest. The discovery prompt can be run in whichever tool the person already has.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

"I am a Customer Success Account Manager at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with."
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation, or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

CSAM-ORIENT.keyTakeaway: The point of the motion is better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake.

For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. activities.name: Keep success plan commitments visible between check-ins
activities.description: Turn the success plan from a document reviewed monthly into a tracked set of commitments with standing visibility on what is slipping.
activities.prompt: Track the commitments in this account's success plan on a recurring basis. For each milestone, tell me whether there is recent evidence of progress, whether the named owner has been active on it, and whether the date is still credible given what has happened since it was set. Flag anything with no evidence of movement and draft the specific question I should ask the owner. Report only changes and exceptions - do not restate the whole plan each time.
activities.expectedOutput: A recurring exceptions-only commitment tracker with an evidence check per milestone and a drafted question for each stalled item.
activities.humanCheckpoint: CSAM confirms the credibility judgement on each date personally before raising it, since absence of visible evidence is not proof of absence of progress.
activities.requiredContext: The current success plan with milestones, owners and dates; access to the engagement activity behind it.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the current success plan with milestones, owners and dates.
2. Run the prompt.
3. Review the exceptions list, remembering that no evidence of movement is not proof that nothing moved.
4. Set the cadence to run before your customer check-in.
5. Ask the named owner the drafted question directly rather than escalating first.
activities.whyThisMatters: Success plans decay quietly. The milestone that slipped is rarely announced - it is simply never mentioned again until the review.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Success planning is not documentation. It is how the customer and Microsoft agree what progress means.
keyTalkingPoints: A plan should name outcomes, milestones, owners, risks and review points. AI can draft and inspect the plan, but only the CSAM can validate the customer priority and commitment.
discussionQuestions: When did your success plan last change because the customer's priorities changed?
Which milestone in it would the customer not recognize as theirs?
What is in the plan because it is genuinely the outcome, and what is there because it was easy to measure?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the plan as it stands to the single outcome you will make observable this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the customer, the one outcome you will make observable this week, and what you will remove from the plan to keep it governable.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one active customer priority, its current CSP or success-plan notes and the latest review or action list.
facilitatorQuestions: Which outcome in your plan is stated in the customer's words rather than ours?
Which milestone has drifted without anyone deciding to move it?
What would you remove from the plan today to make it governable?
listenFor: Listen for plans built around Microsoft milestones rather than customer outcomes, measures chosen because they are available rather than meaningful, owners who have never agreed to their commitment, and plans so long that nobody governs them. Also listen for drift being reported rather than decided.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Make one success plan outcome observable this week, and remove something to keep the plan governable.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the outcome you made measurable and what you removed.

secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Catch the escalation while it is still a conversation
activities.description: Use satisfaction and support-experience thresholds to find the customer heading for escalation before they get there.
activities.prompt: Across my accounts, find where the support experience suggests an escalation is building: OSAT below 3.5, ATQ trending worse, RM score declining, or a cluster of negative verbatims about the same theme. For each, tell me what the evidence supports and what would need to be true for this to become a formal escalation. Separate the evidenced signal from the inference.
activities.expectedOutput: A list of accounts with escalation risk building, the evidence behind each, and the condition that would make each a formal escalation.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM verifies each signal with delivery and support before raising it with the customer. CX Vitals shows dissatisfaction; it does not know what is already being fixed.
activities.requiredContext: Your portfolio with TPIDs; current known escalations; your delivery and support contacts for each account.
activitySteps: 1. Run the prompt across your portfolio.
2. Treat threshold crossings and trend direction as separate signals; a stable low score is different from a fresh drop.
3. Check each against what delivery and support already know before raising it.
4. Choose one account and open the conversation with the customer proactively.
5. Record the escalation threshold you agreed so the next check is measured against it.
activities.whyThisMatters: An escalation you raise yourself is a conversation about a plan. The same issue raised by the customer is a conversation about your credibility.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about moving from signal review to intervention. Scores help, but action changes the customer trajectory.
keyTalkingPoints: Health work spans adoption, usage, support, delivery, sentiment and stakeholder change. The CSAM must separate noise from the risk that matters most right now.
discussionQuestions: Which customer worries you for reasons the health score does not capture?
What did someone say in a recent conversation that has not made it into any system?
Which risk have you been watching rather than acting on, and why?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the ranked health view to one intervention with an owner, a due date, and an escalation threshold.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the top risk, its actual driver rather than its score, the owner who has agreed to the intervention, and the escalation threshold.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account with visible health, adoption, support or delivery risk and the current owner or open question.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the driver behind the score, not the score itself?
Which signal came from a person rather than a system, and did it survive into the record?
Who owns the intervention, and by when does it have to start to matter?
listenFor: Listen for health scores treated as the diagnosis rather than the symptom, risks the team has normalized, interventions without owners, and conversation-based signals that never reached the data. Also listen for the customer's own view of their health being absent from the discussion.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Find the driver behind one health score, then take the intervention to an owner who agrees to it.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the driver, the owner, and the escalation threshold you set.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Executive alignment is where customer success becomes visible to the people who can sponsor, unblock or redirect it.
keyTalkingPoints: Stakeholder maps should show influence, decision rights, relationship health and the next ask. AI can assemble signals; the CSAM decides the message and timing.
discussionQuestions: Who is the most senior person at this customer you have never spoken to directly?
Which stakeholder could stop this work, and do you know what they care about?
When an executive last engaged, what did they actually want from us?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the stakeholder map to the one relationship you will build this month and the reason they would take the meeting.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the stakeholder you will reach this month, what that person needs to believe, and who can make the introduction.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one upcoming executive or sponsor conversation and the latest stakeholder context.
facilitatorQuestions: Which stakeholder can stop this, and what do they need to believe?
Where is your coverage a title on a map rather than a relationship?
What would you ask the executive for if you had fifteen minutes tomorrow?
listenFor: Listen for stakeholder maps built from org charts rather than observed behavior, executive relationships that exist only through an intermediary, engagement plans with no ask, and blockers identified without a plan to reach them. Also listen for assuming a quiet stakeholder is a supportive one.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Reach one stakeholder you have never spoken to directly, and know what they care about before you do.
bringBackEvidence: Bring who you reached, how, and what you learned that you did not expect.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record.
