activities.name: Separate real buying intent from engagement activity
activities.description: Look at the engagement behind a signal and judge whether it indicates someone is buying or merely reading.
activities.prompt: Here is an engagement signal in my solution area: [paste the account, the signal type, and what engagement the record shows]. Help me judge whether this is buying intent or activity. Tell me what the engagement pattern actually supports, what would distinguish genuine evaluation from general interest, and what I would need to see to be confident either way. Be explicit about what you cannot tell from this data. Do not assume that more engagement means more intent.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on what the engagement pattern supports, what would distinguish evaluation from interest, and what evidence is still missing.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what the engagement means. Marketing engagement is a weak proxy for intent, and the specialist who knows the solution area is the only person who can judge whether this particular pattern is meaningful.
activities.requiredContext: One engagement signal in your solution area; the account and what it already owns; the engagement detail the record shows.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one engagement signal in your solution area, ideally one you are unsure about.
2. Paste the account, signal type and engagement into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Look for whether several people at the account engaged or only one. One person reading is not an evaluation.
4. Check whether the engagement matches something they already own or something new. Those mean different things.
5. Decide what you would need to see to be confident, and whether it is worth the time to find out.
activities.whyThisMatters: Engagement data tells you someone clicked. Treating it as intent is how specialists spend a week on an account that was never evaluating anything.

activities.name: Decide the route before the window closes
activities.description: Choose deliberately whether a signal is yours to pursue, belongs with a partner, or should be declined.
activities.prompt: I have to decide what to do with this signal before its window closes: [paste the signal, the account, what I have established about intent, and what capacity I have this week]. Help me choose between pursuing it myself, routing it to a partner, or declining it. For each route, tell me what makes it the right choice and what it costs. Take seriously that declining is a legitimate answer. Where the decision depends on something I have not told you, ask rather than assuming.
activities.expectedOutput: A recommendation across pursue, route to partner and decline, with what makes each right and what it costs, and the decision you have taken with its reason.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS owns the routing decision. Whether a partner is the right home depends on that partner's current capacity and relationship with the account, which is not in any system the agent can read.
activities.requiredContext: The signal and its account; what you have established about intent; your genuine capacity this week; which partners cover this solution area.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the signal you assessed in the previous practice.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, including your honest capacity this week, then run it.
3. Answer its questions rather than letting it guess at your capacity or partner coverage.
4. If routing to a partner, make the decision now rather than after you have half-worked it. A partner picking up a warm signal is very different from a partner inheriting a stalled one.
5. Record the decision and the reason, including for the ones you decline.
activities.whyThisMatters: The worst outcome for a signal is not being declined. It is being half-worked by someone who never decided whether they were working it.

activities.name: Open the conversation without revealing how you found them
activities.description: Prepare a first approach informed by the customer's likely situation, without referencing the internal engagement data that surfaced them.
activities.prompt: I am making first contact with a customer who surfaced through an internal engagement signal. Here is what I know: [paste the account, the solution area, and what I have established about their situation]. Prepare an opening built on their likely business situation and what companies like them are typically working through. Do NOT reference or allude to anything they viewed, clicked, downloaded or attended, and do not imply I know what they have been looking at - that information is internal and referencing it damages trust. Give me the question I should lead with, what I should not assume, and what would tell me quickly that this is not an evaluation after all. Keep it usable in a short call or message, and do not write me a pitch.
activities.expectedOutput: An opening grounded in the customer's likely business situation with no reference to internal engagement data, the assumptions to avoid, and what would show this is not a real evaluation.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS is accountable for what the customer hears. Internal engagement data is exactly that - internal - and an opening that reveals how closely someone has been tracked costs the relationship far more than the signal was ever worth.
activities.requiredContext: The account and its solution area; what you have established about their situation; a contact that exists in MSX if you intend to draft outreach.
activitySteps: 1. Take a signal you have decided to pursue.
2. Paste the account, solution area and situation into the prompt where it asks. Do not paste the engagement detail itself; you are not trying to reference it.
3. Read the opening back and check it does not hint at how you found them. If it would sound like surveillance to the customer, it is wrong regardless of how it was generated.
4. Check the opening question is genuinely open. If it can be answered yes or no, it will be.
5. Confirm the contact exists in MSX before relying on any drafting help, and note that outreach drafting in Sales Home is English only during preview.
activities.whyThisMatters: The signal tells you who to call. It does not give you anything you can say. Openings that leak how the seller found the customer are the fastest way to make a first conversation the last one.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Separate real buying intent from engagement activity

activities.name: Read what the signals are telling you about your solution area
activities.description: Look back at recent signals in your solution area for what customers consistently react to, and what that says about where demand is forming.
activities.prompt: Here are the engagement signals in my solution area recently: [paste the list, with the topic or offer, the account profile, and whether each went anywhere]. Tell me what customers are consistently engaging with, which topics or offers generate engagement that goes nowhere, and whether the pattern differs by customer size or industry. Separate what this genuinely supports from what would be over-reading a small sample. I want to know where demand is actually forming, so be direct if the honest answer is that there is not enough here to say anything.
activities.expectedOutput: What customers consistently engage with, what generates engagement that does not convert, whether patterns hold across customer profiles, and an honest statement where the sample is too small.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS tests the pattern against real conversations. A pattern in engagement data can be an artefact of what marketing happened to send, and the specialist is the only one positioned to know the difference.
activities.requiredContext: Recent engagement signals in your solution area with topic, account profile and outcome; your own recollection of recent customer conversations to test findings against.
activitySteps: 1. Pull the recent signals in your solution area from Sales Accelerator or your own records.
2. Mark each as converted, still open, or went nowhere. The last group is the useful half.
3. Paste the list into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Check whether any pattern holds across customer sizes or is driven by a handful of accounts.
5. Test one finding against what you have actually heard in customer conversations, then bring it to your qualification progression discussion.
activities.whyThisMatters: You see more signals in your solution area than anyone else does. What consistently fails to convert is intelligence nobody else in the territory can give.

activities.name: Watch for the engagement that turns into real intent
activities.description: Set a standing watch across your solution area so repeat engagement surfaces as it builds rather than after the window has closed.
activities.prompt: Watch engagement across the accounts in my solution area and tell me, on a schedule I set, where activity is repeating or building rather than one-off, where a signal has gone quiet after I responded, and where the same pattern is showing up across more than one account. Carry forward what you reported last time so I can see what built and what faded.
activities.expectedOutput: A standing watch across the solution area showing where engagement is building, where it went quiet after a response, and the patterns appearing across more than one account.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what repeat engagement means. Activity that repeats can be a buying signal or one person doing their research, and the difference is not in the count.
activities.requiredContext: The accounts in your solution area, access to the engagement signals for them, and the cadence you want to be told on.
activitySteps: 1. Set the cadence and the accounts in scope.
2. Say what repeat engagement looks like in your solution area.
3. Ask for what changed since the last check, not the full picture.
4. Review the first run before relying on it.
5. Use the cross-account patterns to decide where your solution area is actually landing.
activities.whyThisMatters: A pattern across several touches says something a single event does not, and watching for it by hand is the part that does not get done.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Engagement data tells you someone clicked. This session is about telling the difference between that and someone buying, quickly enough to matter.
keyTalkingPoints: Highly Engaged and program signals carry a 5-day SLA and are yours to action, while Contact Me signals sit with the account executive. Engagement is a weak proxy for intent: several people engaging is a different thing from one person reading. Declining a signal is a legitimate outcome and is far better than half-working it. Facilitator note: Sales Home is in preview and enabled for individual contributors only, with English-only outreach drafting, so some of the room may be working in Sales Accelerator.
discussionQuestions: When did engagement data last mislead you into pursuing something that was never real?
What does genuine evaluation look like in your solution area, as opposed to interest?
How often do you decline a signal outright, and how does that feel?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the intent judgement to the routing decision each person will make and record before the window closes.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the routing decision each person has taken and the reason, including for anything they are declining.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one Highly Engaged or program signal in your solution area that you are genuinely unsure about.
facilitatorQuestions: What in this engagement pattern would you actually bet on?
Is this one person reading or several people evaluating?
If you route this to a partner, what are you handing them?
listenFor: Listen for volume of engagement being read as strength of intent, for signals being carried rather than routed or declined, for partner routing decided after the signal has gone cold, and for openings built on how closely the customer has been tracked.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live signal, use one that was pursued and went nowhere, and work backwards to what in the engagement should have been the warning.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you believe the engagement meant before you looked at it properly?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one engagement signal, decide whether it is real, route or decline it, and record why.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the signal, what you judged, what you decided, and whether the outcome supported your read.

DSS-SIGNAL.keyTakeaway: A signal is an unqualified lead with a clock on it. The skill is deciding quickly which ones deserve your time, not working all of them equally.

DSS-TERRITORY.roleTopicName: Find Where Your Solution Area Actually Lands
DSS-TERRITORY.roleTopicDescription: Work out where your solution area has genuine propensity across the territories you support, test that against real engagement evidence, and decide where your own time goes rather than spreading it evenly.
DSS-TERRITORY.wiifm: Propensity models will happily hand you a long list. The ones that convert are the ones where something has already happened, and telling those apart early is most of the job.
DSS-TERRITORY.name: Plan the Territory With the Partners Who Cover It
DSS-TERRITORY.description: Decide who is genuinely covering which accounts across a territory far larger than one person can work, and build that decision into a joint plan with the partners who cover the rest.
DSS-TERRITORY.todayObjective: Identify the accounts where your solution area has both propensity and evidence, and separate them from the ones that only have propensity.
DSS-TERRITORY.whyItMatters: A territory of roughly fifty accounts cannot be covered account by account, so most of it is covered by partners or not at all. The plan is where that becomes deliberate. Left implicit, the accounts that get worked are the ones that shout, and the ones that quietly lapse were never assigned to anybody.
DSS-TERRITORY.desiredOutcome: A short list of accounts with both propensity and engagement evidence, the difference explained, and one taken into the qualification progression.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Home
primaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Separate propensity from evidence across your solution area
activities.description: Split the accounts your solution area is pointed at into those where something has actually happened and those where only a model says it should.
activities.prompt: For the accounts in my solution area, list each one with any recorded engagement: opportunities open in my solution area, recent activity, and any engagement signal that has come through. Group them into accounts with recorded engagement in my solution area, accounts with recorded engagement elsewhere but not in mine, and accounts with none. Show what the engagement actually was rather than only that it existed.
activities.expectedOutput: Solution-area accounts split by whether engagement is recorded in your area, elsewhere, or nowhere.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what counts as engagement in their area. A model can only see what was recorded, and the strongest signal in this segment is often a conversation the DAE had that never made it into a field.
activities.requiredContext: Your solution area. The territories and accounts you support.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Read the third group and compare it against where you have been spending time.
3. For the second group, note whether the engagement elsewhere gives you a route in.
4. Identify any account you are actively supporting that appears in the third group.
activities.whyThisMatters: Propensity models produce long lists that all look equally promising. The accounts that convert are the ones where something has already started, and that distinction is visible in the record.

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

agents.name: Sales Home
agents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
agents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Find the blocker that repeats across your accounts
activities.description: Look across every territory you support for the objection or dependency that keeps recurring, because a pattern is a solution-area problem while a single instance is an account problem.
activities.prompt: For the open opportunities in my solution area across all the territories I support, show each one with its stage, the date it last moved, and any recorded blocker, objection or competitor. Group the ones that have not moved stage in over a month by what the record says is blocking them. Show me which blockers appear on more than one account and how many accounts each one affects.
activities.expectedOutput: Stalled opportunities grouped by recorded blocker, with the recurring blockers separated from the account-specific ones and a decision on the largest pattern.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides whether a repeated blocker is genuinely one problem or several that were described in similar words. Free-text blocker fields are written by different people in different territories, and only the specialist who knows the solution area can tell a real pattern from a vocabulary coincidence.
activities.requiredContext: The territories you support. Your solution area. The blockers and objections recorded against your open opportunities.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt._x000D_
2. Read the grouped blockers before the individual accounts._x000D_
3. Identify any blocker appearing on three or more accounts - that is a solution-area problem, not a deal problem._x000D_
4. Decide whether it needs a reusable answer, a specialist, or an escalation._x000D_
5. Take the single-account blockers back to the relevant DAE separately.
activities.whyThisMatters: A blocker on one account is that account's problem. The same blocker on five accounts is a solution-area problem with a reusable answer, and only the role that sees across territories is positioned to notice.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Separate propensity from evidence across your solution area

activities.name: Prepare one account for qualification progression
activities.description: Take an account with both propensity and evidence and build the case you would put in front of the weekly qualification progression.
activities.prompt: For [account name], assemble what is known: the workloads already in place, any open opportunity and its stage, the engagement recorded in my solution area, and the decision criteria captured so far. Identify what is missing before this could be treated as a qualified opportunity in my solution area, and state which of those gaps a customer conversation would close and which need internal work.
activities.expectedOutput: A qualification case for one account with the gaps separated into customer-facing and internal, and the single most important question named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides which gap actually blocks qualification. A gap list treats everything as equally missing, and the specialist is the one who knows which single answer would change the decision.
activities.requiredContext: One account with recorded engagement in your solution area. The qualification criteria your solution area applies.
activitySteps: 1. Choose an account that appeared in the propensity-with-evidence group._x000D_
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [account name] with that account._x000D_
3. Separate the gaps that need the customer from the gaps that need the DAE or a specialist._x000D_
4. Decide the single question you most need answered._x000D_
5. Take it into the weekly qualification progression for your solution area.
activities.whyThisMatters: Qualification progression runs weekly and rotates by solution area. Arriving with a specific question is materially different from arriving with a status update.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Separate propensity from evidence across your solution area

activities.name: Test whether you and the DAE are reading the same territory
activities.description: Find the accounts where the solution-area view and the account view disagree, because that gap is usually where the work is.
activities.prompt: For the territory I support, list the accounts with an open opportunity in my solution area. Separately, list the accounts with any activity recorded in the last thirty days. Show which accounts appear in the second list but not the first. For each of those, state what workloads are already in place and whether anything in the record suggests an opening for my solution area.
activities.expectedOutput: The accounts where the account view and the solution-area view disagree, with one investigated.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides whether a disagreement is a gap or a correct exclusion. The DAE may have excluded your solution area for a reason that was never written down, and asking is faster than inferring.
activities.requiredContext: The territory you support. Your solution area.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Look specifically at accounts with recent activity where your solution area has nothing open.
3. Pick one and work out whether that is a genuine gap or a correct exclusion.
4. Raise it in your next conversation with the DAE.
activities.whyThisMatters: The DAE and the DSS read the same territory through different lenses, and the accounts that appear in one view but not the other are where the two roles most often lose each other.

agents.name: Sales Home
agents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
agents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Propensity tells you where your solution area might land. Engagement evidence tells you where something has already started. This session is about not confusing the two.
keyTalkingPoints: The DSS view runs across solution area rather than across account ownership, so the same territory is being read differently by the DAE and by you. Highly Engaged signals carry a five-day SLA and route to DSS, while Contact Me signals carry forty-eight hours and route to the DAE. Weekly Qualification Progression rotates by solution area and is where this work surfaces. Facilitator note: a propensity score is a model output rather than a customer behaviour, and it is worth being explicit about that distinction in the room.
discussionQuestions: Where does your solution area show propensity that you have never acted on?
What is the difference between an account that looks like a fit and one that is showing intent?
How do you currently decide which DAE to spend your time with?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the propensity-versus-evidence split to the one account each person takes into qualification progression.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the account each person takes forward and one they are removing from their list.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your solution-area view across the territories you support, including propensity indicators and any recent engagement signals.
facilitatorQuestions: Which of your high-propensity accounts have shown no actual engagement at all?
Where are you spending time because a DAE asked rather than because the evidence supports it?
What would make you drop an account off your solution-area list?
listenFor: Listen for propensity treated as intent, for effort allocated by relationship rather than evidence, for engagement signals counted without checking whether the contact exists in MSX, and for lists that only ever grow.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If propensity data is unavailable, have them list the accounts they are actively supporting and work backwards to what evidence justified each one.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which account were you working on momentum rather than on evidence?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, separate your solution-area list into propensity-with-evidence and propensity-only, take one of the first into qualification progression, and drop one of the second.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the split you produced, the account you progressed, and the one you dropped.

DSS-TERRITORY.keyTakeaway: Coverage is a decision whether or not you make it. An account nobody named is an account nobody is working.

DSS-ORIENT.roleTopicName: Frontier Accelerator Orientation for Digital Solution Specialists
DSS-ORIENT.roleTopicDescription: Introduce the eight-session motion, where AI reduces the research and triage load across a solution area spanning several territories, and what to bring back each week.
DSS-ORIENT.wiifm: You cover a solution area across more territories than you can hold in your head. This is about spending your time where it changes an outcome.
DSS-ORIENT.name: Frontier Accelerator Orientation
DSS-ORIENT.description: Introduces the motion, the huddle format, the AI tools in scope, and what team members are expected to try between sessions.

DSS-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand how the DSS path runs and where the human checkpoints protect solution and qualification judgement.
DSS-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
DSS-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: DSSs know how the motion works, which tools may show up, and what to try before the next session.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Eight sessions built around parts of the specialist job rather than around tools. This first one covers what is being asked and what is not.
keyTalkingPoints: The motion is about better workflow with human judgement kept explicit rather than tool adoption. Every activity names the judgement that is not delegated. The DSS view runs across solution area rather than account ownership, so the same territory is read differently by you and by the DAE. Highly Engaged signals carry a five-day SLA and route to you, while Contact Me signals carry forty-eight hours and route to the DAE. Facilitator note: Sales Agent is not available in GCC or DoD, so some of the room may be working in different surfaces.
discussionQuestions: How many territories does your solution area cover?
How do you currently decide which DAE to spend time with?
What have you already tried with AI, and what happened?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the discussion to the one thing each person will try before the next session.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person name the account they will run the baseline task against.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: no preparation needed. Bring one example of solution-area work that took longer than it should have.
facilitatorQuestions: What part of the specialist job does not scale across this many territories?
Where would you never want an AI answer?
What would make you distrust an output?
listenFor: Listen for expectations that the tools will do the qualifying, for scepticism worth taking seriously, and for workflows already broken without AI.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the group is quiet, ask what question a DAE asked them most often last month.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which part of your week would you most like to stop doing manually?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, open Sales Agent and ask it to summarize the solution-area position on one account you support but have not looked at this quarter. Note one thing you did not know and one thing it got wrong.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the account, the thing you did not know, and the thing it got wrong.

DSS-ORIENT.keyTakeaway: The point of the motion is better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

activities.name: Find out what the DAE has already promised
activities.description: Get the account history behind a conversation you did not arrange, so you do not contradict what has already been said.
activities.prompt: For [account name], show what has been recorded ahead of this conversation: the open opportunities and their stage, recent activity and who it was with, any commitment or next step logged, the products and workloads already in place, and any open support issue. Focus on anything that has already been said to this customer about my solution area. Where the record is thin, say so rather than filling it.
activities.expectedOutput: The account history relevant to your solution area, with the commitments already made identified and the gaps turned into questions for the DAE.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what to check with the DAE before the conversation rather than discovering it in front of the customer. The record shows what was logged, and in a fast-moving territory the most important commitment is often one the DAE made verbally and has not written down yet.
activities.requiredContext: One customer conversation you have been asked to join, and the account it concerns.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account.
2. Read the commitments first. Contradicting one in the meeting is the fastest way to lose the room.
3. Note what is thin - that is what you ask the DAE before the call, not the customer during it.
4. Send the DAE your two questions rather than arriving with them.
activities.whyThisMatters: A specialist who contradicts what the account owner promised last month damages both the deal and the relationship with the DAE. It is entirely avoidable with ten minutes of preparation.

activities.name: Bring what you have learned elsewhere to this customer
activities.description: Use the objections you have already met across other territories to anticipate what this customer will raise.
activities.prompt: I am proposing [describe your solution-area proposal] at [account name]. First, show what is deployed at that account today. Then, across the other opportunities in my solution area, show any recorded objection, blocker or competitor associated with a similar deployed estate. For each, show the account, what was recorded, and how it was resolved if it was. Do not assume a similar estate means the same objection will arise.
activities.expectedOutput: Objections seen elsewhere on similar estates, filtered to the ones plausible here, with a previously successful answer ready.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS judges whether an objection seen elsewhere actually applies here. The same deployed estate can produce completely different concerns depending on who operates it and what they were burned by last time, and a specialist arriving with a rehearsed answer to the wrong objection is worse than one arriving with none.
activities.requiredContext: Your solution-area proposal and the target account. The other opportunities across the territories you support, including recorded objections.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections._x000D_
2. Read the objections from other accounts before the target account's estate._x000D_
3. Discard any that do not fit this customer's actual situation - a pattern is a prompt to check, not a prediction._x000D_
4. Prepare the answer you already gave successfully somewhere else.
activities.whyThisMatters: The specialist advantage over an account owner is having met this workload at many customers. That only pays if you go and look at what happened rather than relying on what you remember.

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. agents.name: Sales Home
agents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
agents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Agree the boundary with the DAE before you are in the room
activities.description: Settle who covers what, so the customer sees one team rather than two people negotiating live.
activities.prompt: I am joining a customer conversation at [account name] that the DAE is leading. The intended outcome is [describe the outcome]. Help me draft a short note to the DAE proposing the split: which parts I will cover, which parts they keep, and the two questions I need answered before we go in. Keep it to a few lines - this is a working note between colleagues, not a brief.
activities.expectedOutput: A short agreed split of the conversation with your two open questions sent ahead of it.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS proposes the split and the DAE owns the decision, because the account relationship is theirs. Which DAE wants a specialist to lead and which wants them to stay quiet until asked varies by person rather than by process, and the only way to know is to have worked with them.
activities.requiredContext: The conversation you are joining, the account, and the intended outcome. Your DAE.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account and the intended outcome.
2. Cut anything that reads as telling the account owner how to run their meeting.
3. Send it far enough ahead that they can actually reply.
4. If they do not reply, assume they own everything commercial and stay in your lane.
activities.whyThisMatters: Two people improvising a division of labour in front of a customer reads as a team that has not spoken. It takes three lines to prevent.

agents.name: Agent J.ai
agents.shortDescription: Text-based coaching experience grounded in Microsoft 365 context and curated content.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Helps users sharpen messages, rehearse conversations, anticipate objections, and plan next steps.
agents.whenToUseIt: Customer conversation preparation and role-play.
keyBenefits: Rehearsal before the real conversation. Sharpens messages, surfaces objections you had not anticipated, and coaches on clarity and next step, grounded in Microsoft 365 context and curated content.

resources.title: Agent J.ai Reference
resources.description: MCAPS agent reference for coaching and conversation rehearsal.

agents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use as the authoritative source for CRM or commercial data.
stepsToGetStarted: Open Agent J.ai in Microsoft 365 Copilot, then describe the conversation you want to rehearse and who you will be speaking to.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: You are frequently invited into a conversation you did not scope, for an account you do not own, at short notice. This session is about arriving useful anyway.
keyTalkingPoints: Discovery intent is the same as Enterprise - Frontier Conversation and BOAT framing still apply - but the specialist usually joins a conversation the DAE arranged and will lead. Contacts must already exist in MSX before outreach can be drafted against them. The boundary matters: the DAE owns the account relationship and the commercial thread, and the DSS is there for solution depth. Facilitator note: the most common failure here is a specialist answering a question the customer did not ask, because they prepared the demo they wanted to give.
discussionQuestions: How much notice do you usually get?
What do you do when you have thirty minutes to prepare?
When did you last talk past what the customer actually wanted?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the prepared contribution to the boundary each person will confirm with the DAE.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person state what they will contribute and what they will leave to the DAE.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one customer conversation you have been asked to join.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the DAE actually trying to achieve in this conversation?
What is the technical objection most likely to come up, and can you answer it?
Where does your contribution end and the DAE's begin?
listenFor: Listen for preparation aimed at the solution rather than at the customer's decision, for boundaries assumed rather than agreed with the DAE, and for technical answers to commercial questions.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has an upcoming conversation, use the last one that went sideways and identify what preparation would have changed it.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What were you preparing to say that the customer had not asked about?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, prepare one customer conversation this way and agree the boundary with the DAE beforehand rather than discovering it live.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what you prepared, what the customer actually asked, and how close those were.

DSS-CONV.keyTakeaway: Preparation is where the meeting is decided. AI makes good preparation fast enough to actually happen.

DSS-DEAL.roleTopicName: Move the Solution Decision, Not the Deal
DSS-DEAL.roleTopicDescription: Advance the part of a deal that belongs to your solution area, and be clear about where your influence ends and the DAE's ownership begins.
DSS-DEAL.wiifm: Specialists lose credibility by either hovering or bulldozing. Knowing exactly which decision is yours is what makes you useful on the next one.
DSS-DEAL.name: Advance and Structure the Deal
DSS-DEAL.description: Move the deal to its next decision, and structure it so it can actually be approved.

roles.description: Drives customer adoption, expansion, and renewal through success planning.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Leads technical discovery, qualification, and execution of demos, PoCs, and solution designs.

roles.name: Solution Sales Professional
roles.description: Drives solution-specific opportunities by shaping vision and leading value-based conversations.

DSS-DEAL.todayObjective: Identify the solution decision blocking one opportunity and take it forward without taking over the deal.
DSS-DEAL.whyItMatters: Deals stall on structure more often than on merit. The cost of discovering an approval requirement late is measured in weeks.
DSS-DEAL.desiredOutcome: The solution decision named, the evidence it needs assembled, and one action taken inside your own remit.

activities.name: Name the solution decision the deal is waiting on
activities.description: Find the specific technical or solution decision blocking an opportunity, as distinct from the commercial ones.
activities.prompt: For [opportunity name or ID] in my solution area, show the current stage, when it last moved, the recorded next step and owner, any blocker or objection captured, and what has been proposed to the customer. Based on that, identify what appears to be blocking progress and separate anything that is a solution or technical decision from anything commercial or relationship-based. Where the record does not say, say so.
activities.expectedOutput: The blockers split into solution decisions and commercial ones, with the single solution decision named or the deal correctly identified as not yours.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides whether a blocker is genuinely a solution problem. Deals are often described as technical when the real issue is budget or sponsorship, and a specialist who accepts that framing spends weeks solving a problem that was never the obstacle.
activities.requiredContext: One opportunity in your solution area that is not moving.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your opportunity.
2. Work only the solution column. The commercial one belongs to the DAE and the CE.
3. If the solution column is empty, the deal is not blocked on you and your time is better spent elsewhere.
4. Name the single decision that would move it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Specialist time is the scarce resource across a solution area. The most valuable output of this activity is sometimes discovering the deal is not blocked on you at all.

activities.name: Assemble the evidence that settles it
activities.description: Work out what would actually resolve the solution decision, and who has to produce it.
activities.prompt: A deal at [account name] is waiting on this solution decision: [describe the decision]. Based on what is recorded for this account, what evidence exists that bears on it, what is missing, and what would a customer need to see to decide? For each missing piece, state whether it would come from the customer, from a technical proof, from a reference, or from someone else at Microsoft. Do not assume a proof or reference exists.
activities.expectedOutput: The evidence that would settle the decision, split by who must produce it, with one piece started.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what evidence is proportionate. A full technical proof is sometimes the right answer and is frequently a way of delaying a decision the customer was ready to make, and only the specialist can judge which situation this is.
activities.requiredContext: The solution decision blocking the deal, and the account it concerns.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections._x000D_
2. Separate evidence you can produce from evidence you have to ask for._x000D_
3. Pick the single piece most likely to settle it rather than assembling everything._x000D_
4. Start on that one and tell the DAE what you are doing and by when.
activities.whyThisMatters: The instinct on a blocked technical decision is to build a proof. At this deal size that often costs more than the deal is worth, and a reference or a short answer would have done.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Name the solution decision the deal is waiting on

activities.name: Check whether you have answered this before
activities.description: Look across the territories you support for the same solution decision, because you have probably already solved it.
activities.prompt: Across the opportunities in my solution area, show any where the recorded blocker, objection or open question resembles this one: [describe the decision]. For each match, show the account, the current stage, what was recorded, and how it was resolved if it was. Do not assume a similar description means the same underlying problem.
activities.expectedOutput: Prior or parallel instances of the same decision, with a reusable answer identified or the pattern escalated.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides whether two similarly described blockers are actually the same problem. Blocker text is written by different people in different territories, and a vocabulary coincidence sends you reusing an answer that does not fit.
activities.requiredContext: The solution decision you are working. The territories and opportunities in your solution area.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your decision.
2. Check whether the matches are genuinely the same problem or just similar wording.
3. If you resolved one before, reuse the answer rather than rebuilding it.
4. If several are open at once, this is a solution-area problem and needs a reusable answer, not three conversations.
activities.whyThisMatters: A specialist covering many territories answers the same question repeatedly without noticing. Noticing is what converts repeated effort into a reusable asset.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Name the solution decision the deal is waiting on

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: You do not own the deal. You own one decision inside it. This session is about finding that decision and moving it.
keyTalkingPoints: The DSS advises rather than owns, so the lever is influence and evidence rather than control. Weekly Qualification Progression rotates by solution area and is where this work surfaces. In this segment a partner is frequently involved in the transaction, which adds a second party whose decisions you also do not control. Facilitator note: the useful frame is that a specialist is accountable for the quality of a decision rather than for the outcome of a deal.
discussionQuestions: On your last stalled opportunity, what was actually blocking it?
Was that blocker yours to move?
What happens when you and the DAE disagree on whether a deal is real?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the named decision to the one action each person takes inside their own remit.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the decision each person is moving and the action they are taking.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one opportunity in your solution area that is not moving.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the solution decision this deal is waiting on?
What evidence would settle it, and who has to produce that?
What are you doing on this deal that is really the DAE's job?
listenFor: Listen for specialists carrying account-owner work, for solution decisions that are actually commercial ones, for blockers with no named owner, and for evidence assumed to exist.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a stalled opportunity, use the last one that was lost and identify the solution decision that never got made.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Where were you doing the account owner's job?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, name the solution decision blocking one opportunity, assemble the evidence it needs, and take one action that sits inside your own remit.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the decision, what you did, and whether it moved.

DSS-DEAL.keyTakeaway: Deals stall on structure more often than on merit. Getting the shape right early is the cheapest work available.

DSS-VALUE.roleTopicName: Prove the Solution Did What You Said It Would
DSS-VALUE.roleTopicDescription: Evidence the outcome your solution area promised, across the accounts where it was deployed, so the next conversation starts from proof rather than from the pitch.
DSS-VALUE.wiifm: A specialist who can point at a comparable customer wins the next conversation before it starts. That evidence has to be collected before you need it.
DSS-VALUE.name: Prove and Communicate Value
DSS-VALUE.description: Turn what has actually happened into a value story the customer recognizes and will act on.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Manages strategic enterprise accounts with complex multi-stakeholder deals and long sales cycles.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Owns the technical strategy and solution roadmap for enterprise accounts.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Designs and validates cloud and AI architectures for customer success.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Drives customer adoption, expansion, and renewal through success planning.

roles.name: Solution Sales Professional
roles.description: Drives solution-specific opportunities by shaping vision and leading value-based conversations.

DSS-VALUE.todayObjective: Find the accounts where your solution area can be evidenced, and the ones where it cannot.
DSS-VALUE.whyItMatters: Value that is not evidenced reads as opinion, and value never communicated is invisible at renewal. Customers judge us on outcomes they can see.

activities.name: Find where your solution area can actually be evidenced
activities.description: Separate the accounts where the outcome is provable from the ones where it is merely believed.
activities.prompt: For these accounts in my solution area where the solution was deployed [list up to fifteen accounts], show for each what is recorded: what was deployed and when, any usage recorded, support issues raised and whether they were resolved, and any milestone or success activity logged. Group them into accounts with recorded evidence of use, accounts with deployment but no recorded use, and accounts where the record shows only the sale. Do not infer outcomes from deployment.
activities.expectedOutput: A bounded set of deployments grouped by whether outcome is evidenced, compared across territories, with a proof-point candidate identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what counts as evidence of an outcome, and reads the difference between territories rather than averaging it. Usage data shows a product being run rather than a customer getting value, and a solution that lands in one DAE's accounts and not another's is usually telling you something about support rather than about the product.
activities.requiredContext: Up to fifteen accounts from more than one territory where your solution area was deployed.
activitySteps: 1. Write down up to fifteen accounts where your solution area was deployed. Pull from more than one territory - comparing across DAEs is the point._x000D_
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list._x000D_
3. The second group matters most - deployed but not used is a story you must not tell as a success._x000D_
4. Compare across territories: if one DAE's accounts show use and another's do not, that is a coverage difference, not a product difference._x000D_
5. Pick the strongest evidenced account as a proof-point candidate.
activities.whyThisMatters: Specialists are asked for proof constantly and reach for the customer they remember rather than the one they can evidence. The two are often not the same account.

activities.name: Build a proof point you can use with another customer
activities.description: Turn one evidenced deployment into something reusable, without carrying anything that should not travel.
activities.prompt: For [account name], where my solution area was deployed, draft a short proof point usable with a different customer: the problem, what was implemented, the outcome and how it is evidenced, and the conditions that made it work. Write it for an audience outside this account. Do not include the customer name, contact names, seat counts, spend figures, or anything that identifies them. Describe them by industry and size band only.
activities.expectedOutput: An anonymized, evidenced proof point, with account-owner approval sought before reuse.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS establishes who owns the outcome before seeking approval to reuse it. Where a partner led delivery, the account owner cannot consent on the partner's behalf, and a proof point built on somebody else's work and circulated without asking is the fastest way to lose a delivery partner. Customers also recognise themselves from far less detail than sellers expect.
activities.requiredContext: One account with an evidenced outcome in your solution area. The account owner, for approval.
activitySteps: 1. Establish who actually led the delivery before you draft anything. If a partner led it, the outcome is theirs and the DAE cannot approve it on their behalf._x000D_
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [account name]._x000D_
3. Read it as though you were the customer being described. If they would recognise themselves, it is not anonymized._x000D_
4. Check the outcome claim is evidenced rather than asserted - that is the part a prospect will test._x000D_
5. Get approval from the account owner, and additionally from the partner if the partner led delivery. Anonymized is not the same as approved, and approved by us is not the same as approved by them.
activities.whyThisMatters: Reusable proof is the specialist's most valuable asset and the easiest to create carelessly. The anonymization is the technical part; the permission is the part that gets skipped.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Find where your solution area can actually be evidenced

activities.name: Work out whose evidence it actually is
activities.description: Establish where a partner led the delivery, because the proof sits with them and asking is a different conversation.
activities.prompt: For these accounts in my solution area with an evidenced or partial outcome [list the accounts], show what is recorded in MSX about partner involvement: whether a partner is associated with the account, any co-sell or referral record and its recorded status, and the dates on those records. Report only what the record contains. Do not infer or state who led the delivery - that is not determinable from MSX.
activities.expectedOutput: The accounts carrying partner records, identified as requiring a Partner Center check before any outcome is claimed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS establishes who led delivery in Partner Center rather than inferring it from our record, and decides on that basis whether an outcome is ours to claim. MSX shows that a partner was associated, never what they did, and presenting a partner's delivery as our proof point damages the relationship the moment they see it.
activities.requiredContext: Your evidenced accounts. Partner association and co-sell records in MSX. Partner Center or the Partner Timeline view, which is where delivery leadership is actually visible.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list._x000D_
2. Treat the output as a list of where to look, not as an answer._x000D_
3. For every account with a partner record, open Partner Center or the Partner Timeline view. Who led delivery is only determinable there._x000D_
4. Anything partner-led: the outcome evidence is theirs to share, not ours to assume._x000D_

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: The fastest way to win the next conversation is to point at a customer like them where it already worked. That evidence has to exist before you need it.
keyTalkingPoints: A specialist works the same solution area across many accounts, which means proof is reusable in a way it is not for an account owner. In this segment value realization is frequently led by a partner in CSP, so the evidence may sit with them rather than with us. Separate what was deployed from what was used and from what the customer valued - they are three different claims. Facilitator note: anything reused across customers has to be sanitized, and what is unremarkable internally can be sensitive externally.
discussionQuestions: When a customer asks who else has done this, what do you say?
Where is the evidence for your last successful deployment?
What can you not say about one customer to another?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the evidence review to the one proof point each person will assemble properly.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the proof point each person is assembling and who has to approve its reuse.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account where your solution area was deployed and you believe it worked.
facilitatorQuestions: What can you actually evidence about that deployment, as opposed to believe?
Is the proof yours, the customer's, or the partner's to give?
What would you need to remove before using it with another customer?
listenFor: Listen for deployment mistaken for value, for proof points that rest on one enthusiastic contact, for partner-held evidence assumed to be available, and for reuse that would breach what can be said about a customer.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a clear success, use one where the outcome was ambiguous and work out what would have made it provable.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which success could you not actually evidence?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, assemble one reusable proof point from a deployment in your solution area, sanitized so it can be used with another customer, and confirm who needs to approve that.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the proof point and what you had to remove from it.

DSS-VALUE.keyTakeaway: Value that is not evidenced is an opinion. Value that is not communicated is invisible.

activities.prompt: Here is the investment hypothesis for [account and opportunity]: [paste]. Test it. What customer outcome would it unlock that will not happen otherwise? What evidence supports that, and what is assumption? What would need to be true for this to be declined, and is any of that already true? If this is Azure-specific, note that Azure Offer Navigator is the front door rather than a general ECIF request. Recommend proceed, reshape, or stop, and say who owns the next step. Do not assess eligibility or approval likelihood.
activities.expectedOutput: A proceed, reshape, or stop decision with the evidence and assumptions separated, and the owner of the next step named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: AE owns the judgment about whether the customer outcome is real, and routes eligibility, policy, and funding questions to the accountable owners rather than answering them.
activities.requiredContext: The investment hypothesis and its account linkage. What the customer has actually said. Who on the account team would build and own the request.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the investment hypothesis from the previous activity.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Be honest about which supporting points are assumption.
4. Decide proceed, reshape, or stop.
5. If proceeding, name who builds the request and who owns the workscope.
activities.whyThisMatters: The cheapest investment request is the one you decide not to build. Qualifying early costs an hour; qualifying late costs the team weeks.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Investment should be connected to a real customer barrier, not added as a side process. Today is about the AE’s role in naming the investment hypothesis and routing the next decision.
keyTalkingPoints: Eligibility, funding, and approval are governed human decisions. AI may help assemble context, status, and evidence, but the AE should not overstate approval or commitment.
discussionQuestions: Where could investment remove a barrier? Which part is yours to advance? Who owns the next governed decision?
suggestedTransitions: Move from investment concept to the AE’s next governed action on one live case.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the investment hypothesis, evidence gap, and next governed owner.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live opportunity or account barrier where investment may be relevant, plus any approved context you can safely use.
facilitatorQuestions: Where might investment remove a real barrier? What evidence supports that barrier? Who owns eligibility, funding, approval, delivery, or value proof?
listenFor: Listen for funding implied as approved, hidden open questions, unowned handoffs, and investment ideas not tied to an account priority or decision.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized scenario if live data is not appropriate. Do not infer eligibility, approval, or funding status.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Test whether investment could remove one real barrier, then route the next decision without implying approval.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the investment hypothesis, source evidence, open questions, owner, and the next governed action.

AE-INVEST.keyTakeaway: Investment succeeds on role clarity, evidence and clean handoffs. Every role owns one part of that chain.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

stepsToGetStarted: Opens Sales Agent. Sales Home is the seller surface inside it - My View for alerts and quota attainment, Prospecting for signals, account research, contacts and outreach, and Pipeline for opportunities, forecast comments, close plans and deal risks. It is not a separate product and has no separate link.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: AE orchestration works when everyone knows the customer decision, their role, the handoff, and the date. Today is about making that operating model explicit.
keyTalkingPoints: AEs often lead through influence without direct authority. AI can assemble commitments, role gaps, partner context, and follow-up drafts; the AE decides who to pull in and how to lead the motion.
discussionQuestions: Where is the handoff currently vague? Which role or partner is missing? What would reduce follow-up noise this week?
suggestedTransitions: Move from role discussion to an owner/date/input map for one opportunity.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one handoff, role gap, or partner action you will make explicit this week.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live account or opportunity that depends on multiple Microsoft roles, partners, or delivery handoffs.
facilitatorQuestions: Which role, partner, or handoff is missing right now? What input does each owner need? What follow-up should be automated or drafted, and what should remain relationship-led?
listenFor: Listen for responsibility without authority, handoffs assumed rather than confirmed, partner motions added late, and meetings where every role attends but no owner is clear.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If systems are unavailable, map the handoff chain manually and capture the prompt or workflow to run later.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Create or update one account-team operating brief with owners, inputs, dates, and next customer decision.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the role/partner map, handoff list, follow-up message or plan, and what changed after owner validation.
