primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account with a QBR, SBR, renewal, or executive follow-up where value evidence matters.
facilitatorQuestions: What value would the customer recognize? Which outcome is supported by evidence, and which is only expected? What strategic ask should follow from the value story?
listenFor: Listen for value claims without evidence, QBRs that become status readouts, unsupported causality, missing customer commitments, and expansion asks not tied to outcomes.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If evidence sources are unavailable, build the value structure and mark each claim as supported, assumed, or needs review.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Build one executive value or QBR brief and validate which claims are supported before sharing.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the value/QBR brief, source evidence, unsupported claims removed, strategic asks, and owner for follow-up.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Prove the investment produced the technical outcome
activities.description: Collect the technical evidence that the investment delivered what it was funded to deliver, and name what it did not.
activities.prompt: This investment was funded to achieve [paste the original technical outcome and success measures]. Here is what has happened since: [paste delivery status, milestones from ECIF Central, and any technical results]. Assess each success measure as met, partially met, or not met, with the evidence for each judgment. Where a measure cannot be evidenced, say so rather than inferring it. Identify what would need to be true for this to count as a technical success, and what the customer would say if asked independently.
activities.expectedOutput: Each success measure assessed with evidence, and an explicit list of what cannot be evidenced.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS owns the technical judgment about whether an outcome was genuinely achieved, and does not let an unevidenced measure be reported as met.
activities.requiredContext: The original technical outcome and success measures from the workscope. Delivery status and milestones from ECIF Central. Technical results to date.
activitySteps: 1. Retrieve the original success measures from the approved workscope.
2. Gather delivery status and milestones from ECIF Central.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Be honest about measures that cannot be evidenced.
5. Bring the unmet ones to the account team before the realization review, not during it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Investment that cannot be evidenced makes the next request harder for everyone on the account.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about assess the strategic and technical case for investment without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is A strategic and technical investment assessment with dependencies, readiness, risks, and the next governed decision named. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: What technical problem is this investment actually meant to solve?
What would tell you six months from now that it worked?
Which dependency would quietly sink it, and who owns that dependency?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the investment case to the technical evidence it needs and the governed decision that comes next.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the investment, the observable success measure, and the approval question you will route to its correct owner rather than answering themselves.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: What technical outcome does this investment buy that we could not get otherwise?
What is the observable measure that proves it worked?
Which approval or eligibility question are you assuming rather than confirming?
listenFor: Listen for the ATS drifting into eligibility, funding, or approval decisions that belong to other owners, success measures that cannot be observed, deployment paths assumed rather than validated, and handoffs to delivery with no re-engagement trigger.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Test one investment case against its technical dependencies, and route one approval question to its real owner.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the dependency that would sink it and the owner you routed the question to.

ATS-INVEST.keyTakeaway: Investment succeeds on role clarity, evidence and clean handoffs. Every role owns one part of that chain.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Turn the hardest review questions into a readiness edit
activities.description: Find the three questions the content invites, then change the contribution so it answers them before they are asked.
activities.prompt: Here is our technical contribution for a customer business review: [paste]. Identify the three hardest questions this content invites, including about progress that has been slower than planned and any risk we have named. For each question, state what evidence the content currently offers, whether that evidence is sufficient, and the specific edit to the contribution that would answer the question before it is asked. Return the edits as a numbered change list, not as a rewritten document. Do not treat a statement of intent as evidence.
activities.expectedOutput: A numbered change list making the contribution answer its three hardest questions, plus any evidence gap named explicitly.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS decides whether to strengthen the evidence, name the gap openly, or remove the claim, and owns every technical statement made to the customer.
activities.requiredContext: The technical CBR contribution; known risks and slow areas; who attends from the customer side; commitments made in prior reviews.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the reviewed CBR contribution.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Apply the edits where evidence exists.
4. For any question where evidence does not exist, decide whether to name the gap openly in the review or remove the claim.
5. Bring that decision to the huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: The credibility of a business review is decided by the answer to the uncomfortable question.

activities.name: Convert the review into technical decisions
activities.description: Turn what was discussed into the decisions, owners, and dates that make the next review shorter.
activities.prompt: Here are the notes from the customer business review [paste]. Extract only the technical decisions that were actually made, the decisions that were deferred and why, and the ones that were avoided. For each open decision, state who needs to make it, what they need in order to make it, and by when it must happen to protect the roadmap. Do not record a decision as made if the notes show it was only discussed.
activities.expectedOutput: Separated lists of made, deferred, and avoided decisions, with owners and dates for the open ones.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS confirms which decisions were genuinely made and owns the follow-up commitments before they are shared.
activities.requiredContext: Review notes; attendees; the roadmap and its dependencies; commitments made in prior reviews.
activitySteps: 1. Capture review notes.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Separate made, deferred, and avoided.
4. Assign the top open decision an owner and date.
5. Confirm it with the customer.
activities.whyThisMatters: A review that produces no decision guarantees the same conversation next quarter.

activities.name: Raise the risk with the customer before it becomes news
activities.description: Draft the message that tells the customer about a technical risk early, in a way that keeps trust rather than spending it.
activities.prompt: We have identified this technical health risk: [paste risk, evidence, impact, and what we are doing]. Draft a short message to the customer technical owner that states the risk plainly, what we know and do not yet know, what we are already doing, what we need from them, and when we will update them next. Do not minimize the risk, do not over-apologize, and do not commit to a resolution date we have not agreed internally. Keep it under 150 words.
activities.expectedOutput: A short, honest customer message with a named next update date.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS confirms no commitment is made that has not been agreed internally, and owns the decision to communicate and the wording.
activities.requiredContext: The identified risk and its evidence; the intervention plan; what has been agreed internally; the customer relationship and prior communications.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the ranked risk and intervention plan.
2. Confirm internally what can be committed.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Adjust to your relationship with the customer.
5. Send, and diarize the next update.
activities.whyThisMatters: A risk the customer hears about from us early costs far less than one they discover themselves.

activities.name: Find the risk the data does not show
activities.description: Test the health assessment against what people have said, not only against what the systems report.
activities.prompt: Here is our current technical health assessment based on system data: [paste]. Here are recent notes and conversations with the customer team: [paste]. Identify concerns raised by people that do not appear in the system data, and any system signal that people are not talking about. For each mismatch, say which source is more likely to be right and what would confirm it. Do not treat silence as agreement.
activities.expectedOutput: A list of mismatches between reported data and human signals, with what would confirm each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The ATS judges which human signal is credible. A concern raised in a corridor conversation carries no evidence a system can weigh, and dismissing it because it is unrecorded is how the risks that matter stay invisible.
activities.requiredContext: System-derived health assessment, or a hand-built substitute table if system access is unavailable; recent conversation notes with the customer team; who has been quiet and who has been raising concerns.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the data-based assessment.

2. Gather recent conversation notes. If dashboard or transcript access is unavailable, build a lightweight table by hand with source, date, owner, evidence, and your confidence in it, then use that instead.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Pick the mismatch that would hurt most if ignored.
5. Add it to the risk list or record why not.
activities.whyThisMatters: The risks that damage accounts are usually mentioned in conversation long before they appear in a dashboard.

keyBenefits: Turns supplied data into findings and visuals a non-analyst can act on, including trends, outliers, and executive-ready charts, without building the analysis by hand.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about assess technical health and prioritize risk response without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is A prioritized technical risk response with source signals, owner, intervention, and checkpoint. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: Which technical risk have you known about for weeks without acting on?
What is stopping you: evidence, ownership, or the conversation itself?
Which risk would the customer say is most urgent, and does it match yours?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the ranked risk view to one intervention with an owner, a date, and an escalation threshold.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the top technical risk, the intervention, the owner who has agreed to it, and the threshold that would trigger escalation.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: Which risk is most likely to become an escalation, and what is the earliest signal?
Who owns the intervention, and have they agreed to it?
What would you tell the customer today if you had to raise this now?
listenFor: Listen for risks ranked by score rather than by consequence, interventions with no named owner, escalation thresholds that were never defined, and risks the team has normalized because they have lived with them. Also listen for signals from conversations that never made it into the system data.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Take one technical risk to its owner this week with the intervention and the escalation threshold.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the risk, the owner who accepted it, and the threshold you agreed.

activities.name: Define the investment-funded technical scope and decision criteria
activities.description: Bound what the investment is technically meant to prove, including the assumptions, dependencies and explicit out-of-scope items.
activities.prompt: Clarify the technical problem, bounded scope, architecture assumptions, decision criteria, dependencies, risks, and out-of-scope items that the proposed investment should address. Do not infer eligibility or approval.
activities.expectedOutput: Bounded technical scope and decision-criteria brief.
activities.humanCheckpoint: SE validates technical content and confirms that eligibility, policy, commercial, funding, and approval decisions remain with accountable owners.
activities.requiredContext: Customer problem, opportunity context, proposed investment
activities.whyThisMatters: Clear technical scope prevents investment-funded work from expanding beyond the proof it was meant to produce.

agents.name: Sales Agent
agents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
agents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

activities.name: Pressure-test investment scope against failure modes
activities.description: Stress the proposed technical scope for the assumptions and failure modes that would undermine the investment.
activities.prompt: Using the draft technical scope and architecture assumptions, identify the assumptions that would most damage the outcome if wrong, the failure modes that would surface during delivery, and the evidence that would confirm or rule out each one.
activities.expectedOutput: Ranked assumption and failure-mode register with the evidence needed to close each one.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE names the assumption that would most damage the outcome if wrong. Failure modes are easy to list and unequally weighted, and only the engineer knows which one actually breaks the delivery.
activities.requiredContext: Draft technical scope, architecture assumptions, known constraints
activities.whyThisMatters: Failure modes found during scoping are cheaper than failure modes found during delivery.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Investment-funded proof work needs scope, success measures, failure-mode awareness, and handoff boundaries before execution begins.
keyTalkingPoints: SE owns the technical clarity, not eligibility, policy, commercial, or approval decisions.
Success measures must be observable.
Delivery handoff should state what is decided, what remains open, and when SE must be re-engaged.
discussionQuestions: What technical problem is the investment meant to prove or unblock?
Which success measure is observable enough?
What failure mode would make the investment underdeliver?
suggestedTransitions: Move from investment idea to bounded technical proof package.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Commit to to one scoped technical proof artifact, success measure, or delivery handoff update.
preparationChecklist: Bring a proposed investment-funded proof, workshop, PoC, or scoped engagement and the current technical assumptions.
facilitatorQuestions: Which technical scope boundary matters most?
Which success measure proves the investment helped?
What failure mode or handoff gap needs to be closed before review?
listenFor: Listen for eligibility or approval decisions implied by the SE, vague proof measures, hidden open questions, and delivery handoffs without re-engagement triggers.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If live data is inappropriate, use a sanitized case and do not infer eligibility, funding, policy, or approval status.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Define what one investment-funded proof must demonstrate, in measures someone else could verify.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the success measures and the failure mode you named.

SE-INVEST.keyTakeaway: Investment succeeds on role clarity, evidence and clean handoffs. Every role owns one part of that chain.

CE-INVEST.roleTopicName: Clarify Commercial, Policy, and Approval Dependencies for Customer Investment
CE-INVEST.roleTopicDescription: Surface the commercial structure, policy, agreement, exception, and approval dependencies an investment request will encounter.
CE-INVEST.wiifm: Investment requests lose time when commercial dependencies are discovered late. Naming the questions and owners early avoids rework without implying approval authority.
CE-INVEST.name: Plan, Orchestrate and Realize Customer Investment
CE-INVEST.description: Plan, request, deliver and prove the value of customer investment across the roles that touch it.

CE-INVEST.todayObjective: Name the commercial and approval dependencies before the investment request reaches review.
CE-INVEST.whyItMatters: Customer investment succeeds or fails on role clarity, evidence and clean handoffs. Every role owns one link, and the chain breaks where the handoff is vague.
CE-INVEST.desiredOutcome: A dependency and approval map with authoritative questions, owners, unresolved evidence, and the next human decision.

primaryAgents.name: ECIF Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: AI-powered experience layer, available through Sales Agent and Microsoft 365, that connects the systems used across the end-to-end ECIF journey.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Understand eligible investment offers; create compliant ECIF workscopes with guided, auto-populated inputs; identify suitable suppliers; submit requests; and track status, milestones, overdue actions, and delivery progress.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Preparing or refining an ECIF funding request; selecting an eligible offer or supplier for an Opportunity and location; submitting a request; or tracking milestones and delivery across internal or partner-led projects.
keyBenefits: Reduces seller toil by bringing ECIF guidance and actions into one conversational flow; improves workscope completeness and first-pass quality; speeds the path from scope creation to IO/PO; and provides a connected view of requests, milestones, alerts, and delivery progress.

resources.description: The investment path across systems. Sales Agent and the ECIF Agent for guidance, ECIF Central for the workscope, MSX Deal Assistance for submission and tracking, MCAPS Help when blocked. For Azure offers, start at Azure Offer Navigator.

Review the generated workscope, supplier recommendation, or request status before taking the next governed action.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Find where the approval is actually stuck
activities.description: Work out which approval a request is waiting on, who holds it, and what would move it, rather than waiting for it to surface.
activities.prompt: For investment request [request ID or opportunity], I need to work out what is blocking approval. Here is the current status from the tracker: [paste]. Identify which approval it is waiting on, what evidence that approver typically needs, what in our submission is likely to be the sticking point, and what the fastest legitimate way to unblock it is. Distinguish between a request that is genuinely progressing and one that has stalled. Do not represent anything as approved, and do not suggest routing around an approver.
activities.expectedOutput: A clear read on whether the request is progressing or stalled, the specific blocker, its owner, and one action to unblock it.
activities.humanCheckpoint: CE owns the judgment about whether a delay is normal or a genuine block, and never routes around an approver or represents an approval that has not been given.
activities.requiredContext: The request ID and its current tracker status. The submitted package. Knowledge of the approval path for this request type.
activitySteps: 1. Open the request in MSX Deal Assistance and read the tracker view for stage, owner, and blockers.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it with that status.
3. Decide whether it is progressing or stalled.
4. If stalled, contact the named owner with the specific evidence gap rather than a status request.
5. If blocked on access or tooling, use MCAPS Help.
activities.whyThisMatters: Requests rarely get rejected. They go quiet, and quiet looks like progress until the customer asks.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Investment succeeds on role clarity, evidence, and clean handoffs. Today is about the commercial and policy link in that chain.
keyTalkingPoints: Eligibility, funding, exception, and approval remain human decisions. The CE contribution is to surface commercial and policy dependencies, cite authoritative guidance, and route questions to the right owner.
discussionQuestions: Which commercial dependency would slow this investment later? Which decision is genuinely yours? Which question must be routed to an authoritative owner?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the investment lifecycle to the CE-owned dependency and the next governed action.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Map one investment dependency to the authoritative question, owner, and next human decision.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one proposed or in-flight investment, customer agreement context, current policy question, and the known owner or approver.
facilitatorQuestions: Which activity helps clarify the commercial or policy dependency? What would make the output safe to use? Where must a human owner decide?
listenFor: Listen for: eligibility, funding, or approval implied rather than decided; exception ownership unclear; handoffs without named owners; and questions that need authoritative guidance.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized scenario. Do not use live customer data or infer eligibility, approval, exception, or funding status.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Map the approval dependencies for one investment and find where it is actually waiting.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the dependency map and the blocker you identified.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home

secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Investment succeeds on role clarity, evidence and clean handoffs. Today is about your part of that chain.
keyTalkingPoints: Every role owns one link. The chain breaks at the handoff.
Eligibility, funding and approval are human decisions. AI assembles the evidence.
An investment request without named open questions hides them rather than resolving them.
discussionQuestions: Where could investment-funded scope become undeliverable?
Which prerequisite, dependency, or owner must be confirmed before delivery starts?
What technical outcome evidence will be needed later?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the investment lifecycle to the CSA's delivery-readiness or outcome-evidence action on a live or sanitized case.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name one investment delivery-readiness check or outcome-evidence action and its owner.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one proposed or approved investment-funded scope, known technical dependencies, and the delivery checkpoints you would want confirmed.
facilitatorQuestions: Which investment activity is closest to your real delivery responsibility?
What status or milestone data must be verified before acting?
Where could handoff, prerequisite, or ownership failure become customer-visible?
listenFor: Through the CSA lens, listen for: funding or approval inferred from summaries; delivery status not checked against the authoritative record; unowned prerequisites; and technical outcomes that cannot be measured later.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized scenario. Do not use live customer data or infer eligibility, approval or funding status.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Validate delivery readiness for one investment and name the dependency most likely to slip.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the readiness assessment and the dependency you flagged.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.prompt: This investment was intended to deliver [paste the outcome and the success plan linkage]. Here is what was delivered and what the usage and adoption data shows: [paste]. Produce a realization view that separates what we can evidence, what we are inferring, and what has not materialized. activities.humanCheckpoint: CSAM confirms the customer would recognize the value as described, and removes any claim the customer would dispute before it reaches a review.
activities.requiredContext: The investment outcome and success plan linkage. Delivery evidence and milestones. Adoption and usage data. What the customer has said about value.

2. Gather delivery evidence from ECIF Central and adoption data.

4. Read the evidenced list as if you were the customer.
5. Take the unproven items to the account team before the realization review.
activities.whyThisMatters: Value the customer would not describe the same way is not realized value, whatever the internal record says.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Customer investment should be governed through the success plan, not treated as a separate administrative process.
keyTalkingPoints: Investment execution needs owners, milestones, handoffs, risk tracking and value evidence. The CSAM governs the operating rhythm and realization story.
discussionQuestions: Is the investment on this account connected to the success plan, or running beside it?
Who owns delivery, and when did you last confirm status with them rather than assume it?
What evidence would the realization review need that you do not have yet?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the investment rhythm to the one checkpoint you will run this month and the evidence it produces.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the investment checkpoint you will run, the delivery status you will confirm rather than assume, and the realization evidence you will start collecting.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one active or proposed customer investment, scope, milestone list or execution question.
facilitatorQuestions: How does this investment show up in the success plan?
Which delivery status did you confirm rather than assume?
What evidence will the realization review need, and who is producing it?
listenFor: Listen for investment running as a parallel process rather than part of the success plan, delivery status inferred from silence, realization evidence identified only when the review is booked, and the CSAM answering eligibility or approval questions that belong elsewhere.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If the tool or data source is unavailable, map the current workflow manually, name the trusted sources and draft the prompt plus human checkpoint for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Run one investment checkpoint and confirm a delivery status rather than assuming it.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the status you confirmed and how it differed from what you assumed.

CSAM-INVEST.keyTakeaway: Investment succeeds on role clarity, evidence and clean handoffs. Every role owns one part of that chain.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.

activities.name: Brief the specialist so they arrive useful
activities.description: Build the short briefing that lets a partner or specialist contribute in their first meeting rather than spending it catching up.
activities.prompt: A [role] is joining to support this technical priority. First tell me: are they an internal Microsoft specialist or an external partner? I will answer, and you will adjust what may be included accordingly. Here is the context: [paste priority, customer context, and what has already been tried]. Write the briefing they need before their first customer meeting. Include: the customer's outcome in their own words, what has already been attempted and why it did not close the gap, the technical constraints that are fixed, who they will meet and what each person cares about, the specific contribution we need from them, and what they should not commit to. If the recipient is external, generalize or remove customer-identifying detail, internal roadmap references, unannounced product information, and named technical risks, and list separately what I removed so I can decide whether to share it another way. Keep it under 300 words and assume they have no history with this account.
activities.expectedOutput: A short standalone briefing appropriate to the recipient type, plus a separate list of anything withheld because the recipient is external.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS classifies the recipient as internal or external before drafting, then confirms that no customer-identifying detail, roadmap reference, or named technical risk reaches an external partner without approval, and confirms what the recipient may and may not commit to.
activities.requiredContext: Whether the recipient is an internal Microsoft specialist or an external partner; the technical priority and customer outcome; what has been tried; fixed constraints; the stakeholders they will meet; the sensitivity classification of any account detail.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the capability gap assessment and alignment note.
2. Classify the recipient as internal specialist or external partner before writing anything.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Review the removed-items list and decide what, if anything, to share through an approved channel.
5. Send it before the meeting, not during.
6. Ask them what is still unclear.
activities.whyThisMatters: An unbriefed specialist spends their first customer meeting learning what you already knew.

activities.name: Check whether the support actually moved the priority
activities.description: Review what changed after partner or specialist involvement, so the next request is based on evidence rather than habit.
activities.prompt: Gather what has happened on this account since [date] from my recent meetings, notes, chats, and files, and summarize it against this original capability gap and ask: [paste original gap and what we asked for]. Then assess whether the gap is now closed, partially closed, or unchanged, and what evidence supports that judgment. If it is unchanged, identify whether the problem was the brief, the fit, the timing, or the gap itself being misdiagnosed. If you cannot find enough recent activity to judge, say so rather than inferring. Be direct.
activities.expectedOutput: A judgment on whether the gap closed, with evidence, and a diagnosis if it did not.
activities.humanCheckpoint: ATS owns the assessment of a colleague's or partner's contribution and decides how, or whether, it is shared.
activities.requiredContext: The original capability gap and the ask made; the date support began; access to recent meetings, notes, and files, or a manual summary if access is unavailable; the current state of the technical priority.
activitySteps: 1. Restate the original gap and ask.
2. Let the agent gather recent activity, or supply it manually if the agent cannot reach the sources.
3. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
4. Decide whether to continue, change the ask, or stop.
5. Record the lesson for the next request.
activities.whyThisMatters: Support gets added by habit unless someone checks whether the last one worked.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Today is about align partner and specialist support to technical priorities without turning the huddle into a tool demo or a status review.
keyTalkingPoints: The goal is A partner and specialist alignment plan with feature gaps, owners, timing, and next decision. AI can assemble evidence and draft options, but ATS judgment stays accountable for strategy, technical accuracy, and next decisions.
discussionQuestions: Where is technical feature the constraint, rather than time or priority?
When you last brought in a specialist, did it change the outcome?
What would a partner need from you to arrive useful rather than catching up?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the feature gap to one specific, dated ask with the briefing that makes it answerable.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the feature gap, the specific ask you will send, who receives it, and whether that recipient is internal or external.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm access to the named tools, bring one real account or technical strategy example, and review the commitment from the prior huddle.
facilitatorQuestions: Is the gap feature, capacity, or clarity? They need different answers.
What exactly would you ask this partner or specialist to do?
What will you send them so they arrive useful rather than catching up?
listenFor: Listen for support requested by habit rather than by need, asks vague enough that anyone could decline them politely, briefings promised verbally and never sent, and customer-sensitive detail heading to an external partner without a classification step.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tooling is unavailable, map the workflow and human checkpoint manually, then draft the prompt for later testing.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Write one specific partner or specialist ask and send the briefing that makes it answerable.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ask, the briefing, and whether the recipient was internal or external.

activities.whyThisMatters: A request that comes back for missing information costs a cycle. Most of what gets sent back is knowable before submission.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Investment requests slow down when inputs, owners, or open questions are hidden. Today is about readiness.
keyTalkingPoints: Separate facts from assumptions. Name confirmed inputs, gaps, contributors, policy/process questions, and next governed action.
discussionQuestions: Which request input is missing? Who owns it? What should not be represented as approved?
suggestedTransitions: Move from request readiness to next governed action.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the next governed investment action, owner, and evidence needed.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live solution pursuit, solution play, lead list, opportunity, or investment case relevant to this huddle; confirm tool access; review last commitment and evidence.
facilitatorQuestions: What request input is missing? Who owns it? What decision must remain human?
listenFor: Listen for eligibility or funding implied rather than confirmed, hidden open questions, and contributor inputs without owners.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: Use a sanitized scenario if live investment data should not be used.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Check one investment request against what a complete submission needs before you submit it.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what was missing and where the request sits now.

activities.name: Map the workflow the team chose and find where it leaks
activities.description: Make the chosen workflow visible end to end, then locate the specific steps where time, confidence, or quality is lost.
activities.prompt: I run this recurring workflow: [describe the workflow, what triggers it, how often, and who depends on the output]. Here is a recent example of it going badly: [describe what happened]. Break the workflow into its actual steps. For each step, identify what input it needs, what decision it requires, and who owns it. Then tell me which two or three steps most likely cost time or quality, and why you think so. Ask me for anything you need rather than assuming it. Do not propose tools yet.
activities.expectedOutput: A step-by-step map of the chosen workflow with the two or three highest-friction steps named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The person who owns the workflow confirms the step map matches how the work is really done, not how it is supposed to be done.
activities.requiredContext: A recurring workflow you personally run; a recent concrete example; who owns each step; what inputs the workflow depends on.
activitySteps: 1. Describe the workflow and one recent example.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt.
4. Correct the step map where the model got your work wrong; that correction is where the learning is.
5. Agree as a group which step leaks the most.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most workflow friction is invisible to the person living with it, because they have already adapted to it.

activities.name: Design one bounded experiment you can finish this week
activities.description: Turn the highest-friction step into a test small enough to run before the next huddle and specific enough to judge.
activities.prompt: Here is the workflow step I want to test: [paste the step and why it costs time or quality]. Design a one-week experiment. Specify: the exact input I will supply, the action I will take, the output I expect, who reviews it before it is used, what evidence I will bring back, and the stop condition that tells me to abandon it. Keep it small enough to run in under an hour total. If the step as described is too large to test in a week, tell me how to narrow it rather than proposing a bigger plan.
activities.expectedOutput: A bounded experiment card with input, action, output, reviewer, evidence, and stop condition.
activities.humanCheckpoint: You decide whether the experiment is genuinely small enough to finish, and you own the judgment about what output is safe to use in real work.
activities.requiredContext: The friction step from the previous activity; what data or systems you can actually access this week; who could review the output.
activitySteps: 1. Take the step your group identified.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Cut the experiment down until it fits in an hour.
4. Name your reviewer and your stop condition out loud.
5. Put it in your calendar before you leave the huddle.
activities.whyThisMatters: An experiment that does not fit in a week does not get run, and an experiment without a stop condition never ends.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This huddle has no pre-written workflow. The team chooses one, which means the value depends entirely on picking a workflow people actually run. Anchor the session in real work and trusted context before anyone opens a tool.
keyTalkingPoints: The workflow must be recurring, not a one-off.
Someone in the room must actually own it.
A specific recent example beats a general description.
If the team cannot name a real example, the workflow is too abstract to work on.
discussionQuestions: What workflow are we improving today?
What triggers it, and how often does it run?
What inputs, constraints, and approvals shape it?
Whose work is it, and who else depends on the output?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the friction people named to one specific assistable step, then from that step to a single bounded experiment with an owner.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the workflow you chose, the one step you will test, the human checkpoint you will keep, and the evidence you will bring back. If you cannot name an owner or a date, the experiment is not real yet; shrink it until it is.
preparationChecklist: Bring one recurring workflow you personally run and one recent example of it, including what made that run harder than it needed to be.
facilitatorQuestions: Where in this workflow is effort or quality lost today?
What is the smallest step AI could assist, rather than the whole workflow?
What must a person verify before the output is used?
What would a one-week version of this experiment look like?
listenFor: Listen for scope that is too broad to test in a week, inputs the person cannot actually access, an output nobody would notice if it were wrong, and enthusiasm for a tool without a workflow behind it. Also listen for the opposite problem: a step so small that automating it changes nothing.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If a tool or data source is unavailable, map the workflow on paper and design the experiment for later execution. Use a hypothetical process shape if needed, but do not invent business facts, customer detail, or system behavior.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: What will you test this week? State the input, the action, the output, who reviews it, and what would tell you to stop.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the actual output from your experiment, whether it worked or not. A failed experiment with evidence is more useful to the group than a success without it.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

activities.name: Find out what this customer actually owns
activities.description: Retrieve the agreements, enrollments, and license estate for one of your own accounts, so you know what the customer already has before you talk to them.
activities.prompt: List all agreements for [Account name or TPID] with type and status, and show me the list of enrollments. For the agreement I name next, provide the license estate details grouped by SKU. Lead with the identifier I gave you. If you cannot retrieve something, say so rather than estimating it, and do not infer entitlements that are not in the data.
activities.expectedOutput: A list of agreements and enrollments for the account, plus license estate grouped by SKU for one agreement.
activities.humanCheckpoint: You confirm the retrieved data matches the account you meant, and treat entitlement and licensing detail as information to verify with the deal owner before making any customer-facing commitment.
activities.requiredContext: An account you work on, and ideally an agreement number, enrollment number, or TPID. Access to Sales Agent with your CRM scope connected.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one account you actually work on.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Run the prompt with the account name or TPID.
4. Pick one agreement from what comes back and ask for the license estate grouped by SKU.
5. Note anything you did not know.
6. Note anything you had assumed that turned out to be different.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most roles walk into customer conversations without knowing what the customer already bought. The answer takes about ninety seconds to retrieve.

activities.name: See what is expiring and what that means for your work
activities.description: Surface upcoming renewals and consumption trend for your account, then work out what it changes for your own role rather than for the deal owner's.
activities.prompt: What are the upcoming renewals for [Account name or TPID]? Show expiry dates and current agreement details, then give me the ACR trend month over month for this account. Do not recommend a renewal strategy. I want the facts and the timing so I can work out what my own role needs to do before that date.
activities.expectedOutput: Upcoming renewals with expiry dates, agreement detail, and consumption trend, plus one action your own role owns ahead of that date.
activities.humanCheckpoint: You decide what the timing means for your own work, and leave renewal strategy, pricing, and commercial approach to the account owner and Commercial Executive.
activities.requiredContext: The account and identifier from the previous activity. Your own role's commitments on that account.
activitySteps: 1. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
2. Run the prompt for your account.
3. Note the nearest expiry date.
4. Work backwards: what does your role need to have done before that date?
5. Name the one thing you would otherwise have found out too late.
activities.whyThisMatters: A renewal date is a deadline for every role touching the account, not only for the person who owns the deal.

activities.name: Draw the line between what you can answer and what you should hand off
activities.description: Sort the deal questions you get asked into ones you can now answer yourself and ones that belong to the deal owner, so you stop escalating retrievable facts and stop answering commercial questions you should not.
activities.prompt: Here are deal-related questions I have been asked recently by customers or colleagues: [paste the questions]. For each one, tell me whether it can be answered by retrieving facts from agreements, enrollments, licensing, or consumption data, or whether it requires a commercial, pricing, policy, or approval decision. For the retrievable ones, give me the prompt I would use. For the rest, say what kind of decision it is. Do not answer the commercial ones yourself.
activities.expectedOutput: Your questions sorted into retrievable and decision-requiring, with a prompt for the first group and an owner for the second.
activities.humanCheckpoint: You own the judgment about where the line sits on your accounts, and confirm that anything commercial, pricing, policy, or approval related routes to the accountable owner rather than being answered from retrieved data.
activities.requiredContext: Real questions you have been asked. Knowledge of who owns commercial decisions on your accounts.
activitySteps: 1. List the deal questions you have been asked in the last month.
2. Paste what you gathered into the prompt where it asks for it, then run it.
3. Check the split against your own judgment.
4. Pick one question you used to escalate and commit to answering it yourself next time.
5. Pick one you should always route, and confirm who owns it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Two failures cost time: escalating a question you could have answered, and answering one you should have escalated.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Deal making features live inside Sales Agent. There is no separate agent to select: when you ask Sales a deal-related question, those features answer. This session is not about learning to run deals. It is about being able to find deal facts for your own accounts, whatever your role, instead of waiting for someone to send them to you.
keyTalkingPoints: Deal Agent is a skill inside Sales Chat, reached by picking the Sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot. There is nothing separate to install or select.
Its primary motion is renewals, specifically EA and MCA-E. That is where it is strongest.
The trigger is specificity. A TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number returns real data; a vague account reference returns a generic answer.
Keep one chat thread per deal. Mixing several deals into one thread confuses the context and makes the history hard to audit.
Looking up deal facts is open to every role. Commercial decisions, approvals, and material amendments are not.
discussionQuestions: When did you last need agreement, licensing, or renewal information and have to ask someone for it?
How long did that take, and what did you do while waiting?
What have you assumed about a customer's entitlements that you have never actually verified?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the lookup you ran to the single fact that changes how you would open your next conversation with that customer.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Name the account you looked up, the one fact that surprised you, and one question you previously would have escalated but can now answer yourself. If nothing was new, pick a less familiar account before the next session.
preparationChecklist: Bring one real account you work on, and if you have it, an agreement number, enrollment number, or TPID. If you do not have an identifier, bring the account name and we will find one in the session.
facilitatorQuestions: What did the lookup return that you did not already know?
What did you previously assume about this customer's estate that turned out to be wrong or unverified?
Where does this stop being your call and become the deal owner's?
listenFor: Listen for vague prompts producing vague answers, which is the most common reason people conclude deal making does not work. Listen for a first response being treated as final on a complex deal, when the guidance is to re-run and verify against current data. Listen for several unrelated deals being worked in one chat thread. Listen for someone treating a retrieved figure as approved pricing or a commitment, or stepping past retrieval into structuring a deal that belongs to the AE or Commercial Executive. Also listen for the opposite: someone escalating a question they could now answer themselves.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If Sales Agent access is unavailable or a lookup returns nothing, work from an account you know and list what you would need to verify before the next customer conversation, then name who currently holds each answer. Do not guess at entitlements, pricing, or discount levels.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you learn today? Name one thing AI made easier, one thing that still needed your judgment, and one thing you would do differently next time.
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: What will you do this week? Look up one account before a real customer conversation and use one retrieved fact in that conversation.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the prompt you used, what came back, and whether it changed how the conversation went. If the lookup returned nothing useful, bring the prompt so the group can sharpen it.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Read what the customer's satisfaction data already says
activities.description: Pull the satisfaction, support and relationship signals for one account and separate what the data shows from what you assumed.
activities.prompt: Give me a CX health summary for [Customer name - TPID]. Show OSAT, DSAT and VSAT with their trend over the last four fiscal months, the ATQ and RM scores, and the most recent verbatims. Tell me which metric moved most and when it moved. Where a metric has no data for this account, say so rather than leaving it out.
activities.expectedOutput: A satisfaction summary for one account with OSAT, DSAT, VSAT, ATQ and RM trends, recent verbatims, the metric that moved most, and any metric with no coverage named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The AE decides whether the data matches the relationship they actually have. Where the score and the lived relationship disagree, that gap is the finding, and the AE names which one they trust and why.
activities.requiredContext: One account you own and its TPID; your own current read on how that customer feels; Sales Agent access.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one account you own, with its TPID. CX Vitals only covers TPID-mapped accounts.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details.
3. Open Sales Agent and run the prompt. There is no setup and no separate tool.
4. Compare what the data shows against what you believed about this account before you ran it.
5. Note any metric returned as no data, and treat that as unknown rather than healthy.
6. Keep the output internal. CX Vitals content is Microsoft internal and must not be shared with the customer.
activities.whyThisMatters: You already have a satisfaction signal on most accounts. Not looking at it is a choice, and it is usually the reason a deteriorating account becomes a surprise.
