activities.name: Turn a repeated prompt into a reusable skill
activities.description: Take a prompt you run often and work out whether it should become a saved skill your whole team can use.
activities.prompt: Here is a prompt I run repeatedly: [paste the prompt and describe when you use it]. Help me decide whether this should become a reusable skill rather than something I retype. Tell me what would need to be parameterised so it works for someone else's accounts, what context it silently assumes, what could go wrong if a colleague ran it without understanding it, and what the human checkpoint should be. Then draft the version that would work for the team rather than only for me.
activities.expectedOutput: A judgement on whether the prompt should become a shared skill, what needs parameterising, its silent assumptions, the failure modes and a team-ready draft with a human checkpoint.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides whether the prompt is safe to generalise. A prompt that works because of what the author knows about their own accounts becomes dangerous when someone runs it without that knowledge.
activities.requiredContext: A prompt you run repeatedly; the situations you use it in; what data access it depends on; the colleague who would test it.
activitySteps: 1. Choose a prompt you have run more than three times.
2. Paste it into the prompt where it asks, along with when you use it, then run it.
3. Look hard at what it assumes about your accounts, your data access and your role.
4. Name the human checkpoint explicitly; a skill that runs without one will eventually run wrong.
5. Share the draft with one colleague and watch them use it before publishing it more widely.
activities.whyThisMatters: The prompt you have retyped four times is a skill waiting to be written. Most never get written because nobody notices they are repeating themselves.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Everyone in this room has rebuilt something a colleague had already solved, and everyone has had their own work rebuilt by someone else. This session is about breaking that cycle with one thing you have already made.
keyTalkingPoints: The best reuse candidate is the thing you keep sending to people, not the thing you are proudest of. An asset without prerequisites and limitations will be used once and abandoned. An asset nobody owns is one nobody trusts.
discussionQuestions: What have you sent to more than one colleague in the last month?
What have you rebuilt that you suspect someone else had already done?
What would you need to see before you trusted a colleague's asset enough to use it with a customer?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the chosen asset to what each person must write down before anyone else could use it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the asset each person will publish and where they will put it. An asset that stays in a personal folder has not been captured.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one thing you have built that worked, ideally something you have already shared with at least one person.
facilitatorQuestions: What in your asset only makes sense because of what you already know?
What would you have to tell someone before they could safely use it?
What does it genuinely not do?
listenFor: Listen for assets chosen because the author is proud of them rather than because they are repeatedly needed, for customer detail nobody has noticed, for limitations left unstated, and for material about to be stored where only its author would look.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If someone has nothing built, have them take a prompt they run repeatedly. The packaging exercise is identical and the reuse value is often higher.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you have to explain about your own work that you had never noticed you were assuming?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, publish one asset with its purpose, prerequisites, limitations and your name on it, somewhere a colleague would look.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the asset, where you put it, what you had to strip out, and whether anyone has used it.

activities.name: Check whether committed milestones are actually progressing
activities.description: Test each committed milestone against evidence of real delivery progress, rather than against its status field.
activities.prompt: For [Account name or TPID], review the committed milestones I own. First tell me which sources you can actually reach for this account: milestone records, delivery activity, deployment or consumption data, and customer engagement. Then for each milestone, tell me what evidence exists that it is genuinely progressing, and separate milestones with real evidence from those where only the status field has been updated. Flag any milestone whose date has passed or is approaching with no supporting evidence. Where you cannot see a source, say so and treat that milestone as unknown rather than as stalled.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on each committed milestone separating evidenced progress from status-only updates and from milestones the agent could not see, with unsupported approaching dates flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM verifies with the delivery team before treating a milestone as stalled, and treats anything the agent could not see as unknown rather than as bad news. Delivery work often runs ahead of what is recorded, and raising a false alarm costs credibility with the people you need.
activities.requiredContext: One account and its TPID; the committed milestones you own; access to delivery and consumption activity for that account.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one account with committed milestones you own.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details, then run it.
3. Read what it says it could not reach first. Unknown and stalled are not the same thing, and acting on the difference is the whole point.
4. Separate genuine progress from a status field somebody updated.
5. Check the dates approaching in the next month first; those are still recoverable, then pick the milestone with the weakest evidence and find out what is actually happening.
activities.whyThisMatters: A milestone status is a claim, not evidence. The ones that fail were usually failing quietly for weeks while the status said otherwise.

activities.name: Diagnose why a milestone stopped and route it correctly
activities.description: Establish what is actually blocking a stalled milestone and get it to the person who can move it, rather than escalating in the wrong direction.
activities.prompt: A committed milestone has stalled. Here is what I know: [paste the milestone, its dates, what has and has not happened, and any blocker I am aware of]. Help me work out what is most likely blocking it: a technical dependency, a customer-side resource or decision, a Microsoft delivery constraint, or a commercial issue. For each possibility, tell me what evidence would confirm or rule it out, and which role or function would own it at Microsoft and at the customer. Name the role rather than a person, since you cannot know either org chart; I will map the role to a name. Do not guess at a cause the evidence does not support.
activities.expectedOutput: A ranked set of likely causes with the confirming evidence and the owning role at Microsoft and at the customer for each, the person you have mapped each role to, and the cause you have chosen to act on.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM confirms the cause before routing. Every misrouted milestone costs a cycle, and the commitment date does not move to accommodate the mistake.
activities.requiredContext: The stalled milestone with its dates; what has and has not happened; any blocker you already know about; your Microsoft and customer contacts for that workload.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the milestone with the weakest evidence from the previous practice.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Rule out causes before acting on one. Routing a customer-side problem to a technical owner loses a week.
4. Map each named role to an actual person yourself, and confirm the likely cause with someone closer to the work.
5. Hand it to that person with the evidence attached, not just the problem.
activities.whyThisMatters: Stalled milestones usually have one cause and three plausible explanations. Picking the wrong one costs a week you did not have.

activities.name: Test whether completed milestones produced real usage
activities.description: Check that milestones marked complete actually resulted in the customer using what was delivered.
activities.prompt: For [Account name or TPID], look at the milestones marked complete in the last two quarters and compare them against actual usage of what was delivered. Here is the intended rollout scope as far as I know it: [paste the intended scope, and say plainly where you do not know it]. Tell me first which usage data you can actually reach. Then identify anything marked complete where usage is flat, where usage started and then declined, or where adoption sits with a much smaller group than was intended. Tell me what the data supports and what would need checking with the customer before I draw a conclusion.
activities.expectedOutput: A comparison of completed milestones against real usage, identifying flat, declining or narrowly concentrated adoption, with what needs customer confirmation.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM confirms the intended rollout before calling adoption a failure. A deliberately phased deployment looks identical to a failed one in the data.
activities.requiredContext: An account with recently completed milestones; usage data for the delivered workloads; the customer's intended rollout scope, or an honest statement of where you do not know it.
activitySteps: 1. Bring an account with milestones completed in the last two quarters.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your account and the intended rollout scope, then run it.
3. Distinguish a phased rollout from an adoption failure before reacting. If you did not know the intended scope, that is the first thing to go and find out.
4. Identify who owns adoption on the customer side; it is rarely whoever owned the deployment.
5. Raise flat usage as a finding to work on together, not as a criticism of the delivery.
activities.whyThisMatters: A milestone marked complete that nobody uses is a renewal problem you have already been paid for and will pay for later.

activities.name: Prepare the conversation that unblocks a customer-side delay
activities.description: Plan how to raise a milestone stalled on the customer's side without turning it into a complaint about them.
activities.prompt: A committed milestone is stalled because of something on the customer's side. Here is the situation: [paste the milestone, the blocker, who at the customer is involved, what I am genuinely able to offer to help, and the customer outcome this milestone supports]. Help me prepare the conversation: how to raise it as a shared problem rather than a failure on their part, how to use what I have told you I can offer to make it easier for them, what specifically I need from them, and what the consequence is for them, in their own terms, if it does not move. Do not invent resources, funding or commitments I have not told you I can make. Keep it customer-safe and avoid anything that sounds like chasing a Microsoft number.
activities.expectedOutput: A conversation plan framing the delay as a shared problem, with what you will offer, the specific ask, and the consequence expressed in the customer's terms.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSAM decides how hard to push. A milestone date that matters to Microsoft may not matter to the customer, and pressing on Microsoft's timeline damages the relationship the renewal depends on.
activities.requiredContext: The stalled milestone and its customer-side blocker; who at the customer is involved; what you are genuinely authorised to offer; the customer outcome the milestone supports.
activitySteps: 1. Take a milestone stalled on the customer side.
2. Decide what you can genuinely offer before you run anything. If you do not tell it, it will invent something you cannot deliver.
3. Paste the situation into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Check the consequence is stated in the customer's terms, not Microsoft's.
5. Have the conversation with the person who can actually move it, not the person you usually speak to.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most committed milestones stall on the customer side, and most of those conversations go badly because they sound like Microsoft chasing its own number.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: You inherit milestones the customer has committed to, and you are measured on whether they complete. This session is about finding the ones that are quietly not going to land, while there is still time.
keyTalkingPoints: A milestone status is a claim, not evidence. Committed milestones transfer to customer success to be driven to completion, which means to real usage rather than to a completion flag. Most stalls sit on the customer side, and those conversations go badly when they sound like Microsoft chasing its own number.
discussionQuestions: Which of your committed milestones would you actually bet on landing?
When a milestone stalls, how long does it usually take you to find out?
Which completed milestone do you suspect nobody is using?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the milestone review to the single stalled milestone each person will diagnose and route this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the stalled milestone each person will diagnose and the owner they will route it to with evidence attached.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account with committed milestones you own, their current dates, and whatever delivery or consumption data you can reach.
facilitatorQuestions: Which milestone has a status but no evidence behind it?
What is actually blocking the one that stopped, and who owns that?
Where has something completed without anyone using it?
listenFor: Listen for status fields treated as evidence, for causes guessed at rather than confirmed, for milestones escalated to the wrong owner, and for phased rollouts being mistaken for failed adoption.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If delivery data is not reachable, work from the milestone dates and recent customer engagement alone, and treat the missing data as the first thing to fix.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which milestone turned out to be stalled for a different reason than you assumed, and what did that change?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one committed milestone with no supporting evidence and find out what is actually happening with it.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the milestone, what you assumed was blocking it, what was actually blocking it, and who you routed it to.

CSAM-CONSUME.keyTakeaway: A signed commitment is a promise to consume, not consumption. The plan is what converts one into the other, and it decays unless someone owns each milestone by name.

activities.name: Test your uncommitted milestones against what commitment requires
activities.description: Check each uncommitted milestone against the criteria a commitment is supposed to satisfy, and identify which criteria are not yet met.
activities.prompt: For [Account name or TPID], review the uncommitted milestones I own. A milestone should not be committed until there is a named sponsor who has agreed the outcome, an agreed value and date, confirmed feasibility, available customer and delivery resources, an available budget, and a chosen delivery model. Tell me first which sources you can actually reach. For the sponsor, outcome, value, date and budget, tell me which are evidenced in the record, which are asserted without evidence, and which are simply absent. For feasibility, resources and the delivery model, tell me only whether each is recorded as confirmed and by whom; do not assess the technical position yourself, because the Solution Engineer owns settling those and you do not have the technical context. Rank the milestones by how close they are to being genuinely committable, and do not treat a populated field as evidence on its own.
activities.expectedOutput: Each uncommitted milestone scored against the commitment criteria, with sponsor, value, date and budget separated into evidenced, asserted and absent, the technical criteria reported only as recorded or not and by whom, a readiness ranking, and the unreachable sources named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides what counts as evidence of sponsorship, and routes the technical criteria rather than judging them. A named contact in a field is not a sponsor who has agreed the outcome, and a feasibility box ticked by nobody in particular is not confirmed feasibility.
activities.requiredContext: One account and its TPID; the uncommitted milestones you own; the sponsor, value, date and budget position on each as far as you know it.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one account with uncommitted milestones you own.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details, then run it.
3. Separate a populated field from an evidenced one. Most milestones fail on evidence, not on data entry.
4. Take the closest milestone to commitment, not the largest one.
5. Split the missing criteria into the ones you close and the ones your SE closes, and send the technical half to them today rather than carrying it.
activities.whyThisMatters: A milestone gets committed once. Everything after that is measured against it, so the cost of committing an unready one lands months later on someone who did not make the call.

activities.name: Build the case the sponsor has to agree to
activities.description: Turn the milestone into the outcome, value and commitment a named sponsor would actually put their name to.
activities.prompt: I need a sponsor to commit to a milestone. Here is what I have: [paste the milestone, the outcome it is meant to produce, the sponsor and what I know about what they are measured on, and the value and date I am proposing]. Help me build the case in the sponsor's terms rather than in ours: what outcome they are being asked to own, what they get, what they have to put in including budget and their own people, and what happens to their outcome if the date slips. Tell me which parts of this I have not actually given you, and ask me for them rather than filling them in yourself.
activities.expectedOutput: A sponsor-facing case stating the outcome they would own, what they receive, what they must contribute, and the consequence to their outcome if the date moves, with the gaps you still need to fill named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP judges whether this person can actually commit. Agreement from someone without budget or authority reads identically in the record and fails identically later.
activities.requiredContext: The milestone and the outcome it produces; the named sponsor and what they are measured on; the value and date you intend to propose; what the customer would need to contribute.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the milestone you took forward in the previous practice.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Answer whatever it asks for rather than letting it assume. What the sponsor is measured on is the part that decides this.
4. Check the ask is proportionate to what they get. A commitment that costs them more than it returns will be agreed and then quietly dropped.
5. Take it to the sponsor directly. A commitment relayed through someone else is not a commitment.
activities.whyThisMatters: Sponsorship is the criterion most often recorded and least often true. The test is not whether they are supportive; it is whether they would defend the date to their own leadership.

activities.name: Pressure-test the value and the date before you commit to them
activities.description: Challenge the value and date on a milestone against the evidence behind them, before they become a commitment you are measured on.
activities.prompt: Here is the value and date I am about to commit to on a milestone: [paste the milestone, the value, the date, and how I arrived at each]. Challenge both from the commercial side. For the value, tell me what it assumes about scope, adoption and timing, and which of those assumptions I have evidence for. For the date, work only on what the customer and I control: budget cycle, approval and procurement timing, the customer's own decision cadence, and any contractual or fiscal date it depends on. Do not construct the technical delivery sequence behind the date; the Solution Engineer owns that and you do not have the technical context for it. Then tell me what the value and date would look like if the least-evidenced assumption turned out to be wrong. Do not propose a different number; show me what mine depends on.
activities.expectedOutput: The commercial assumptions the value and date rest on, which are evidenced and which are not, the approval, budget and customer-timing dependencies on the date, and what both would become if the weakest assumption failed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP owns the number and knows to get the delivery sequence from the SE rather than from a model. The decision to commit a value and a date in front of a customer and a forecast is not one to take on a commercial read alone.
activities.requiredContext: The milestone with its proposed value and date; how you arrived at each; the scope and adoption assumptions behind the value; the budget, approval and customer decision timing the date depends on.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the value and date you intend to commit to, and how you arrived at each.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Look for the assumption carrying the most of the number. There is usually one.
4. Get the technical side of the date from your SE rather than from the model. A commercial date that ignores the delivery sequence is half a commitment.
5. Record what the commitment depends on alongside it, so the reason is still there when someone asks in a quarter.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most missed milestones were mis-estimated rather than mismanaged, and the commercial half of the estimate fails as often as the technical half. The assumption that broke was usually visible at the moment of commitment and never written down.

activities.name: Find the uncommitted milestones that are never going to commit
activities.description: Identify uncommitted milestones that have stopped moving and should be closed or reset rather than carried.
activities.prompt: For [Account name or TPID], look at my uncommitted milestones and find the ones that are not progressing: dates that have been moved more than once without the underlying position changing, and milestones with no logged activity against them since they were created. For each of those, also tell me who is recorded as the sponsor and when that contact record was last updated, so I can check myself whether they are still in the role. Do not tell me whether anyone has left; you only know what someone typed into the record. For each milestone, tell me what the record shows and what it does not, and whether the honest action is to reset it with a new basis or close it. Do not recommend closing anything on absence of data alone; say what you would need to see.
activities.expectedOutput: The uncommitted milestones with repeated date moves or no logged activity, the recorded sponsor and how stale that record is, what the record does and does not show, and a reset-or-close recommendation with the evidence still needed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SSP decides what to close. Closing a milestone removes it from the picture everyone else is working from, and a quiet customer is not the same as a dead opportunity.
activities.requiredContext: One account and its TPID; your uncommitted milestones with their date history; the recorded sponsor on each; what you know yourself about recent customer engagement.
activitySteps: 1. Use the same account and its uncommitted milestones.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details, then run it.
3. Check the recorded sponsors yourself. A stale contact record looks identical to a current one, and the agent cannot tell them apart.
4. Check each candidate before acting. A milestone can be quiet because the customer is quiet, not because it is dead.
5. Reset the ones with a real basis and a stale date, close the ones without, and say why in the record. A closed milestone with a reason is reusable evidence; one without is just a gap.
activities.whyThisMatters: Uncommitted milestones that nobody will close make the consumption picture look healthier than it is, and the sponsor who left is usually discovered by the person who inherits the milestone rather than the one who carried it.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Test your uncommitted milestones against what commitment requires

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Committing a milestone is a one-way door. Everything after it is measured against the date and the value you put on it. This session is about the moment before that door closes.
keyTalkingPoints: A milestone is ready to commit when there is a sponsor who has agreed the outcome, an agreed value and date, confirmed feasibility, available customer and delivery resources, an available budget and a chosen delivery model. A populated field is not evidence. Once the milestone is committed it transfers to customer success to be driven to completion, so what you commit becomes someone else's number to defend.
discussionQuestions: Which of your uncommitted milestones would you personally defend the date on?
When a milestone gets committed early, what usually forces it?
Which committed milestone in your patch was committed before it was ready, and what did that cost?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the readiness read to the single milestone each person will either take to a sponsor or deliberately hold.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the milestone each person will take forward and the criterion they still have to close, or the milestone they are choosing to hold and why.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account with uncommitted milestones you own, and for one of them the sponsor, the value, the date and how you arrived at each.
facilitatorQuestions: Which commitment criteria are populated on your milestone but not actually evidenced?
Would your sponsor defend this date to their own leadership?
Which single assumption is carrying most of your value?
listenFor: Listen for a named contact being treated as an agreed sponsor, for values built from scope assumptions nobody has tested, for dates set from when the number is needed rather than when the work can be done, and for milestones being carried rather than closed.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has an uncommitted milestone in front of them, use one that was committed and missed, and run the same criteria backwards to find which one failed.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which commitment criterion did you find you had been treating as met without evidence?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one uncommitted milestone and either close the weakest criterion or make the case for holding it, and write the reason into the record either way.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the milestone, the criterion that was weakest, what you did about it, and whether it moved.

SSP-CONSUME.keyTakeaway: A signed commitment is a promise to consume, not consumption. The plan is what converts one into the other, and it decays unless someone owns each milestone by name.

SE-CONSUME.description: Turn a customer commitment into a consumption plan with owned milestones, and drive those milestones through deployment to usage the customer actually gets value from.

activities.name: Separate what is technically confirmed from what is assumed
activities.description: Establish which parts of the technical path behind a milestone are proven and which are still assumptions carrying the date.
activities.prompt: Here is a milestone we are considering committing to: [paste the milestone, the workload, the target architecture or approach, and what has been proven so far]. Separate what is technically confirmed from what is assumed. For each assumption, tell me what would prove or disprove it, roughly how hard that is to establish, and what breaks if it turns out to be false. Then tell me which single assumption carries the most of the date. Do not treat something we have done at another customer as confirmed here; say what would make it transferable.
activities.expectedOutput: A split of the technical basis into confirmed and assumed, what would settle each assumption and at what effort, what breaks if it fails, and the assumption carrying most of the date.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE decides what counts as proven in this environment. A pattern that worked elsewhere is a hypothesis here, and the difference is invisible in the record once the milestone is committed.
activities.requiredContext: The milestone and its workload; the target architecture or approach; what has already been proven and where; the customer's environment constraints as far as you know them.
activitySteps: 1. Bring one uncommitted milestone with a technical dependency you are not certain about.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Check that it has not quietly promoted a pattern from another customer into a confirmed fact here.
4. Take the assumption carrying the most of the date and work out what would settle it.
5. Say plainly which assumptions remain open. That sentence is what protects the date.
activities.whyThisMatters: Technical commitments fail on the assumption nobody wrote down. Naming them before the commitment is the only point at which naming them is cheap.

activities.name: Name the dependencies and resources the date actually needs
activities.description: Work out what the customer and Microsoft must each provide for the milestone to land, and where those are not yet secured.
activities.prompt: For this milestone: [paste the milestone, the technical approach, and the open assumptions from the previous practice]. Work out what the date actually depends on. Separate what the customer must provide, including people, environment access, data and decisions, from what Microsoft or a partner must provide, and from what depends on the chosen delivery model. For each, tell me whether it is secured, requested or not yet raised as far as I have told you, and flag anything you cannot tell from what I have given you rather than assuming it is in place. Then tell me which dependency, if it is not secured this month, makes the date unachievable.
activities.expectedOutput: The dependencies split into customer, Microsoft or partner, and delivery model, each marked secured, requested or not yet raised, with the dependency that decides the date identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE confirms what the customer has actually agreed to provide rather than what was discussed. Assumed customer resource is the most common reason a technically sound milestone misses its date.
activities.requiredContext: The milestone and its technical approach; the open assumptions; what the customer has agreed to provide; the intended delivery model; which partner or Microsoft resources are involved.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the assumptions you produced in the previous practice.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Check the customer-side list honestly. It is the half that is usually assumed and rarely secured.
4. Identify the dependency that decides the date and who owns it on the customer side.
5. Raise the unsecured ones now, while the milestone is still uncommitted and the date can still move.
activities.whyThisMatters: The technical work is rarely what slips. What slips is an environment nobody had access to and a customer engineer nobody had booked.

activities.name: Turn the proof result into a commit or hold recommendation
activities.description: Convert what a proof of concept or pilot actually showed into a clear recommendation on whether the milestone can be committed.
activities.prompt: Here is what our proof of concept or pilot actually produced: [paste what was tested, what the results showed, what was not tested, and any conditions that differed from production]. Turn this into a recommendation on whether the milestone can be committed. Tell me what the result genuinely supports, what it does not support because it was not tested, and what would behave differently at production scale or under production conditions. Then give me the recommendation, either commit, commit with a named condition, or hold, with the reason in one sentence I could say out loud to the account team. Do not extrapolate beyond what was tested.
activities.expectedOutput: What the proof result supports and what it does not, what would differ at production scale, and a commit, commit-with-condition or hold recommendation with a one-sentence reason.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE owns the recommendation. A proof result is routinely reported as broader than it was, and the person who ran it is the only one who can say where the boundary is.
activities.requiredContext: The proof of concept or pilot scope and results; what was explicitly not tested; how the test conditions differed from production; the milestone the result is meant to support.
activitySteps: 1. Bring a proof of concept or pilot result behind an uncommitted milestone.
2. Paste what was tested and what was not into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Pay attention to what it says was not tested. That is the part the account team will hear as proven.
4. Take a position. Commit, commit with a stated condition, or hold.
5. Give the account team the one-sentence reason as well as the recommendation, so it survives being repeated.
activities.whyThisMatters: A pilot that succeeded on a narrow scope becomes, three retellings later, a proven solution. The correction is far cheaper before the milestone is committed than after.

activities.name: Work the date backwards from the technical path
activities.description: Build the sequence of technical work a milestone date implies and find where it has no room to absorb a delay.
activities.prompt: Here is a milestone date being proposed and the technical work behind it: [paste the date, the work that has to happen, and the dependencies from the previous practice]. Work backwards from the date. Lay out what has to happen in what order, what can run in parallel and what genuinely cannot, and where a delay in one step consumes the whole margin. Tell me which step has the least certainty and the most consequence. Do not invent how long anything takes; where you need a duration, ask me for it.
activities.expectedOutput: A backwards-planned sequence from the proposed date showing order, genuine parallelism, where the margin is consumed, and the step with the least certainty and most consequence.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The SE supplies the durations and owns the sequence. The model can structure the dependencies but has no basis for estimating how long work takes in this customer's environment.
activities.requiredContext: The proposed milestone date; the technical work required; the dependencies and who owns each; your own estimate of how long each step takes.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the proposed date and the dependency list from the previous practice.
2. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Supply the durations yourself when it asks. It has no basis for guessing them and a guessed sequence is worse than none.
4. Find the step with the least certainty and the most consequence.
5. Take the sequence to whoever proposed the date, before it is committed rather than after it is missed.
activities.whyThisMatters: A date is usually set from when it is needed rather than from when the work can be done. Laying the sequence out is how that gets discussed while it can still change.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Name the dependencies and resources the date actually needs

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: You are usually the person in the room who knows whether the date is achievable. This session is about the window where saying so still changes the outcome rather than explaining the miss.
keyTalkingPoints: Feasibility, resources and the delivery model are part of what makes a milestone committable, and they are the part most often assumed. A pattern that worked at another customer is a hypothesis here, not a proven fact. A proof of concept proves what it tested and nothing else, and it gets retold as broader than it was.
discussionQuestions: Which milestone in your patch has a date nobody has worked backwards from?
What is the last thing you assumed the customer would provide and they did not?
Where has a pilot result been repeated back to you as more than it actually showed?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the confirmed-versus-assumed split to the one dependency each person will secure or escalate before the date is committed.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the assumption or dependency each person will settle, and the position they will give the account team in the meantime.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one uncommitted milestone with a technical dependency you are not certain about, along with whatever has been proven so far and what has not.
facilitatorQuestions: Which part of your technical basis is confirmed here, as opposed to confirmed somewhere else?
What does the customer have to provide, and has anyone actually asked them?
What did your proof deliberately not test?
listenFor: Listen for patterns from other customers being treated as confirmed, for customer-side resource being assumed rather than secured, for proof results described more broadly than their scope, and for durations being guessed rather than supplied.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has an uncommitted milestone, take a committed one whose date is at risk and run the same split. The output is the same and the urgency is higher.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which assumption were you carrying as a fact until you had to write it down?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take the assumption carrying most of a milestone date and either settle it or tell the account team plainly that it is open.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the assumption, what you did to settle it, what you found, and how the account team reacted to being told it was open.

SE-CONSUME.keyTakeaway: A signed commitment is a promise to consume, not consumption. The plan is what converts one into the other, and it decays unless someone owns each milestone by name.

ALL-CLOSE.roleTopicName: Land the Fiscal Year Without Damaging Next Year
ALL-CLOSE.roleTopicDescription: Separate what is genuinely pinned to the fiscal calendar from what only feels urgent, and act on the part that is real while there is still time.
ALL-CLOSE.wiifm: The costly year-end mistakes are a record nobody fixed in time and a deal that was forced early and discounted for no reason. Both are avoidable and both are decided now.
ALL-CLOSE.name: Land the Fiscal Year and Protect What Books
ALL-CLOSE.description: Work out what can still book before the fiscal year closes, get the records right before the systems stop accepting changes, and tell the difference between a real deadline and a self-imposed one.

activities.name: Work out what can still realistically book this fiscal year
activities.description: Separate the deals that can still be fully executed and processed before the period ends from the ones that are already next year's.
activities.prompt: For [my patch, or a named account or TPID], list the opportunities with a close date in the current fiscal period. For each, tell me what the record shows about its approval state, what is still outstanding, whether it has been signed, and whether anything indicates it will arrive for processing after the guaranteed cutoff. Tell me first which of these you can actually see. Do not tell me whether it will book, because the rule that decides that is set by my own segment's bookings policy and you do not have it. Tell me what still has to happen for each deal to be capable of booking in the period.
activities.expectedOutput: Each in-period opportunity with its approval state, what is still outstanding, its signature position, any indication it will miss the processing cutoff, and what still has to happen for it to be capable of booking.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms the bookings rule locally and decides what is genuinely closeable. An approval state in the record is a snapshot, and only the person in the deal knows whether the customer will actually sign in time or is simply being polite about the date.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one account and its TPID; the opportunities you expect to close in the period; their current approval state; what each is waiting on; your Deal Desk or operations contact for the bookings rule that applies to your segment.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your own patch or one account, and the deals you believe are landing this period.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details, then run it.
3. Confirm the bookings rule that applies to your own segment with Deal Desk or operations rather than assuming it. What has to be true for a deal to book in a period, and by when, is set locally.
4. Separate deals waiting on Microsoft approvals from deals waiting on the customer. Only one of those is inside your control, and check the processing runway rather than only the signature date.
5. Decide which deals you are deliberately leaving in the new year, and say so out loud rather than carrying them as hope.
activities.whyThisMatters: Every year some deals get forced into June that were always going to close in July, and are discounted for the privilege. The deals worth pushing are the ones that only need a signature, not the ones that still need a decision.

activities.name: Find the renewals whose expiration timing will cost you the booking
activities.description: Identify renewals whose expiration date sits at the period boundary, where how they are handled decides whether they land in this year or the next.
activities.prompt: For [my patch, or a named account or TPID], list the renewals with expiration dates at or near the end of the current fiscal period. For each, tell me the actual expiration date, whether it has been committed as on-time, what is still outstanding to complete it, and what the record shows about customer engagement on it. Flag any renewal where the expiration falls on the final day of the period, since the booking and billing calendars treat that date differently and it needs handling deliberately rather than by default. Tell me what you cannot see rather than assuming it is fine.
activities.expectedOutput: Renewals at the period boundary with their actual expiration dates, commitment status, outstanding work and customer engagement, with last-day expirations flagged for deliberate handling.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller confirms the processing runway with the person who owns it. Renewal processing has a real lead time and the deadline that matters is when the work has to arrive, not when the agreement expires.
activities.requiredContext: Your patch or one account and its TPID; renewals with expiration dates near the period end; their commitment status; your renewals or operations contact.
activitySteps: 1. Bring your patch or one account with renewals near the period boundary.
2. Replace the bracketed placeholders in the prompt with your own details, then run it.
3. Pay particular attention to anything expiring on the last day of the period. That is the case that behaves differently and gets missed.
4. Confirm the processing runway with your renewals or operations contact rather than assuming it.
5. Commit the ones that are genuinely on-time and stop describing the others as on-time.
activities.whyThisMatters: A renewal at the period boundary is the easiest booking to lose and the hardest to explain, because nothing about it looked at risk until it was.

activities.name: Correct the records that stop being correctable at close
activities.description: Find the records whose correction window closes with the fiscal year, and separate them from the hygiene items that are worth fixing but can be fixed at any time.
activities.prompt: For [my patch, or a named account or TPID], help me find records on my accounts that look wrong, and separate them into two groups. The first is detail that stops being correctable once the fiscal year closes: agreement, licensing and enrollment detail and the amounts tied to them. The second is pipeline hygiene, such as close dates already in the past, mis-categorised forecast or stale commitments, which is worth fixing but is not tied to the fiscal calendar. For each item, tell me what looks wrong, what the correct position appears to be, and what evidence you are basing that on. Tell me which of these you can actually see and which I would have to check somewhere else.
activities.expectedOutput: Records that appear incorrect, split into detail that stops being correctable at close and year-round hygiene, each with the apparent correct position and the evidence for it, and a separation of what you can correct yourself from what must be raised with another team.

activitySteps: 1. Bring your patch or one account.

activities.whyThisMatters: Once the year closes, the agreement and licensing detail stops being editable and only limited fields remain open. The hygiene backlog will still be there in July. This group will not.

activities.name: Separate the real deadlines from the ones you have invented
activities.description: Sort your year-end pressure into work genuinely pinned to the fiscal calendar and work that belongs on the customer's own timeline.
activities.prompt: Here is everything I am treating as urgent because of year end: [paste the list, and for each say what I believe the deadline is and where that deadline comes from]. Sort it into two groups. The first is work genuinely pinned to the fiscal calendar, meaning it must happen before the period closes because a system, an approval chain or a booking rule requires it. The second is work I am pulling forward into this month even though the real driver is the customer's own decision, contract or delivery timeline. For anything in the second group, tell me what it would cost to force it early. Where I have not said where a deadline comes from, ask me rather than assuming there is one.
activities.expectedOutput: Your year-end work sorted into genuinely fiscal-dated and customer-dated, the cost of forcing each item that is being pulled forward, and an owner and date for the items that are genuinely fixed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides what to force. Some work is worth pulling forward even at a cost, and that is a judgement about the customer relationship and the number, not one a model can make.
activities.requiredContext: Your own list of what you are treating as year-end urgent; where you believe each deadline comes from; the customer decision or contract timing behind each item.
activitySteps: 1. Write down everything you are treating as urgent because of year end, and where you think each deadline comes from.
2. Paste the list into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Be honest about the ones where the only deadline is that it is June.
4. For anything you are pulling forward, decide whether the cost of forcing it is worth it. Often it is; the point is to decide rather than to drift.
5. Take the genuinely fiscal-dated items and make sure each one has an owner and a date that is earlier than the cutoff.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most of what feels like a June deadline is a deal on its own clock being pulled forward. Doing that deliberately is fine. Doing it because the month feels urgent is how good deals get discounted and customers get pushed.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Work out what can still realistically book this fiscal year

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Year end generates a lot of urgency and only some of it is real. This session separates the part that is genuinely fixed by the calendar from the part that only feels that way, and acts on the first while there is still room.
keyTalkingPoints: There is no single worldwide month-by-month year-end calendar for Enterprise sellers, and looking for one is why people end up inventing deadlines. What is genuinely fixed is the systems close: for the FY26 close, licensing and agreement detail had to be submitted by 26 June, all revenue had to reach MS Sales by close of business on 30 June, and the close publish landed on 2 July, after which only limited fields remain editable. Confirm this year's exact dates locally, because they shift by a few days. For a deal to book in a period it must be fully approved, final and fully executed before the end of the last day of that period, and it needs processing runway on top of that. Renewals expiring on the final day of a period are treated differently by the booking and billing calendars and need deliberate handling. Facilitator note: ECIF publishes its own detailed year-end milestone calendar, but the milestone quarter-end validation warning is documented for the Americas only, so do not present it as a worldwide rule.
discussionQuestions: Which of the things you are rushing right now would still be urgent if it were March?
What did you find out too late at the last year end?
Which deal did you pull forward last year, and what did it cost to do it?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the closeable list to the single record each person will correct and the single deal each person will deliberately release into the new year.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming, for each person, one record they will correct before cutoff and one thing they are deliberately not forcing into this period.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your own patch or one account, the deals and renewals you expect to land in this period, and a written list of everything you are currently treating as year-end urgent.
facilitatorQuestions: Which of your in-period deals is waiting on Microsoft, and which is waiting on the customer?
What could you correct today that stops being correctable after close?
Which of your urgent items has a deadline you could actually point to?
listenFor: Listen for signature dates being treated as booking dates with no processing runway, for renewals at the period boundary assumed to be fine, for corrections being deferred to the week when every queue is longest, and for deadlines whose only source is that it is June.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If someone carries no quota and no renewals, run the third practice only. The record-correction window applies to anyone who owns milestones or agreement detail, and it is the part most often left to somebody else.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which of your year-end deadlines turned out to have no source other than the month it is?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, correct one record that stops being correctable at close, and tell one customer or one internal owner that a deal you had been pushing is landing in the new year instead.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the record you corrected, the deal you released, and what happened when you said so.

ALL-CLOSE.keyTakeaway: Almost nothing about June is a seller deadline. What is genuinely fixed is when the systems stop accepting changes, and that is the part most often discovered too late.

PSS-PARTNER.todayObjective: Establish where your pinned-partner deals are stuck and take one of them into the next partner conversation with a specific ask.

PSS-PARTNER.desiredOutcome: A stage-by-stage read on your pinned-partner deals, the stalled ones identified with a likely cause, and one specific ask prepared for the partner.

secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. activities.name: See where your pinned-partner deals actually sit
activities.description: Build a stage-by-stage picture of the partner deals you track, and find where the picture and the evidence disagree.
activities.prompt: Here are the pinned-partner deals I track: [paste the list from Partner Center, with the co-sell stage of each, when it last moved, and what the partner last reported]. The co-sell stages run Created and Accepted at 10 percent, Qualified at 20, Developed at 40, Proposed at 60, Negotiated at 80 and Won at 100. For each deal, tell me what the stage claims is true and what would need to be true for that stage to be genuine. Identify deals whose stage has not moved for a long time relative to the others, and deals where the reported stage looks ahead of what the partner has actually described. Do not assume a stage is accurate because it is recorded.
activities.expectedOutput: A read on each deal covering what its stage claims, what would make that stage genuine, which have not moved, and which look stage-inflated.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS judges whether a stage is real. Partners set their own stages and have every reason to be optimistic, and the specialist who knows the deal is the only one who can tell an advancing deal from an advancing number.
activities.requiredContext: Your pinned-partner deals and their current co-sell stage from Partner Center; when each last moved; what the partner last reported; your partner meeting cadence.
activitySteps: 1. Open Partner Center and pull the current stage of each pinned-partner deal you track. The agent cannot see Partner Center, so this list has to come from you.
2. Paste it into the prompt where it asks, with when each last moved, then run it.
3. Look for stages that are ahead of what the partner has actually described. Optimistic stage-setting is the most common distortion.
4. Pick the deal with the longest gap since it last moved.
5. Take that one into your next partner meeting rather than raising all of them at once.
activities.whyThisMatters: Partner deals rarely fail loudly. They sit at a stage that looks respectable while nothing underneath it moves, and nobody asks because the number is not obviously wrong.

activities.name: Work out what is actually blocking the stalled one
activities.description: Establish why a partner deal has stopped between stages and who is genuinely able to move it.
activities.prompt: A pinned-partner deal has stopped moving between stages. Here is what I know: [paste the deal, its current stage, how long it has been there, what the partner has told me, and anything I know from the customer side]. Help me work out what is most likely blocking it: partner capacity or skills, a customer-side decision, a technical dependency, a commercial or licensing issue, or the partner deprioritising it. For each possibility, tell me what evidence would confirm or rule it out, and which role would own it - partner seller, partner development manager, the account executive, or me. Name the role rather than a person, since you cannot know the individuals. Do not guess at a cause the evidence does not support.
activities.expectedOutput: Ranked likely causes with the evidence that would confirm each, the owning role for each, and the cause you have chosen to act on.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS confirms the cause before escalating. A deal stalled because the partner lacks capacity and one stalled because the customer went quiet need completely different interventions, and guessing wrong costs the deal a cycle it may not have.
activities.requiredContext: The stalled deal, its stage and how long it has been there; what the partner has reported; anything you know from the customer side; your PDM and account executive contacts.
activitySteps: 1. Take the deal with the longest gap from the previous practice.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Rule out causes before acting on one. Treating a partner capacity problem as a customer problem loses weeks.
4. Map each named role to the actual person on this deal.
5. If the cause is partner performance rather than this specific deal, that belongs with the PDM, not in another deal conversation.
activities.whyThisMatters: A stalled partner deal has one cause and several plausible stories. The stories are usually more comfortable than the cause.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: See where your pinned-partner deals actually sit

activities.name: Prepare the partner conversation with one specific ask
activities.description: Turn a stalled deal into a partner conversation that produces a commitment rather than an update.
activities.prompt: I am taking a stalled deal into a conversation with the partner. Here is the situation: [paste the deal, its stage, what I believe is blocking it, and what I am able to offer to help]. Help me prepare the conversation: how to raise it as a shared problem rather than an inspection, the one specific thing I am asking them to commit to, what I will do in return, and how we will both know within a short period whether it moved. Do not invent support or resources I have not told you I can offer. Keep it to a single ask; a conversation with four asks produces none.
activities.expectedOutput: A conversation plan framing the stall as a shared problem, with one specific ask, what you will do in return, and how both sides will know shortly whether it moved.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides how hard to push. Partners choose where to put their capacity, and a conversation that feels like an audit moves this deal at the cost of the next five.
activities.requiredContext: The stalled deal and its stage; what you believe is blocking it; what you are genuinely able to offer; your partner meeting or deal clinic cadence.
activitySteps: 1. Take the stalled deal and its likely cause.
2. Decide what you can genuinely offer before you run anything, and include it. If you do not, it will invent something you cannot deliver.
3. Paste the situation into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Cut it down to one ask. This is the step people skip and it is the one that decides whether anything happens.
5. Raise it in the deal clinic or partner rhythm rather than as a separate escalation, so it lands as working the deal rather than checking up on them.
activities.whyThisMatters: Partner conversations default to status updates, which change nothing. A single specific ask with something offered in return is what turns a rhythm into progress.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Work out what is actually blocking the stalled one

activities.name: Look at where your recent deals stopped
activities.description: Take a small number of recent partner deals and check whether they stopped at the same stage.
activities.prompt: Here are a few partner deals I have tracked recently and what happened to each: [paste up to five, with the partner, the stage each reached, and whether it progressed or stalled]. Looking only at these, tell me whether they stopped at a similar stage and what is different about any that got through. Be explicit that this is too small a set to establish a pattern, and tell me what I would need to see to know whether it is real. Give me one thing worth watching for rather than a conclusion.
activities.expectedOutput: Whether the small set stopped at a similar stage, what differs about any that progressed, an explicit caveat about sample size, and one thing worth watching for.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides whether a repeated stage is a real bottleneck. It may equally be the stage where optimistic early staging finally meets reality, and telling those apart needs someone who saw the deals.
activities.requiredContext: Up to five recent partner deals with the partner, the stage reached and the outcome; your partner rhythm or deal clinic.
activitySteps: 1. Bring up to five recent partner deals from Partner Center. The agent cannot see Partner Center, so this comes from you.
2. Note the partner, the stage reached and the outcome for each.
3. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Treat any apparent stage boundary as something to watch for, not as a finding. Five deals cannot tell you where your portfolio stalls.
5. If it does keep recurring, raise it in your partner rhythm as something to look at earlier, not as a scorecard.
activities.whyThisMatters: Chasing individual stalled deals is endless. Noticing that several stopped at the same point is what turns it into something you can change upstream.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Partner deals rarely fail loudly. They sit at a respectable stage while nothing underneath them moves, and nobody asks because the number does not look wrong.
keyTalkingPoints: The co-sell stages run Created and Accepted at 10 percent, Qualified at 20, Developed at 40, Proposed at 60, Negotiated at 80 and Won at 100. Partners set their own stages and have every reason to be optimistic, so a stage is a claim rather than evidence. Your accountability is visibility and Stage 2 to 3 acceleration rather than execution ownership; the partner owns delivery in the later stages and partner performance issues belong with the partner development manager. Facilitator note: Partner Center is a separate system from MSX, so the agent cannot read it - sellers must bring their own stage data into the session.
discussionQuestions: Which of your partner deals would you actually bet on at the stage it claims?
Where do your deals most often stop moving?
When did you last ask a partner for a specific commitment rather than an update?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the stage review to the one stalled deal each person will take into their next partner conversation with a specific ask.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the deal each person will raise, the single ask they will make, and what they are offering in return.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: pull the current co-sell stage of your pinned-partner deals from Partner Center, with when each last moved.
facilitatorQuestions: Which stage is ahead of what the partner has actually described?
What is genuinely blocking the one that stopped?
What is the single thing you would ask this partner to commit to?
listenFor: Listen for recorded stages treated as evidence, for causes assumed rather than confirmed, for partner performance problems being worked one deal at a time instead of raised with the PDM, and for conversations planned with several asks and therefore no ask.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If Partner Center data is not to hand, work from what each partner last told you and treat the missing data as the first thing to fix.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which deal turned out to be stalled for a different reason than the one you had been assuming?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one stalled partner deal into a partner conversation with a single specific ask and something offered in return.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the deal, the ask you made, what the partner committed to, and whether the stage moved.

PSS-PARTNER.keyTakeaway: Handing something to a partner is not the end of your involvement. The windows run whether or not anyone is watching them, and the system closes the lead for you if nobody acts.

DCSA-CONSUME.roleTopicDescription: Read consumption movement across a portfolio far larger than you can work individually, decide where your own time changes the outcome, and route the rest deliberately.

DCSA-CONSUME.description: Turn a customer commitment into a consumption plan with owned milestones, and drive those milestones through deployment to usage the customer actually gets value from.

DCSA-CONSUME.todayObjective: Decide which handful of accounts get your own attention this month, and stop pretending the rest are covered.

DCSA-CONSUME.desiredOutcome: A triaged portfolio with the movement explained, a short list you are personally working, an explicit routing decision on the rest, and one intervention started.

activities.name: Explain the consumption movement before you react to it
activities.description: Take the accounts whose consumption has moved sharply and work out which movements actually mean something.
activities.prompt: Here are the accounts in my portfolio whose consumption has moved sharply: [paste the list, with the account, the direction and rough size of the movement, and anything I already know about what changed]. For each, give me the plausible explanations and what would distinguish them: a genuine change in usage, a workload landing or completing, a migration or seasonal pattern, a billing or reporting artefact, or something going wrong. Tell me which movements look like they need a human and which look self-explanatory. Do not treat a sharp move as automatically bad, and do not treat a rise as automatically good.
activities.expectedOutput: Each significant movement with its plausible explanations, what would distinguish them, and a split between movements needing a human and movements that explain themselves.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides what a movement means. Consumption data shows the shape of a change but not its cause, and a decline during a planned migration and a decline from a failing deployment look identical in the number.
activities.requiredContext: Your portfolio and its consumption movement; the direction and rough size of each move; anything you already know about workloads landing, migrating or completing.
activitySteps: 1. Pull the accounts in your portfolio with significant consumption movement. If you have no other filter, a swing of around a quarter month on month in either direction is a reasonable place to start.
2. Paste the list into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Separate the movements you can already explain from the ones you cannot. Only the second group is work.
4. Watch for rises that are not good news, such as a workload running hotter than the customer intended.
5. Carry forward only the accounts where the explanation genuinely needs a person.
activities.whyThisMatters: Movement in a consumption number tells you something changed, not what changed. Chasing the movement rather than the reason is how a month's attention gets spent on accounts that were always going to be fine.

activities.name: Decide where you go and what the partner takes
activities.description: Split the accounts that need attention into the few you will work yourself, the ones a partner is better placed to take, and the coverage gap that is left.
activities.prompt: Here are the accounts from my portfolio that need attention, and here is roughly what capacity I have: [paste the accounts with what each appears to need, and say honestly how many I can realistically work myself this month]. Help me split them into the ones where my own technical involvement changes the outcome, and the ones a partner is better placed to take. For each, say what makes it that category. Do not distribute them evenly to make the list look covered. Then tell me how much of what needs attention is left over once my capacity and the partner's are accounted for, and help me describe that gap in terms of what it would take to close it. Do not name individual accounts in that summary; I need the size and shape of the gap, not a list.
activities.expectedOutput: Your accounts split into personally worked and partner-routed with the reason for each, plus a description of the remaining coverage gap in terms of scale and what would close it.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA owns the split and decides what to escalate. At this coverage ratio some demand will exceed what you and your partners can absorb, and the useful response is a capacity conversation with your manager rather than a private list of accounts you are not reaching.
activities.requiredContext: The accounts needing attention and what each appears to need; your genuine capacity this month; which partners cover your workloads and where they have capability; your next manager conversation.
activitySteps: 1. Bring the accounts that survived the previous practice, and be honest about your capacity.
2. Paste both into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Push back on any split that quietly assumes you have more capacity than you said.
4. For the partner group, check the partner actually has coverage and capability for that workload before routing.
5. Take the leftover gap to your manager as a capacity question rather than carrying it privately. Coverage at this ratio is set above you, and it can only be solved where it was set.
activities.whyThisMatters: Coverage at scale is a series of choices about what not to do. Made explicitly it is a strategy you can defend and escalate; made by default it is whichever account shouted loudest getting the time.

activities.name: Design an intervention that works after you leave
activities.description: Take a stalled milestone and build the fix around the fact that you will not be back on this account for some time.
activities.prompt: Here is a stalled committed milestone on one of my accounts: [paste the milestone, the workload, what has been deployed, what usage looks like, and who is involved on the customer and partner side]. I cover a large portfolio, so assume I get one substantive intervention here and will not be back on this account for months. Work out what stands between this and real usage, then design the intervention around that constraint: what I must do myself while I am engaged, what has to be handed to the partner or the customer to carry on without me, what would tell them it is going wrong after I have gone, and who they escalate to. Reject any option that only works if I stay involved. Name roles rather than individuals, since you cannot know the people.
activities.expectedOutput: What stands between the milestone and real usage, an intervention split into what you do now and what is handed on, the failure signal the carrier should watch for, and the escalation route once you have disengaged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides what can safely be handed over. Handing work to a partner or a customer who cannot carry it is worse than not intervening at all, because everyone then believes it is covered, and at this coverage ratio nobody will check for months.
activities.requiredContext: One stalled committed milestone and its workload; what has been deployed; what usage shows; the customer and partner people involved; a realistic view of when you would next touch this account.
activitySteps: 1. Take one account you decided to work yourself, and one stalled milestone on it.
2. Paste what you know into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Separate deployed from used. A milestone can be technically complete and commercially worthless.
4. Check every step of the plan against whether it survives you leaving. Anything that needs you next month is not a plan, it is a delay.
5. Name the person who carries it and the signal that tells them it is failing, then tell them both, before you disengage.
activities.whyThisMatters: At a large coverage ratio the intervention that only works while you are watching is not an intervention. The test of the fix is whether it is still working the month after you moved on.

activities.name: Look for the thing several declining accounts share
activities.description: Take a small number of accounts whose consumption has fallen and check whether the cause is the same one.
activities.prompt: Here are a few accounts in my portfolio where consumption has declined recently: [paste up to five, with the workload, roughly when the decline started, and what I know about each]. Looking only at these, tell me whether they appear to share a cause, such as the same workload, a similar point after deployment, the same partner, or a similar customer profile. Be explicit that a handful of accounts cannot establish a pattern, and tell me what I would need to look at to know whether it is real. Give me one thing worth testing rather than a conclusion.
activities.expectedOutput: Whether the small set appears to share a cause, an explicit caveat about sample size, and one thing worth testing next.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA judges whether an apparent shared cause is real. Several accounts declining on the same workload may be a product problem or may simply be the workload you sold most of last year.
activities.requiredContext: Up to five declining accounts with the workload, roughly when the decline began, and what you know about each; your team rhythm for raising systemic findings.
activitySteps: 1. Bring up to five accounts you have seen declining. Five you can describe accurately beats twenty you cannot.
2. Note the workload, roughly when each started declining, and anything you know about the cause.
3. Paste them into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
4. Treat any shared cause as a hypothesis. Five accounts cannot tell you about a portfolio of this size.
5. If it does look systemic, that is worth raising in your rhythm, because a shared cause is the only kind you can fix at this coverage ratio.
activities.whyThisMatters: One-by-one intervention does not scale to this many accounts. A cause shared across several of them is the only kind of finding that changes more than one outcome.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: You cover more accounts than you can work. This session is about making that a set of decisions rather than something that happens to you.
keyTalkingPoints: Coverage in this role runs at roughly one architect to fifty pinned accounts, which means most accounts will not receive individual attention in any given month and some will receive none at all. Naming those deliberately is the job. A consumption movement is a shape, not a cause: a decline during a planned migration and a decline from a failed deployment look the same in the data, and a rise can be a workload running hotter than the customer intended. Deployed is not used, and the milestone that completed and then flatlined is the one discussed at renewal. Facilitator note: Unified accounts are covered by customer success and cloud solution architects; this role covers the non-Unified pinned base alongside partners, so routing to a partner is a normal outcome rather than an escalation.
discussionQuestions: How many of your accounts did you personally touch last month, out of how many?
When consumption drops on an account, how do you currently decide whether to look?
Which accounts are you quietly hoping nobody asks you about?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the triaged portfolio to the single milestone each person will drive from deployed to actually used.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the accounts each person is personally working this month, the ones going to a partner, and the ones nobody is covering.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your portfolio's recent consumption movement, and an honest number for how many accounts you can realistically work yourself this month.
facilitatorQuestions: Which of these movements can you already explain, and which genuinely need you?
Which accounts are you routing to a partner, and does that partner actually cover the workload?
Which accounts is nobody working?
listenFor: Listen for sharp movements being treated as automatically bad, for rises assumed to be good news, for splits that quietly assume more capacity than the person just said they had, for partner routing without checking partner capability, and for reluctance to name the accounts nobody is covering.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If consumption data is not to hand, work from the accounts each person already suspects are drifting. The triage judgement is the transferable part and the missing data becomes the first thing to fix.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which account did you find you had been assuming someone else was covering?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one committed milestone that completed without producing usage and find out why, then start the intervention.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the milestone, what you thought was blocking it, what actually was, and what you did about it.

DCSA-CONSUME.keyTakeaway: A signed commitment is a promise to consume, not consumption. The plan is what converts one into the other, and it decays unless someone owns each milestone by name.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.
