secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

secondaryAgents.name: GitHub Copilot
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: AI pair programmer available in VS Code, the CLI and the GitHub Copilot app. It works against a repository or a working folder rather than against your mail and meetings.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Write, explain, refactor and test code; scaffold infrastructure-as-code and deployment artifacts; build the smallest spike that proves or disproves an architecture assumption; generate sample data and validation scripts; and reproduce a reported failure so you can see it rather than describe it.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: When the next step is to build something rather than to plan or describe it. Validating an architecture assumption with a spike, standing up a demo or workshop environment, iterating a proof of concept, reproducing a deployment or integration failure, or packaging a reusable asset with tests and setup steps.
keyBenefits: Turns a technical opinion into evidence. A spike that takes twenty minutes settles an argument that would otherwise run for a week, and a reproduced failure is a fact the account team can act on rather than a claim the customer has to accept.
secondaryAgents.whenNotToUseIt: Do not use it for customer, market or account research; that is Researcher. Do not use it to assemble a customer-facing document or deck; that is Cowork. Do not point it at production without the review your team already requires, and do not paste customer data into it. It works on code and configuration, not on the CRM record.
stepsToGetStarted: Use it where the code already is: the Copilot extension in VS Code, the gh copilot CLI, or the GitHub Copilot app in the browser for work not tied to a local checkout. Open the repository or folder first so it has the context. Start with: Explain what this deployment does, then write the smallest test that would prove the assumption I am least sure about.

activities.name: Find what your design assumes that you never wrote down
activities.description: Surface the technical context sitting in your head that a partner would need and does not have.
activities.prompt: Here is a solution design I have been working on: [paste the design, the customer situation, and the constraints as I understand them]. A partner who was not in any of the discovery conversations is going to build this. Read it the way they would and tell me what they could not work out from what is written: decisions I have made without recording why, customer constraints I know but have not stated, dependencies I am assuming are handled, and anything where I have used shorthand that only makes sense internally. Be specific about what is missing rather than telling me to add more detail. If a section would leave a competent engineer guessing, say which section and what they would guess wrong about.
activities.expectedOutput: The specific gaps a partner would hit, covering unrecorded decisions, unstated constraints, assumed dependencies and internal shorthand, with what they would get wrong in each case.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what genuinely needs recording. Only the person who was in the room knows which constraint was casually mentioned and turns out to be load-bearing, and that is exactly the kind of thing that never reaches the partner.
activities.requiredContext: A design a partner will deliver; the customer situation and constraints as you understand them; the decisions you made and why.
activitySteps: 1. Bring a design you are working on that a partner will deliver.
2. Paste it into the prompt where it asks, along with the constraints as you understand them, then run it.
3. Look hardest at the decisions you made without recording the reason. Those are what get reversed by someone who did not know why.
4. Add the missing context rather than removing the part that needs it.
5. Check whether any gap is something the customer told you verbally. Those never make it across unless you write them down.
activities.whyThisMatters: The design in your head is always more complete than the one on the page. The gap between them is where delivery goes wrong, and it is invisible to the person who wrote it.

activities.name: Check the design against who is actually going to build it
activities.description: Test whether the partner you have in mind can deliver this design, and change the design if they cannot.
activities.prompt: Here is the design and here is what I know about the partner who will deliver it: [paste the design, and what I know about this partner's capability, capacity, and what they have built before]. Tell me where the design and the partner do not match: capability the design assumes that I have no evidence this partner has, parts that would be straightforward for them, and parts where a different approach would reach the same customer outcome with less risk. Where I have not told you enough about the partner, ask rather than assuming they can do it. Do not simply lower the ambition of the design; if a simpler approach genuinely costs the customer something, say so.
activities.expectedOutput: Where the design and the partner do not match, what would be straightforward, lower-risk alternatives that reach the same outcome, and what the customer gives up if the approach changes.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE judges partner capability. There is no system view of what a given partner can actually build, only what they have been certified for, and the difference between those two is usually discovered during delivery.
activities.requiredContext: The design; what you know about the partner's capability, capacity and delivery history; who to talk to if a different partner is needed.
activitySteps: 1. Start from the design you worked on in the previous practice.
2. Paste it into the prompt where it asks, with what you actually know about the partner, then run it.
3. Answer its questions about the partner rather than letting it assume. The agent has no view of partner capability.
4. Decide whether to change the design or change the partner. Both are legitimate; carrying on with a mismatch is not.
5. If you change the design, note what the customer gives up. That is a conversation someone will need to have.
activities.whyThisMatters: A design is only as good as the team that will build it. Engaging the partner after the design is fixed means either a rebuild or a disappointed customer.

activities.name: Diagnose something a partner built
activities.description: Work out what is wrong with a deployed solution you did not build, when the person who built it made decisions nobody recorded.
activities.prompt: A solution a partner built is not working as intended. Here is what I have: [paste the symptoms, the intended design, what the partner has told me about how they actually built it, and what the customer is experiencing]. Help me work out where to look. Separate the possibilities into where the build has diverged from the intended design, where the design itself was wrong for this environment, where something in the customer's environment has changed since it was delivered, and where the solution is working as built but not as the customer expected. For each, tell me what evidence would confirm it and what I should ask the partner. Do not assume the build matches the design; that is the thing I am testing.
activities.expectedOutput: Candidate causes separated into build divergence, design error, environment change and expectation mismatch, with the confirming evidence for each and the specific questions to put to the partner.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether this is a build problem or a design problem before raising it. Telling a partner their build is wrong when the design was wrong damages a relationship you will need on the next twenty deals, and the two look identical from the symptoms.
activities.requiredContext: The symptoms and what the customer is experiencing; the intended design; whatever the partner has said about how they actually built it; your contact at the partner.
activitySteps: 1. Bring a partner-delivered solution that is not working as intended.
2. Paste the symptoms and both the intended design and what you know of the actual build into the prompt where it asks, then run it.
3. Establish what was actually built before diagnosing why it fails. The design tells you the intent, not the implementation.
4. Ask the partner the specific questions rather than requesting a general update. A general update returns a general answer.
5. Separate a broken build from a design that was wrong. Those go to different people and confusing them costs a cycle.
activities.whyThisMatters: You get called when something a partner built stops working, and you will not have the decisions they made along the way. Working out what was actually built is most of the diagnosis.

activities.name: Work out whether the partner can run this proof instead of you
activities.description: Decide whether a proof genuinely needs your hands on it, or whether the partner can run it with the right preparation from you.
activities.prompt: A proof of concept is going ahead and I need to decide whether I run it or the partner does. Here is the situation: [paste what the proof has to demonstrate, what I know about this partner's capability with this technology, what the customer expects, and my own read on whether the customer needs to see Microsoft in the room]. I cover a territory, so my time on one proof is time off everything else. Help me decide: which parts genuinely need me, which the partner could run with preparation, and what I would have to give them for that to work. If my read is that the customer needs Microsoft present, take that as given rather than arguing with it, and tell me the smallest presence that satisfies it.
activities.expectedOutput: A split of the proof into what needs you, what the partner can run with preparation, what you must give them, and the reporting you have agreed if you hand it over.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE judges whether the customer needs Microsoft in the room. That is a read on the relationship rather than on the technology, the seller is the only one who has it, and getting it wrong either burns a week of territory time or loses the customer's confidence in the proof.
activities.requiredContext: What the proof must demonstrate; what you know of the partner's capability with this technology; what the customer expects; your own judgement on whether Microsoft needs to be present.
activitySteps: 1. Take a proof that is going ahead, and the partner assessment from the previous practice.
2. Decide your own read on whether the customer needs Microsoft in the room before you run anything. The agent cannot judge that and should not try.
3. Paste the situation into the prompt where it asks, including that read, then run it.
4. Be honest about what the partner would need from you. A proof handed over without preparation comes back as an escalation.
5. If you hand it over, agree in advance what they tell you and when, so you find out it is going wrong before the customer does.
activities.whyThisMatters: At territory coverage the proofs you personally run are the ones you are not spending elsewhere. Deciding what genuinely needs your hands, rather than defaulting to running everything, is what makes the coverage work.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Someone who was not in any of your discovery conversations is going to build what you designed. This session is about finding out whether they can, while there is still time to change it.
keyTalkingPoints: Technical design in this segment is largely the same job as anywhere else, with one difference that changes everything downstream: partner delivery capacity is engaged earlier, and the partner owns delivery in the later stages. That means a design is not finished when it is technically sound, it is finished when someone else can build it from what is written. The design in your head is always more complete than the one on the page, and the gap between them is invisible to the person who wrote it. At territory volume, the proofs you decline and the designs you make reusable are what create room for the work that matters.
discussionQuestions: When did a partner last build something differently from what you intended, and where did the misunderstanding start?
What do you know about your current design that is not written down anywhere?
When did you last agree to a proof of concept that did not change anyone's mind?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the design gaps to the one thing each person will write down or ask the partner before delivery starts.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the gap each person will close and whether they are changing the design, changing the partner, or asking a question before delivery starts.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one design a partner will deliver, and whatever you know about that partner's capability and delivery history.
facilitatorQuestions: What would a competent engineer guess wrong about, reading only what you wrote?
Do you actually have evidence this partner can build this, or a certification that suggests it?
What single uncertainty would that proof resolve?
listenFor: Listen for verbal customer constraints that never reached the document, for partner capability inferred from certification rather than from delivery history, for proofs agreed to because they were asked for rather than because they would settle something, and for designs described as reusable that hide a decision behind every section.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live design, use one a partner has already built and work backwards to where the misunderstanding started. The gap-finding exercise is the transferable part and hindsight makes it sharper.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you have to explain about your own design that you had not realised you were assuming?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one design a partner will deliver and either write down the context they are missing or ask them the question that would change it.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the design, the gap you found, what you did about it, and what the partner said when you raised it.

PSS-JOINTPLAN.roleTopicName: Build a Joint Plan the Partner Will Actually Work
PSS-JOINTPLAN.roleTopicDescription: Assess what a partner can genuinely deliver rather than what they have agreed to, build the joint plan inside the data rules that govern partner exchange, and set the trigger that tells you the plan has stopped being true.
PSS-JOINTPLAN.wiifm: Partners agree to plans in the meeting and work the deals that pay them. A plan that ignores that is a plan you will be explaining at the quarterly review.
PSS-JOINTPLAN.name: Plan the Territory With the Partners Who Cover It
PSS-JOINTPLAN.description: Decide who is genuinely covering which accounts across a territory far larger than one person can work, and build that decision into a joint plan with the partners who cover the rest.
PSS-JOINTPLAN.todayObjective: Test one joint plan against partner capacity and incentive rather than against partner intent.
PSS-JOINTPLAN.whyItMatters: A territory of roughly fifty accounts cannot be covered account by account, so most of it is covered by partners or not at all. The plan is where that becomes deliberate. Left implicit, the accounts that get worked are the ones that shout, and the ones that quietly lapse were never assigned to anybody.
PSS-JOINTPLAN.desiredOutcome: A joint plan tested against capacity and incentive, the data-sharing boundary respected, and a named trigger for revisiting it.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Assess what the partner has actually delivered, not agreed to
activities.description: Build the capacity picture from what has moved rather than from what was promised in the last planning session.
activities.prompt: For [partner name], list the co-sell opportunities and referrals currently associated with them: the stage of each, the date it last moved, and how long it has been at its current stage. Separate the ones progressing from the ones static for more than a month. Do not infer partner capacity or intent from the pattern; just show me what has moved and what has not.
activities.expectedOutput: A movement-based read on one partner separating progressing work from static work, with the oldest static item identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS interprets what the pattern means. Movement data shows what happened and not why, and capacity, incentive and attention produce very similar-looking stalls while needing completely different conversations.
activities.requiredContext: One partner you work with. Their associated co-sell opportunities and referrals in MSX. Partner Center or the Partner Timeline view for partner-side status.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [partner name] with your partner._x000D_
2. Read the static group and note how long the oldest has been sitting._x000D_
3. Check the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center directly for anything approaching the fourteen-day accept or sixty-day convert window._x000D_

activities.whyThisMatters: Partner capacity assessed from the planning conversation reflects intent. Assessed from what actually moved, it reflects reality, and the two are often a long way apart.

activities.name: Build the joint plan inside the data rules
activities.description: Assemble the joint plan content that can legitimately be shared, and find what you were about to include that cannot.
activities.prompt: Draft a joint planning input for a partner covering these accounts [list the accounts]. For each, include the industry, the size band, the workloads in place, the open opportunity and its stage, and the specific help being asked of the partner. Write it for an audience outside Microsoft. Exclude contact names and details, seat counts, spend or consumption figures, and anything that reads as an export or screenshot from our systems.
activities.expectedOutput: A joint planning input that respects the data-sharing boundary, with the excluded material listed explicitly rather than silently dropped.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS checks the draft against the source records before it leaves Microsoft, rather than asking the model to confirm its own compliance. A model told to exclude something will usually comply and will occasionally rephrase it instead, and it cannot report an instruction it did not register.
activities.requiredContext: The accounts in scope for the joint plan. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [list the accounts] with the accounts in scope._x000D_
2. Put the output side by side with the account records you drew from._x000D_

3. Go field by field through what you can see in MSX and check whether each one made it into the draft. Do not ask the model what it left out - if it missed the instruction, it cannot tell you it missed it._x000D_
4. Remove anything CELA rules exclude: personal data, seat or spend detail, anything resembling an export._x000D_
5. Decide what genuinely needs to be in the plan versus what you were including out of habit.
activities.whyThisMatters: Partner exchange is governed by CELA rules covering personal data, exports and commercial detail. The failure mode is not malice; it is a helpful summary that includes one field too many.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Assess what the partner has actually delivered, not agreed to

activities.name: Find where the plan asks more of the partner than it looks like
activities.description: Test the joint plan for the operational load it actually places on the partner, and take the economics to the PDM rather than guessing at them.
activities.prompt: I am building a joint plan with a partner covering [describe the accounts and the ask]. Working only from what I have described, analyze the operational shape of what I am asking: which parts require significant partner effort before any revenue is realized, which depend on the partner holding skills or capacity I have not confirmed, which have long lead times, and which would compete for the same people at the same time. Do not speculate about partner incentives, margins, programs, or compensation - you do not have access to those and I will confirm them separately. Return the operational load analysis only.
activities.expectedOutput: An operational load analysis of what the plan asks of the partner, with the economic question routed to the PDM rather than answered by the agent.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS owns the economic judgement and takes it to the PDM. Partner incentive and program detail is outside what this agent can see, so anything it offers on margin or compensation is invention wearing a confident sentence, and the operational analysis is the only part worth carrying forward.
activities.requiredContext: Your draft joint plan and the specific ask it makes of the partner. Access to your PDM for anything incentive, margin or program related.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [describe the accounts and the ask] with your plan._x000D_
2. If the output mentions incentives, margin, rebates or program tiers, discard those lines - it does not have that data._x000D_
3. Take the operational load analysis into your PDM conversation and ask the economic question there: does this plan pay the partner enough to prefer it over what else they could be doing._x000D_
4. Pick the one conflict most likely to matter and raise it directly with the partner.
activities.whyThisMatters: Plans fail where they ask a partner to do something that pays less than the alternative. The operational load is visible in the plan itself; the economics are not, and guessing at them is how a joint plan gets built on a false premise.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Assess what the partner has actually delivered, not agreed to

activities.name: Set the trigger that tells you the plan has stopped being true
activities.description: Decide in advance what observable change would mean the joint plan needs revisiting, rather than discovering it at the quarterly review.
activities.prompt: For this joint plan [summarize the plan and its key assumptions], help me define what I should watch to know it is drifting. For each key assumption, suggest an observable change that would indicate it is no longer holding, where that change would be visible, and how soon it would realistically show. Distinguish changes I can see in our own systems from changes I would only learn from the partner directly.
activities.expectedOutput: One named trigger with a place to observe it and a date to check it, tied into the existing partner rhythm.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides which single trigger is worth committing to. A monitoring plan with six triggers gets checked once, and choosing the one that would actually change your behaviour is the judgement that makes it survive.
activities.requiredContext: Your agreed joint plan and its underlying assumptions. Your partner meeting cadence.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [summarize the plan and its key assumptions] with your plan._x000D_
2. Separate the signals visible in MSX from the ones that require a partner conversation._x000D_
3. Choose one trigger you will genuinely check rather than several you will not._x000D_
4. Set the date and put it in the partner rhythm.
activities.whyThisMatters: Joint plans degrade quietly. The quarterly review is where drift is usually discovered, which is one quarter after it could have been corrected.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Partners agree to joint plans in the meeting and then work the deals that pay them. This session is about building a plan that survives that.
keyTalkingPoints: Formal joint planning is structurally required in this segment rather than being optional assistance. Partner Center is the partner-facing surface and sits outside what our agents can reach, so partner-side status has to be read there directly or through the Partner Timeline view on the plan priority. CELA rules govern the exchange: personal data, MSX screenshots and exports, and financial or seat-level detail are off-limits, and signals shared with partners are unqualified leads until confirmed. Facilitator note: the fourteen-day accept window and the sixty-day convert window are system-enforced, so a plan that assumes a slower partner rhythm will lose leads automatically.
discussionQuestions: When a joint plan fails, is it usually capacity, incentive or attention?
What do you actually know about what else your partner is carrying?
What can you not share with a partner, and where does that boundary get uncomfortable?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the capacity and incentive test to the specific trigger each person will set.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the assumption each person is going to confirm with their partner and the trigger they are setting.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one current joint plan and, if you have it, a read on what that partner has accepted and converted recently.
facilitatorQuestions: What in this plan depends on partner capacity you have never confirmed?
Where does the plan pay the partner less than the alternative work they could be doing?
What would tell you early that the partner has quietly deprioritized this?
listenFor: Listen for capacity inferred from enthusiasm, for plans that assume a partner rhythm faster than the fourteen and sixty day windows allow, for data being prepared for partner exchange that CELA rules exclude, and for the absence of any trigger that would reveal drift.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live joint plan, use the most recent partner engagement that underdelivered and reconstruct which of capacity, incentive or attention actually caused it.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you assume about your partner's capacity that you have never actually asked?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, test one joint plan assumption directly with the partner and set a named trigger that would tell you the plan has stopped being true.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what the partner said about capacity and the trigger you set.

PSS-JOINTPLAN.keyTakeaway: Coverage is a decision whether or not you make it. An account nobody named is an account nobody is working.

DSE-ORIENT.roleTopicDescription: Introduce the eight-week huddle motion: why Frontier Accelerator exists, what happens in a thirty-minute huddle, the five roles that make it work, and what is expected of you between sessions.
DSE-ORIENT.wiifm: You are Customer Zero. Before we ask a customer to put AI at the centre of how they work, we do it on our own work and find out honestly where it helps and where it does not. The aim is to get time back from the assembling, and to find out first-hand where AI earns that time and where it does not.
DSE-ORIENT.name: Frontier Accelerator Orientation
DSE-ORIENT.description: Introduces the motion, the huddle format, the AI tools in scope, and what team members are expected to try between sessions.

DSE-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand how the huddle motion runs, what you are being asked to do each week, and where your own judgment stays yours.
DSE-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
DSE-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: You know how the motion works, what happens in each huddle, what is expected of you between sessions, and you leave with one thing to try before the next one.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This is the first of eight huddles, and the one with no AI activity in it. Today is about what the motion is and what it asks of you. Frontier Accelerator exists because we are asking customers to reshape how they work around AI, and that argument is stronger when we have done it ourselves first. That is what Customer Zero means here: we apply these tools to our own real work, and we are straight about where they help and where they do not.
keyTalkingPoints: Weekly and short, led by the manager with a facilitator. The cadence carries the motion, so if the slot has to move, move it rather than drop it.

Four principles hold every week: keep the weekly rhythm, learn from what colleagues have actually tried, ground every session in real work rather than hypothetical scenarios, and try something between huddles so there is an experience to bring back.

Every huddle from next week runs to the same shape, and the agenda and timings are set out on the huddle page: a short framing of why the topic matters, then sharing what you tried since last time, then hands-on work on a real scenario, then a close where you pick the one thing you will carry into the week.

Five roles make the motion work. The Leader connects it to strategy and clears barriers. The Manager owns the huddle and opens with the why. The Facilitator runs it and draws every voice in. The Team Member experiments in their own workflow and brings back wins and friction. The Coach reviews patterns across huddles and feeds insight back.

The journey ahead: this week you get grounded, weeks two to eight you build the habit on real work, week nine the team decides which habits stick and what comes next, and from week ten you choose your own topics.
You are here as a peer, not an expert. You do not need prior AI experience, and “I do not know” is a good answer.

Two things on feedback. The facilitator posts one question in the chat each week, asking how useful the huddle was on a scale of one to ten. Huddle transcripts are reviewed for themes to improve the sessions, so keep confidential detail out of the room, whether that is customer, partner, enrollment or commercial, and put product problems into the tool's own feedback control rather than here.
discussionQuestions: Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you deliberately avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted output in front of a customer?
What would make thirty minutes a week worth protecting for this?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the discovery prompt below. Week one is for finding the recurring work worth handing to AI. Post the usefulness question in the chat before people leave.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: complete the baseline survey if it has been sent to you, confirm the huddle series is on your calendar, confirm you can open at least one of the tools named for your path, since the commitment at the end of this session runs in one of them, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. If your access is blocked, come anyway and say so, because that is a different problem from not being interested. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
facilitatorQuestions: Which work do you repeat every week without ever thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where does your judgment have to stay human no matter how good the output gets?
What would have to happen in these thirty minutes for you to want the next one?
listenFor: Listen for unvoiced skepticism, for access blockers stated as disinterest, and for the assumption that this is a tool rollout. Listen for people describing only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat, because the recurring and unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping. Listen for anyone who thinks they need to be an AI expert to take part, and correct that in the room.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the conversation and record access blockers separately from interest, since they need different fixes. The discovery prompt runs in whichever tool the person already has. If the room stays quiet, start with your own example of work you repeat every week.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

“I am a [your role] at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with.”
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

activities.name: Find out who has already spoken to this customer
activities.description: Establish what is already known about the estate and who holds the rest, before you take a single question to the customer.
activities.prompt: For [account name], show me what is already recorded about their technical estate: the products and workloads in place and when they were deployed, any open support or delivery issue, the opportunities open and what they are for, every recorded activity and which role it came from, and whether a partner or co-sell record exists on the account. Report only what the record contains. Do not describe what any partner has done - that is not in MSX.
activities.expectedOutput: What the record already establishes about the estate, and the named colleagues or partners likely holding the rest.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what the record genuinely establishes versus what it merely mentions. A workload appearing in the record says it was bought rather than how it was configured, and the configuration is what you will be held to when you design against it.
activities.requiredContext: One customer where you are about to start technical discovery.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your customer.
2. Read the activity list by role. Whoever has been active is the person who knows what is not written down.
3. If a partner record exists, check the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center - the partner may have run discovery of their own.
4. Write down what the record answers, and what it only appears to answer.
activities.whyThisMatters: At this customer count you are arriving after a partner and a seller have both already been there. Starting from what they found is faster than starting again and does not spend the customer's patience.

activities.name: Test your criteria against what they already run
activities.description: Check draft decision criteria against the customer's recorded estate, and work out which ones a partner would have to satisfy.
activities.prompt: Here are the technical decision criteria I am proposing for [account name]: [paste your draft criteria]. Show me what that customer has deployed today and, for each criterion, whether anything in the record bears on it - an existing workload, an open support issue, a prior opportunity - or whether the record says nothing. Do not assess technical effort or judge whether a criterion is reasonable. I want to know which of these the record can already speak to.
activities.expectedOutput: Your criteria split by whether the record already speaks to them, with the partner-satisfied ones marked.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE writes the criteria and decides which a partner could realistically meet. A criterion only the engineer can satisfy quietly commits you to every future deal of that shape, and at this customer count that is a commitment you cannot keep.
activities.requiredContext: Your draft technical decision criteria, and the customer they are for.
activitySteps: 1. Draft your criteria first. This is your judgment, not the agent's.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
3. Criteria the record says nothing about are the ones you will have to establish with the customer or the partner.
4. Mark which of those a delivery partner would have to satisfy rather than you.
5. Agree the surviving set with the DAE before it reaches the customer.
activities.whyThisMatters: Criteria written for yourself do not survive being handed to a delivery partner. Checking them against what the customer already runs is the cheap part; deciding who can meet them is the part that matters.

activities.name: Find where the technical record has gone quiet
activities.description: Rank the technical record by how long each part of it has gone without an update, then decide what you still have to verify yourself.
activities.prompt: For [account name], show me how current the technical record actually is. For each deployed product and workload give the date it was last updated, list any open support or service record with the date it last moved, and name the areas where nothing has been logged in the last [number] months. Sort by longest silence first, and lead with the gaps rather than a full inventory of the estate.
activities.expectedOutput: The technical record ranked by how long each part of it has gone untouched, with anything showing no entry inside the chosen period named separately.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE owns the design and therefore decides which recorded facts are safe to build on. A fact nobody has touched in a long time is not necessarily wrong, and the difference between an inaccuracy caught at design time and one found in production is entirely a matter of which fact it was.
activities.requiredContext: The customer, and how far back you want the currency check to run.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections - the account and the number of months you want checked.

2. Read the dates, not just the facts. Silence is not evidence either way: it means no entry was found in MSX for that period, not that nothing happened or that nobody recorded it somewhere you cannot see.
3. Now do the part the agent cannot: decide which of these facts you will confirm with a person before you design against them, and which are safe to take as read.
activities.whyThisMatters: You cannot verify everything at this customer count. The record will not tell you what is true, but it will tell you which facts are fresh and which have gone untouched long enough to be worth checking before you design against them.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Somebody has usually asked this customer most of your questions already. This session is about finding out what they said before you ask again.
keyTalkingPoints: In this segment a partner is frequently engaged before the engineer is, and may have run discovery of their own. The DAE owns the account relationship and the DSS covers the solution area, so three people may hold pieces of the same picture. Partner-side conversations are not in MSX and return through the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center. Facilitator note: the failure mode here is not missing information, it is asking for information somebody already has, which reads to the customer as a team that does not talk to itself.
discussionQuestions: How do you currently find out what has already been asked?
When did you last repeat a question the customer had already answered?
What do you need to establish yourself, whatever anyone else has done?
suggestedTransitions: Move from what is already known to the short list only this person can establish.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the one thing each person will ask a colleague or partner rather than the customer.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one customer where you are about to start technical discovery.
facilitatorQuestions: What does the record already tell you about this customer's estate?
Who else has spoken to them, and what would they know that is not written down?
What must you see for yourself rather than take on trust?
listenFor: Listen for discovery restarted from scratch out of habit, for partner-held knowledge assumed to be unavailable rather than asked for, for the record treated as complete, and for engineers accepting a second-hand answer on something they will be accountable for.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has upcoming discovery, use the last engagement where something important surfaced late and work out who already knew it.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What were you about to ask a customer that somebody on your own side already knew?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, establish what is already known about one customer's estate from the record and from whoever else is engaged, and take only your genuinely unanswered questions to the customer.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what you learned without asking the customer, and what you still had to ask.

DSE-DISC.keyTakeaway: Discovery that does not end in decision criteria is a conversation, not discovery.

DSE-PROOF.roleTopicName: Prove It Without Building It Again
DSE-PROOF.roleTopicDescription: Decide the smallest proof that would settle the decision, and reach for something that already exists before building anything bespoke.
DSE-PROOF.wiifm: A bespoke proof per customer does not scale to the number of customers you cover. The engineers who keep up are the ones who reuse.
DSE-PROOF.name: Design and Validate the Technical Solution
DSE-PROOF.description: Design the solution, then prove it works well enough for the customer to decide.
DSE-PROOF.todayObjective: Settle one customer's technical doubt without building a proof from scratch.
DSE-PROOF.whyItMatters: A design the customer cannot see or test is a document. Proof is what converts technical work into a customer decision, and criteria set afterwards get argued about forever.
DSE-PROOF.desiredOutcome: The decision the proof must settle named, an existing asset found or ruled out, and the smallest sufficient proof scoped.

activities.name: Look for the proof before you build one
activities.description: Check whether you or a colleague have already proven this, at a customer with a comparable estate.
activities.prompt: I need to prove [describe what the customer doubts] for a customer running [describe their estate]. Across the opportunities in my patch, show me any where a similar workload or configuration was involved, what stage they reached, and any recorded notes, objections or outcomes. For each, show what the customer environment looked like. Do not assume a similar environment means the same proof will transfer.
activities.expectedOutput: Comparable prior work identified with an honest read on whether it transfers, or a clear statement that this proof is genuinely new.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE judges whether a prior proof actually transfers. Two customers on the same product can differ in the one respect the proof depended on, and a borrowed proof that quietly does not apply is worse than building a new one, because nobody re-examines it.
activities.requiredContext: The technical doubt to be settled, and the customer's environment as you understand it.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Look for the closest environment rather than the closest product name.
3. If something transfers, find out who ran it before rebuilding it.
4. If nothing transfers, you now know why this one is genuinely new.
activities.whyThisMatters: A bespoke proof for every customer does not survive the customer count in this segment. Reuse is the constraint that makes the job possible, and it only works if somebody looks first.

agents.name: Sales Home
agents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
agents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Cut your proof down before you build it
activities.description: State the proof you are considering, then test it against what comparable customers actually needed.
activities.prompt: A customer at [account name] is unsure about [describe the doubt]. I am considering this proof: [describe the proof you have in mind]. Across the opportunities in my patch, show me any where a similar doubt or objection was recorded, what was proposed, what stage the opportunity reached, and any note about what convinced the customer. Do not design a proof or judge whether mine is the right size.
activities.expectedOutput: Your proposed proof tested against what comparable customers actually needed, cut to the smallest sufficient version with exclusions stated.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what the customer is really doubting, which is frequently not what they asked to see. A request for a pilot is often a request for reassurance about operational effort, and building the pilot answers a question nobody had while leaving the real one open.
activities.requiredContext: The customer, what they are unsure about, and the proof you are considering including its exclusions.
activitySteps: 1. Write down the proof you have in mind first, including what it will not cover. That scoping is yours.
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace all three bracketed sections.
3. Look at what actually convinced comparable customers. It is frequently smaller than what was offered.
4. Cut yours to the smallest version that still settles the doubt, and write down explicitly what it excludes.
5. Get the customer to agree that this settles it, before you build anything.
activities.whyThisMatters: Proof work expands to fill whatever time it is given, and at this customer count that time comes straight out of another customer. What convinced somebody comparable is the cheapest available check on your own scoping.

activities.name: Leave it in a state the next engineer can use
activities.description: Spend the extra hour that makes this proof reusable, rather than rebuilding it from memory next quarter.
activities.prompt: I have built a proof demonstrating [describe what it shows] for a customer running [describe the environment]. Help me write it up so another engineer could reuse it: what it demonstrates, what environment it assumes, what it deliberately does not cover, what would have to change for a different customer, and what someone should check before reusing it. Write it for an engineer who was not involved. Do not include the customer name, contact details, or anything identifying them.
activities.expectedOutput: A reuse note covering what the proof shows, what it assumes, what it excludes, and what to check before reusing it, with the customer anonymized.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE states what the proof deliberately does not cover. A reuse note that lists only capabilities gets applied to a situation it was never valid for, and the engineer who inherits the failure will not know which assumption broke.
activities.requiredContext: The proof you built, what it demonstrates, and the environment it assumed.
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the assumptions section as somebody who was not there. Anything implicit will be missed.
3. Remove anything identifying the customer.
4. Put it where your colleagues will actually find it, and tell the ones covering similar estates.
activities.whyThisMatters: Reuse only works if somebody wrote down the limits. The capabilities are obvious from the artifact; the boundaries exist only in the head of whoever built it.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Cut your proof down before you build it

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Building a bespoke proof for every customer does not survive contact with this many customers. This session is about proving the point with less.
keyTalkingPoints: Enterprise engineers can afford a tailored proof per pursuit; at this customer count that arithmetic does not work, so reuse is the constraint rather than a nice-to-have. A partner may be able to run the proof instead, which is covered separately in the design session. What matters here is deciding the smallest thing that would actually settle the customer's doubt. Facilitator note: the most common failure is building a technically impressive proof of something the customer was never doubting.
discussionQuestions: How long does a proof take you, and how many can you run at once?
When did you last build something that already existed?
What was the customer actually unsure about?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the decision in doubt to what each person will reuse or scope.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming what each person is reusing rather than building.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one customer asking for a demo, pilot or proof.
facilitatorQuestions: What decision is this proof supposed to settle?
Does something already exist that would settle it?
What is the smallest version that would still be convincing?
listenFor: Listen for proofs scoped to what is interesting to build rather than to what is in doubt, for reuse dismissed without looking, for success criteria that were never agreed with the customer, and for effort that exceeds the value of the deal.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live request, use the last proof that was built and work out what the smallest sufficient version would have been.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you build that you could have borrowed?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, name the decision one customer's proof must settle, look for something that already exists before building anything, and scope the smallest sufficient version.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what you found already existing, and what you still had to build.

activities.name: Work out what was actually asked
activities.description: Reconstruct the customer's real question from the version that reached you second-hand.
activities.prompt: A technical question has reached me through a partner or seller. Here is how it was relayed: [paste the question as you received it]. It concerns [account name]. Using what is recorded about that customer's estate, help me work out what they might actually be asking. Give the most likely readings, what each would imply about their concern, and the single clarifying question that would tell them apart. Do not answer the question yet.
activities.expectedOutput: The plausible readings of the question with the one clarifying question that would resolve them.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether to answer or to ask. A relayed question has already lost the tone and the follow-up that would have disambiguated it, and answering the wrong reading with confidence is how a technically correct answer becomes a customer problem.
activities.requiredContext: The relayed question as you received it, and the customer it concerns.
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the alternative readings against what the customer actually runs.
3. If two readings need completely different answers, ask the clarifying question before answering.
4. Answering the wrong reading confidently costs more than the delay of asking.
activities.whyThisMatters: You are not in the room in this segment, so every question arrives already translated once. Treating the relayed wording as the actual question is how engineers give confidently wrong answers.

activities.name: Write an answer that survives being forwarded
activities.description: Produce a technical answer for the person who will relay it, not for a technical peer.
activities.prompt: Here is a technical question about [account name]: [state the question you have established]. Here is my answer: [paste your answer in your own words]. Rewrite it for a partner or seller who will relay it to the customer and who is not a specialist in this area. Lead with the direct answer, then the conditions it depends on. Keep every qualification I have written - do not simplify one away. Mark clearly which parts must be passed on word for word and which can be summarized. Do not add technical claims I have not made.
activities.expectedOutput: Your answer rewritten for relay, with qualifications intact, the must-not-paraphrase parts marked, and the data-sharing boundary checked.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE writes the technical answer and checks that nothing was added or softened in the rewrite. A model asked to make an answer clearer will drop the qualification that made it accurate, and the person relaying it has no way to know a sentence went missing.
activities.requiredContext: The question you have established, your own technical answer, and the account. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
activitySteps: 1. Write your answer first, in your own words. The technical content is yours.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace all three bracketed sections.
3. Check nothing has been added that you did not say, and no qualification has been softened.
4. Read it as the relayer. If a sentence needs you present to make sense, rewrite it.
5. Check the word-for-word section is genuinely short - if everything is marked critical, nothing is.
6. Check it against the CELA rules before it goes to a partner: no personal data, no seat or spend detail, nothing resembling an export.
activities.whyThisMatters: An answer written for a technical peer gets compressed by whoever passes it on, and the part they drop is the qualification. Having it rewritten for the relayer is useful; letting it be written from scratch is how a confident wrong answer reaches a customer.

activities.name: Work out what is not yours to answer
activities.description: Identify the parts of a technical question that belong to product, legal, security or commercial owners, and route them.
activities.prompt: Here is a technical question I have been asked about [account name]: [state the question]. Break it into its separate parts and, for each, say whether answering it needs current product behavior, an unreleased or roadmap capability, licensing or commercial terms, or a security, legal or compliance position. Do not answer any part and do not suggest who should own it.
activities.expectedOutput: The question split by the kind of answer each part needs, with your portion answered and the rest routed by you to a named owner.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE answers the technical part and routes the rest rather than being helpful across the boundary. An engineer's answer about licensing or a roadmap date is read as authoritative because it came from the technical person, and it is repeated long after it stops being true.
activities.requiredContext: The technical question and the account it concerns. Your CE for anything commercial, and the authoritative owner for security or compliance.
activitySteps: 1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. You route these, not the agent. Licensing and commercial go to your CE; security and compliance to the authoritative owner.
3. Anything touching roadmap goes nowhere near a customer until it has shipped.
4. Answer your part fully and name who is picking up the rest, so the question does not stall.
activities.whyThisMatters: A relayed question arrives as one question and unpacks into several. Splitting it is what stops an engineer accidentally giving a commercial commitment.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Most technical questions reach you second-hand, and your answer goes back the same way. This session is about writing for the relay.
keyTalkingPoints: At this scale the engineer is frequently not in the room. A partner or a seller carries the question in and the answer back, which means the question has already been through one translation before you see it and the answer goes through another on the way out. CELA rules govern what may be exchanged with a partner: personal data, MSX screenshots and exports, and financial or seat-level detail are off-limits. Facilitator note: an answer that requires your presence to make sense is not finished, because you will not be there.
discussionQuestions: How often are you answering a question the customer asked somebody else?
When has an answer of yours arrived at a customer distorted?
What do you put in writing differently when a partner will forward it?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the reconstructed question to the answer each person will write for relay.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the part of each answer that must not be paraphrased.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one technical question that reached you through somebody else.
facilitatorQuestions: What do you think the customer actually asked, as opposed to what reached you?
Which part of your answer would you least like to see paraphrased?
What would this look like if the person relaying it did not understand it?
listenFor: Listen for the relayed question taken at face value, for answers written for a technical peer rather than for the relayer, for caveats that will not survive being summarized, and for detail that CELA rules exclude from partner exchange.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live question, use one that came back a second time and work out what was lost in the first answer.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which of your answers has been repeated to a customer in a form you would not recognize?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, answer one relayed technical question in a form that survives being forwarded, and mark explicitly what must be passed on word for word.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the answer you wrote and what came back.

activities.name: Find who else is running the thing you know breaks
activities.description: Take a problem you have already met and find the other customers exposed to it.
activities.prompt: I have found a technical problem at one customer: [describe the configuration or workload and what goes wrong]. Across the accounts in my patch, show me which others have the same workload or product combination deployed, with what is recorded about their deployment and any open support issue. Do not conclude that a matching product list means the same problem is present.
activities.expectedOutput: The customers plausibly exposed to the same problem, narrowed by configuration rather than product match, and ordered by customer-visible impact.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides which matches are genuinely exposed. A product list is not a configuration, and two deployments that share a product name can differ in exactly the setting that determines whether the problem occurs.
activities.requiredContext: A technical problem you have already diagnosed at one customer. The accounts in your patch.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your problem described.
2. Treat the output as a list of customers to check, not a list of customers affected.
3. Narrow it using what you know about the configurations rather than the product names.
4. Order the survivors by how visible the failure would be to the customer.
activities.whyThisMatters: You do not operate any of these environments and there are too many to inspect. The only scalable way to find a problem before the customer does is to already know its shape.

agents.name: Sales Home
agents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
agents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Check whether the problem is already being worked
activities.description: Find out whether an exposed customer already has a support issue open on the problem, before you warn anyone about it.
activities.prompt: For these customers [list the exposed accounts], show every support or service issue recorded in the last six months: what it concerns, when it was raised, its current status, and whether it has been resolved. Show the deployed workloads alongside so I can see which issues touch the configuration I am worried about. Report only what is recorded and do not judge whether any issue relates to my problem.
activities.expectedOutput: The exposed customers split by whether an issue is already open, already resolved, or nothing is recorded at all.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether an existing issue is actually the same problem. Support records describe a symptom in the customer's words rather than the cause in yours, and a ticket that looks unrelated is often the same fault reported by someone who did not know what they were seeing.
activities.requiredContext: Your list of exposed customers from the previous activity.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list.
2. Read the open issues first. An issue already raised on the same workload means somebody found this before you.
3. A resolved issue on the same configuration is worth reading too - it may be the fix you were about to describe.
4. Only for accounts with nothing recorded should you check the Partner Timeline view, since a partner may be working it outside our systems.
5. Warn only the customers where nobody appears to be on it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most of these environments are operated by somebody else, so a problem you have just spotted has often already been raised by the people living with it. Warning them about it costs you standing you will need later.

activities.name: Send the fix to whoever can actually apply it
activities.description: Write the problem up so the person who operates the solution can act on it without needing you.
activities.prompt: I need to tell the people operating a solution about this problem: [describe the problem, the trigger, and the fix]. Draft a short technical note for whoever operates the environment: what the symptom looks like, what causes it, how to confirm whether they are affected, and what to do about it. Write it for a competent engineer who was not involved in the original design. Keep it to what is technically necessary and exclude customer names, personal data, seat counts and spend figures.
activities.expectedOutput: A technical note the operating team can act on unaided, with the check they can run themselves and the customer detail removed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether the note is genuinely actionable by somebody who was not there, and checks it against the data rules before it goes to a partner. A problem report that requires the author to explain it will sit unactioned, and the customer will find the problem first.
activities.requiredContext: The problem, its trigger and its fix. The partners or customer teams operating the affected environments. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Check the confirm-whether-affected step is something they can actually run themselves.
3. Remove anything a partner should not receive under the CELA rules.
4. Send it, and record where you sent it so this does not come back to you as new in three months.
activities.whyThisMatters: You are not going to fix these yourself across this many customers. The work is making the fix travel, and a note that needs you attached to it does not travel.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: You will not notice a customer's technical problem by looking at them, because you are not looking at most of them and you do not operate any of it. You notice by recognizing a pattern you have already met.
keyTalkingPoints: The technical estate here is operated by partners and customers rather than by us, and there are far more customers per engineer than in Enterprise, so risk is found by pattern rather than by inspection. The problems worth tracking are the ones you have already diagnosed once: a configuration that fails under load, a version combination that breaks on upgrade, an integration that degrades quietly. Consumption movement belongs to the D-CSA and is not the engineer's signal. The intervention normally runs through whoever operates the solution. Facilitator note: the judgment here is about noticing and routing rather than fixing.
discussionQuestions: How would you currently find out a customer's solution was in trouble?
Which technical problem have you now seen at more than one customer?
Who actually fixes it when you find one?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the exposed list to the one fix each person routes.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the customer each person is warning and who is actually going to fix it.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one technical problem you have seen at more than one customer.
facilitatorQuestions: Which of your customers are running the configuration you already know is fragile?
Which of them has a partner who probably knows already?
What can you actually do about it from where you sit?
listenFor: Listen for problems treated as one-offs when they have already recurred, for partner-operated estates assumed to be unmonitored, for engineers taking on a fix that belongs to whoever operates it, and for warnings sent without a route to action.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a recurring problem, use the last customer escalation and ask whether anything about it was predictable.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which problem had you already seen twice without treating it as a pattern?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, identify which of your customers are exposed to a technical problem you have already met elsewhere, and route one fix to whoever operates the solution.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the pattern, who was exposed, and where you routed it.
