DCSA-ORIENT.roleTopicDescription: Introduce the eight-week huddle motion: why Frontier Accelerator exists, what happens in a thirty-minute huddle, the five roles that make it work, and what is expected of you between sessions.
DCSA-ORIENT.wiifm: You are Customer Zero. Before we ask a customer to put AI at the centre of how they work, we do it on our own work and find out honestly where it helps and where it does not. The aim is to get time back from the assembling, and to find out first-hand where AI earns that time and where it does not.
DCSA-ORIENT.name: Frontier Accelerator Orientation
DCSA-ORIENT.description: Introduces the motion, the huddle format, the AI tools in scope, and what team members are expected to try between sessions.

roles.name: Account Executive
roles.description: Manages strategic enterprise accounts with complex multi-stakeholder deals and long sales cycles.

roles.name: Account Technology Strategist
roles.description: Owns the technical strategy and solution roadmap for enterprise accounts.

roles.name: Commercial Executive
roles.description: Structures pricing, licensing, and commercial terms for deals and coordinates across team.

roles.name: Cloud Solution Architect
roles.description: Designs and validates cloud and AI architectures for customer success.

roles.name: Customer Success Account Manager
roles.description: Drives customer adoption, expansion, and renewal through success planning.

roles.name: Solution Engineer
roles.description: Leads technical discovery, qualification, and execution of demos, PoCs, and solution designs.

roles.name: Solution Sales Professional
roles.description: Drives solution-specific opportunities by shaping vision and leading value-based conversations.

DCSA-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand how the huddle motion runs, what you are being asked to do each week, and where your own judgment stays yours.
DCSA-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
DCSA-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: You know how the motion works, what happens in each huddle, what is expected of you between sessions, and you leave with one thing to try before the next one.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This is the first of eight huddles, and the one with no AI activity in it. Today is about what the motion is and what it asks of you. Frontier Accelerator exists because we are asking customers to reshape how they work around AI, and that argument is stronger when we have done it ourselves first. That is what Customer Zero means here: we apply these tools to our own real work, and we are straight about where they help and where they do not.
keyTalkingPoints: Weekly and short, led by the manager with a facilitator. The cadence carries the motion, so if the slot has to move, move it rather than drop it.

Four principles hold every week: keep the weekly rhythm, learn from what colleagues have actually tried, ground every session in real work rather than hypothetical scenarios, and try something between huddles so there is an experience to bring back.

Every huddle from next week runs to the same shape, and the agenda and timings are set out on the huddle page: a short framing of why the topic matters, then sharing what you tried since last time, then hands-on work on a real scenario, then a close where you pick the one thing you will carry into the week.

Five roles make the motion work. The Leader connects it to strategy and clears barriers. The Manager owns the huddle and opens with the why. The Facilitator runs it and draws every voice in. The Team Member experiments in their own workflow and brings back wins and friction. The Coach reviews patterns across huddles and feeds insight back.

The journey ahead: this week you get grounded, weeks two to eight you build the habit on real work, week nine the team decides which habits stick and what comes next, and from week ten you choose your own topics.
You are here as a peer, not an expert. You do not need prior AI experience, and “I do not know” is a good answer.

Two things on feedback. The facilitator posts one question in the chat each week, asking how useful the huddle was on a scale of one to ten. Huddle transcripts are reviewed for themes to improve the sessions, so keep confidential detail out of the room, whether that is customer, partner, enrollment or commercial, and put product problems into the tool's own feedback control rather than here.
discussionQuestions: Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you deliberately avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted output in front of a customer?
What would make thirty minutes a week worth protecting for this?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the discovery prompt below. Week one is for finding the recurring work worth handing to AI. Post the usefulness question in the chat before people leave.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: complete the baseline survey if it has been sent to you, confirm the huddle series is on your calendar, confirm you can open at least one of the tools named for your path, since the commitment at the end of this session runs in one of them, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. If your access is blocked, come anyway and say so, because that is a different problem from not being interested. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
facilitatorQuestions: Which work do you repeat every week without ever thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where does your judgment have to stay human no matter how good the output gets?
What would have to happen in these thirty minutes for you to want the next one?
listenFor: Listen for unvoiced skepticism, for access blockers stated as disinterest, and for the assumption that this is a tool rollout. Listen for people describing only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat, because the recurring and unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping. Listen for anyone who thinks they need to be an AI expert to take part, and correct that in the room.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the conversation and record access blockers separately from interest, since they need different fixes. The discovery prompt runs in whichever tool the person already has. If the room stays quiet, start with your own example of work you repeat every week.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

“I am a [your role] at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with.”
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

DCSA-ORIENT.keyTakeaway: The point of the motion is better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake.

DCSA-PARTNER.roleTopicName: Get Technical Work Done by People You Do Not Manage
DCSA-PARTNER.roleTopicDescription: Hand technical work to a delivery partner with enough for them to act, and set up a way of knowing whether it landed, without a support agreement or an escalation path behind you.
DCSA-PARTNER.wiifm: On these accounts there is no Unified agreement and no funded delivery. If the partner cannot act on what you gave them, nothing happens at all.
DCSA-PARTNER.name: Hand Work to a Partner and Keep It Moving
DCSA-PARTNER.description: Decide what genuinely belongs with a partner, hand it over with enough for them to act, and stay on it through the acceptance and conversion windows rather than assuming it landed.
DCSA-PARTNER.todayObjective: Hand one piece of technical work to a partner in a form they can act on without you.
DCSA-PARTNER.whyItMatters: Partner-led is structural in this segment rather than optional help, which means referrals that quietly expire are lost coverage you chose to give away. The difference between a partner motion that works and one that does not is almost entirely about what happens after the handoff.
DCSA-PARTNER.desiredOutcome: One technical handover a partner can act on unaided, with a named signal that would tell you whether it worked.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

activities.name: Find out what is actually behind each account
activities.description: Establish which accounts have a delivery partner genuinely engaged and which have a support agreement, because on these accounts one of those may be all there is.
activities.prompt: For these accounts [list up to fifteen accounts from your portfolio], show two things. First, whether any support or services agreement is recorded on the account, and of what kind. Second, whether a partner is associated, with any co-sell or referral record and its recorded status and dates. Report only what the record contains and do not describe what any partner is doing or infer what support entitlement implies.
activities.expectedOutput: Your accounts sorted by what is actually behind them: an agreement, an engaged partner, both, or nothing.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides what counts as an engaged partner and what an absent agreement really means for a given account. A referral accepted eight months ago and a partner deploying this week look identical in our record, and an account with neither is one where your own time is the entire coverage.
activities.requiredContext: Up to fifteen accounts from your portfolio.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list with up to fifteen of your accounts.
2. Read the support agreement column first. An account with neither an agreement nor an engaged partner has nothing behind it at all.
3. An association is not an engagement - check the dates before assuming anyone is active.
4. For anything that looks live, open the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center; partner-side progress is only visible there.
5. Rank by what would happen at each account if something broke tomorrow.
activities.whyThisMatters: At this coverage ratio you are not the delivery mechanism, the agreement or the partner is. Knowing which accounts have neither tells you where a problem becomes yours by default.

agents.name: Sales Home
agents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
agents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Write a handover the partner can act on without you
activities.description: Turn your own technical assessment into something a partner engineer can execute, inside the rules that govern what may be shared.
activities.prompt: I need to hand technical work to a delivery partner at [account name]. Here is my assessment and what I want done: [paste your own technical assessment and the work required]. Restructure this for a competent engineer at the partner who was not in any of my conversations: what the situation is, what needs doing, what order, and what they should check to confirm it worked. Do not add technical steps or recommendations I have not written. Exclude contact names and details, seat counts, spend figures, and anything that reads as an export from our systems.
activities.expectedOutput: A partner-executable technical handover derived from your own assessment, checked for added content and for the data-sharing boundary.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA owns the technical content and confirms nothing was invented in the restructuring, then checks it against the data rules before it goes out. A partner engineer will execute what is written without knowing which line came from you and which was generated to make the sequence read well.
activities.requiredContext: One account, and your own technical assessment of what needs doing. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
activitySteps: 1. Write your technical assessment and the required work first. That content is yours.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
3. Check nothing technical has been added that you did not write.
4. Read it as the partner engineer. Anything that assumes a conversation they were not in has to be spelled out.
5. Check it against the CELA rules before sending: no personal data, no seat or spend detail, nothing resembling an export.
activities.whyThisMatters: Without a Unified agreement there is no delivery manager to interpret your intent. The handover is the whole intervention, and if it needs you attached to it, nothing happens.

activities.name: Decide how you will know it worked
activities.description: Name the observable signal that would tell you the partner's work landed, before you stop thinking about the account.
activities.prompt: I have handed technical work to a partner at [account name]. The intended technical outcome is [describe what should change if it worked]. Show me what is currently recorded for that account that relates to it: deployed workloads, open or resolved support issues, recorded activity, and any usage or consumption figures held in the record. Show the current state only. Do not project what should happen or judge whether the work will succeed.
activities.expectedOutput: A dated baseline of what is currently recorded, with one observable signal and a date to check it.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA defines what would count as success and whether it is observable at all. Some technical outcomes leave no trace in any system we can see, and finding that out now rather than in three months is the difference between a check you can run and a hope.
activities.requiredContext: One account with work handed to a partner, and your own definition of what would change if it succeeded.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Take this as your baseline and write it down with today's date.
3. Decide which single observable would change if the work landed, and by when you would expect it.
4. Put that check in your calendar. Nothing else in the week will surface it.
5. If the observable is not visible in any record you can reach, you need the partner to report it - agree that now, not later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Work handed to a partner without a check is work you have stopped tracking. At this account count nothing will bring it back to your attention until the customer escalates.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: On these accounts the technical work is done by a partner you have no authority over, with no support agreement behind you. This session is about making a handover that actually gets acted on.
keyTalkingPoints: Consumption execution in this segment runs through the D-CSA and partner delivery, particularly on non-Unified Azure. Unlike a Unified engagement there is no funded delivery vehicle and no contractual escalation route, so the handover has to stand on its own. Partner Center sits outside what our agents can reach, so partner-side progress returns through the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center directly. CELA rules govern the exchange: personal data, MSX screenshots and exports, and financial or seat-level detail are off-limits. Facilitator note: the useful frame is that you are writing for a competent engineer who was not in any of your conversations.
discussionQuestions: When you hand technical work to a partner, how do you find out whether it happened?
What do you end up doing yourself because handing it over felt slower?
What does a partner need from you that you usually leave out?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the handover to the signal each person will use to check it landed.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming what each person is handing over and the signal they will check.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account where a partner is doing or should be doing the technical work.
facilitatorQuestions: What would this partner need to act on this without calling you?
How would you know in a month whether anything happened?
What are you holding onto that you should have handed over?
listenFor: Listen for handovers that assume context the partner does not have, for work retained because delegating felt slower, for progress assumed from silence, and for detail being prepared that CELA rules exclude.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live handover, use the last one that stalled and work out what was missing from it.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you keep because explaining it felt like more work than doing it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, hand one piece of technical work to a partner in a form they can act on unaided, and write down the specific signal you will check to know whether it worked.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what you handed over and what the signal showed.

DCSA-PARTNER.keyTakeaway: Handing something to a partner is not the end of your involvement. The windows run whether or not anyone is watching them, and the system closes the lead for you if nobody acts.

DCSA-CONV.roleTopicDescription: Prepare for a technical conversation you may not get to repeat, and leave the customer with something that keeps working after you have moved on to the next account.
DCSA-CONV.wiifm: At this coverage you are not building a relationship, you are making a single intervention. What you leave behind matters more than what you say.
DCSA-CONV.name: Prepare and Lead a Customer Conversation
DCSA-CONV.description: Prepare for the conversation that moves the decision, anticipate what will be asked, and lead it with evidence.

DCSA-CONV.todayObjective: Prepare one customer conversation on the assumption that it is the only one you will get.
DCSA-CONV.whyItMatters: Customer conversations are where decisions actually move. They are won or lost in preparation, and preparation is the first thing dropped when the calendar fills.
DCSA-CONV.desiredOutcome: A conversation prepared around one decision, with something durable left behind and the next owner named.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

activities.name: Pick the one thing worth their attention
activities.description: Assemble what is known about the account and choose the single technical priority, on the assumption you get one conversation.
activities.prompt: For [account name], show me what is recorded: the products and workloads deployed and when, any open or recently resolved support issue, any usage or consumption figures held in the record, recent activity and which role it came from, and whether a partner is associated. Present it as a factual summary. Do not rank the findings by importance or recommend what to focus on.
activities.expectedOutput: A factual account summary, with your own decision on the single technical priority for the conversation.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA chooses the priority. The record shows what was bought and what has broken, but which risk actually matters for this customer depends on what they are trying to do, and a summary that ranks findings would be ranking them on the wrong criteria.
activities.requiredContext: One customer with a technical conversation coming up.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account.
2. Read it for what is missing as much as for what is there.
3. Now do the part the agent cannot: decide the single technical thing that most needs to be right at this customer.
4. Build the conversation around that one thing and let the rest go.
activities.whyThisMatters: With one conversation available, covering everything means the customer leaves with nothing. Choosing is the work, and it is not something the record can do for you.

activities.name: Leave something behind that works without you
activities.description: Turn your technical guidance into a short written artifact the customer or their partner can act on after you have moved on.
activities.prompt: I am advising [account name] on [state the priority you have chosen]. Here is my guidance in my own words: [paste your guidance]. Turn it into a short written note for the customer's own technical people and whoever supports them, covering what to do, in what order, what to check afterwards, and what would indicate it is going wrong. Do not add recommendations I have not written. Keep it to one page and write it for someone who was not in the conversation.
activities.expectedOutput: A one-page durable note the customer or their partner can act on without you, derived from your own guidance.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA owns the guidance and confirms nothing was added in the rewrite. Advice that gets acted on months later with nobody available to interpret it has to be right as written, and a generated clarification that changes the meaning will not be caught by the person following it.
activities.requiredContext: One customer, your chosen technical priority, and your own guidance written out.
activitySteps: 1. Write your guidance first, in your own words. The technical judgment is yours.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace all three bracketed sections.
3. Check nothing has been added, and that no caveat you wrote has been smoothed away.
4. Test it against the question: could they follow this in three months with you unavailable?
5. Send it to the customer and, if a partner supports them, to the partner as well.
activities.whyThisMatters: At this coverage the value you leave is more durable than the value you deliver in the room. A conversation with nothing written down is gone the week after.

activities.name: Name who has this account after you
activities.description: Establish which Microsoft roles have been active recently and who realistically holds the technical relationship next.
activities.prompt: For [account name], list every recorded activity in the last six months with the date and the role it came from, and show any open support issue with its recorded owner. Show the roles by how recently each was active. Do not include partner or co-sell records, and do not infer who is responsible for the account technically.
activities.expectedOutput: The Microsoft roles active on the account ordered by recency, with a named technical successor or an explicit acknowledgement that there is not one.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides who genuinely picks this up, including the honest answer that nobody does. Naming a successor who has not agreed is worse than admitting the gap, because the customer will call someone who is not expecting them.
activities.requiredContext: One customer you are unlikely to revisit soon.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account.
2. If the only recent activity is yours, that is the finding.
3. Decide who realistically holds this next - the DAE, a partner you already identified, or nobody - and be honest about the last option.
4. Tell them, and tell the customer who to contact. An unnamed successor is the same as none.
activities.whyThisMatters: Accounts at this coverage ratio quietly lose their technical contact and nobody notices until something breaks. Saying out loud that there is no successor is what turns it into a decision somebody can make.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: You are probably not coming back to this account. This session is about preparing for a conversation on that assumption.
keyTalkingPoints: A Unified engagement supports an ongoing advisory relationship with recurring contact. At this coverage ratio and without that agreement, most customers get a single technical conversation and then nothing until something breaks. That changes the objective from building understanding over time to making one intervention that survives your absence. Facilitator note: the temptation is to cover everything because you may not be back, and that reliably produces a conversation the customer remembers nothing from.
discussionQuestions: How many of your accounts have you spoken to more than once?
What happens at an account after you leave it?
When did you last try to cover everything in one meeting?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the single priority to what each person will leave behind.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the one thing each person is leaving behind and who is picking it up.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one customer you have a technical conversation coming up with.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the single thing this customer most needs to get right?
Who will be here after you are not?
What would still be true in six months if you did nothing else?
listenFor: Listen for agendas that try to cover everything, for advice that depends on the architect returning, for no named owner on the customer or partner side, and for durable guidance never written down.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has an upcoming conversation, use an account they have not revisited and ask what is still standing from the last one.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which of your advice quietly assumed you would be coming back?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, prepare one customer conversation around a single priority, and leave something written that a customer or partner could act on without you.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what you left behind and who owns it now.

secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

activities.prompt: For these accounts [list up to fifteen accounts where you believe the technical outcome was good], show for each whether a support or services agreement is recorded, any support issue raised and how it was resolved, any milestone or success activity logged, and any usage or consumption figures held in the record. Separate the accounts that produced some record of delivery work from those where the only thing recorded is the purchase and whatever usage figures exist. Do not infer an outcome from deployment or from usage.
activities.expectedOutput: Your accounts split by whether any delivery record exists, with an explicit read on what can be evidenced for those where none does.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides whether usage figures alone amount to evidence of an outcome. On an account with no delivery record they are all there is, and consumption showing a service running is a much weaker claim than a customer saying it solved something.
activities.requiredContext: Up to fifteen accounts where you believe the technical outcome was good.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list.
2. The accounts with no delivery record are the normal case here, not the failures. That is what non-Unified looks like.
3. For those, usage figures are the only evidence that will ever exist, so decide now whether they say anything useful.
4. For the accounts that did produce a record, check whether the work recorded is actually connected to the outcome you have in mind.
5. Pick the account with the strongest case and carry it into the attribution step.
activities.whyThisMatters: A Unified engagement leaves milestones and hours behind it. Most of these accounts leave nothing, so knowing which ones produced any record at all tells you where a value story is even possible before somebody asks you for one.

agents.name: Sales Home
agents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
agents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
agents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.description: Establish who actually performed the delivery work, so that outcomes are described by whoever earned them.

activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides what is honestly ours to claim. Our record shows what Microsoft logged, which on a partner-delivered account is a small fraction of what happened, and presenting that fraction as the whole story is visible to the partner immediately.
activities.requiredContext: Your evidenced accounts from the previous activity.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list.

activities.name: Get the evidence to whoever owns the renewal
activities.description: Pass the technical evidence to the account and commercial roles before the renewal conversation happens without it.
activities.prompt: For [account name], I have technical evidence of the outcome delivered. Here is what I can evidence: [paste what you established]. Draft a short internal note for the account executive and the commercial executive covering what was delivered, what the evidence is, what the partner contributed, and what remains unproven. Keep it brief and factual. Do not add claims I have not made and do not characterize the commercial implications.
activities.expectedOutput: A brief factual internal note for the account and commercial roles, stating what is evidenced, what the partner contributed, and what is not proven.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA states what is not proven alongside what is. A technical note that reads as advocacy gets discounted entirely by the people preparing a renewal, and the unproven items are exactly what they need to know before they meet the customer.
activities.requiredContext: One account with evidenced technical outcomes, your own summary of them, and the renewal date if known.
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Check nothing has been added, particularly anything that reads as a commercial recommendation.
3. Say plainly what remains unproven. A note that only lists wins is discounted by whoever reads it.
4. Send it to the DAE and the CE, and note the renewal date so you know whether it arrived in time.
activities.whyThisMatters: Renewal conversations belong to the account and commercial roles. Technical evidence that stays with the architect does not reach them, and at this coverage nobody will come and ask for it.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Somebody else delivered most of what worked at your accounts. This session is about what you can honestly say about it.
keyTalkingPoints: A Unified engagement leaves a delivery record - milestones, hours, an engagement manager - that can be pointed at. On non-Unified accounts none of that exists, so the evidence is telemetry plus whatever the partner is willing to share. Separate what was deployed from what is being used and from what the customer got value from; those are three different claims and only the first is reliably in the record. The renewal conversation belongs to the DAE and the CE, so evidence that stays with you does not reach it. Facilitator note: partner-delivered outcomes are the partner's to describe, and claiming them damages the relationship that is doing the work.
discussionQuestions: When an account goes well, where is the proof?
How much of what worked was delivered by a partner?
Who asks you for value evidence, and when?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the evidence review to what each person passes on and to whom.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming what each person is passing on and who is receiving it.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring two or three accounts where you believe the technical outcome was good.
facilitatorQuestions: What can you evidence about that outcome as opposed to believe?
Whose outcome is it to describe?
Who needs this before the renewal, and have they got it?
listenFor: Listen for deployment presented as value, for partner-delivered outcomes claimed as ours, for evidence that exists only in the architect's head, and for renewals approaching with nobody having asked.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a clear success, use an account that renewed quietly and ask what evidence would have been available if anyone had wanted it.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which good outcome would have gone unrecorded if nobody asked?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, establish what one account's technical outcome can actually be evidenced with, separate what the partner delivered, and send it to whoever owns the renewal.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what you could evidence, what you could not, and who you sent it to.

DCSA-VALUE.keyTakeaway: Value that is not evidenced is an opinion. Value that is not communicated is invisible.

PSS-ORIENT.roleTopicDescription: Introduce the eight-week huddle motion: why Frontier Accelerator exists, what happens in a thirty-minute huddle, the five roles that make it work, and what is expected of you between sessions.
PSS-ORIENT.wiifm: You are Customer Zero. Before we ask a customer to put AI at the centre of how they work, we do it on our own work and find out honestly where it helps and where it does not. The aim is to get time back from the assembling, and to find out first-hand where AI earns that time and where it does not.
PSS-ORIENT.name: Frontier Accelerator Orientation
PSS-ORIENT.description: Introduces the motion, the huddle format, the AI tools in scope, and what team members are expected to try between sessions.

PSS-ORIENT.todayObjective: Understand how the huddle motion runs, what you are being asked to do each week, and where your own judgment stays yours.
PSS-ORIENT.whyItMatters: Eight weeks of huddles only works if everyone understands what is being asked, what good participation looks like, and where human judgment stays non-negotiable.
PSS-ORIENT.desiredOutcome: You know how the motion works, what happens in each huddle, what is expected of you between sessions, and you leave with one thing to try before the next one.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This is the first of eight huddles, and the one with no AI activity in it. Today is about what the motion is and what it asks of you. Frontier Accelerator exists because we are asking customers to reshape how they work around AI, and that argument is stronger when we have done it ourselves first. That is what Customer Zero means here: we apply these tools to our own real work, and we are straight about where they help and where they do not.
keyTalkingPoints: Weekly and short, led by the manager with a facilitator. The cadence carries the motion, so if the slot has to move, move it rather than drop it.

Four principles hold every week: keep the weekly rhythm, learn from what colleagues have actually tried, ground every session in real work rather than hypothetical scenarios, and try something between huddles so there is an experience to bring back.

Every huddle from next week runs to the same shape, and the agenda and timings are set out on the huddle page: a short framing of why the topic matters, then sharing what you tried since last time, then hands-on work on a real scenario, then a close where you pick the one thing you will carry into the week.

Five roles make the motion work. The Leader connects it to strategy and clears barriers. The Manager owns the huddle and opens with the why. The Facilitator runs it and draws every voice in. The Team Member experiments in their own workflow and brings back wins and friction. The Coach reviews patterns across huddles and feeds insight back.

The journey ahead: this week you get grounded, weeks two to eight you build the habit on real work, week nine the team decides which habits stick and what comes next, and from week ten you choose your own topics.
You are here as a peer, not an expert. You do not need prior AI experience, and “I do not know” is a good answer.

Two things on feedback. The facilitator posts one question in the chat each week, asking how useful the huddle was on a scale of one to ten. Huddle transcripts are reviewed for themes to improve the sessions, so keep confidential detail out of the room, whether that is customer, partner, enrollment or commercial, and put product problems into the tool's own feedback control rather than here.
discussionQuestions: Which part of your week is assembling information rather than deciding anything?
Where do you already use AI, and where have you deliberately avoided it?
What would you need to see before you trusted an AI-drafted output in front of a customer?
What would make thirty minutes a week worth protecting for this?
suggestedTransitions: Move from how the motion works to the recurring work each person will map with the discovery prompt this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by pointing the team to the resources for next week's topic and to the discovery prompt below. Week one is for finding the recurring work worth handing to AI. Post the usefulness question in the chat before people leave.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: complete the baseline survey if it has been sent to you, confirm the huddle series is on your calendar, confirm you can open at least one of the tools named for your path, since the commitment at the end of this session runs in one of them, and come ready to describe the work you repeat most weeks. If your access is blocked, come anyway and say so, because that is a different problem from not being interested. No prior AI experience is needed for this session.
facilitatorQuestions: Which work do you repeat every week without ever thinking of it as a workflow?
Which of those steps is assembling information rather than making a decision?
Where does your judgment have to stay human no matter how good the output gets?
What would have to happen in these thirty minutes for you to want the next one?
listenFor: Listen for unvoiced skepticism, for access blockers stated as disinterest, and for the assumption that this is a tool rollout. Listen for people describing only their exceptional work rather than the work they repeat, because the recurring and unglamorous tasks are the ones worth mapping. Listen for anyone who thinks they need to be an AI expert to take part, and correct that in the room.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If tool access is not confirmed, still run the conversation and record access blockers separately from interest, since they need different fixes. The discovery prompt runs in whichever tool the person already has. If the room stays quiet, start with your own example of work you repeat every week.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which part of your week had you never thought of as a workflow until now? What would have to be true before you trusted AI with it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt:
Run this in Microsoft 365 Copilot, Cowork, or Scout before the next huddle, then bring the result to the session:

“I am a [your role] at Microsoft and I want to find the recurring work in my week that AI could take on.
1. First, look at my calendar, mail and Teams activity from the last four weeks and tell me what you can see about where my time actually goes. If you cannot access that data, say so and move to step 2 rather than guessing.
2. Then ask me up to five short questions, one at a time, to cover the work that never shows up in a calendar or an inbox.
3. Then list the five things I do most often. For each one give an estimate of the time it costs me per month, whether it is best handled as a saved prompt, a reusable skill, a scheduled automation or an existing agent, and the one judgment that must stay mine.
4. Rank them by time returned and tell me which one to start with.”
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ranked list of the five things you repeat most, which of them looked like a prompt, skill, automation or agent fit, and any AI experience from the week, including anything that did not work.

PSS-ORIENT.keyTakeaway: The point of the motion is better workflow with human judgment kept explicit, not tool adoption for its own sake.

activities.name: Separate what you know from what you were told
activities.description: Establish what our own record can independently confirm about an opportunity a partner brought you.
activities.prompt: A partner has brought me an opportunity at [account or company name]. Here is what they have told me: [paste what the partner told you]. Show me what our record independently contains about that customer: whether they exist as an account and under whose ownership, any products or workloads already in place, any prior or open opportunity, any recorded activity and from which role, and any existing partner association. State plainly which of the partner's claims our record can speak to and which it cannot. Do not assess whether the opportunity is likely to close.
activities.expectedOutput: The partner's claims split into what our record can confirm and what rests entirely on their word, with an explicit decision on what to invest against the latter.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides how much to invest against a claim only the partner can make. Their qualification bar is not ours and their incentive is to get Microsoft engaged, and a partner who is habitually right about this is a different proposition from one who is not, which is a judgment about the relationship rather than about the deal.
activities.requiredContext: One opportunity brought to you by a partner, and what the partner told you about it.
activitySteps: 1. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the cannot-speak-to list first. That is the part you are taking on the partner's word.
3. If the account is owned by a DAE, tell them before you invest anything.

activities.name: Check the conditions before anyone counts on it
activities.description: Establish whether a partner-originated deal meets the recorded conditions for registration, before it is treated as one.
activities.prompt: For [opportunity name or ID], show me what is recorded that bears on co-sell registration: the account and whether it is Microsoft-managed, the recorded deal value and currency, the solution area and products attached, the opportunity creation date, and the current stage and status. Also show any existing co-sell or referral record on the opportunity with its dates. Report only what is recorded and do not assess eligibility.
activities.expectedOutput: The recorded facts assembled against the registration conditions, with the gaps identified and raised with the partner early.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS confirms eligibility against the authoritative source rather than against a summary. Registration conditions change and a deal that fails one at close costs the partner real money, which is the kind of thing that ends a partnership rather than a deal.
activities.requiredContext: One partner-originated opportunity. The current co-sell registration conditions from the authoritative source.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Home and paste the prompt with the opportunity.

2. Check the recorded facts against the conditions yourself: a Microsoft-managed account, Azure IP co-sell eligibility, a value of at least twenty-five thousand US dollars, and at least seventy-two hours between creation and being marked won.
3. Anything you cannot confirm from the record, confirm with the authoritative owner rather than assuming.
4. Tell the partner what is missing now. Finding out at close is too late for both of you.
activities.whyThisMatters: The conditions are checkable long before close, and nothing prompts anyone to check them until it is nearly there. The whole cost of getting this wrong lands on the partner, and they will remember.

activities.name: Find the partner who keeps letting things lapse
activities.description: Look across your partners for the ones whose referrals and co-sell records consistently stall, because that is a relationship problem rather than a record problem.
activities.prompt: For these partners [list three to five partners], show me the co-sell and referral records associated with each: the account, the recorded status, the date the record was created, and the date of the last recorded change. Group the output by partner. Report the recorded dates only - do not calculate elapsed time, judge which are close to expiring, or compare the partners.
activities.expectedOutput: Records grouped by partner with the window arithmetic done by you, separating one-off lapses from a partner-level pattern.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides whether a pattern of lapsed records is a capacity problem, a fit problem, or a partner who was never going to work them. Those need completely different conversations, and the records look identical in all three cases.
activities.requiredContext: Three to five partners from your portfolio. The Partner Timeline view or Partner Center for anything near a boundary.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Home, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list with three to five of your partners.
2. Do the arithmetic yourself against the windows: fourteen days for a partner to accept a referral before it expires, sixty days after acceptance to convert before it is marked lost.
3. Read down each partner rather than across all the records. One lapsed referral is an accident; a partner with several is a conversation.
4. Check anything near a boundary in the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center, since our recorded status can lag what the partner has already done.
5. Chase the individual items with days left, and raise the pattern with the partner who has one.
activities.whyThisMatters: Individual expiring referrals are chased by whoever sent them. Nobody else is positioned to notice whether the lapses concentrate on one partner, and that is the finding worth having.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Most roles here decide what to send out to a partner. You also have to decide what to do with what comes back the other way.
keyTalkingPoints: Partner-originated demand arrives qualified to the partner's standard rather than ours, and the windows are already running: a partner has fourteen days to accept a referral before it expires, and sixty days to convert it before the system marks it lost. IP co-sell registration has its own conditions - the deal must be won on a Microsoft-managed account, be Azure IP co-sell eligible, be at least twenty-five thousand US dollars, and have a seventy-two hour gap between creation and being marked won. CELA rules limit what can be exchanged in either direction. Facilitator note: the honest difficulty here is that you often cannot verify what the partner is telling you, and deciding how much to invest on their word is the actual skill.
discussionQuestions: How much of your pipeline originates with a partner rather than with us?
How do you decide whether to believe a partner's qualification?
When did a partner-sourced deal turn out not to be real?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the verification read to the one opportunity each person progresses or declines.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the opportunity each person is progressing and the one they are declining.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one opportunity that came to you from a partner.
facilitatorQuestions: What do you actually know about this opportunity as opposed to what you were told?
What would you need to see to invest Microsoft resource behind it?
Which of your open partner-sourced items are closest to a window closing?
listenFor: Listen for partner qualification accepted at face value, for registration conditions assumed rather than checked, for windows running unnoticed, and for reluctance to push back on a partner in case it damages the relationship.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live partner-sourced opportunity, use the last one that went nowhere and work out what would have revealed it earlier.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which partner-sourced opportunity have you been carrying on trust?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, establish what can actually be verified about one partner-originated opportunity, check its registration conditions, and either progress it or tell the partner why you are not.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what you could verify, what you could not, and what you decided.

activities.name: Decide which partners need you this month
activities.description: Triage a portfolio of partners into the ones with something to decide and the ones that only need contact.
activities.prompt: For these partners [list three to five partners], show for each: the co-sell and referral records currently associated with them and the recorded status of each, and any opportunity where they are the associated partner along with its stage and the date it last moved. Group the output by partner. Do not rank the partners, compare them, or recommend where to spend time.
activities.expectedOutput: Those partners split into meetings that need an agenda and contacts that meet the cadence commitment.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides which partner genuinely needs time this month. Activity in the record tracks how much business is flowing rather than how much attention the relationship needs, and meeting a cadence minimum is a floor rather than a plan.
activities.requiredContext: Three to five partners from your portfolio, and your own record of when you last spoke to each.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed list with three to five partners.
2. Look for partners with something stalled or something approaching a decision - those need a meeting with an agenda.
3. Partners with everything moving need a check-in, not a meeting.
4. Separately, check your own cadence commitment: a minimum of monthly contact per partner seller. Anyone you have not spoken to in that window needs contact regardless of what the record shows.
5. Split the month into meetings that need preparation and contacts that satisfy the cadence.
activities.whyThisMatters: A minimum contact cadence is an obligation, not a strategy. Without a deliberate split the calendar fills with the partners who ask for time, and the meetings that needed preparation get none.

activities.name: Give the meeting something to decide
activities.description: Turn a recurring partner meeting into one with a decision attached, using what has actually moved.
activities.prompt: I have a partner meeting with [partner name]. Show me what has changed on their associated records since a month ago where the record supports that: opportunities that moved stage, co-sell or referral records created or changed status, and any new recorded activity. Also show what has not moved. Present the changes factually and do not propose an agenda or suggest what to discuss.
activities.expectedOutput: A factual read on what has and has not moved for that partner, with one decision chosen and sent ahead as the agenda.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS chooses the decision the meeting is for. What has not moved may be a partner problem, a Microsoft problem or a customer problem, and walking in with the wrong attribution turns a working session into a defensive one.
activities.requiredContext: One partner with a meeting coming up.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [partner name].
2. The things that have not moved are the meeting. The things that have moved are the update.
3. Pick one decision you want out of the conversation and build the agenda around it.
4. Send the partner the decision you want to reach beforehand, so they can arrive able to make it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Recurring partner meetings drift into status reporting, which both sides can do by email. A meeting with a decision attached is the only kind worth the cadence.

activities.name: Find out who else is talking to your partner
activities.description: Establish which Microsoft roles are engaged with the same partner, so the partner is not receiving three different asks.
activities.prompt: For these accounts where [partner name] is engaged [list three to five accounts], show which Microsoft roles have recorded activity on each in the last quarter and the date of the most recent from each role. Present it account by account with the roles named. Do not infer coordination or judge whether the engagement is aligned.
activities.expectedOutput: The accounts where your partner is engaged, showing which Microsoft roles are active on each and where nobody is.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides whether several roles engaging one partner is coordination or confusion. The record shows activity rather than intent, and a partner being asked for different things by three people will do the easiest one and tell nobody.
activities.requiredContext: One partner, and three to five accounts where they are engaged.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your partner and three to five of the accounts they work.
2. Look for accounts where several roles are active - the partner may be receiving conflicting asks.
3. Look for accounts where only the partner appears and no Microsoft role does.
4. Raise the conflicts at the territory health review rather than by chasing each role individually.
activities.whyThisMatters: Partners work with many people at Microsoft, and one receiving mixed messages does not necessarily say so; they prioritize. Seeing the overlap is the only way to find out it is happening.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A cadence commitment across a portfolio of partners becomes a diary full of status calls unless somebody decides what each one is for. This session is about that decision.
keyTalkingPoints: The partner rhythm in this segment includes a weekly partner meeting with the account roles and a minimum of monthly contact per partner seller, alongside deal clinics and the bi-weekly territory health review. Meeting a minimum is not the same as running a portfolio, and the partners who most need attention are rarely the ones who ask for it. Facilitator note: the useful distinction is between a meeting that needs an agenda because something has to be decided, and one that needs only a check-in because nothing has changed - treating them the same is what fills the week.
discussionQuestions: How many partner meetings do you hold in a month, and how many changed anything?
Which partner have you not spoken to in longer than you should admit?
What makes a partner meeting worth having?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the triage to the agenda each person will set for their one substantive meeting.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the partner each person is giving real time to and the ones they are handling lightly.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring your partner list and roughly when you last spoke to each.
facilitatorQuestions: Which of your partners has something that actually needs deciding this month?
Which are you meeting out of obligation?
Who is quietly getting no attention at all?
listenFor: Listen for cadence treated as the objective rather than the floor, for the loudest partners absorbing the time, for meetings with no decision attached, and for the quiet partners going unmentioned.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If someone has few partners, work the last month of meetings and ask which produced a decision.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which partner has been getting your time because they ask for it rather than because they need it?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, triage three to five of your partners for the month, set a real agenda for the one meeting that needs a decision, and make sure your monthly contact commitment is met across the partner sellers you carry.
bringBackEvidence: Bring your triage and what the substantive meeting decided.

activities.name: Find out what happened after one partner's deals closed
activities.description: Take a single partner and establish what our record knows about the customers they closed, and where it goes silent.
activities.prompt: For [partner name], show me the opportunities recorded as closed won where they are the associated partner, going back two quarters. For each, show the account, the close date, and then what has been recorded on that account since that date: any activity and from which role, any support issue, and any usage or consumption figures held in the record. Show the most recent record date for each account alongside the close date. Do not infer customer satisfaction or outcome from any of it.
activities.expectedOutput: The visibility gap across one partner's closed customers, read as a pattern for that partner, with the customer where it matters most identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides where a gap in our visibility actually matters. Silence after a partner-led close is normal rather than alarming, and treating every quiet customer as a risk will exhaust both your time and the partner's patience.
activities.requiredContext: One partner whose closed deals you want to understand.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [partner name] with one partner.
2. Look at the gap between each close date and the most recent record. That gap is what Microsoft cannot see.
3. Read it as a pattern for this partner rather than as a list of accounts. If every one of their customers goes silent immediately, that tells you something about how they work.
4. Long silence is not evidence of a problem or of success. It is the normal condition when a partner owns the relationship.
5. Pick the customer where not knowing would cost the most, usually one with a renewal ahead.
activities.whyThisMatters: Our record ends roughly where the customer's experience begins on these deals. Looking partner by partner rather than account by account shows you whether the blind spot is about one customer or about how that partner works.

activities.name: Ask the partner something worth answering
activities.description: Draft the question that gets a partner to tell you how a customer is actually doing, without it reading as an audit.
activities.prompt: I want to ask [partner name] how a customer is getting on since they closed and delivered. Here is what I already know from our record: [paste what you found]. Draft a short message asking about the customer's experience and any difficulty they have hit. Write it as a colleague with a shared interest in the customer, not as an inspection. Keep it to a few lines. Do not request seat counts, consumption figures, financial detail or anything commercially sensitive, and do not imply any obligation to report to us.
activities.expectedOutput: A short colleague-to-colleague question about a specific customer, checked against the data rules and with something offered in return.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS owns how this reads to the partner. A partner has no obligation to report customer outcomes to Microsoft, so the answer depends entirely on whether the question sounds like interest or like inspection, and only the person in the relationship can judge which.
activities.requiredContext: One partner and one customer they closed, plus what our record already shows. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
activitySteps: 1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read it as the partner. If it sounds like a request for a status report, it will be answered like one.
3. Check it against the CELA rules in both directions - what you are asking for as well as what you are sharing.
4. Send it, and be ready to offer something in return. A question with nothing behind it gets a short answer.
activities.whyThisMatters: This is the only route Microsoft has back to a customer a partner owns. Getting the tone wrong does not just fail to get an answer, it makes the next question harder.

activities.expectedOutput: A short internal note separating the partner's report from our record, with discrepancies left visible and attribution clear.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: When a partner closes and delivers, Microsoft largely stops seeing the customer. You are the only route back.
keyTalkingPoints: In CSP the partner frequently leads the later stages and often closes, which means our record ends roughly where the customer's experience begins. The PSS has visibility into the partner relationship without owning execution, so the realistic goal is closing an information gap rather than driving an outcome. What the partner will tell you is governed by the CELA rules in both directions, and a partner is under no obligation to report customer outcomes to us at all. Facilitator note: the value of asking is as much about the partner relationship as about the answer - a partner who is asked how the customer is doing behaves differently from one who is only asked about pipeline.
discussionQuestions: What do you know about customers your partners closed last quarter?
Who would tell you if one of them was unhappy?
When did you last ask a partner about a customer rather than about a deal?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the visibility gap to the one question each person will put to a partner.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the partner each person is asking and the question they are asking.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring two or three deals a partner closed in the last few quarters.
facilitatorQuestions: What does our record actually show about these customers since the close?
What would you want to know that only the partner can tell you?
What is in it for the partner to tell you?
listenFor: Listen for usage data mistaken for customer satisfaction, for the assumption that silence means success, for questions framed as inspection rather than as interest, and for renewal dates approaching with nobody having asked anything.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has recent closed deals, use a renewal that was lost and ask when the first sign was available.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which customer do you know nothing about since the day it closed?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, map what our record can and cannot tell you about customers a partner closed, and ask one partner directly how a specific customer is getting on.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what you could not see, what the partner told you, and whether it surprised you.

activities.name: Route the question so it comes back usable
activities.description: Frame a policy question so the authoritative owner can answer it once, rather than starting a conversation.
activities.prompt: I need to ask an authoritative owner a policy question about [account name]. Here is the question and the context: [paste your question and the deal facts that bear on it]. Restructure this as a single question that can be answered without a follow-up: what is being asked, the specific facts that determine the answer, what I have already checked, and what decision the answer will drive. Do not answer the question or suggest what the answer might be.
activities.expectedOutput: A single self-contained question that can be answered without a follow-up, with the answer recorded against the account.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE owns the question and confirms the rewrite did not change what is being asked. A model asked to make a question clearer will often make it more general, and a general answer to a specific eligibility question is worse than no answer because it feels like one.
activities.requiredContext: Your policy question and the deal facts that bear on it. The authoritative owner for that question.
activitySteps: 1. Write the question yourself first, including the deal facts that determine the answer.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
3. Check the restructured version still asks YOUR question rather than a cleaner adjacent one.
4. Send it, and record the answer against the account so the next person does not ask again.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most policy delay is not the owner being slow, it is the question arriving without the facts needed to answer it. One well-formed question beats three exchanges.

activities.name: Say out loud what you are relying on
activities.description: Make an inherited policy position explicit enough that its owner can confirm or correct it.
activities.prompt: For [account name], show every amendment, exception or non-standard term recorded against this account: what each one is, the date it was recorded, and which agreement it sits against. activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE states precisely what position they are relying on and has the owner confirm it before building on it. Reuse is invisible - a previous answer gets carried forward as an assumption rather than re-examined as a decision - and only the person relying on it can notice they are doing it. Whether it still stands is the owner's call, not a matter of how recent it looks.
activities.requiredContext: One live deal and the policy position you intend to rely on.

3. Check whether the record actually says what you remember it saying. Often it says something narrower.
4. Send your one sentence and the relevant record to the authoritative owner and ask whether it still stands.
activities.whyThisMatters: The most expensive policy error is not a wrong answer, it is a right answer that has expired. Nothing in the record marks a position as superseded, so the only reliable move is to name what you are assuming and have it confirmed.

activities.name: Read what the guidance actually says
activities.description: Establish what published commercial and licensing guidance states on a question, before asking anyone to interpret it.
activities.prompt: I need to understand what published guidance says about [describe the policy, licensing or eligibility question]. Using approved Microsoft sources and authoritative public documentation, set out what the published position is, what conditions or exceptions the documentation names, what it explicitly does not cover, and where different sources say different things. Cite each source and give its date. Do not tell me whether it applies to my deal and do not resolve any conflict you find.
activities.expectedOutput: The published position with its conditions, its explicit gaps, and any conflicts between sources, each cited and dated.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE decides which fact about this deal takes it outside the published general case. Guidance is written for the standard shape and commercial eligibility turns on the specifics that differ, so the judgment is which of your deal's particulars actually changes the answer - that is what determines whether you need a ruling or already have one.
activities.requiredContext: The policy or licensing question your deal raises.
activities.bestFitJob: Read what the guidance actually says
activitySteps: 1. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Check the dates before the content. Commercial guidance gets revised without being re-read.
3. Where sources conflict, that is your question for the authoritative owner - not something to resolve yourself.
4. Take the citations with you when you ask. A question that shows what you have already read gets a faster and better answer.
activities.whyThisMatters: Arriving at the policy owner having read nothing wastes their time and yours. Arriving having read it and knowing exactly where it stops being clear is the difference between one exchange and four.
