facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Every deal meets the policy questions eventually. This session is about meeting them while the structure is still a question rather than a commitment.
keyTalkingPoints: Policy, licensing and eligibility interpretation always routes to the authoritative owner rather than to an agent or to your own reading. In this segment a substantial share transacts through CSP, which carries its own eligibility conditions - Modern Commerce and an accepted agreement with a pre-existing partner billing relationship, with legacy arrangements excluded - so the route matters as much as the structure. Facilitator note: the failure mode is not getting a policy answer wrong, it is answering at all when the question belonged to somebody else, because an answer from the commercial person is treated as authoritative.
discussionQuestions: When did a policy question last surface too late to change anything?
Which questions do you find yourself answering that you should be routing?
How long does an authoritative answer actually take to get?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the question list to the one each person will route today.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the question each person is routing and who they are routing it to.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live deal where the commercial structure is not yet fixed.
facilitatorQuestions: What in this deal has an eligibility or licensing condition attached to it?
Which of those can you answer from approved guidance, and which need the owner?
What would it cost to find out at approval instead of now?
listenFor: Listen for policy answered from memory or from a previous deal, for eligibility assumed because a similar customer qualified, for CSP conditions treated as the same as direct, and for questions deferred because getting an answer feels slow.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live deal, use the last one where a policy issue surfaced late and work out when it first became answerable.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which policy question have you been answering yourself?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, run one live deal against the policy and eligibility questions it will face, and route every unresolved one to its authoritative owner rather than carrying it.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the question you routed and what the answer changed.

primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. activities.name: Establish what can be conceded without asking
activities.description: Fix the concession boundary from approved guidance before any pressure is applied to it.
activities.prompt: For [account name], show any discount, concession or non-standard term already in force on this account: what each one is, which agreement it sits on, and whether a partner transacts it. Report what is recorded. Do not advise what concession would be appropriate and do not propose a boundary.
activities.expectedOutput: A concession boundary set from approved guidance, with the concessions already in force on the account recorded as constraints on it.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE sets the boundary from current approved guidance rather than from what comparable deals happen to carry. What was granted elsewhere may have been an exception, may have been wrong, or may have been approved under guidance that has since changed, and inheriting it silently converts one exception into a standard.
activities.requiredContext: One live deal heading toward a negotiation. Current approved commercial guidance for concession authority.
activitySteps: 1. Set your concession boundary from current approved guidance before you look at anything. That anchor does not come from the record.
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace [account name] with your deal.
3. Treat what is already in force as a constraint on the boundary, not as evidence for it. It may itself have been an exception.
4. Write the boundary down, with the existing concessions noted against it, before anyone asks you to move.
activities.whyThisMatters: A boundary set before the pressure arrives is a decision. The same boundary set during the negotiation is a reaction, and it will be argued with.

activities.name: Test whether your briefing gives away the floor
activities.description: Check what a partner could infer from the boundary you are about to hand them.
activities.prompt: A partner will negotiate [describe the deal] with the customer. Here is the briefing I have written for them, covering what is fixed, what is theirs to use without asking, and what has to come back to me: [paste your briefing]. Read it as the partner would. Tell me what could be inferred from it about how much room exists beyond what I have stated, what is vague enough to be read as permission I did not intend, and anything in it resembling internal cost, margin, approval thresholds, seat counts, spend figures or personal data. Do not rewrite the briefing and do not tell me where the boundary should sit.
activities.expectedOutput: A partner briefing whose stated limits cannot be read as more room than you intended, with everything inferable closed before it is sent.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE decides how much of the boundary the partner needs to see. Too little and they concede something they should have escalated; too much and your floor becomes their opening position with the customer. That judgment depends on the specific partner, and only the person in the relationship can make it.
activities.requiredContext: The partner briefing you have written, setting out what is fixed, what is theirs to use, and what must return to you for approval. The CELA rules on partner data exchange.
activitySteps: 1. Write the briefing yourself, in three parts: what is fixed, what is theirs to use without asking, and what must come back to you. All three are your decisions and none of them are delegated.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
3. Close anything that could be read as permission you did not intend to give. Vagueness reads as room.
4. Check it against the CELA rules yourself as well. The agent is a second reader, not the control.
5. Send it through your normal partner channel before the negotiation, not during it.
activities.whyThisMatters: A boundary is only as good as what the other side can infer around it. Partners are commercially sophisticated and will read the shape of what you did not say.

activities.name: Decide now what would make you escalate
activities.description: Name the specific condition that would take a concession decision above you, before it arrives.
activities.prompt: For the deal at [account name], my concession boundary is [paste your boundary]. Help me think through what circumstances would put a decision beyond that boundary: what the customer might reasonably ask for, what a partner might commit to on their own, and what timing pressure might create. For each, frame it as a condition to watch for rather than a prediction. Do not recommend whether to escalate or what the answer should be.
activities.expectedOutput: One or two observable escalation triggers named in advance, with the approver forewarned.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE decides what genuinely warrants escalation. Escalating everything trains your approver to stop reading, and escalating nothing means the boundary was never real, and only you can judge where this deal sits between those.
activities.requiredContext: Your concession boundary and the deal it applies to. Your approval route.
activitySteps: 1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Pick the one or two conditions most likely to actually occur.
3. Write the trigger as something observable - a specific ask, a specific number - not as a feeling.
4. Tell your approver now that it may be coming, so the escalation is expected rather than a surprise.
activities.whyThisMatters: An escalation raised before the pressure is a decision with time attached. The same escalation raised during a negotiation is an emergency, and gets a worse answer.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: In this segment the negotiation is frequently conducted by a partner. Your concession logic has to work when applied by somebody who does not report to you.
keyTalkingPoints: The Commercial Executive owns concession authority and the commercial boundary, but in a partner-transacted deal the conversation with the customer is often the partner's. That changes the artefact from a negotiation plan you will execute into a boundary somebody else has to hold. CELA rules govern what can be shared with the partner: personal data, screenshots and exports, and financial or seat-level detail are off-limits. Facilitator note: the useful question in the room is what happens to your boundary when you are not there to defend it.
discussionQuestions: On your last partner-transacted deal, who actually did the negotiating?
What did you concede that you had not planned to?
How do you tell a partner what they cannot offer without telling them your floor?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the boundary to how each person will communicate it to the partner.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the boundary each person is setting and how the partner will learn it.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live deal heading toward a negotiation.
facilitatorQuestions: What can be conceded on this deal without approval, and what cannot?
How does the partner know where that line is?
What would trigger you to escalate rather than concede?
listenFor: Listen for concession authority assumed rather than confirmed, for boundaries that exist only in the CE's head, for partner briefings that reveal the floor, and for escalation triggers defined after the pressure has started.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live negotiation, use one that conceded more than intended and work out where the boundary failed.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Where has a concession been made in your name that you would not have made?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, write down the concession logic and authority limits for one live deal, name the escalation trigger, and brief the partner on what cannot be conceded without revealing your floor.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what you told the partner and whether the boundary held.

activities.name: Find every approval this structure triggers
activities.description: Assemble the full set of approvals a commercial structure will need, rather than meeting them one at a time.
activities.prompt: For [account name] I am taking this commercial structure to approval: [paste the structure]. Show what is already recorded that an approver would need to see: any exception or non-standard term already approved on this account and when it was recorded, the current deal stage and value, and whether a partner is associated with the account. Report what is recorded. Do not determine which approvals are required or who approves them.
activities.expectedOutput: The full approval set for this structure, each classified by whether you obtain it, request it, or the partner obtains it.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE determines which approvals are required, because that mapping changes with guidance and the record cannot know it. The classification matters more than the list: an approval you can obtain and one the partner must obtain from their own organization look identical on a plan and behave completely differently.
activities.requiredContext: One deal with an agreed commercial structure needing approval. Current approved guidance on approval requirements.
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your deal.
2. Work out the required approvals yourself from current approved guidance - that mapping is yours and it changes.
3. For each, decide whether it is one you obtain, one you request, or one the partner obtains from their own organization.
4. Confirm current lead times rather than assuming last quarter's.
activities.whyThisMatters: Approvals met one at a time cost a week each. Mapping them together can show which ones run in parallel, and the sequence that looked fixed may be habit.

activities.name: Replace every implied owner with a named one
activities.description: Turn an approval path expressed in roles into one expressed in people who know it is coming.
activities.prompt: Here is the approval path I have mapped for [account name]. For each step I have listed the owning role and the evidence that approval requires: [paste your approval list]. Draft the short note I would send to secure each one: what is being asked, the evidence I have listed against it, the date it is needed by, and what happens if it slips. Keep each to a few lines. Do not add evidence I have not listed, do not invent approver names, and do not state who the owner is.
activities.expectedOutput: A named owner and a sent request for every approval step, with the partner-side steps raised with the partner.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE confirms who currently holds each approval and that the evidence listed against it is what that approver actually asks for. Both change without announcement - a role moves, or a threshold is revised - and a note sent to last quarter's owner citing last quarter's evidence is a week lost before anyone notices it went to the wrong place.
activities.requiredContext: Your mapped approval path, with the owning role for each step and the evidence that step requires taken from current approved guidance. The people who currently hold those roles.
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Put a real name against every role before you send anything. A role is not an owner.
3. For partner-side steps, send the note to your partner contact rather than assuming they will discover it.
4. Send them all now rather than in sequence. Most of these are not actually dependent on each other.
activities.whyThisMatters: The approval path can be entirely correct and still unowned. Naming people converts a diagram into something that moves.

activities.name: Find the approval that never landed
activities.description: Check the approvals you have already requested against what the record now shows, before a customer date makes it urgent.
activities.prompt: Here are the approvals I have outstanding and the date I requested each one: [paste your list with dates]. For each, show what is currently recorded on that opportunity: the current stage, the recorded next step and who owns it, and the close date. Report what is recorded and do not infer why anything is waiting.
activities.expectedOutput: Outstanding approvals separated into those that landed, those that never registered, and those sitting with a partner organization.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE decides which approvals have genuinely stalled and which are simply waiting their turn. An approval nobody ever submitted and one sitting correctly in a queue look identical from inside our systems, and a partner-side approval leaves no trace here at all - chasing that one through our own record costs the week you were trying to save.
activities.requiredContext: The approvals you have already requested, and the date you requested each one.
activitySteps: 1. List your outstanding approvals and the date you asked for each. If you cannot produce that list, that is itself the finding.
2. Open Sales Agent, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
3. Compare the recorded next step against what you actually asked for. Where they do not match, the request never landed.
4. Chase the ones you own with the named person rather than the queue. For partner-side approvals, ask your partner contact - our record will not show their progress at all.
activities.whyThisMatters: Approvals fail quietly. The request that was never registered looks exactly like the one being worked, and the difference only becomes visible when the close date arrives.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Approvals discovered one at a time cost a week each. This session is about finding them all at once, including the ones that are not yours to obtain.
keyTalkingPoints: On a partner-transacted deal the approval path runs across two organizations, and the steps on the partner side are visible only through the Partner Timeline view or Partner Center rather than through our own systems. Approval lead times drift with quarter load, so a plan built on last quarter's turnaround will miss. Facilitator note: the distinction worth drawing is between an approval you can obtain, one you can only request, and one the partner has to obtain from their own side - all three look the same on a plan and behave completely differently.
discussionQuestions: How do you currently find out what approvals a structure will need?
Which approvals on your last deal were discovered late?
What happens when the partner needs an approval from their own organization?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the mapped path to the one approval each person will start today.

Customer Zero cue - use only if it happens: when someone reverts, rejects or overrides what the agent produced, stop and name it. Ask what the agent could not see. Huddle transcripts are reviewed for themes, so what is said here does reach us - keep customer-confidential detail out of it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the approval each person is starting and what evidence it needs.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one deal with a commercial structure that needs approving.
facilitatorQuestions: Which approvals does this structure trigger, and who owns each?
Which are genuinely sequential and which have you been treating as sequential out of habit?
What does the partner have to obtain that you cannot?
listenFor: Listen for approval owners named by role rather than by person, for parallel approvals treated as a chain, for partner-side steps assumed to be quick, and for evidence requirements discovered at submission.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live deal, reconstruct the approval path of the last one that slipped and identify where the time went.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which approval did you assume somebody else was handling?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, map the approval path for one deal with a named owner and the required evidence for each step, mark which belong to the partner, and start the one on the critical path.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the map and what you found was missing from it.

activities.name: State the decision you are asking someone to make
activities.description: Turn a commercial structure into an explicit decision, so the approver is not left to work out what is being asked.
activities.prompt: I am taking a commercial structure to approval. Here is the structure and what I am asking for: [paste the structure and the ask]. Restate this as a decision: what specifically is being approved, what the alternatives were and why they were set aside, what happens if it is declined, and what the approver is accepting responsibility for. Use only what I have given you. Do not add commercial detail, do not recommend a decision, and do not soften the ask.
activities.expectedOutput: The structure restated as an explicit decision, with the alternatives, the consequence of declining, and what the approver is accepting.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE decides what the approver is actually being asked to accept. An approval request that understates what the approver is taking on gets granted quickly and withdrawn later, and the second conversation is far more expensive than the first.
activities.requiredContext: One commercial structure you have agreed and intend to take to approval. The approval you are seeking.
activitySteps: 1. Write the structure and the ask down yourself first. If you cannot state the ask in one sentence, it is not ready to send.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
3. Check the alternatives are the ones you genuinely considered, not ones that make the recommendation look inevitable.
4. Confirm the responsibility line is accurate. That sentence is the one the approver will remember.
activities.whyThisMatters: Approvers are sent structures and left to infer the decision. The ones that stall are the ones where the ask was never stated plainly, and nobody wants to admit they could not find it.

activities.name: Make the numbers checkable by someone else
activities.description: Lay out the economics so an approver can verify them rather than take them on trust.
activities.prompt: Here are the economics of the commercial structure I am proposing: [paste your figures and where each came from]. Lay them out so someone else can check them: what is committed, over what period, what the customer pays and when, and what varies from standard and by how much. Show each figure alongside the source I have given for it. Do not calculate anything I have not supplied, do not estimate missing values, and flag any figure I have given without a source.
activities.expectedOutput: The economics laid out with a source against every figure, and unsourced figures either sourced or stated as ranges.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE owns every number in the narrative and confirms each against where it came from. A figure that appears in an approval document becomes the figure everyone quotes afterwards, and the person who typed it is the only one who knows whether it was measured or estimated.
activities.requiredContext: The economics of your proposed structure, with the source of each figure.
activitySteps: 1. Assemble your figures first, and write the source next to each one as you go.
2. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
3. Look at what it flags as unsourced. Those are the ones you will be asked about.
4. Replace any figure you cannot source with the range you can defend, and say it is a range.
activities.whyThisMatters: A commercial narrative can fail review on one unsourced number rather than on the strength of the case. The figure nobody can trace is the one that stops the meeting.

activities.name: Find what you have asserted without showing
activities.description: Read your own narrative as someone who was not in any of the conversations behind it.
activities.prompt: Here is the commercial decision narrative I have written: [paste the narrative]. Read it as someone who was not part of any conversation behind it. List every claim asserted without evidence attached, every figure whose source is not stated, and every place where a judgment is presented as though it were a fact. Do not rewrite it, do not supply the missing evidence, and do not tell me whether the case is a good one.
activities.expectedOutput: The narrative's unevidenced claims identified, with the central ones closed and the remaining judgments attributed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE decides which gaps must be closed before this goes and which can stand. A narrative that evidences every claim is unreadable and a narrative that leaves the central commercial claim unevidenced is returned, and telling those apart is the whole skill.
activities.requiredContext: Your drafted commercial decision narrative.
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Read the list before defending anything. The first reaction to most of these is that the context is obvious.
3. Close the gaps on the central commercial claim. Leave the peripheral ones open if closing them would bury the argument.
4. Where a judgment is being presented as a fact, say whose judgment it is.
activities.whyThisMatters: You cannot see the assumptions you carried into your own document. Everything in it was obvious to you at the time, which is exactly why it reads as unsupported to the person approving it.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A commercial structure that cannot be explained without you in the room will not get approved when you are not. This session is about making one reviewable.
keyTalkingPoints: In this segment the CE is frequently absent from the conversation where the structure is actually decided - the partner is in the room and the approver reads a document. That makes the written case the product, not a summary of it. Separate the three things an approver needs: what decision they are being asked to make, whether the numbers can be checked, and what is being asserted without support. Facilitator note: the instinct is to make the case persuasive. Push the group towards making it inspectable instead, because an approver who cannot verify a figure will not approve around it.
discussionQuestions: When did an approval last stall on something other than the merits?
What in your last commercial case could the approver not have checked?
Who has to be able to read this when you are not there?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the narrative to the one gap each person will close before sending it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the single unevidenced claim each person is going to close before their case goes out.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one commercial structure you have agreed and still need to take to approval.
facilitatorQuestions: What exactly is the approver being asked to decide?
Which figure in this could someone else not verify?
What have you asserted that you have not shown?
listenFor: Listen for cases that argue rather than evidence, for figures whose source nobody can name, for judgments stated as facts, and for people describing what they would say in the room when they will not be in the room.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live structure awaiting approval, use the last one that was approved and ask what the approver had to take on trust.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What in your last approval request did the approver have to take on trust?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, write the decision narrative for one commercial structure, have it read back for unsupported claims, and close the gap on the central one.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ask as you stated it, the gap that came back, and what you changed.

activities.name: Compare the options on what happens when nobody tunes them
activities.description: Research architecture options for a customer with no platform team, judging them on how they behave unattended.
activities.prompt: I am designing [describe the workload] for a customer with [describe their technical capacity and who will operate it]. activities.expectedOutput: Architecture options compared on unattended behavior and operator skill assumed, with sources cited and gaps named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides what this customer can realistically operate. Published guidance assumes a competent platform team because it is written for the general case, and a design chosen on capability alone will be technically correct and quietly abandoned within two quarters.
activities.requiredContext: The workload and the customer's technical constraints. What you know about who will operate it.
activities.bestFitJob: Compare the options on what happens when nobody tunes them
activitySteps: 1. Write down who will operate this before you look at any options. That constraint decides the answer.
2. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
3. Check the citations. Guidance written for a customer with a platform team will not say so, and you have to notice.
4. Discard any option whose operational assumptions this customer cannot meet, however good it looks.
activities.whyThisMatters: For a portfolio of non-unified customers there is no support relationship to absorb an operationally demanding design. The question is not which architecture is best but which one survives contact with the people who will actually run it.

activities.description: Turn a chosen architecture into something a partner or customer team can implement without you present.
activities.prompt: Here is the architecture I have chosen and what I know about who will implement it: [paste the design, the constraints, and what the implementer has built before]. Turn this into an implementation-ready description covering the sequence and the dependencies, marking which dependencies are outside the implementer's control. Separately, list every configuration decision the implementer will have to make that my design does not already settle, and for each state what the design implies but does not say. Do not choose any of those configurations for me and do not add architectural decisions I have not made.
activities.expectedOutput: An implementation-ready design with the sequence and dependencies, plus the configuration decisions your design leaves open, each answered by you.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA answers every configuration decision the design leaves open. The implementer will resolve anything left silent using their own defaults, which are reasonable for their usual customer and may be wrong for this one - and the divergence only becomes visible when something behaves unexpectedly months later.
activities.requiredContext: Your chosen architecture and its constraints. Who will implement it and what they have built before.
activities.bestFitJob: Write the design for the person who will build it
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Read the unsettled configuration list. Those are the decisions the implementer will otherwise make for you, at the point you are least available.
3. Write your recommended choice against each one yourself. That is a design decision and it does not get delegated.
4. Send it to the implementer and ask which step they would want to talk through.
activities.whyThisMatters: The design is not the artefact. What the implementer does with it is the artefact, and everything you left implicit becomes their judgment call.

activities.name: Find what your design assumes the customer has
activities.description: Read your own design for the support, skills and tooling it quietly takes for granted.
activities.prompt: Here is a design I am about to hand over: [paste the design]. Here is what I actually know about the customer's operating capability: [describe their team, skills, tooling and support arrangements]. Identify every point where the design assumes capability, tooling, support or availability I have not confirmed they have. For each, state what the design expects and what happens if it is absent. Do not redesign anything and do not tell me whether the design is good.
activities.expectedOutput: The design's unconfirmed assumptions listed with the consequence of each, and the silent-failure ones closed or disclosed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides which unconfirmed assumptions are acceptable to hand over. Every design assumes something, and closing all of it is not possible in this segment - the judgment is which assumption fails quietly, because that is the one that turns into a consumption problem nobody traces back to the design.
activities.requiredContext: Your implementation-ready design. What you actually know about the customer's operating capability and support arrangements.
activities.bestFitJob: Find what your design assumes the customer has
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the list before defending it. Most of these assumptions felt obvious when you made them.
3. Confirm or close the ones that would cause a silent failure. An assumption that fails loudly is survivable.
4. Where you cannot close one, say so in the handover rather than leaving it to be discovered.
activities.whyThisMatters: You cannot see what you assumed. Everything in the design was reasonable when you wrote it, which is exactly why the gaps are invisible to you and obvious to the customer six months later.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Architecture in this segment is judged by whether it still works six months after you have moved on. This session is about designing for that.
keyTalkingPoints: A DCSA carries a portfolio of non-unified customers - no dedicated support relationship, often no in-house platform team, and frequently a partner doing the implementation. That changes what a good design is. The elegant option that assumes someone will tune it is worse than the plain option that runs untouched. Separate the design decisions that need your expertise from the ones the customer or partner will end up making anyway, and make the second group hard to get wrong. Facilitator note: the instinct is to compare architectures on capability. Push the group to compare them on what happens when nobody is watching.
discussionQuestions: Who is actually going to build this?
What does this design assume somebody will maintain?
What breaks first if nobody touches it for six months?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the design to the single assumption each person will go and verify.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the one operability assumption each person will confirm with the implementer this week.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one architecture you are designing or reviewing now, and know who will implement it.
facilitatorQuestions: What does this design assume about the people running it?
Which decision here did you make because it was right, and which because it was familiar?
What would you simplify if you knew nobody would ever tune it?
listenFor: Listen for designs justified by capability rather than by operability, for assumptions about customer skill that nobody has tested, for a partner implementer who has not been consulted, and for support models being assumed rather than confirmed.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live design, take an architecture already deployed on one of their accounts and ask what it assumed that turned out not to be true.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which of your designs needed you more than it should have?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one design to the person who will build it and confirm they can operate it without you.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the assumption you tested and what the implementer said.

secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. activities.name: Find the accounts where something technical has changed
activities.description: Scan the portfolio for the recorded signals that precede a consumption problem.
activities.prompt: Across the accounts in my portfolio, identify those where consumption or usage has moved against plan, and separately those with a support or service record raised in the period I specify but no recorded technical activity from us. For the accounts that match, show the recorded movement, the support activity and the date of our last recorded technical engagement. Use this period: [state the period]. Do not return the accounts that do not match and do not diagnose a cause.
activities.expectedOutput: The portfolio split into accounts moving against plan and accounts with unattended support activity, ranked by cost of delay.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides which movement is technically significant. Consumption drops for reasons that have nothing to do with the technology - a project ending, a budget cycle, a seasonal workload - and spending your limited portfolio time on those is how the real problem stays undiscovered.
activities.requiredContext: Your portfolio of accounts. Whatever consumption, usage and support views you can reach. The period you want assessed.
activities.bestFitJob: Find the accounts where something technical has changed
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Treat the two groups differently: movement against plan is a question, support activity with no engagement from us is a gap.
3. For each candidate, form your own technical hypothesis before opening the account. The record will not give you one.
4. Rank by how expensive the problem becomes if it is still there next quarter, not by size.
activities.whyThisMatters: At this portfolio size you cannot inspect accounts individually, so the scan is the only way in. It will not tell you what is wrong; it tells you where to spend the attention you have.

activities.name: Raise a problem the customer has not noticed yet
activities.description: Prepare the conversation where you tell a customer about a technical risk they did not ask you to look for.
activities.prompt: I need to raise a technical risk with a customer who has not asked about it. Here is the risk and my evidence: [describe the risk and what supports it]. Here is who I would raise it with and our history: [describe the contact and the relationship]. Help me rehearse this conversation: how to open it without implying they have been negligent, what they are likely to push back on, how to respond if they say it is not a priority, and how to close with a specific next step. Do not tell me whether to raise it.
activities.expectedOutput: A rehearsed conversation with the likely objections worked through and a specific next step prepared.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides whether the evidence is strong enough to raise unasked. A technical risk surfaced on partial evidence and then disproved by the customer's own team costs the standing you would need to raise the next one, and the record may not contain enough to settle it either way before the conversation.
activities.requiredContext: The technical risk you have identified and the evidence for it. Who at the customer you would raise it with.
activities.bestFitJob: Raise a problem the customer has not noticed yet
activitySteps: 1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Rehearse the pushback you find hardest rather than the opening you find easiest.
3. Decide in advance what you will do if they decline to act. That answer is yours, not the agent's.
4. Have the conversation, and record what they said so the next person does not raise it cold again.
activities.whyThisMatters: Finding the risk is the easy part. The conversation is where it either becomes an intervention or becomes a note nobody acted on, and in this segment you may get one attempt.

activities.name: Set a standing check so the next one finds you
activities.description: Put a recurring watch on the portfolio so technical movement reaches you when it happens rather than at the next review.
activities.prompt: Set up a recurring weekly check across the accounts in my portfolio. Each week, tell me where consumption or usage has moved against plan, where a new support or service record has appeared on an account with no recent technical engagement from us, and where something I flagged previously has not changed. For each one, state what the data shows, what it does not tell us, and the single technical question I should ask next. Remember what you reported before, so you can tell me what is genuinely new and what is unchanged.
activities.expectedOutput: A weekly check running across the portfolio, separating new movement from unchanged risk, with a next technical question for each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA confirms the technical reading of each signal and decides what is worth acting on. A standing check makes the finding cheaper, not the judgment - and the failure mode of automation here is a weekly report that everyone stops reading by week three.
activities.requiredContext: Your portfolio of accounts. The consumption, usage and support sources you can reach. The risks already on your list.
activities.bestFitJob: Set a standing check so the next one finds you
activitySteps: 1. Open Scout and set the check running against your portfolio.
2. Give it the period and the movement threshold you actually care about, so it does not report everything.
3. Read the first run against what you already believed about these accounts.
4. Keep only the accounts where the movement is technically explainable and worth a conversation.
5. Prune it after two weeks. A check that reports everything gets ignored exactly like a dashboard nobody opens.
activities.whyThisMatters: Manual portfolio scans do not survive a busy quarter, which is exactly the quarter you need them. The value is that it keeps running when you have forgotten about it.

activities.name: Check whether the technical explanation actually holds
activities.description: Test the most likely technical cause against documented behavior before raising it with anyone.
activities.prompt: I have a hypothesis about why a customer's workload is behaving the way it is. Here is what I observed and what I think is causing it: [describe the movement and your suspected technical cause]. Here is the configuration as far as I know it: [describe the workload and any relevant settings]. Using approved Microsoft and authoritative internal documentation, tell me whether this cause is consistent with documented behavior for this configuration. Give me at most three documented alternatives that would produce the same symptom on this configuration, and for each, what I would need to observe to tell them apart. Cite each claim. Where the documentation does not settle it, say so rather than choosing.
activities.expectedOutput: The hypothesis either retained or rejected, with up to three documented alternatives and the observation that would separate them, each claim sourced.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides whether the hypothesis survives contact with the documentation, and which observation would settle it. Documentation describes the general case and this customer is a specific one, so consistency raises confidence without confirming, and carrying an unrejected hypothesis forward as a finding is how a technical conversation goes wrong before it starts.
activities.requiredContext: The account you ranked highest, what you observed, and your suspected technical cause.
activities.bestFitJob: Test the technical hypothesis before you take it to a customer
activitySteps: 1. Open Researcher and paste the prompt with your observation and your suspected cause.
2. Read the alternative explanations before the confirming ones. You already believe your own.
3. Check the citations reach current documentation. A behavior that changed in a recent release is the case this step is for.
4. Note what you would need to observe to separate the explanations. That is your question for the customer's team.
5. Decide whether your hypothesis survived. If it did not, say so now rather than carrying it into the conversation.
activities.whyThisMatters: A ranked list tells you which account to look at, not what is wrong with it. Testing the explanation is what turns a suspicion into something worth a customer's time.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Every consumption problem has a technical cause that appeared first. This session is about catching it at that point rather than at the review.
keyTalkingPoints: Across a portfolio of this size nobody can inspect accounts individually, so technical risk is found either by a signal or by a complaint. The gap between those two is where the DCSA earns their place. Distinguish three things that look identical from outside: a workload that was never fully deployed, one that was deployed and abandoned, and one that is working but small. Only the first two are yours. Facilitator note: this session pairs with a standing check - the point is not the one-off scan but the rhythm that replaces it.
discussionQuestions: When did you last find a technical problem before the customer did?
What told you about your last consumption drop, and how late was it?
Which of your accounts could be in trouble without you knowing?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the scan to the standing check that means they do not have to remember to run it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person name the risk they are acting on and confirm their standing check is running.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: know which consumption or usage view you can actually reach for your portfolio.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the earliest signal you could realistically have seen?
Which risks here would the customer dispute?
What would you want to be told automatically every week?
listenFor: Listen for risk lists with no owner, for signals being read as problems without a technical hypothesis, for people describing manual checks they know they will not sustain, and for accounts nobody has looked at in months being called healthy.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If consumption data is not reachable, use support and service records instead and ask what those alone can and cannot tell you.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you find late that you could have found early?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, start one technical intervention and leave a standing check running on your portfolio.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the risk you acted on, what the check has surfaced since, and whether any of it was new.

activities.name: Find the workload that is genuinely working
activities.description: Identify where a customer is succeeding with something, as the only reliable starting point for expansion.
activities.prompt: For the accounts in my portfolio, show for each the workloads deployed, what usage is recorded against each, when each was deployed, and any support or service record raised against them. Identify the accounts where recorded usage has been stable or growing over the period I specify: [state the period you want assessed]. Report what is recorded and do not infer readiness or recommend anything.
activities.expectedOutput: Accounts where a workload has demonstrably held or grown over two quarters, with the strongest candidate chosen.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides what counts as genuinely succeeding. Recorded usage can reflect one team, one automated process, or a workload nobody has switched off, and expanding from a false positive costs the credibility you would need for the real conversation.
activities.requiredContext: Your portfolio of accounts and whatever deployment and usage evidence you can reach.
activities.bestFitJob: Find the workload that is genuinely working
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Look for stable and growing, not just large. A big workload that has flattened is not a readiness signal.
3. Decide for yourself how long usage has to hold before it evidences adoption rather than a pilot. That depends on the workload and the customer.
4. Pick the one account where the succeeding workload is closest to something the customer has said they care about.
activities.whyThisMatters: Expansion built on a workload that is merely deployed fails in a predictable way. Expansion built on one the customer is visibly getting value from is a conversation they will start themselves.

activities.name: Test what usually comes next after this
activities.description: Check an expansion hypothesis against documented adoption patterns rather than against what we would like to sell.
activities.prompt: A customer is running [describe the workload] successfully and I am considering whether [describe the expansion you have in mind] is the next logical step. Using approved Microsoft and authoritative public sources, show what the documented technical prerequisites are for that expansion, what the common adoption sequence is from the first workload, and what the documented reasons are for that sequence failing. Cite each claim. Do not tell me whether this customer is ready.
activities.expectedOutput: The expansion's documented prerequisites and common failure reasons, checked against what this customer actually has.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides whether the documented sequence applies to this customer. Adoption patterns describe the average case and this segment is full of customers who are not average - the judgment is which prerequisite genuinely blocks and which is an assumption from a larger deployment.
activities.requiredContext: The workload the customer is succeeding with, and the expansion you are considering.
activities.bestFitJob: Test what usually comes next after this
activitySteps: 1. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the failure reasons before the prerequisites. They are more useful and less often looked at.
3. Check the prerequisites against what you actually know this customer has, not what a customer of this size usually has.
4. If the documented sequence puts something else before your expansion, take that seriously rather than skipping it.
activities.whyThisMatters: The expansion that follows a documented sequence is the one the customer can absorb. Skipping a step is how a technically valid expansion turns into a stalled deployment that damages the workload it grew from.

activities.name: Hand it over in a form somebody can sell
activities.description: Turn technical readiness evidence into something the person who owns the commercial conversation can actually use.
activities.prompt: I have technical evidence that a customer is ready for [describe the expansion]. Here is the evidence: [paste what you found - the succeeding workload, the usage pattern, the prerequisites met and any not yet met]. Draft a short handover for the person who owns the commercial conversation: what the customer is already succeeding with, what that makes possible, what is technically confirmed and what is not, and what would need to be true before it could start. Keep it factual. Do not write a pitch and do not include commercial or pricing framing.
activities.expectedOutput: A factual technical handover separating confirmed readiness from open questions, with the commercial owner named.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA states what is technically evidenced and stops there. Technical readiness and commercial timing are different judgments owned by different people, and a handover that strays into whether the customer will buy undermines the person who has to have that conversation.
activities.requiredContext: Your evidenced expansion hypothesis. Who owns the commercial conversation on this account.
activities.bestFitJob: Hand it over in a form somebody can sell
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Check that what is unconfirmed is as prominent as what is confirmed. A handover that reads as certainty will be sold as certainty.
3. Send it to whoever owns the commercial conversation and say explicitly that the technical readiness is your view and the timing is theirs.
4. Record it against the account so the next person does not rediscover it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Uncovering the next workload is the DCSA's accountability; selling it is not. The handover is where that boundary is either respected or quietly crossed.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Expansion in this segment is found in the telemetry of what is already working, not built in a deck. This session is about reading that evidence.
keyTalkingPoints: A DCSA is accountable for uncovering the next logical workload, but not for selling it - that boundary matters and gets blurred under pressure. Readiness has three parts and all three have to hold: the customer is succeeding with something adjacent, they have the technical capacity to take on more, and somebody on their side wants it. Two out of three produces a stalled deployment that damages the account you were trying to grow. Facilitator note: watch for expansion proposed from what Microsoft wants to sell rather than from what the customer has proven they can run.
discussionQuestions: Which of your accounts is genuinely succeeding with something right now?
What did your last expansion attempt assume that was not true?
Who on the customer side would actually want the next workload?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the hypothesis to who owns the conversation and what they need from it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the owner of each expansion conversation and what evidence goes with it.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one account where a workload is deployed and working.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the evidence this customer is ready rather than just suitable?
Who asked for this, or did we?
What would have to be true technically before this could start?
listenFor: Listen for expansion built on product fit rather than customer readiness, for deployed being read as adopted, for no named customer sponsor, and for DCSAs carrying the commercial conversation themselves rather than handing it over.

activities.name: Package it with what it assumes
activities.description: Turn something you built into a reusable asset, with the constraints that decide whether it fits.
activities.prompt: Here is something I built and want to make reusable: [paste or describe the artefact - a script, design, demo, response or checklist]. It was built for this situation: [describe the customer context, constraints and what it assumed]. Produce a reusable package covering what it does, what it requires before use, the steps to use it, what someone would need to change for their own situation, how to check it worked, where it does not apply, and who owns it. Flag anything customer-identifying that should be removed. Do not add capability it does not have.
activities.expectedOutput: A reusable package with prerequisites, adaptation points, validation steps and stated limits, sanitized for internal sharing.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what is safe to hand to someone who will not know what it assumed. Automated flagging may surface names and identifiers but cannot be relied on to catch a configuration that only made sense for one customer, so the review is the seller's and it is not delegable.
activities.requiredContext: The artefact you want to make reusable. The customer situation it was built for. Your team's rules on what may be shared internally.
activities.bestFitJob: Package it with what it assumes
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Check the removal flags yourself. The agent will catch names and identifiers; it will not catch a configuration that only one customer would ever run.
3. Write the "where it does not apply" section properly. It is the part that stops the asset being misused and the part everyone skips.
4. Check the community hubs before publishing. If something close already exists, improve that instead of adding a second.
activities.whyThisMatters: An artefact without its constraints is not reusable, it is just findable. The next engineer either rebuilds it or applies it somewhere it was never validated.

activities.name: Catch the question that has started arriving
activities.description: Set a standing check that surfaces technical questions which have begun recurring since you last looked, rather than re-listing what you already know.
activities.prompt: Check my messages and meetings from the last [state a period] for technical questions I have answered more than once. Group them by the underlying technical problem rather than by wording, and show how many different people or customers each came from. On each later run, report only groups that are new since your previous report, or where the number of distinct askers has grown. Do not draft answers and do not repeat groups you have already reported unless they have grown.
activities.expectedOutput: Technical question groups that are new or growing since the previous run, with the breadth of askers for each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether a newly recurring question reflects a genuine change or a coincidence of timing. A question that starts appearing may mean a product update, a competitor claim or a shift in what customers are attempting - and only someone who knows what changed recently can tell which, or whether it is simply two customers who happened to ask in the same two weeks.
activities.requiredContext: Your mail, chats and meetings. The assets your team has already published.
activities.bestFitJob: Notice what you are answering repeatedly
activitySteps: 1. Open Scout, run the prompt, and set your own lookback period for the first run.
2. Treat the first run as a backlog. Everything it finds is historical and most of it you already half-knew.
3. From the second run onward, the value is only in what is new or growing. That is a signal that something has changed in the product, the market or your patch.
4. Pick candidates by breadth of asker rather than by count, and judge for yourself what breadth means for your patch.
5. When you publish an asset, check the next report to see whether the question stopped arriving.
activities.whyThisMatters: A one-off scan finds the backlog once. What is worth knowing afterwards is which questions have STARTED arriving, because that is a change in the field you would otherwise notice months later.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: The same technical problem arrives at this team repeatedly wearing different customer names. This session is about answering it once.
keyTalkingPoints: Reuse fails for a predictable reason: the asset gets saved and the context does not. Another engineer finds a script or a design and cannot tell what it assumed, so they rebuild it, and now there are two. The reusable unit is the artefact plus its constraints - what it was built for, what it depends on, and where it does not apply. Sanitization matters more here than in Enterprise because at this volume an asset gets reused many times before anyone reviews it. Facilitator note: the community hubs already hold field-contributed assets; check before building.
discussionQuestions: What have you built more than once?
What have you looked for and failed to find?
What would somebody need to know before reusing your last piece of work?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the artefact to where it will live and who will find it.

Customer Zero cue - use only if it happens: when someone reverts, rejects or overrides what the agent produced, stop and name it. Ask what the agent could not see. Huddle transcripts are reviewed for themes, so what is said here does reach us - keep customer-confidential detail out of it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by confirming where each asset is going and who else has been told it exists.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one artefact you built recently that you think somebody else could use.
facilitatorQuestions: Could somebody use this without talking to you?
What does it assume that is not written down?
Where would this be wrong to apply?
listenFor: Listen for assets shared without their constraints, for customer-identifying detail left in, for reuse being treated as filing rather than as writing, and for people describing things they rebuilt that already existed somewhere.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has an artefact, use the last question they answered twice and capture the answer instead.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you rebuild this quarter that already existed?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, publish one asset with its limitations stated, and tell the team where it is.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the asset, where it now lives, and whether anyone has used it.

primaryAgents.name: Sales Home
primaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Find where the same partner keeps needing you
activities.description: Look across partner-led opportunities for the technical dependency that keeps coming back to you.
activities.prompt: For the opportunities in my area where a partner is associated and that have been open during [state the period], group them by partner and return only the partners with more than one. For those partners only, show for each opportunity the current stage, how long it has been at that stage, the recorded next step and its owner, and any recorded technical activity from me. Report what is recorded and do not infer why anything has stalled.
activities.expectedOutput: Partner-led opportunities grouped by partner, with the recurring technical dependency identified for each.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides whether a partner is genuinely lacking capability or has learned that asking is faster than doing. Both look identical in the record and in the request, and enablement fixes only the first - offering it for the second is politely ignored.
activities.requiredContext: The partner-led opportunities you support, which partner is associated with each, and the period you want to look at.
activities.bestFitJob: Find where the same partner keeps needing you
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt.
2. Look at the grouping by partner before the individual deals. One deal needing you is normal; one partner repeatedly needing you is the finding.
3. For each recurring partner, work out what specific technical step they hand back. The record will not say - you know it from the asks.
4. Separate what they cannot do from what they simply prefer you to do. Those need different responses.
activities.whyThisMatters: One deal at a time, absorbing the technical step looks like helpfulness. Across a partner's portfolio it is the reason their capability never grows and your time never comes back.

activities.name: Have the capability conversation without causing offence
activities.description: Prepare the conversation that names a partner's technical gap and offers to close it rather than cover it.
activities.prompt: I need to raise a technical capability gap with a partner. Here is the gap and what makes me think it exists: [describe the gap and the evidence]. Here is my relationship with them and who I would speak to: [describe the contact and the history]. Help me rehearse this: how to open it as an offer rather than a criticism, what they may say to deflect it, how to respond if they say they have it covered when the evidence says otherwise, and how to close with a specific action they own. Do not tell me whether the gap is real.
activities.expectedOutput: A rehearsed capability conversation opened as an offer, with the likely deflections worked through and a partner-owned action prepared.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what evidence is sufficient to call something a capability gap rather than a preference. Repeated requests can mean the partner cannot do the work, or that they have learned we will, and naming the wrong one produces enablement that is politely attended and never applied.
activities.requiredContext: The capability gap you have identified and the evidence for it. Your relationship with the partner and who you would raise it with.
activities.bestFitJob: Have the capability conversation without causing offence
activitySteps: 1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Rehearse the deflection you expect, not the version where they agree with you.
3. Decide beforehand what you will do if they decline. Continuing to absorb the work is a decision too, and it should be a deliberate one.
4. Close with an action the partner owns and a date. Enablement you own is not enablement.
activities.whyThisMatters: This conversation is the whole workflow. Everything before it is preparation, and the alternative to having it is doing the partner's technical work indefinitely.

activities.name: Leave them something that works when you are not there
activities.description: Turn a resolved technical gap into material the partner can use themselves next time.
activities.prompt: A partner had this technical gap and here is how it was resolved this time: [describe the gap and what was done]. Here is what the partner's team already knows and works with: [describe their technical background and tooling]. Draft something they could use to do this themselves next time: the steps, the decisions they will face and what to consider for each, how to check it worked, and when to come to us anyway. Write it for their engineers, not for ours. Do not include internal-only detail, customer-identifying information, or anything that reads as an export from our systems.
activities.expectedOutput: Partner-usable technical material with the decision points explained and the escalation boundary stated, checked before it leaves Microsoft.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides what is genuinely safe to hand to another company and where the boundary of self-service sits. Material that is too complete invites a partner to attempt something they should escalate, and the failure lands on a customer who never knew the difference.
activities.requiredContext: The capability gap and how it was resolved. What the partner already knows and what they use.
activities.bestFitJob: Leave them something that works when you are not there
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Check it against your data-sharing rules before it leaves Microsoft. This is going to another company.
3. Be specific about when they should still come to us. Material that implies they never need us again is inaccurate and will be trusted anyway.
4. Send it to the person who owns the action, not to the account contact, and ask them to try it on the next one.
activities.whyThisMatters: A gap closed in one conversation reopens on the next deal. Something the partner keeps is the only version of this that reduces your load permanently.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: When a partner-led deal stops moving, the cause is usually that somebody on the partner side is not confident enough to take the next technical step. This session is about finding that and fixing it properly.
keyTalkingPoints: This is the one part of the DSE path with no Enterprise equivalent, and it carries a genuine tension: the fastest way to unblock a partner-led deal is to do the technical work yourself, and that is exactly what prevents the partner ever becoming self-sufficient. The distinction to hold is between a gap in knowledge, which enablement fixes, and a gap in capacity, which it does not. Facilitator note: partner-side detail is limited in our systems, so most of the evidence here comes from what the partner tells you and how their deals actually behave.
discussionQuestions: Which of your partner-led deals keep needing you?
What do you end up explaining more than once?
Is the partner missing knowledge, or missing people?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the gap to the specific enablement action and who owns it on the partner side.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the enablement action, its owner on the partner side, and the date.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one partner-led opportunity that has stalled or that keeps returning to you.
facilitatorQuestions: What exactly can the partner not do yet?
Is that knowledge, capacity, or willingness?
What would let them do this without you next time?
listenFor: Listen for DSEs absorbing partner work and calling it enablement, for capability gaps described as attitude problems, for enablement with no owner or date, and for the same partner appearing behind several stalled deals.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a stalled partner deal, use the last one they unblocked and ask what would have happened if they had been unavailable.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What are you doing for a partner that they should be able to do themselves?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, name one partner technical gap and agree an enablement action with a named owner and a date.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the gap, the action agreed, and whether the partner did it.

activities.name: Find out what the competitor actually does well
activities.description: Build an evidenced view of a competitor's real strengths in your solution area, from sources rather than from internal belief.
activities.prompt: A customer is comparing our [describe the solution area] against [name the competitor]. Using authoritative public sources and approved Microsoft material, set out what that competitor's offering does well in this area, what its documented limitations are, and where independent sources disagree with either vendor's marketing. Cite each claim and state where evidence is thin. Do not tell me how to position against them and do not characterize the competitor as weak.
activities.expectedOutput: An evidenced view of the competitor's genuine strengths and documented limitations, with sources cited and thin areas flagged.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what is safe to assert. A competitive claim that a customer can disprove in one search costs the whole position, not just that point, and internal competitive material is written to persuade rather than to survive being checked.
activities.requiredContext: The competitor and the solution area. The customer's stated decision criteria if you have them.
activities.bestFitJob: Find out what the competitor actually does well
activitySteps: 1. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Read the competitor strengths first. That is the part internal material will not give you honestly.
3. Check the citations. A claim about a competitor that turns out to be out of date loses a technical audience.
4. Mark anything you would be uncomfortable saying if the competitor were in the room. That is the material to drop.
activities.whyThisMatters: You will be positioned against a competitor the customer has already researched. Arriving with a view that is less accurate than theirs ends the technical credibility you need for everything else.

activities.name: Check what this competitor has actually cost you
activities.description: Look across your solution area for what happened in past opportunities where this competitor was involved.
activities.prompt: Across the opportunities in my solution area, show any where [name the competitor] is recorded as involved: the account, the stage reached, whether it closed and how, and any recorded objection, blocker or competitor note. Group them by outcome. Report what is recorded and do not infer why any of them went the way they did.
activities.expectedOutput: Past opportunities involving this competitor grouped by outcome, with the recurring objection identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides which recorded objection reflects a real competitive pattern. Notes are written by whoever was losing at the time and often record the last thing said rather than the actual reason, so the same words can mean several different problems.
activities.requiredContext: The competitor. Your solution-area opportunities.
activities.bestFitJob: Check what this competitor has actually cost you
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Home and paste the prompt with your competitor.
2. Look at the losses before the wins. The recorded objection on a loss is the most useful sentence in the system.
3. Where the record says nothing, treat that as unknown rather than as no objection.
4. Pick the objection that appears most often across different accounts. That is the one worth preparing properly.
activities.whyThisMatters: The objection you will meet has almost certainly been met before somewhere in your solution area. It is written down badly, but it is written down.

activities.name: Write the position against their criteria, not ours
activities.description: Turn competitive evidence into a position expressed in the customer's decision criteria.
activities.prompt: Here is what I know about how we compare to a competitor in my solution area: [paste your evidence and the recurring objection]. Here are the customer's decision criteria as they have expressed them: [paste or describe the criteria]. Map each criterion to what we can evidence, what the competitor can evidence, and where neither of us has evidence. Identify the criteria where the comparison genuinely favors us and those where it does not. Do not write positioning language and do not resolve the criteria where we are behind.
activities.expectedOutput: Decision criteria mapped to what each side can evidence, with the winnable criteria separated from the ones to concede.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides which criteria to concede. Contesting everything reads as a vendor who has not listened, and choosing what to give up is a judgment about this customer's priorities that no comparison table contains.
activities.requiredContext: Your competitive evidence and the recurring objection. The customer's decision criteria in their own words.
activities.bestFitJob: Write the position against their criteria, not ours
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Look at the criteria where we are behind. Deciding what to do about those is the actual work.
3. Concede the ones you cannot win rather than arguing them. A concession buys credibility for the criteria that matter.
4. Build the conversation around the two or three criteria where the advantage is both real and valued.
activities.whyThisMatters: Customers decide on their criteria, not on ours. A position organized around our strengths answers a question they were not asking.

activities.name: Rehearse the objection you know you will get
activities.description: Prepare to meet the recurring competitive objection in the room, rather than only knowing what it is.
activities.prompt: I am going into a technical conversation where a competitor is in play. Here is the objection that comes up repeatedly: [paste the recurring objection you identified]. Here is what we can evidence and what I have decided to concede: [paste the criteria mapping]. Help me rehearse meeting it: how to acknowledge the part that is true without conceding the decision, what they are likely to say next, and how to respond if they press on something I have already decided to concede. Do not write competitive claims for me and do not tell me the competitor is wrong.
activities.expectedOutput: A rehearsed response to the recurring objection, with the acknowledgement and the concession both prepared as deliberate choices.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides whether the rehearsed response is accurate and which part of it to withhold. Rehearsal smooths an answer, and a smoothed answer can acquire confidence the underlying evidence does not support, so what gets said is a separate decision from what was practiced.
activities.requiredContext: The recurring objection from your competitive review, and the criteria you decided to contest and concede.
activities.bestFitJob: Prepare to meet the objection you already know is coming
activitySteps: 1. Open Agent J.ai and paste the prompt with the objection and your criteria mapping.
2. Practice the acknowledgement first. Decide how much of the objection you are willing to grant out loud.
3. Work the follow-up, not the opening. The opening is the part you have already thought about.
4. Say out loud the thing you decided to concede. If it sounds like a loss rather than a choice, it is not ready.
5. Take one sentence into the meeting, not a script.
activities.whyThisMatters: Knowing the objection and being ready to meet it are different states. Rehearsal is where you find out which one you are in.
