facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Competitive positions usually fail because they answer a comparison the customer was not making. This session is about finding the real one.
keyTalkingPoints: A DSS carries a solution area across many accounts, so the same competitive conversation recurs with small variations - which makes it worth getting right once. Three things get confused: what we do better, what the customer values, and what they are actually comparing us to. Only the overlap of all three is a differentiator. Being honest about where a competitor is stronger is what makes the rest of the position credible, and sellers consistently underrate how obvious the omission is to a customer who has already seen the other vendor. Facilitator note: push for the specific competitor and the specific criteria, not a general positioning discussion.
discussionQuestions: What is this customer actually comparing us to?
Which of our advantages have they told you they care about?
Where is the competitor genuinely better?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the position to the one objection each person will prepare properly.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the objection each person will prepare and the evidence they will bring to it.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one live opportunity where a competitor is involved and you know who it is.
facilitatorQuestions: What are the customer's own decision criteria, in their words?
Which differentiator survives contact with those criteria?
What will you concede, and when?
listenFor: Listen for feature comparisons standing in for customer criteria, for competitor weaknesses asserted without a source, for positions that concede nothing, and for the same objection appearing across several accounts without anyone having prepared for it.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live competitive deal, take the objection they hear most often across the solution area and build the position around that instead.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which competitive claim have you made that you could not evidence?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, test one competitive position with a customer and record which part of it actually landed.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the position, what the customer responded to, and what you dropped.

activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides what would actually unblock this rather than what would be useful to have. In a segment with no assigned v-team every ask spends credit with someone who has their own targets, and asking for the wrong thing costs the same as asking for the right one.
activities.requiredContext: One opportunity in your solution area that is not moving as it should.
activities.bestFitJob: Work out what the opportunity is actually missing
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your opportunity.

4. Write the need down as a task somebody could do, not as a description of the situation.
activities.whyThisMatters: Most support asks describe a situation and hope the reader works out the task. Naming the missing thing precisely is what separates an ask that gets actioned from one that gets acknowledged.

activities.name: Write the ask so it can be said yes to
activities.description: Turn a support need into a request with a task, a date and a consequence.
activities.prompt: I need support on an opportunity and here is what is missing: [describe what you need and the opportunity context]. I am asking [describe who you are asking and what they are accountable for]. I need it by [state your date] because [state what happens to the opportunity if it does not arrive]. Draft the request using those: what specifically I am asking them to do, by my stated date, what I have already done so they are not repeating it, and my stated consequence. Keep it to a few lines. Do not set a date I have not given you, do not invent a consequence, and do not pad it with background.
activities.expectedOutput: A short request with a specific task, a date, what has already been done, and the consequence of it not arriving.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides how much of the consequence to state. Overstating it is noticed and quietly discounted from then on; omitting it leaves the reader to guess the priority, and they will guess low because everything else they have been sent also looked urgent.

activities.name: Notice when an ask has gone quiet
activities.description: Set a standing check that tells you which of your requests never got answered.
activities.prompt: Set up a recurring weekly check across my sent messages for requests I have made that have not received a reply. For each, show who it went to, when it was sent, what was being asked, and whether any date I set has now passed. Group them by how overdue they are. Remember what you reported before so you can tell me which are newly overdue and which I have already been told about. Do not draft follow-ups.
activities.expectedOutput: Outstanding requests grouped by how overdue they are, separating newly overdue from previously reported.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides which silence needs chasing and which means the answer is no. Some unanswered asks are a queue and some are a declined request nobody wanted to say out loud, and chasing the second repeatedly costs the relationship you will need for the next one.
activities.requiredContext: The support asks you have outstanding and who each went to.
activities.bestFitJob: Notice when an ask has gone quiet
activitySteps: 1. Open Scout and run the prompt.
2. Read the newly-overdue group first. The long-overdue ones need a different approach rather than another chase.
3. For anything twice reported and still unanswered, go to the person a different way rather than resending.
4. Prune what you are tracking every few weeks. A list that includes everything you ever sent stops being useful immediately.
activities.whyThisMatters: Support asks fail silently. Nobody tells you they are not doing it, and by the time you notice, the opportunity has moved past the point where it would have helped.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: In this segment nobody is assigned to your opportunity. Everything you need comes from someone who is also doing their own job. This session is about asking well.
keyTalkingPoints: An ask that describes a situation gets sympathy; an ask that describes a specific task with a date gets done. The three things that make an ask answerable are what exactly is needed, by when, and what happens if it does not arrive - the last one is almost always omitted and is what moves an ask up someone's list. Separate asks that need a person from asks that need a decision, because they go to different places and have different lead times. Facilitator note: watch for people who have absorbed a task themselves rather than asking, and ask what that cost them.
discussionQuestions: What are you doing yourself that you should have asked for?
What did you last ask for that never arrived?
Would the person receiving your ask know exactly what to do?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the ask to the standing check that tells them when it has gone quiet.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by confirming each ask has a person, a task and a date, and that a check is running.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one opportunity where you need support you have not yet asked for.
facilitatorQuestions: What exactly do you need, and by when?
Who specifically, not which team?
What happens to the deal if it does not come?
listenFor: Listen for asks addressed to a team rather than a person, for needs described as context rather than as tasks, for no date, and for people who have stopped asking because previous asks went unanswered.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live need, use the last support ask that went unanswered and rewrite it as it should have been sent.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you stop asking for because it never came?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, send one specific support ask and set a check that tells you if it goes unanswered.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the ask, whether it was answered, and how long it took.

activities.name: Look at what the partner has actually delivered
activities.description: Establish a partner's delivery record from what is recorded, before deciding what to route to them.
activities.prompt: For [partner name], show what is recorded: the opportunities where they are associated and the stage each reached, any co-sell or referral record and its status, what closed and over what period, and the workloads or solution areas involved. Group by outcome and by solution area. Report what is recorded and do not assess their capability.
activities.expectedOutput: The partner's recorded delivery grouped by outcome and solution area, with the gaps in the record noted.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides what the delivery record actually evidences. A partner who closed several deals two years ago with a team that has since left looks identical in the record to one delivering now, and the record has no way of showing you the difference.
activities.requiredContext: The partner you are assessing. The work you are considering routing to them.
activities.bestFitJob: Look at what the partner has actually delivered
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your partner.
2. Look at what they have delivered in the specific solution area you are considering, not their overall record.
3. Note where the record thins out. A partner with three closed deals and nothing recorded since is a different proposition from one with steady flow.
4. Treat this as the capability half only. Nothing here tells you whether they have anyone available.
activities.whyThisMatters: Capability is the half of partner readiness we have evidence for. Getting it from the record rather than from the relationship is what makes the routing decision defensible when it is questioned.

activities.name: Ask about capacity without implying doubt
activities.description: Prepare the conversation that establishes whether a partner actually has people available, which no system will tell you.
activities.prompt: I need to find out whether a partner genuinely has capacity to take on [describe the work], and our systems cannot tell me. Here is what I know about their delivery record: [paste your findings]. Help me prepare that conversation: how to ask about available people without implying I doubt them, what answers would tell me they are overcommitted, how to respond if they say yes when the evidence suggests otherwise, and how to leave the door open if the answer is no. Do not tell me whether to route the work.
activities.expectedOutput: A prepared capacity conversation with the tell-tale answers identified and a safe route to no.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides whether a named-people answer is specific enough to route work on. A partner naming individuals and dates has given you something checkable; a partner describing capability in general has not, and accepting the second because the first felt intrusive is how work gets routed to a firm rather than to a team.
activities.requiredContext: The partner and what you are considering routing to them. Your delivery-record findings.
activities.bestFitJob: Ask about capacity without implying doubt
activitySteps: 1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Rehearse the case where they say yes and you do not believe them. That is the hard one and it is common.
3. Ask about named people and current commitments rather than about capacity in general. General questions get general reassurance.
4. Decide in advance what you will do with a no. A partner who can say no safely will tell you the truth next time.
activities.whyThisMatters: Nothing in our systems shows partner capacity. It only comes from a conversation, and how you ask determines whether the answer is real.

activities.name: Watch for the partner who has stopped moving
activities.description: Set a standing check across your partners for the delivery signals that appear before a partner-led engagement stalls.
activities.prompt: Set up a recurring check across the partners I work with. Each time, show me for each partner-associated opportunity and referral: its current status, the date that status was last recorded, and how long it has held. Show the same for any partner with no recorded activity in the period. Report the elapsed times and do not classify anything as stalled, at risk or normal. Remember what you reported before so you can tell me which elapsed times have grown since last time.
activities.expectedOutput: Elapsed time against each partner-associated record, with the times that have grown since the previous run identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides what a gap in partner activity means. There is no general answer - partners work to their own cadence, and two weeks of quiet that is routine for one is a warning for another - so the elapsed time is a prompt to ask rather than a conclusion to act on.
activities.requiredContext: The partners you carry. The opportunities and referrals associated with each.
activities.bestFitJob: Watch for the partner who has stopped moving
activitySteps: 1. Open Scout and confirm which partner and opportunity sources it can reach.
2. Choose your own cadence. Partner rhythms differ and a frequency that suits one portfolio buries another.
3. Decide for yourself what counts as too long for each partner. A quiet period that is routine for one partner is a warning for another.
4. Remember our record shows nothing about partner-side activity. Silence here is a prompt to ask, not a finding.
5. Prune what you track once you can see which categories actually move.

activities.name: Decide whether this partner is ready, and who closes the gap
activities.description: Put capability and capacity together into a readiness decision with a named owner and a date.
activities.prompt: Here is what the record shows about a partner's delivery capability: [paste your findings]. Here is what they told me about capacity: [paste what they said, including anything vague]. Bring these together into a readiness view for [describe the work]. Separate what they have demonstrated from what they have asserted. Set out the candidate gaps with the evidence for each, the possible impact of each on this work, and what is not known. Do not rank the gaps for me, do not decide whether to proceed, and do not assume any gap can be closed.
activities.expectedOutput: A readiness view with demonstrated capability separated from asserted capacity, the candidate gaps evidenced, and the seller's chosen gap with a closing action, an owner and a date.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS chooses which gap matters and names who closes it by when. The evidence supports several readings and selecting among them is the decision; an unowned gap has no date, and a readiness view without a date has not decided anything.
activities.requiredContext: Your findings on the partner's delivery record, and what they said about capacity.
activities.bestFitJob: Turn the two halves of partner readiness into one decision
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork and paste both halves - what the record showed and what the partner said.
2. Look first at anything demonstrated on one side and only asserted on the other. Demonstrated and asserted are different kinds of evidence and the difference is the point of this step.
3. Name one gap, not several. A readiness view with four gaps is a list, and lists do not get owned.
4. Decide who closes it and by when. If the honest answer is that you would close it yourself, that is a finding about this partnership rather than a plan.
5. Write down what happens to the work if the gap is not closed. That is the part that makes the date real.
activities.whyThisMatters: Capability and capacity are each half an answer. The decision that routes work needs both, joined, with somebody's name on what is missing.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Partner capability and partner capacity look identical from the outside and fail in completely different ways. This session is about telling them apart before you route work.
keyTalkingPoints: Capability is whether they know how; capacity is whether they have anyone free. Enablement fixes the first and does nothing for the second, which is why so much partner enablement is politely attended and never applied. The evidence available to us is partial - program participation and past delivery tell you about capability, and almost nothing tells you about capacity, which usually has to be asked. Facilitator note: a partner rarely says no to work, so absence of refusal is not evidence of readiness.
discussionQuestions: Which of your partners have you routed work to without checking?
When a partner-led engagement last went wrong, was it skill or bandwidth?
How would you know a partner was overcommitted?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the assessment to the specific action and who on the partner side owns it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the gap, the closing action, its partner-side owner and the date.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one partner you are currently routing work to or considering.
facilitatorQuestions: Is this a knowledge gap or a people gap?
What evidence do you have, and what are you assuming?
What would you have to see to route confidently?
listenFor: Listen for capability judged from the partner's own claims, for capacity never being asked about, for program certifications treated as delivery evidence, and for partners being chosen by relationship rather than by readiness.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live routing decision, use a partner engagement that went badly and work out which of the two gaps it actually was.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which partner have you kept using out of habit rather than evidence?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, assess one partner's readiness properly and agree one closing action with them.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the gap you found, what you agreed, and whether the partner acted.

activities.name: Reframe the ask in what their business gains
activities.description: Turn a Microsoft priority into an ask expressed in the partner's own economics.
activities.prompt: I want a partner to [describe the one thing you want them to do]. Here is what I know about their business and performance: [paste your partner picture]. Here is what I know about how they make money, and what I do not know: [describe their model and state the gaps]. Set out the questions I would have to answer before I could claim this is good for their business: what it would cost them, what they would gain, and over what period. For each question, say whether what I have given you answers it. Do not estimate any figure I have not supplied, do not construct a return calculation, and do not use Microsoft targets or incentive language.
activities.expectedOutput: The economic questions the ask depends on, marked by whether your material answers them, with the unanswerable ones turned into questions for the partner.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides which economic claims can be made and which must be asked. A partner's cost base is not visible to us, and a return figure constructed from our side is both wrong and recognisably wrong to the person who runs the business - which costs the credibility the ask depends on.
activities.requiredContext: Your partner picture. The one thing you want the partner to do. Whatever you actually know about how they make money, including what you do not know.
activities.bestFitJob: Reframe the ask in what their business gains
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace all three bracketed sections, including what you do NOT know.
2. Look at which questions your material cannot answer. Those are what you ask the partner, not what you assert to them.
3. Do not fill a gap with an estimate. A partner will recognize a number you invented about their own business immediately.
4. Reduce it to one ask, framed by the questions you can actually answer.
activities.whyThisMatters: Partners commit to things that improve their business. Claiming to know their economics when you do not is how you get treated as a vendor rather than a partner.

activities.expectedOutput: A rehearsed conversation covering the likely pushback, the history, and a close specific enough to follow up.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides which previous commitment is solid enough evidence to raise. A commitment that was implied, or made by someone who has since left, will be disputed and turns the conversation into a disagreement about history - so the judgment is whether this specific instance is documented well enough to survive being questioned.
activities.requiredContext: Your reframed ask and the partner picture. The history of what this partner has and has not done before.
activities.bestFitJob: Rehearse the part where they push back
activitySteps: 1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Rehearse the response to a past Microsoft failure honestly. Deflecting it is remembered longer than the original failure.
3. Prepare for agreement-without-action specifically - it is the most common outcome and the hardest to name politely.
4. Close on something checkable with a date, and put it in writing the same day.
activities.whyThisMatters: The partner conversation that changes anything is the one where the difficult part was prepared. The rest is a status meeting with a friendlier name.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Partners agree to a great deal in meetings and act on very little of it. The difference is almost always whether the ask made sense in their economics.
keyTalkingPoints: You influence without authority across more partners than you can meet, so each conversation has to carry weight. A partner's economics are not a mystery - margin, utilization of their consultants, recurring revenue and how quickly they get paid - and framing an ask against any of those changes the response. The most common failure is a conversation that reports Microsoft's view of the partnership back to a partner who experiences it completely differently. primaryAgents.name: Sales Agent
primaryAgents.shortDescription: Conversational sales agent in Microsoft 365 Copilot, reached through the agent picker as Sales, on desktop and on mobile through the Microsoft 365 Copilot app as well as in Teams and Outlook. Deal Agent runs as a skill inside Sales Chat and triggers automatically when you ask about a renewal or a deal.
primaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Search, synthesize, and act on sales data, and support repeatable execution-focused sales workflows. Through the Deal Agent skill it also runs enterprise renewals end to end: deal discovery and history, Deal Book generation, EA quotes and proposals, amendments, pre-approvals, and licensing questions, traversing more than a dozen source systems from a natural language prompt.
primaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Account, opportunity, pipeline, meeting preparation, CRM updates, and configured sales actions. Also on mobile immediately before or after a customer meeting: account summaries, pipeline and usage health, decision makers on an opportunity, list price lookups, and updating MSX in the moment by creating an opportunity, changing a close date or adding a forecast comment. For renewals and deals, ask about enrollments, renewal agreements, agreement summaries, license estate, Azure consumption against commitment, Deal Books, EA quotes, proposals, amendments, and pre-approvals. EA and MCA-E renewals are the primary motion. Lead with an identifier such as a TPID, agreement number, or enrollment number; specific prompts return real deal data and vague prompts return generic answers.
keyBenefits: Brings sales data and actions into the flow of work, including on a phone between meetings. For renewals, work that previously meant gathering data from seven or eight portals over two to three weeks becomes a few natural language prompts, with the Deal Book assembled across more than a dozen source systems. MSX records can be created or amended from the field behind a confirmation card, so context captured after a meeting does not wait until you are back at a desk.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Establish what the deal actually looks like
activities.description: Assemble the recorded facts that determine which investment routes are even open to this opportunity.
activities.prompt: For [opportunity name or ID] in my solution area, show what is recorded: the account, the products and workloads involved, the deal value and stage, any existing agreement and its type, whether a partner is associated and any co-sell or referral record, and any consumption or usage recorded on the account. Report what is recorded. Do not determine eligibility for any investment program and do not recommend a route.
activities.expectedOutput: The recorded facts that bear on route selection, with the barrier the investment would remove stated in one sentence.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS decides whether there is a real barrier that money removes. Investment attached to a deal that is simply slow does not speed it up, and a request built on a barrier nobody can name is declined late, after the effort has been spent.
activities.requiredContext: One solution-area opportunity where customer investment might remove a barrier.
activities.bestFitJob: Establish what the deal actually looks like
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your opportunity.
2. Note the partner association first. It changes which routes are even in scope.
3. Write down the barrier the investment would remove, in one sentence. If you cannot, investment is not the answer yet.
4. Take the facts and the barrier to the next step rather than deciding eligibility here.
activities.whyThisMatters: Route selection depends on facts about the deal that are already recorded. Starting from the program rather than the deal is how sellers end up building a case for a vehicle the opportunity never fitted.

activities.name: Find out what the routes actually require
activities.description: Establish from published guidance what each candidate investment route requires, before choosing between them.
activities.prompt: I am considering customer investment for an opportunity with these characteristics: [paste the deal facts and the barrier]. Using approved Microsoft sources and authoritative internal documentation, set out what the published requirements are for each investment route that could apply, what evidence each requires, what each explicitly excludes, and where the documentation is silent. Cite each source and give its date. Do not tell me which route to use and do not assess whether my opportunity qualifies.
activities.expectedOutput: Each candidate route's published requirements, evidence and exclusions, cited and dated, with the silent areas identified.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS confirms every eligibility reading with the authoritative owner rather than acting on the documentation alone. Published requirements describe the general case and investment decisions turn on specifics the documentation cannot see, so this shortens that conversation instead of replacing it.
activities.requiredContext: Your deal facts and the barrier you named. The routes you are considering.
activities.bestFitJob: Find out what the routes actually require
activitySteps: 1. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Read the exclusions before the requirements. That is where most requests fail and it is the part least often read.
3. Check the dates. Investment guidance changes between fiscal years and last year's version is still findable.
4. Where the documentation is silent, that is a question for the authoritative owner, not a gap for you to fill.
activities.whyThisMatters: Sellers learn one route and apply it everywhere - the one that worked first. Reading what the alternatives actually require is the only way that habit gets corrected.

activities.name: Write the case against the route you chose
activities.description: Turn the barrier and the route requirements into a request that answers what that route actually asks.
activities.prompt: I am requesting customer investment through [name the route] for an opportunity. Here are the route's published requirements: [paste them]. Here is the barrier and the deal context: [paste them]. Draft the request so that it answers each requirement in turn: what is being asked for, the barrier it removes, the evidence for that barrier, what changes if it is approved, and how that change would be observed. Mark any requirement I have not evidenced. Do not assert eligibility, do not estimate any figure I have not supplied, and do not claim approval is likely.
activities.expectedOutput: A request answering each published requirement in turn, with unevidenced requirements marked and the observable change stated specifically.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSS states what will be observably different if the investment is approved. A request that promises acceleration without naming what would be measured is approved on trust and cannot be defended at review, which is what makes the next request from your team harder.
activities.requiredContext: Your chosen route and its published requirements. The barrier and the deal facts.
activities.bestFitJob: Write the case against the route you chose
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace all three bracketed sections.
2. Look at what it marks as unevidenced. Those are the questions a reviewer will ask first.
3. Make the observable change specific. "Accelerates adoption" is not something anyone can check afterwards.
4. Send it through the route's own process rather than to whoever answered last time.
activities.whyThisMatters: Investment requests are compared against each other, not judged in isolation. The one that answers the stated requirements in order is easier to approve than a better opportunity described loosely.
activities.prerequisiteActivityName: Find out what the routes actually require

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Investment in SME&C is not one thing. This session is about picking the right route before you build anything.
keyTalkingPoints: Investment in this segment is a selection problem before it is a submission problem. There are several routes - direct customer investment, partner-led programs, and voucher-based offers - and most sellers learn one and use it for everything. The FY27 SME&C customer investment analysis records that Azure post-sales investment expects first-year ACR above roughly 500,000 US dollars, and that below that threshold the motion routes partner-led; it also records vouchers as the scale vehicle, at around 20,000 US dollars for Corporate against 50,000 for Enterprise. Treat those as orientation from that analysis rather than as current policy - confirm any figure with the authoritative owner before it reaches a customer. The point of the session is that choosing the wrong route wastes weeks that the right route would not have cost. For a DSS the relevant question is usually whether the solution-area opportunity is large enough to carry direct investment or whether it belongs in a partner-led or voucher motion. Facilitator note: resist letting this become an ECIF mechanics session - the mechanics only matter once the route is right.
discussionQuestions: Which investment route do you reach for by default?
When did an investment request last fail, and at what stage?
Who tells you whether something is eligible?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the route to the eligibility question each person will route to an owner.

Customer Zero cue - use only if it happens: when someone reverts, rejects or overrides what the agent produced, stop and name it. Ask what the agent could not see. Huddle transcripts are reviewed for themes, so what is said here does reach us - keep customer-confidential detail out of it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by confirming each person has a route and one eligibility question sent to a named owner.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one solution-area opportunity where customer investment might help.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the barrier the investment would actually remove?
Which route fits the size and shape of this deal?
What do you not know about eligibility?
listenFor: Listen for one route being used for everything, for eligibility being assumed from a previous deal, for investment proposed before the barrier is clear, and for people who have stopped requesting because a past request failed late.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live candidate, take the last investment request that failed and work out which route it should have taken.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you last build that turned out to be the wrong vehicle?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, match one opportunity to an investment route and get one eligibility question answered authoritatively.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the route you chose, the question you asked and the answer you got.

activities.name: Check what this partner has already signed up to
activities.description: Establish what program commitments a partner already carries before adding another one.
activities.prompt: For [partner name], show any co-sell or referral record currently open and the status and date of each, and any record showing a program or campaign this partner has been nominated into. For each, show whether it progressed after it was opened and the date of the last change. Report what is recorded. Do not assess their program eligibility and do not recommend an investment route.
activities.expectedOutput: The partner's open commitments with the ones that never progressed identified, and a view on whether they have room for another.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides whether this partner can absorb another commitment. Partners accept nominations readily and complete far fewer, so adding one to a partner already carrying unfinished commitments produces another unfinished commitment and makes the next conversation harder to have.
activities.requiredContext: The partner and the opportunity you are considering investment for. Whatever partner program reporting you can reach.
activities.bestFitJob: See what this partner has already been nominated for
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your partner.
2. Look for records opened and never progressed. A partner carrying several of those has an acceptance habit rather than a delivery habit.
3. Check program participation in the partner reporting you have access to - our opportunity record shows nominations, not completions.
4. Decide whether this partner has room for another commitment before you offer one.
activities.whyThisMatters: A partner-led route only works if the partner does their part. What they have already agreed to and not delivered is the most direct evidence available, and it sits in a record nobody checks before nominating.

activities.name: Find out what the route asks of the partner
activities.description: Establish from published guidance what a partner-led route requires the partner to do, not just what it offers.
activities.prompt: I am considering [name the partner-led investment route] for a partner opportunity. Using approved Microsoft sources and authoritative internal documentation, set out what the route requires from the PARTNER specifically: what they must nominate, what activity they must complete, what evidence they must produce, over what period, and what they receive in return. Also show what it requires from Microsoft. Cite each source and give its date. Do not assess whether this partner qualifies.
activities.expectedOutput: The route's partner-side obligations, Microsoft-side obligations, timeframe and partner return, cited and dated.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS confirms the partner-side obligations with the authoritative owner before committing a partner to them. activities.requiredContext: The route you are considering and the partner it would run through.
activities.bestFitJob: Find out what the route asks of the partner
activitySteps: 1. Open Researcher, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Separate what the partner must do from what we must do, and list each partner obligation on its own line.
3. Note the period. A program requiring activity over two quarters is a different ask from one requiring a single nomination.
4. Take the partner-side obligations into the conversation with them rather than nominating first and explaining later.
activities.whyThisMatters: Partner-led investment fails when the partner did not know what they had agreed to. The obligations are published, and nothing in the nomination flow requires anyone to read them.

activities.name: Get the partner to agree to their half
activities.description: Prepare the conversation where the partner commits to what the route requires of them, rather than simply accepting a nomination.
activities.prompt: I want a partner to take part in an investment route that requires this of them: [paste the partner-side obligations]. Here is their record of completing what they have started before: [describe it]. Help me prepare the conversation: how to present the obligations without making it sound like paperwork, what they are likely to agree to in the room and not do, how to raise a previous unfinished commitment without it becoming an argument, and how to close on something specific enough to check. Do not tell me whether to nominate them.
activities.expectedOutput: A prepared conversation covering the partner's obligations, the previous record, and a close naming a person and a date.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The PSS decides how directly to raise a partner's record of not finishing. Naming it risks the relationship; not naming it means nominating into the same outcome again, and only the person in the relationship can judge which this partner will take better.
activities.requiredContext: The route's partner-side obligations. The partner's record of completing what they start.
activities.bestFitJob: Get the partner to agree to their half
activitySteps: 1. Open Agent J.ai, paste the prompt, and replace both bracketed sections.
2. Rehearse raising the unfinished commitment. Avoiding it guarantees the same outcome.
3. Get agreement on a named person on their side, not on the firm. A firm cannot complete an activity.
4. Confirm in writing the same day, with what they agreed and by when.
activities.whyThisMatters: A nomination is not a commitment. The conversation where the partner agrees to their specific half is the whole difference between a program that runs and one that appears in a report as unstarted.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: The investment routes that matter most in this segment run through partners. This session is about using them deliberately.
keyTalkingPoints: Investment in this segment is a selection problem before it is a submission problem. There are several routes - direct customer investment, partner-led programs, and voucher-based offers - and most sellers learn one and use it for everything. The FY27 SME&C customer investment analysis records that Azure post-sales investment expects first-year ACR above roughly 500,000 US dollars, and that below that threshold the motion routes partner-led; it also records vouchers as the scale vehicle, at around 20,000 US dollars for Corporate against 50,000 for Enterprise. Treat those as orientation from that analysis rather than as current policy - confirm any figure with the authoritative owner before it reaches a customer. The point of the session is that choosing the wrong route wastes weeks that the right route would not have cost. For a PSS the additional dimension is that partner-led routes place obligations on the PARTNER - nomination, activity completion, evidence - and a partner who does not know what they have signed up to is the most common reason a partner-led investment produces nothing. Facilitator note: the partner's incentive under each route is worth naming explicitly; it is rarely the same as ours.
discussionQuestions: Which partner-led routes do you actually use?
When did a partner-led program last produce nothing, and why?
Does the partner know what the program requires of them?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the route to the specific obligation the partner has agreed to and the date.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by confirming each person has a route and a partner-side obligation agreed with a name and a date.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one partner and one opportunity where investment could help.
facilitatorQuestions: What does this route require the partner to do?
What does the partner get out of it?
Who is tracking whether they do it?
listenFor: Listen for partner obligations being assumed rather than agreed, for programs nominated and never started, for the partner's incentive being taken for granted, and for PSS carrying activity that the program expects the partner to carry.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live candidate, use a partner program that was nominated and never completed and work out where it stalled.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Which partner program did you nominate and never follow up?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, match one partner opportunity to a route and confirm with the partner what it requires of them.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the route, what the partner agreed to, and whether they started.

activities.name: Tell a funding barrier from a decision barrier
activities.description: Assemble the recorded facts your role needs before contributing to an investment decision.
activities.prompt: For [account name], show what is recorded that would bear on whether investment could help: the open opportunities and their stage, any recorded blocker or objection, the existing agreement and its type, what is deployed against it, whether a partner is associated, and any recorded activity in the last six months. Report what is recorded and do not assess whether investment is appropriate.
activities.expectedOutput: The account's recorded position with the barrier stated, and your own read on whether it is one funding removes.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DAE decides whether the barrier is one money removes. A customer who has not decided is not blocked by cost, and investment offered into indecision reads as discounting and is remembered as a price signal on the next deal.
activities.requiredContext: One account where something is blocked and money might move it.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Customer investment reaches your role even though you do not own the request. This session is about the part that is yours.
keyTalkingPoints: Investment in this segment is a selection problem before it is a submission problem. There are several routes - direct customer investment, partner-led programs, and voucher-based offers - and most sellers learn one and use it for everything. The FY27 SME&C customer investment analysis records that Azure post-sales investment expects first-year ACR above roughly 500,000 US dollars, and that below that threshold the motion routes partner-led; it also records vouchers as the scale vehicle, at around 20,000 US dollars for Corporate against 50,000 for Enterprise. Treat those as orientation from that analysis rather than as current policy - confirm any figure with the authoritative owner before it reaches a customer. The point of the session is that choosing the wrong route wastes weeks that the right route would not have cost. A DAE does not own investment requests but meets the barriers that investment removes, across more accounts than anyone else. The value is in recognition and routing rather than in submission. Facilitator note: keep this session on the role's own contribution rather than letting it drift into submission mechanics owned elsewhere.
discussionQuestions: Where have you seen investment help, and where have you seen it wasted?
What does your role actually contribute to an investment decision?
Who owns the request once you have raised it?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the assessment to the one thing each person routes or confirms this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming what each person will route or confirm, and to whom.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one situation where customer investment is or was in play.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the barrier, precisely?
What is yours to decide here and what is not?
What would you need to see to be confident?
listenFor: Listen for investment proposed as a discount by another name, for barriers that are really timing, and for DAEs building requests themselves rather than routing them.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live case, use the last investment situation they encountered and work through what their role should have contributed.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: When did you last see investment used for something it could not fix?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one investment situation and contribute the part your role owns.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what you found, who you took it to, and what happened.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Decide what would count as proof
activities.description: Assemble the recorded facts your role needs before contributing to an investment decision.
activities.prompt: A customer investment would fund this technical work: [describe the work and what the customer doubts]. Define what it would need to demonstrate for the customer's doubt to be resolved: the observable success criteria, what would constitute a clear negative result, the exit criteria that end the work either way, and the evidence a reviewer would need afterwards. Do not assume the investment is approved and do not estimate cost or duration.
activities.expectedOutput: What the funded work would have to demonstrate, expressed as things somebody could observe happening.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE decides how much the funded work must prove before the customer would act on the result. Proving too little leaves the doubt intact and the funding spent; proving too much turns a bounded piece of work into a project, and where that line sits depends on what this specific customer said they doubted.
activities.requiredContext: One proposed piece of technical work that customer investment might fund.
activities.bestFitJob: Decide what would count as proof
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account or opportunity.
2. Separate the recorded technical position from what you were briefed. The gap is where the success criteria will have to do their work.
3. Form your own view before reading anyone else's assessment.
4. Route what you find to whoever owns the request rather than acting on it yourself.
activities.whyThisMatters: Funded technical work is assessed at closure against whatever criteria existed at the start. If none did, the assessment becomes a matter of opinion and the next request is harder.

activities.name: Write the criteria down before the work is funded
activities.description: Record the technical success and exit criteria in a form a reviewer can assess against afterwards.
activities.prompt: I have defined what an investment-funded piece of technical work must demonstrate. Here are my criteria: [paste them]. activities.expectedOutput: Success and exit criteria written for the request, with anything unobservable marked before it is submitted.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DSE owns which criteria survive into the request. Criteria are negotiated down when the request is assembled, and the ones removed are the ones that would have shown a negative result - which is exactly what makes the remaining set unfalsifiable.
activities.requiredContext: Your assessment and the evidence behind it. Who owns the investment request.
activities.bestFitJob: Write the criteria down before the work is funded

activities.whyThisMatters: Criteria that live only in your head are renegotiated at closure by people who were not there. Written into the request, they set the terms of the assessment before anyone has a stake in the answer.

activities.expectedOutput: The account's recorded technical position, with your read on whether this customer could absorb the funded work.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA decides which customer-side dependency would genuinely block delivery. activities.bestFitJob: Check the environment, not the opportunity

4. Route what you find to whoever owns the request rather than acting on it yourself.
activities.whyThisMatters: Investment converts into consumption only if the customer can absorb the work. In a portfolio of non-unified customers that is the assumption the request does not test.

activities.name: Name the dependency that would stop it
activities.description: Set out the customer-side dependencies that would block funded delivery, and who would have to resolve each.
activities.prompt: I have assessed whether a customer could absorb investment-funded technical work. Here is what I found: [paste your findings]. Set out the customer-side dependencies that would have to be in place before the work could start or complete: what each is, who on the customer or partner side would have to provide it, and what happens to the engagement if it is not there. Separate the ones I have confirmed from the ones I am assuming. Do not assess whether the investment should proceed.
activities.expectedOutput: The customer-side dependencies that would block delivery, separated into those confirmed and those assumed.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The DCSA distinguishes a dependency the customer has been told about from one they have agreed to. Those look identical in any write-up and behave completely differently at delivery, and only the person who had the conversation knows which one it was.
activities.requiredContext: Your assessment and the evidence behind it. Who owns the investment request.
activities.bestFitJob: Name the dependency that would stop it
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork, paste the prompt, and replace the bracketed section.
2. Check that what you could not determine is as visible as what you found. Silence on a gap reads as a clear result.
3. Say what your role would still have to do. Requests are approved without that and then stall on it.
4. Send it to the named owner, not to a distribution list.
activities.whyThisMatters: Funded work can stall on a customer-side dependency that no technical review would surface, and the stall is recorded as a Microsoft delivery failure regardless of whose dependency it was. Testing for them is separate work from testing the technical plan.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Customer investment reaches your role even though you do not own the request. This session is about the part that is yours.
keyTalkingPoints: Investment in this segment is a selection problem before it is a submission problem. There are several routes - direct customer investment, partner-led programs, and voucher-based offers - and most sellers learn one and use it for everything. The FY27 SME&C customer investment analysis records that Azure post-sales investment expects first-year ACR above roughly 500,000 US dollars, and that below that threshold the motion routes partner-led; it also records vouchers as the scale vehicle, at around 20,000 US dollars for Corporate against 50,000 for Enterprise. Treat those as orientation from that analysis rather than as current policy - confirm any figure with the authoritative owner before it reaches a customer. The point of the session is that choosing the wrong route wastes weeks that the right route would not have cost. A DCSA does not own the investment request but is accountable for whether the funded work converts into consumption. Non-unified customers have less capacity to absorb delivery than the request usually assumes. Facilitator note: keep this session on the role's own contribution rather than letting it drift into submission mechanics owned elsewhere.
discussionQuestions: Where have you seen investment help, and where have you seen it wasted?
What does your role actually contribute to an investment decision?
Who owns the request once you have raised it?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the assessment to the one thing each person routes or confirms this week.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming what each person will route or confirm, and to whom.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: bring one situation where customer investment is or was in play.
facilitatorQuestions: What is the barrier, precisely?
What is yours to decide here and what is not?
What would you need to see to be confident?
listenFor: Listen for prerequisites the customer has been told about but not agreed to, for partner delivery capacity being assumed, and for readiness judged from the opportunity rather than the environment.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has a live case, use the last investment situation they encountered and work through what their role should have contributed.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: When did you last see investment used for something it could not fix?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, take one investment situation and contribute the part your role owns.
bringBackEvidence: Bring what you found, who you took it to, and what happened.

activities.name: Test whether the structure survives without the investment
activities.description: Check whether a commercial structure you are building depends on funding that has not been approved.
activities.prompt: For [account name], I am structuring a deal where customer investment is expected to form part of it. Show what is recorded: the existing agreement and its type, the products and quantities involved, any amendment or exception already recorded, the deal stage and value, and whether a partner is associated. Report what is recorded. Do not assess the investment, do not determine eligibility, and do not comment on approval.
activities.expectedOutput: The structure described with and without the investment, and any dependency on an unapproved decision made explicit.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CE decides whether a structure that depends on unapproved investment should be presented at all. A structure contingent on someone else's decision looks complete to a customer and to an approver, and the dependency only surfaces when the investment is declined and the commitment has already been made.
activities.requiredContext: One deal you are structuring where customer investment is expected to be part of it.
activities.bestFitJob: Test whether the structure survives without the investment
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with your account.
2. Describe the structure twice: once assuming the investment arrives and once assuming it does not.
3. If the second version does not work, the structure depends on a decision you do not own. Say so now rather than at approval.
4. Route any eligibility or investment question to the role that owns it rather than answering it.
activities.whyThisMatters: Investment decisions sit outside the CE's authority in this segment, but the commercial consequence of one not arriving lands entirely on the structure. That exposure is worth seeing before the customer does.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: This is a short awareness session rather than a workflow. The CE does not own investment requests in this segment, but investment lands on deals you structure.
keyTalkingPoints: Investment in this segment is a selection problem before it is a submission problem. There are several routes - direct customer investment, partner-led programs, and voucher-based offers - and most sellers learn one and use it for everything. The FY27 SME&C customer investment analysis records that Azure post-sales investment expects first-year ACR above roughly 500,000 US dollars, and that below that threshold the motion routes partner-led; it also records vouchers as the scale vehicle, at around 20,000 US dollars for Corporate against 50,000 for Enterprise. Treat those as orientation from that analysis rather than as current policy - confirm any figure with the authoritative owner before it reaches a customer. The point of the session is that choosing the wrong route wastes weeks that the right route would not have cost. No source assigns the SME&C Commercial Executive ownership of investment requests, which is why this is an awareness card rather than a full workflow. What IS yours: whether an investment changes the commercial structure, whether it creates a precedent that the next similar customer will expect, and whether the structure still works if the investment is declined. Facilitator note: keep this short and do not let it become an ECIF mechanics session - route those questions to the roles that own them.
discussionQuestions: When has an investment changed a structure you built?
What would you want to know before structuring around one?
Who would you ask?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the discussion to the single question each person would raise next time.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by naming the one question each person would raise if investment appeared on a deal they were structuring.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: think of one deal where investment was involved.
facilitatorQuestions: What would change about the structure if the investment did not come?
What precedent does this set?
Whose decision is the investment itself?
listenFor: Listen for CEs taking on investment requests that belong elsewhere, for structures that only work if investment is approved, and for precedent implications going unnoticed.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If nobody has an example, use a deal with a non-standard term and ask what would have changed if investment had been part of it.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: Have you ever built a structure that depended on funding you did not control?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, if investment appears on a deal you are structuring, test whether the structure still holds without it.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the deal, the dependency you found, and what you did about it.

SMEC-CE-INVEST.keyTakeaway: Investment succeeds on role clarity, evidence and clean handoffs. Every role owns one part of that chain.

secondaryAgents.name: Sales Home
secondaryAgents.shortDescription: The seller landing surface inside Sales Agent, opened from Microsoft 365 Copilot. It brings your alerts and quota attainment, your prospecting signals and your pipeline into one place, and answers questions against what MSX holds. It is in preview for SME&C sellers on MSX and is enabled for individual contributors, not managers.
secondaryAgents.whatItHelpsYouDo: Pull the real state of an opportunity out of MSX and read it back plainly: the current stage and when it last moved, the recorded next step and who owns it, the close date and what supports it, and any blocker or objection captured against the account. It works across your whole book, so you can ask which opportunities in your solution area have a named competitor recorded, which partners keep letting co-sell records lapse, or which accounts already carry a discount or non-standard term. It also drafts first-touch outreach to contacts that already exist in MSX, in English.
secondaryAgents.whenToUseIt: Use it when the question is what is on the record. Deal preparation, pressure-testing a close date, working your prospecting signals, checking the concessions already in force on an account before you negotiate, or finding the other opportunities where this same objection has already come up. Reach for it first whenever you would otherwise open MSX and click through an opportunity by hand. If Sales Home has not been turned on for you, Sales Accelerator covers the same prospecting and signal work and is where your queue lives. Sales Agent is the wider conversational surface that Sales Home sits inside, so if you are already in a Sales Agent chat you do not need to switch.
keyBenefits: Replaces the click-through: stage, next step, owner, close date and open objection come back in one answer instead of four screens in MSX. Because it reads across your whole book at once, questions that used to mean opening opportunities one at a time, such as where a competitor has shown up, which partners keep lapsing, or what you have already conceded on an account, become a single prompt. Most usefully, it shows you where the record is empty, which is normally the thing costing you the deal.

activities.name: Find the closes you cannot account for
activities.description: List recent closed-won opportunities in your book and separate the ones you closed from the ones that closed some other way.
activities.prompt: Show me the opportunities in my book that were marked closed won with a close date in the last [state a short period, for example 30 days]. For each, show the account, the value, the close date, the products or SKU lines attached, and the recorded close reason or status if one is set. Report what is recorded. Do not assess whether any close was correct.
activities.expectedOutput: Recent closed-won opportunities with the ones the seller cannot account for identified, or an explicit statement that there were none.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides which closes they can account for. A closed record can be well-formed and still describe something that did not happen, and the check is whether the value, products and date match what was actually sold.
activities.requiredContext: Your own opportunities and the date range you want to review.
activities.bestFitJob: See which of your deals closed without you closing them
activitySteps: 1. Open Sales Agent and paste the prompt with a short recent period. Keep it small enough to read in one sitting.
2. Go down the list and mark the ones you do not remember closing. You are working from your own memory of the deal here, not from a field.
3. For each one you marked, ask whether you can account for the value, the products and the date. Mark anything you cannot.
4. Take the marked ones forward. If there are none, say so - that is a result worth the room hearing.
activities.whyThisMatters: A closed record carries your number whether or not you set it. A wrong one raises no error and blocks nothing, so it survives until somebody has to explain it.

activities.name: Work out what to do about the one you cannot explain
activities.description: Take a closed record you cannot account for and decide whether to accept it, correct it, or raise it.
activities.prompt: Here is a closed-won opportunity I cannot fully account for: [paste the record - account, value, close date, close reason, products]. Here is what I know was actually happening on this account: [paste what you know - what was sold, what was signed, what was delivered, what was still open]. Lay out where the record and my account knowledge agree, where they disagree, and what would settle each disagreement. Do not tell me whether the close was correct.
activities.expectedOutput: One questionable close resolved into accepted, corrected by the seller, routed to whoever can act on it, or held pending a specific check.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The seller decides whether the record matches what was sold, and whether the correction is theirs to make or somebody else's. Account knowledge is one input rather than the deciding one, and a correction made without the contract in front of you replaces one wrong record with another.
activities.requiredContext: One closed record you could not account for, and what you know was happening on that account.
activities.bestFitJob: Decide what to do about a close you cannot account for
activitySteps: 1. Open Cowork and paste both the record and what you know about the account.
2. Work the disagreements, not the agreements. The agreements are why you did not notice sooner.

3. Decide which of four this is: the close is right and you had forgotten; it is wrong on detail you are able to correct yourself; it is wrong in a way that needs somebody else; or you cannot yet tell and need to check something first.
4. If it is yours to correct, correct it now while you still have the context.
5. If it needs somebody else or more evidence, write down what you checked and what you found, so the next person does not start from nothing.
activities.whyThisMatters: A wrong close is easy to leave alone because nothing breaks. It shows up later as revenue that cannot be explained or a customer conversation that starts from a false position.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: A closed-won record carries your number whether or not you were the one who set it. Closes arrive through your own work, through automation, and through other people acting on the account. This session is about reading your own recent closes and deciding which ones you can stand behind.
keyTalkingPoints: A wrong close raises no error and blocks nothing. It stays in the book until somebody has to explain it, and by then the context has gone.
The test is not whether the record is well-formed. It is whether the value, the products and the date describe what was actually sold.
Your account knowledge is the input here, not the verdict. A correction made without the contract in front of you replaces one wrong record with another.
Finding nothing is a real result. Say so in the room rather than treating the exercise as having failed.
discussionQuestions: When did you last read your own closed-won list rather than your open pipeline?
If a close in your book were wrong, how would you find out?
Which part of a closed record would you struggle to explain in a review?
suggestedTransitions: Move from the list of closes nobody could account for to the single record each person will resolve, and how they will resolve it.
facilitatorGuide.wrapUpGuidance: Close by having each person name the one record they will resolve, and which of the four it is: accepted, corrected by them, routed to somebody who can act on it, or held pending a specific check.
preparationChecklist: Before the session: confirm you can open Sales Agent, and choose a recent period short enough to read in one sitting. Bring what you remember about the accounts in it, because that memory is the instrument this exercise runs on.
facilitatorQuestions: Which close in your list did you not recognise straight away?
What in that record does not match what you remember selling?
Is this one yours to correct, or does it need somebody else?
listenFor: Listen for sellers scrolling past records they do not recognise because the totals look right. Listen for “that must have been the partner” or “that came from the team” offered as an explanation rather than as something to check. Listen for reluctance to raise a close that flatters the number, and for the assumption that a well-formed record is a correct one.
facilitatorGuide.fallbackGuidance: If Sales Agent access is not available, run it from a report export or the opportunity list, since the exercise is reading your own closes rather than the tool that surfaces them. If nobody finds an unexplained close, use the time to ask how they would notice one.
facilitatorGuide.reflectPrompt: What did you find in your own closed book that you had not looked at before? What would have to be true for you to notice it sooner next time?
facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Before the next huddle, resolve one closed-won record you could not account for: accept it, correct it, route it to whoever can act on it, or write down the specific thing you need to check.
bringBackEvidence: Bring the record, what you could not account for, what you did about it, and whether it turned out to be yours to correct.

facilitatorGuide.sessionIntroduction: Satisfaction is decided during the delivery, not at the survey. Today is about reading it early enough to act.

facilitatorGuide.commitPrompt: Take one live delivery, name the satisfaction risk you would least like to see in the survey, and act on it this week.

activities.name: Build the credibility plan for one gap
activities.description: Turn the highest-value gap into a specific plan with a first step this week.
activities.prompt: Take the highest-value technical gap and build a plan to close it: what being credible on this looks like in a customer conversation, the smallest first step, what I will use to get there, how I will test whether it worked, and the date I will have it by. Keep it to one gap.
activities.expectedOutput: A one-gap credibility plan with a first step and a date.
activities.humanCheckpoint: The CSA keeps this to one gap. A plan covering every gap is a plan that closes none of them before the customer needs the answer.
activities.requiredContext: Gap map, customer timeline, available time; your delivery context, whether global delivery, field delivery or SME&C coverage, since it changes which next action is right.
activitySteps: 1. Pick the gap the customer will hit soonest.
2. State what credible looks like in their words, not ours.
3. Name the smallest first step.
4. Decide how you will test it, ideally on a real conversation.
5. Put a date on it.
activities.whyThisMatters: One closed gap before the customer needs it beats a broad plan that arrives after they asked.
